questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Three layers surround each kidney. Which one is the outer connective tissue layer that anchors the kidney to the abdominal wall?
options: The adipose capsule
The renal capsule
The parietal peritoneum
The renal fascia
questions.why: From deep to superficial, the three layers around each kidney are the renal capsule, the adipose capsule, and the renal fascia. The renal fascia is the outermost of the three, a layer of connective tissue that anchors the kidney and its fat to the abdominal wall. The capsule shapes the kidney, the fat cushions it, and the fascia ties it down.
notes: The adipose capsule is the layer of fat around the renal capsule that cushions the kidney and helps hold it in place. Pick it for the layer whose loss lets the kidney drop in nephroptosis.
The renal capsule is the smooth fibrous layer lying directly on the kidney's surface. It maintains the kidney's shape, so pick it if the question asked for the innermost covering.

The parietal peritoneum lines the abdominal cavity and passes in front of the kidneys, which is why the kidneys are called retroperitoneal. It is not one of the kidney's own three layers; choose it if the question asked which membrane lies anterior to the kidneys.
Correct. The renal fascia is the outer connective tissue layer that anchors the kidney to the abdominal wall.

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Which kidney usually sits slightly lower, and why?
options: The right kidney, because the stomach sits above it
The left kidney, because the spleen sits above it
The right kidney, because the liver sits above it
The left kidney, because the heart sits above it
questions.why: Both kidneys lie retroperitoneally between about T12 and L3, but they are not perfectly level. The liver, the largest organ in the abdomen, fills the upper right side, so the right kidney sits slightly lower than the left. This is one of the questions on the lab structure list, so be ready to say both the side and the reason.
notes: The right kidney is the lower one, but the stomach is mostly on the left side of the upper abdomen, so it is not the reason. The liver above the right kidney is what pushes it down.

The spleen does sit near the upper left kidney, but it is small compared with the liver, and the left kidney is the higher one. Students who reason by symmetry pick this; remember the liver makes the right side the low side.
Correct. The large liver above the right kidney pushes it slightly lower than the left.
The heart sits in the thorax above the diaphragm, well away from the kidneys, and the left kidney is the higher one. This choice comes from mixing up the left-sided heart with the low kidney.
questions.answerText: The right kidney, because the liver sits above it

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the renal cortex and the renal medulla?
options: The cortex is the inner region made of renal pyramids; the medulla is the outer region holding the renal corpuscles.
The cortex is the outer region holding the renal corpuscles; the medulla is the inner region made of renal pyramids.
The cortex is the fat layer around the kidney; the medulla is the funnel that drains into the ureter.
The cortex and the medulla are both made of renal pyramids, separated by the renal capsule.
questions.why: The renal cortex is the outer region of kidney tissue, just beneath the capsule. It holds the renal corpuscles and the convoluted tubules, and it sends renal columns down between the pyramids. The renal medulla is the inner region, made of cone-shaped renal pyramids that hold the nephron loops and collecting ducts. Together the cortex and pyramids form the parenchyma, the working tissue that houses the nephrons.
notes: This statement swaps the two regions. Cortex comes from the Latin word for bark, the outer layer of a tree, while the medulla is the inner core, so the pyramids belong to the medulla.
Correct. The cortex is the outer region with the renal corpuscles, and the medulla is the inner region of pyramids.

These descriptions belong to other structures. The fat layer is the adipose capsule, and the funnel that drains into the ureter is the renal pelvis, so choose those names if the question asked what cushions the kidney or what passes urine to the ureter.

Only the medulla is made of pyramids, and the renal capsule is the fibrous covering on the outside of the kidney, not a divider inside it. Pick the renal capsule if the question asked for the kidney's outer fibrous covering.
questions.answerText: The cortex is the outer region holding the renal corpuscles; the medulla is the inner region made of renal pyramids.

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Which sequence correctly traces blood through the arteries of the kidney, from the renal artery to the glomerulus?
options: Segmental, arcuate, interlobar, cortical radiate, afferent arteriole
Segmental, interlobar, arcuate, cortical radiate, afferent arteriole
Segmental, interlobar, cortical radiate, arcuate, afferent arteriole
Interlobar, segmental, arcuate, cortical radiate, efferent arteriole
questions.why: The renal artery enters at the hilum and splits into segmental arteries, which give off interlobar arteries that run between the renal pyramids. At the bases of the pyramids these bend into arcuate arteries, which arch along the border between cortex and medulla. Cortical radiate (interlobular) arteries then branch up into the cortex, and each one gives off afferent arterioles that feed the glomeruli. The names help: interlobar means between the lobes, and arcuate means arched.
notes: This order places the arcuate arteries before the interlobar arteries. The interlobar arteries climb between the pyramids first, and only at the pyramid bases do they arch over as arcuate arteries.
Correct. Segmental, interlobar, arcuate, cortical radiate, then the afferent arteriole into the glomerulus.
This order has the cortical radiate arteries before the arcuate arteries. The cortical radiate arteries branch up into the cortex from the arcuate arteries, so they come after them.

This order starts with interlobar instead of segmental and ends with the efferent arteriole. The efferent arteriole carries blood out of the glomerulus, so it would be the answer for the vessel leaving the glomerulus.
questions.answerText: Segmental, interlobar, arcuate, cortical radiate, afferent arteriole

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Which group of structures enters or leaves the kidney at the renal hilum?
options: Renal artery, renal vein, ureter, and nerves
Renal artery, renal vein, suprarenal gland, and ureter
Collecting ducts, nephron loops, and arcuate arteries
Renal artery, renal vein, urethra, and nerves
questions.why: The renal hilum is the notch on the medial border of the kidney, and it is the kidney's only doorway. The renal artery enters there, while the renal vein and the ureter (continuing from the renal pelvis) leave there, along with the nerves and lymphatic vessels that serve the kidney. Everything that connects the kidney to the rest of the body passes through this one notch.
notes: Correct. The renal artery, renal vein, ureter, and nerves all pass through the hilum.
The suprarenal (adrenal) gland sits like a cap on the superior pole of the kidney, not at the hilum. Pick it if the question asked which gland rests on top of each kidney.
These structures lie inside the kidney tissue. Collecting ducts and nephron loops run in the pyramids, and arcuate arteries arch along the pyramid bases, so they never reach the hilum.
The urethra does not touch the kidney at all. It is the tube that carries urine from the bladder to the outside; the tube leaving the hilum is the ureter, which carries urine to the bladder.
questions.answerText: Renal artery, renal vein, ureter, and nerves

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Which paired organs filter the blood and form urine?
options: The urinary bladder
The ureters
The urethra
The kidneys
questions.why: The kidneys are the paired, bean-shaped organs against the back wall of the abdomen that filter the blood and form urine. Inside each one, about a million nephrons do the actual filtering. Every other organ of the urinary system only carries or stores the urine the kidneys make.
notes: The urinary bladder is a single muscular sac that stores urine until it is released. It would be the answer if the question asked where urine is held.
The ureters are paired too, but they are tubes that carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder by peristalsis. Pick them if the question asked what transports urine down to the bladder.
The urethra is a single tube that carries urine from the bladder to the outside. Choose it if the question asked which structure releases urine from the body.
Correct. The kidneys filter the blood and form urine.

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: What is the smooth, fibrous layer that lies directly on the kidney's surface and maintains its shape?
options: The renal capsule
The adipose capsule
The renal cortex
The renal fascia
questions.why: The renal capsule is the innermost of the three layers around the kidney. It is a smooth, fibrous covering that sits right on the kidney's surface, holds its shape, and helps protect the tissue beneath it. Outside it lie the adipose capsule and then the renal fascia.
notes: Correct. The renal capsule is the smooth fibrous layer on the kidney's surface.
The adipose capsule is the fat layer between the renal capsule and the renal fascia. Choose it if the question asked which layer cushions the kidney and holds it in place.

The renal cortex is kidney tissue, the outer region just beneath the capsule that holds the renal corpuscles. Pick it if the question asked for the outer tissue region of the kidney rather than its covering.
The renal fascia is also connective tissue, but it is the outermost of the three layers and anchors the kidney to the abdominal wall. It would be the answer for the anchoring layer.

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Which vessel branches directly from the abdominal aorta to bring blood to the kidney?
options: The efferent arteriole
The renal artery
The renal vein
The afferent arteriole
questions.why: The renal artery branches from the abdominal aorta and enters the kidney at the hilum. Inside the kidney it divides into smaller and smaller arteries until afferent arterioles deliver blood to each glomerulus. Because the kidneys filter the blood, they receive a large share of the blood the heart pumps.
notes: The efferent arteriole carries blood out of the glomerulus toward the peritubular capillaries. It would be the answer for the vessel leaving the glomerulus.
Correct. The renal artery comes straight off the abdominal aorta.
The renal vein carries blood out of the kidney at the hilum and drains into the inferior vena cava. Choose it if the question asked which vessel drains the kidney.
The afferent arteriole is a tiny vessel at the far end of the arterial chain, delivering blood into one glomerulus. Pick it if the question asked which vessel feeds a glomerulus.

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: What is the tip of a renal pyramid, where urine drains out, called?
options: The renal hilum
The minor calyx
The renal papilla
The renal column
questions.why: Each renal pyramid is a cone with its broad base toward the cortex and its tip pointing toward the center of the kidney. That tip is the renal papilla. Papillary ducts open on its surface, and urine drains from there into a minor calyx.
notes: The renal hilum is the notch on the medial border of the kidney where the vessels, ureter, and nerves pass. It would be the answer for the kidney's doorway, not the tip of a pyramid.
The minor calyx is the cup that catches urine from the papilla, so it sits just beyond the tip rather than being the tip itself. Choose it if the question asked what receives urine from the papilla.
Correct. The renal papilla is the tip of the pyramid.
A renal column is an extension of cortical tissue that dips down between two pyramids. Pick it if the question asked what separates neighboring pyramids.

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: What is the notch where the renal artery, renal vein, and ureter connect to the kidney?
options: The renal hilum
The trigone
The renal column
The renal papilla
questions.why: The renal hilum is the notch on the kidney's medial border. It is the only place where structures enter or leave the kidney: the renal artery comes in, and the renal vein and ureter go out, along with nerves and lymphatic vessels. Other organs, such as the lungs, also have a hilum that serves the same doorway role.
notes: Correct. The renal hilum is where the vessels and ureter connect.
The trigone is a triangular area on the floor of the urinary bladder, not part of the kidney. It would be the answer for the region marked by the ureter openings and the urethral opening.
A renal column is cortical tissue that dips down between pyramids inside the kidney. Choose it if the question asked what lies between two renal pyramids.
The renal papilla is the tip of a renal pyramid, deep inside the kidney, where urine drains into a minor calyx. Pick it if the question asked where urine leaves a pyramid.

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: The renal pyramids are found in which region of the kidney?
options: The renal pelvis
The renal medulla
The renal capsule
The renal cortex
questions.why: The renal medulla is the inner region of kidney tissue, and it is made of cone-shaped renal pyramids. Each pyramid points its base toward the cortex and its tip, the renal papilla, toward the center of the kidney. The pyramids look striped because they are packed with nephron loops and collecting ducts running in parallel.
notes: The renal pelvis is a hollow funnel at the center of the kidney that collects urine, so it holds urine rather than tissue. Choose it if the question asked where the calyces drain.
Correct. The pyramids make up the renal medulla.
The renal capsule is the fibrous covering on the kidney's surface, not a region of tissue. It would be the answer for the layer that maintains the kidney's shape.
The renal cortex is the outer tissue region, which holds the renal corpuscles and dips between the pyramids as renal columns. Pick it if the question asked where the glomeruli are found.

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: The renal columns that dip down between the renal pyramids are extensions of which tissue?
options: Adipose tissue
Fibrous capsule tissue
Medullary tissue
Cortical tissue
questions.why: The renal columns are extensions of the renal cortex that reach down between neighboring pyramids. Because the columns are cortex, the medulla is broken up into separate cone-shaped pyramids rather than forming one solid inner layer. The arteries that run between the pyramids travel in these columns.
notes: Adipose tissue forms the adipose capsule that cushions the kidney from the outside. Choose it if the question asked which layer holds the kidney in place and is lost in nephroptosis.
Fibrous capsule tissue forms the renal capsule on the outside of the kidney. It would be the answer for the smooth covering that maintains the kidney's shape.
Medullary tissue makes up the pyramids themselves, which the columns separate. Pick it if the question asked what the renal pyramids are made of.
Correct. The renal columns are extensions of the cortex.

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: The kidneys are described as retroperitoneal. What does that tell you about where they lie?
options: They lie in the thoracic cavity, behind the pleura.
They hang inside the peritoneal cavity, suspended by a mesentery.
They lie behind the parietal peritoneum, against the posterior abdominal wall.
They sit low in the pelvic cavity, behind the urinary bladder.
questions.why: Retro means behind, so retroperitoneal organs lie behind the peritoneum, the serous membrane that lines the abdominal cavity. The kidneys sit against the posterior abdominal wall, between about T12 and L3, with only the parietal peritoneum passing in front of them. Instead of hanging from a mesentery, each kidney is held in place by its own fat and fascia.
notes: The thoracic cavity holds the lungs and heart above the diaphragm, and the pleura covers the lungs. The kidneys are below the diaphragm, so this choice confuses the abdomen with the chest.

Organs that hang inside the peritoneal cavity on a mesentery, such as most of the small intestine, are called intraperitoneal. Pick this description if the question asked about an organ like the jejunum.
Correct. Retroperitoneal means behind the peritoneum, against the posterior abdominal wall.
The kidneys sit high in the abdomen, near the lowest ribs, not in the pelvis. The urinary bladder is the urinary organ found low in the pelvic cavity.
questions.answerText: They lie behind the parietal peritoneum, against the posterior abdominal wall.

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Which chambers collect urine directly from the renal papillae?
options: The major calyces
The collecting ducts
The minor calyces
The renal pelvis
questions.why: Each minor calyx is a small cup that fits around the tip of a renal papilla and catches the urine draining out of it. Several minor calyces join to form a major calyx, and the major calyces empty into the renal pelvis. The sequence runs from small to large: minor calyx, major calyx, renal pelvis.
notes: The major calyces form when several minor calyces join, so they receive urine one step after the minor calyces. Pick them if the question asked what drains into the renal pelvis.

The collecting ducts carry fluid down through the pyramids toward the papillae, so they deliver urine to the papillae rather than collect it from them. Choose them if the question asked which ducts gather fluid from many nephrons.
Correct. The minor calyces catch urine straight from the papillae.
The renal pelvis is the funnel that gathers urine from the major calyces and passes it to the ureter. It would be the answer for the last collecting space before the ureter.

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Which vessel carries blood directly into a glomerulus?
options: The efferent arteriole
The afferent arteriole
The peritubular capillaries
The cortical radiate artery
questions.why: The afferent arteriole is the last vessel in the kidney's arterial chain, and it delivers blood straight into the glomerulus. Afferent means carrying toward, the same word used for sensory neurons that carry signals toward the brain. Blood then leaves the glomerulus through the efferent arteriole, meaning carrying away.
notes: The efferent arteriole carries blood out of the glomerulus, the opposite direction. Pick it if the question asked which vessel leaves the glomerulus and leads to the peritubular capillaries.
Correct. The afferent arteriole carries blood into the glomerulus.

The peritubular capillaries are the second capillary bed, wrapping the renal tubules after blood leaves through the efferent arteriole. Choose them if the question asked which capillaries surround the tubules.

The cortical radiate (interlobular) artery runs up into the cortex and gives off the afferent arterioles, so it is one step upstream. It would be the answer for the artery that branches into afferent arterioles.

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: After blood leaves the efferent arteriole, which capillaries wrap around the convoluted tubules in the cortex?
options: The cortical radiate veins
The glomerular capillaries
The vasa recta
The peritubular capillaries
questions.why: Blood in the kidney passes through two capillary beds in a row. The first is the glomerulus, where filtration happens. The efferent arteriole then carries the blood to the second bed, the peritubular capillaries, which wrap the convoluted tubules in the cortex. Peritubular means around the tubules.
notes: The cortical radiate veins are veins that drain blood away from the capillaries toward the arcuate veins. They would be the answer for the first veins blood enters after the peritubular capillaries.

The glomerular capillaries are the first capillary bed, the filtering tuft inside the glomerular capsule. They come before the efferent arteriole, so pick them if the question asked where filtration happens.

The vasa recta also come from efferent arterioles, but they are long, straight capillaries that run deep into the medulla beside the loops of juxtamedullary nephrons. Choose them if the question asked about capillaries in the medulla.
Correct. The peritubular capillaries wrap the convoluted tubules after the efferent arteriole.

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Which structure is the funnel that gathers urine from the major calyces and passes it to the ureter?
options: The renal pelvis
The renal cortex
The renal papilla
The minor calyx
questions.why: The renal pelvis is the funnel-shaped cavity at the center of the kidney. The major calyces empty into it, and it narrows at the hilum to become the ureter. It is the last collecting space inside the kidney before urine leaves for the bladder.
notes: Correct. The renal pelvis funnels urine into the ureter.
The renal cortex is the outer region of kidney tissue, holding the renal corpuscles. Pick it if the question asked where the glomeruli are.
The renal papilla is the tip of a pyramid, where urine first leaves the kidney tissue. It sits upstream of the calyces, so choose it if the question asked where papillary ducts open.
The minor calyx is the small cup that catches urine from a papilla, two steps before the renal pelvis. It would be the answer for the first chamber urine enters after leaving a pyramid.

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Which vessel carries blood out of the glomerulus?
options: The efferent arteriole
The cortical radiate artery
The peritubular capillaries
The afferent arteriole
questions.why: Blood leaves the glomerulus through the efferent arteriole, meaning the arteriole that carries away. Unusually, blood leaving this capillary bed is still in an arteriole rather than a venule. The efferent arteriole then leads to a second capillary bed, the peritubular capillaries and vasa recta, around the renal tubules.
notes: Correct. The efferent arteriole carries blood out of the glomerulus.

The cortical radiate (interlobular) artery runs up into the cortex and gives off afferent arterioles, upstream of the glomerulus. It would be the answer for the artery that branches into afferent arterioles.
The peritubular capillaries receive blood from the efferent arteriole, so they are one step downstream. Choose them if the question asked which capillaries wrap the convoluted tubules.
The afferent arteriole carries blood into the glomerulus, the opposite direction. Pick it if the question asked which vessel feeds the glomerulus.

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Which sequence correctly traces blood from the renal artery through the filtering vessels to the renal vein?
options: Renal artery, glomerulus, afferent arteriole, efferent arteriole, peritubular capillaries, renal vein
Renal artery, afferent arteriole, glomerulus, efferent arteriole, peritubular capillaries, renal vein
Renal artery, efferent arteriole, glomerulus, afferent arteriole, peritubular capillaries, renal vein
Renal artery, afferent arteriole, efferent arteriole, glomerulus, peritubular capillaries, renal vein
questions.why: Blood reaches each nephron through an afferent arteriole, which empties into the glomerulus, the first capillary bed, where filtration happens. It leaves the glomerulus through the efferent arteriole, flows into the second capillary bed, the peritubular capillaries around the tubules, and then drains through a chain of veins to the renal vein. The efferent arteriole is the vessel between the two capillary beds.
notes: This order places the glomerulus before the afferent arteriole. The afferent arteriole is what delivers blood into the glomerulus, so it has to come first.
Correct. Afferent arteriole, glomerulus, efferent arteriole, peritubular capillaries.
This order reverses the two arterioles. Afferent means carrying toward and efferent means carrying away, so the afferent arteriole must come before the glomerulus.
This order puts both arterioles before the glomerulus. The glomerulus sits between them, with the afferent arteriole feeding it and the efferent arteriole draining it.
questions.answerText: Renal artery, afferent arteriole, glomerulus, efferent arteriole, peritubular capillaries, renal vein

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: A frontal section of the kidney shows the outer tissue region, the inner tissue region, and the funnel that empties into the ureter. Which sequence names them from outermost to innermost?
options: Renal medulla, renal cortex, renal pelvis
Renal pelvis, renal cortex, renal medulla
Renal cortex, renal pelvis, renal medulla
Renal cortex, renal medulla, renal pelvis
questions.why: On a frontal section, the renal cortex forms the outer band of tissue just under the capsule. Deep to it is the renal medulla, made of cone-shaped pyramids with their tips pointing inward. At the center, the calyces open into the renal pelvis, the funnel that narrows into the ureter at the hilum. Tissue regions are on the outside and the collecting spaces are in the middle.
notes: This order puts the medulla on the outside. The cortex is the outer region, and the pyramids of the medulla lie deep to it, pointing toward the center.
This order starts with the renal pelvis, which is actually the innermost space. The pelvis sits at the center of the kidney where the calyces drain, so it belongs last.
This order places the renal pelvis between the two tissue regions. The pelvis is a collecting space at the very center, so the medulla must come before it.
Correct. Cortex, then medulla, then renal pelvis.
questions.answerText: Renal cortex, renal medulla, renal pelvis

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Between which vertebral levels do the kidneys lie?
options: Between S1 and S3
Between T12 and L3
Between L3 and L5
Between T6 and T10
questions.why: The kidneys lie retroperitoneally against the posterior abdominal wall, between about T12 and L3. Their upper ends are protected by the lowest ribs. The right kidney sits slightly lower than the left because the liver lies above it.
notes: The sacral vertebrae form the back of the pelvis, where the urinary bladder and rectum lie. This choice confuses the kidneys with the pelvic organs of the urinary system.
Correct. The kidneys lie between about T12 and L3.
This range is too low. The lower lumbar vertebrae sit near the level of the iliac crests, below the kidneys, so this choice confuses the kidneys with the lower abdomen.
This range is too high. The T6 to T10 vertebrae lie mostly behind the thoracic cavity, at the level of the heart and lower lungs, above where the kidneys sit.

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: On which part of the kidney is the renal hilum found?
options: The medial border
The inferior pole
The lateral border
The superior pole
questions.why: The renal hilum is a notch on the medial (concave) border of the kidney, the side that faces the vertebral column. This is where the ureter, renal vessels, and nerves enter and leave, which keeps them close to the aorta and inferior vena cava running along the spine. The notch is what gives the kidney its bean shape.
notes: Correct. The hilum is on the medial border, facing the spine.
The inferior pole is the lower, rounded end of the kidney. This choice usually comes from picturing the ureter hanging straight down, but the ureter leaves from the medial notch.
The lateral border is the smooth, convex outer edge of the kidney, facing away from the spine. It has no opening, so pick it only if the question asked for the outer curved edge.
The superior pole is the upper end of the kidney, where the suprarenal (adrenal) gland sits like a cap. It would be the answer for where the adrenal gland rests.

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Which sequence names the three layers around the kidney from innermost to outermost?
options: Renal fascia, adipose capsule, renal capsule
Renal cortex, renal medulla, renal pelvis
Renal capsule, renal fascia, adipose capsule
Renal capsule, adipose capsule, renal fascia
questions.why: Three layers cushion and anchor each kidney. The renal capsule is the smooth fibrous layer on the kidney's surface that maintains its shape. Around it is the adipose capsule, a layer of fat that cushions the kidney and holds it in place. Outermost is the renal fascia, connective tissue that anchors the kidney to the abdominal wall.
notes: This is the correct list read in the opposite direction, from outermost to innermost. It would be right if the question asked you to start at the abdominal wall.
The cortex, medulla, and renal pelvis are regions inside the kidney, not the layers around it. Pick this list if the question asked what a frontal section shows from outside to center.
This order puts the renal fascia in the middle. The fat of the adipose capsule lies between the capsule and the fascia, so the fascia is the outermost layer.
Correct. Renal capsule, then adipose capsule, then renal fascia.
questions.answerText: Renal capsule, adipose capsule, renal fascia

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Blood enters the kidney through the renal artery, which splits into segmental arteries in the renal sinus. Which arteries come next, running up through the renal columns between the pyramids?
options: The afferent arterioles
The cortical radiate arteries
The interlobar arteries
The arcuate arteries
questions.why: Inside the renal sinus, the renal artery divides into segmental arteries. These give off interlobar arteries, which run up through the renal columns between the renal pyramids. Interlobar means between the lobes, and each lobe is one pyramid with the cortex around it. At the bases of the pyramids the interlobar arteries turn into arcuate arteries.
notes: The afferent arterioles are the last arterial vessels in the chain, each delivering blood into one glomerulus. Choose them if the question asked which vessel feeds a glomerulus.
The cortical radiate (interlobular) arteries branch from the arcuate arteries up into the cortex. They would be the answer for the arteries that give off the afferent arterioles.
Correct. The interlobar arteries branch from the segmental arteries and run through the renal columns between the pyramids.
The arcuate arteries come one step later, arching along the bases of the pyramids at the border of the cortex and medulla. Pick them if the question asked which arteries run along the pyramid bases.

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Which arteries branch from the arcuate arteries up into the cortex and give off the afferent arterioles?
options: The efferent arterioles
The interlobar arteries
The cortical radiate (interlobular) arteries
The segmental arteries
questions.why: The cortical radiate arteries, also called interlobular arteries, radiate outward from the arcuate arteries into the cortex. Along their length they give off the afferent arterioles that feed the glomeruli. Watch the look-alike names: interlobar arteries run between the pyramids, while interlobular arteries run up into the cortex.
notes: The efferent arterioles carry blood out of the glomeruli, after the afferent arterioles. Choose them if the question asked which vessel leaves the glomerulus.

The interlobar arteries run between the pyramids before the arcuate arteries, so they come earlier in the chain. The name differs from interlobular by only a few letters; pick interlobar if the question asked which arteries pass between pyramids.
Correct. The cortical radiate (interlobular) arteries give off the afferent arterioles.
The segmental arteries are the first branches of the renal artery inside the kidney. They would be the answer for the vessels the renal artery divides into right after the hilum.

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Several minor calyces join to form which larger chamber?
options: The renal pelvis
The renal sinus
A major calyx
The ureter
questions.why: Each minor calyx catches urine from one renal papilla, and several minor calyces merge into a major calyx. The major calyces in turn empty into the renal pelvis. Calyx means cup, and the chambers grow larger as urine moves from minor calyx to major calyx to renal pelvis.
notes: The renal pelvis receives urine from the major calyces, so it is one step beyond the chamber the minor calyces form. Pick it if the question asked where the major calyces drain.
The renal sinus is the space inside the kidney, deep to the hilum, that holds the calyces, renal pelvis, vessels, and fat. It surrounds the calyces rather than being formed by them.
Correct. Minor calyces join to form a major calyx.
The ureter begins where the renal pelvis narrows at the hilum, two steps after the minor calyces. Choose it if the question asked which tube carries urine out of the kidney.

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: A kidney biopsy needs to include renal corpuscles for the pathologist to examine. Which region of the kidney must the needle sample?
options: The renal medulla
The renal pelvis
The renal sinus
The renal cortex
questions.why: All of the renal corpuscles, the glomeruli inside their capsules, sit in the renal cortex, the outer region of kidney tissue. The medulla holds the nephron loops and collecting ducts, but no corpuscles. So a sample that must show glomeruli has to come from the cortex.
notes: The renal medulla is made of pyramids holding the nephron loops and collecting ducts, with no renal corpuscles. Pick it if the question asked where the long loops of juxtamedullary nephrons reach.
The renal pelvis is a hollow funnel that collects urine, so it holds no nephrons at all. It would be the answer if the question asked where kidney stones often form.
The renal sinus is the space deep to the hilum that holds the renal pelvis, calyces, vessels, and fat. It contains no nephron tissue; choose it if the question asked what space the hilum opens into.
Correct. All renal corpuscles are in the renal cortex.

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Unlike most capillary beds, the glomerulus drains into an arteriole instead of a venule. Where does blood in that efferent arteriole go next?
options: Back into the afferent arteriole
Directly into the renal vein
Into the capsular space with the filtrate
Into a second capillary bed around the renal tubules
questions.why: Blood in the kidney meets two capillary beds, one after the other. The first is the glomerulus, where filtration happens. The efferent arteriole carries the blood to the second bed, the peritubular capillaries and vasa recta that wrap the renal tubules, and only then does the blood drain into veins leading to the renal vein. The efferent arteriole is the vessel that links the two beds.
notes: The afferent arteriole carries blood into the glomerulus, so blood cannot flow back into it. Pick the afferent arteriole if the question asked which vessel feeds the glomerulus.
The renal vein is reached only after the second capillary bed and a chain of veins. This choice skips the peritubular capillaries, which are the reason the glomerulus drains into an arteriole.
The capsular space receives filtrate, the fluid pushed out of the blood, but blood itself stays inside the vessels. Choose the capsular space if the question asked where filtrate first collects.
Correct. The efferent arteriole leads to the peritubular capillaries and vasa recta.
questions.answerText: Into a second capillary bed around the renal tubules

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Which list correctly names the roles of the kidneys?
options: Storing urine, then contracting the bladder wall to push it out through the urethra
Filtering wastes, balancing water, ions, and pH, and helping regulate blood pressure
Exchanging oxygen and carbon dioxide between the blood and the air
Producing bile, storing glycogen, and breaking down old and worn-out red blood cells
questions.why: The kidneys filter wastes out of the blood and form urine, but their work goes further. By adjusting how much water and salt they keep or let go in the urine, they balance the body's water, ions, and pH. Because the amount of water in the blood affects blood volume, the kidneys also help regulate blood pressure.
notes: Storing urine and pushing it out is the job of the urinary bladder and its detrusor muscle. Pick this list if the question asked about the bladder.
Correct. These are the roles of the kidneys.
Exchanging oxygen and carbon dioxide is the job of the lungs, at the alveoli. Choose this description if the question asked about the respiratory membrane.
Producing bile and storing glycogen are jobs of the liver, and breaking down old red blood cells is a job of the spleen. This list mixes up the kidneys with other abdominal organs.
questions.answerText: Filtering wastes, balancing water, ions, and pH, and helping regulate blood pressure

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: What is the space inside the kidney, just deep to the hilum, that holds the renal pelvis, calyces, vessels, and fat?
options: The renal medulla
The capsular space
The renal sinus
The adipose capsule
questions.why: The hilum is the notch on the medial border of the kidney, and it opens into a space inside the kidney called the renal sinus. The sinus holds the renal pelvis and calyces along with the branches of the renal vessels, nerves, and fat that cushions them. On a frontal section, it is the central area surrounded by the kidney tissue.
notes: The renal medulla is solid kidney tissue made of renal pyramids, not an open space holding the pelvis. Pick it if the question asked which region contains the pyramids.
The capsular space is a microscopic space inside one glomerular capsule where filtrate collects. It would be the answer for where filtrate gathers before the proximal tubule.
Correct. The renal sinus is the space deep to the hilum.
The adipose capsule is the fat layer around the outside of the kidney, between the renal capsule and the renal fascia. Choose it if the question asked which outer layer cushions the kidney.

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Which capillaries run deep into the medulla alongside the long loops of juxtamedullary nephrons?
options: The arcuate arteries
The vasa recta
The glomerular capillaries
The peritubular capillaries
questions.why: The vasa recta are long, straight capillaries that branch from the efferent arterioles of juxtamedullary nephrons and run deep into the medulla beside their long nephron loops. Vasa recta means straight vessels. Cortical nephrons, with their short loops, are wrapped by peritubular capillaries instead.
notes: The arcuate arteries are arteries, not capillaries, and they arch along the bases of the pyramids rather than running down into them. Choose them if the question asked which arteries mark the border of cortex and medulla.
Correct. The vasa recta run alongside the long loops of juxtamedullary nephrons.
The glomerular capillaries form the filtering tuft inside the glomerular capsule, upstream of the efferent arteriole. They would be the answer for where filtration happens.

The peritubular capillaries also come from efferent arterioles, but they wrap the convoluted tubules and short loops of cortical nephrons. Pick them if the question asked which capillaries surround tubules in the cortex.

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Which arteries arch along the bases of the renal pyramids, at the border between the cortex and medulla?
options: The interlobar arteries
The cortical radiate arteries
The arcuate arteries
The segmental arteries
questions.why: The arcuate arteries arch over the bases of the renal pyramids, right along the border between the cortex and medulla. Arcuate means arched, which names their shape. They receive blood from the interlobar arteries and send cortical radiate arteries up into the cortex.
notes: The interlobar arteries run between the pyramids, one step before the arcuate arteries. Pick them if the question asked which arteries pass between neighboring pyramids.
The cortical radiate (interlobular) arteries branch from the arcuate arteries and run up into the cortex. Choose them if the question asked which arteries give off the afferent arterioles.
Correct. The arcuate arteries arch along the pyramid bases.
The segmental arteries are the first branches of the renal artery after it enters at the hilum. They would be the answer for the vessels the renal artery divides into first.

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Which sequence correctly traces blood from the peritubular capillaries back to the renal vein?
options: Interlobar veins, arcuate veins, cortical radiate veins, renal vein
Cortical radiate veins, arcuate veins, interlobar veins, renal vein
Arcuate veins, cortical radiate veins, interlobar veins, renal vein
Cortical radiate veins, interlobar veins, arcuate veins, renal vein
questions.why: The veins of the kidney retrace the arterial path in reverse. Blood from the peritubular capillaries drains into cortical radiate veins in the cortex, then into arcuate veins along the pyramid bases, then into interlobar veins between the pyramids, and finally into the renal vein, which leaves at the hilum. If you know the arteries in order, read them backward to get the veins.
notes: This order runs from the hilum outward, the direction of the arteries rather than the veins. It would fit a question about arteries if the names were changed to arteries.
Correct. Cortical radiate, arcuate, interlobar, then the renal vein.
This order starts with the arcuate veins, which sit at the pyramid bases. Blood from the cortex must first collect in cortical radiate veins before reaching the arcuate veins.
This order skips over the arcuate veins and adds them too late. The arcuate veins lie between the cortical radiate and interlobar veins, just as the arcuate arteries do.
questions.answerText: Cortical radiate veins, arcuate veins, interlobar veins, renal vein

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Which list orders the three tissue layers around the kidney from innermost to outermost?
options: Adipose capsule, renal capsule, renal fascia
Renal fascia, adipose capsule, renal capsule
Renal capsule, adipose capsule, renal fascia
Renal capsule, renal fascia, adipose capsule
questions.why: The renal capsule is the smooth fibrous layer that sits right on the kidney surface and keeps its shape. Around it is the adipose capsule, a layer of fat that cushions the kidney and holds it in place. The renal fascia is the outermost layer of dense connective tissue that anchors the kidney and its fat to the back wall of the abdomen.
notes: This puts the fat directly on the kidney surface, but the fibrous renal capsule is the layer touching the kidney. The fat lies outside that capsule, which is why the two layers share the word capsule but sit in different places.

This is the correct sequence written backward, from outermost to innermost. Students choose it when they miss the words inner to outer in the stem; it would be right if the question asked for the order from the outside in.
Correct. The fibrous capsule touches the kidney, the fat surrounds it, and the fascia anchors everything to the body wall.
This swaps the fat and the fascia. The renal fascia is the outermost anchoring sheet, and the adipose capsule lies between it and the renal capsule, so the fat cannot be the outer layer.
questions.answerText: Renal capsule, adipose capsule, renal fascia

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the positions of the renal cortex and the renal medulla?
options: The cortex forms the renal pelvis; the medulla forms the outer shell of the kidney
The cortex and medulla are side by side, with the cortex nearer the hilum
The cortex is the inner region and holds the pyramids; the medulla lies beneath the capsule
The cortex lies under the capsule; the medulla is deeper and holds the pyramids
questions.why: Cortex means bark, the outer layer, and medulla means marrow, the inner part, and the kidney follows that pattern. The renal cortex is the outer band of tissue just under the renal capsule, and the renal medulla lies deeper, divided into cone-shaped renal pyramids. Strips of cortex called renal columns dip down between the pyramids.
notes: Neither region forms the renal pelvis, which is the funnel-shaped space that collects urine from the calyces. The outer shell is the cortex, not the medulla, so this statement gets both halves wrong.

The two regions are layered one inside the other, not set side by side. The structures nearest the hilum are the renal pelvis and the major calyces, which would be the answer if the question asked what lies at the medial notch where the ureter leaves.
This reverses the two regions. The pyramids belong to the medulla, which is the deeper region; students choose this when they mix up which word means outer.
Correct. The cortex is the outer zone under the capsule, and the medulla is the deeper zone made of renal pyramids.
questions.answerText: The cortex lies under the capsule; the medulla is deeper and holds the pyramids

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: After rapid, severe weight loss, a patient's kidney drops out of its normal position and kinks the ureter. Loss of which layer most likely allowed this?
options: Renal capsule
Renal fascia
Adipose capsule
Parietal peritoneum
questions.why: The adipose capsule is the layer of fat around the kidney that cushions it and helps hold it in place. When a person loses a large amount of body fat quickly, this fat pad can shrink, and the kidney may drop lower in the abdomen. This condition is called nephroptosis, or a floating kidney, and the dropped kidney can kink the ureter and block the flow of urine.
notes: The renal capsule is the thin fibrous layer on the kidney surface that maintains the kidney's shape. It is not fat, so weight loss does not shrink it; pick it if the question asked which layer touches the kidney directly.

The renal fascia is the outer connective tissue sheet that anchors the kidney to the abdominal wall. It is not lost with weight loss; choose it if the question asked which layer is the outermost anchor of the kidney.
Correct. Loss of the fatty adipose capsule removes the cushion that holds the kidney in place.

The kidneys are retroperitoneal, meaning they lie behind the parietal peritoneum rather than wrapped in it, so the peritoneum is not one of the kidney's own supporting layers. Pick it if a question asked which membrane lies in front of the retroperitoneal organs.

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: What are the renal pyramids, and which way do their bases face?
options: Cup-shaped spaces of the medulla, with their bases toward the hilum
Cone-shaped masses of the medulla, with their bases toward the pelvis
Cone-shaped masses of the cortex, with their bases toward the pelvis
Cone-shaped masses of the medulla, with their bases toward the cortex
questions.why: The renal medulla is divided into cone-shaped renal pyramids. Each pyramid has a broad base that faces outward toward the cortex and a pointed tip, the renal papilla, that faces inward toward the renal sinus where it drains into a minor calyx. Picture each pyramid pointing its tip at the center of the kidney.
notes: This describes the calyces, the cup-shaped spaces that collect urine near the renal sinus, rather than solid tissue. Pick a minor calyx if the question asked what cup receives urine from a papilla.
This gets the tissue right but flips the pyramid. The tip of the pyramid, the papilla, points toward the pelvis and calyces, so the base must face the opposite way, out toward the cortex.

The pyramids are part of the medulla, not the cortex. The cortical tissue that dips between the pyramids forms the renal columns, which would be the answer if the question asked about cortex extending into the medulla.
Correct. The pyramids are medullary tissue, broad at the cortex and narrowing to a papilla.
questions.answerText: Cone-shaped masses of the medulla, with their bases toward the cortex

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: The renal papilla is the tip of a renal pyramid. Into which space does it drain urine?
options: A major calyx
The ureter
A minor calyx
The renal pelvis
questions.why: Each renal papilla, the pointed tip of a pyramid, fits into a small cup called a minor calyx, and urine drips from the papilla into that cup. Several minor calyces join to form a major calyx, and the major calyces empty into the renal pelvis. The minor calyx is therefore the first collecting space urine reaches after it leaves the kidney tissue.
notes: A major calyx forms where several minor calyces merge, so it is one step later in the path. Pick it if the question asked what the minor calyces drain into.

The ureter leaves the kidney at the hilum and carries urine to the bladder. It is several steps downstream of the papilla, and it would be the answer if the question asked what the renal pelvis drains into.
Correct. The papilla empties straight into a minor calyx.
The renal pelvis is the funnel that collects urine from the major calyces, two steps after the papilla. Choose it if the question asked what passes urine directly into the ureter.

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: What are the renal columns?
options: Extensions of the cortex that dip down between the renal pyramids
Bundles of collecting ducts that form the tip of each pyramid
Strips of medulla that rise up into the cortex between nephrons
Branches of the renal pelvis that cup the tip of each pyramid
questions.why: The renal columns are bands of cortical tissue that reach inward between neighboring renal pyramids, separating one pyramid from the next. They carry blood vessels, such as the interlobar arteries and veins, between the pyramids toward the cortex. Because they are cortex, they look the same as the outer cortex in a sectioned kidney.
notes: Correct. Renal columns are cortex reaching down between the pyramids.
Collecting ducts gathering at the tip of a pyramid form the renal papilla region, not a column. Pick the renal papilla if the question asked about the tip of a pyramid where urine drains out.
This reverses the direction. The columns are cortex pushing inward, not medulla pushing outward; students choose this when they forget which tissue the columns are made of.
This describes the minor calyces, the cup-shaped branches of the collecting system around each papilla. Choose a minor calyx if the question asked what receives urine from the tip of a pyramid.
questions.answerText: Extensions of the cortex that dip down between the renal pyramids

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: What is the renal pelvis, and what does it do?
options: The funnel that collects urine and passes it to the ureter
The cup that receives urine directly from a single renal papilla
The bony pelvic basin that supports the kidney from below
The muscular sac that stores urine until it is released
questions.why: The renal pelvis is a flat, funnel-shaped space inside the renal sinus, near the hilum. The major calyces empty into it, and it narrows as it leaves the kidney to become the ureter. Its job is to gather all the urine from the calyces and channel it into that one tube.
notes: Correct. The renal pelvis gathers urine from the major calyces and funnels it into the ureter.
This describes a minor calyx, the small cup that fits over a single papilla. Pick it if the question asked what receives urine first after it leaves the pyramid.

The word pelvis means basin, which is why students link it to the bony pelvis, but the renal pelvis is a hollow space inside the kidney. The kidneys sit high on the posterior abdominal wall, well above the bony pelvis.
This describes the urinary bladder, which stores urine until urination. Choose the bladder if the question asked which organ holds urine between trips to the restroom.
questions.answerText: The funnel that collects urine and passes it to the ureter

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Which list orders the urine-collecting spaces from the renal papilla to the ureter?
options: Minor calyx, renal pelvis, major calyx, ureter
Major calyx, minor calyx, renal pelvis, ureter
Minor calyx, major calyx, renal pelvis, ureter
Renal pelvis, minor calyx, major calyx, ureter
questions.why: The collecting spaces get larger as they merge. Each papilla drains into a small minor calyx, several minor calyces join to form a major calyx, and the major calyces empty into the single renal pelvis. The renal pelvis then narrows into the ureter as it leaves the kidney at the hilum.
notes: This places the renal pelvis between the two calyces. The major calyces empty into the pelvis, so both calyces come before it.
This puts the larger cup first. Minor calyces merge to form the major calyx, so the minor calyx must come first; students pick this when they mix up minor and major.
Correct. Small cups merge into larger cups, which merge into the funnel that becomes the ureter.

The renal pelvis is the last space inside the kidney, formed where the major calyces meet, so it cannot come before the calyces. It would be first only if the question traced urine backward from the ureter.
questions.answerText: Minor calyx, major calyx, renal pelvis, ureter

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Which vessel delivers blood into the glomerulus, and which carries it out?
options: Interlobular artery in; peritubular capillary out
Efferent arteriole in; afferent arteriole out
Afferent arteriole in; efferent arteriole out
Afferent arteriole in; interlobular vein out
questions.why: Afferent means carrying toward, and efferent means carrying away. The afferent arteriole brings blood into the glomerulus, and the efferent arteriole carries it out. Unusually, the vessel leaving the glomerulus is still an arteriole, which then feeds a second capillary bed, the peritubular capillaries and vasa recta around the tubules.
notes: The interlobular artery feeds the afferent arteriole, one step earlier, and the peritubular capillaries come after the efferent arteriole. Neither one connects directly to the glomerulus.
This reverses the two arterioles. Students mix them up because the words differ by one letter; remember that afferent arrives and efferent exits.
Correct. The afferent arteriole brings blood in and the efferent arteriole takes it out.
The afferent half is right, but blood leaving the glomerulus does not go straight into a vein. It passes through the efferent arteriole and a second capillary bed first.
questions.answerText: Afferent arteriole in; efferent arteriole out

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Which list traces blood from the renal artery to the glomerulus?
options: Renal, segmental, interlobar, interlobular, arcuate, afferent arteriole, glomerulus
Renal, interlobar, segmental, arcuate, interlobular, afferent arteriole, glomerulus
Renal, segmental, arcuate, interlobar, interlobular, afferent arteriole, glomerulus
Renal, segmental, interlobar, arcuate, interlobular, afferent arteriole, glomerulus
questions.why: The renal artery enters at the hilum and splits into segmental arteries, which give rise to interlobar arteries running between the pyramids. At the bases of the pyramids, the interlobar arteries become arcuate arteries that arch along the border of cortex and medulla. Interlobular arteries (also called cortical radiate arteries) rise from the arcuate arteries into the cortex and give off the afferent arterioles that feed each glomerulus.
notes: This swaps the arcuate and interlobular arteries. The arcuate arteries arch along the pyramid bases, and the interlobular arteries rise from them into the cortex, where the glomeruli are.
This swaps the segmental and interlobar arteries. The segmental arteries branch first from the renal artery, and the interlobar arteries come from them.
This puts the arcuate arteries before the interlobar arteries. The interlobar arteries travel between the pyramids first and then curve into the arcuate arteries at the pyramid bases.
Correct. The arteries branch from large to small, ending at the afferent arteriole and glomerulus.
questions.answerText: Renal, segmental, interlobar, arcuate, interlobular, afferent arteriole, glomerulus

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Which vessels are long, straight capillaries that follow the loops of juxtamedullary nephrons deep into the medulla?
options: The interlobar veins
The peritubular capillaries
The vasa recta
The arcuate arteries
questions.why: Vasa recta means straight vessels. These long capillaries come off the efferent arterioles of juxtamedullary nephrons and run beside their long nephron loops deep into the medulla. Juxtamedullary nephrons sit near the medulla, make up about 15 percent of nephrons, and concentrate the urine.
notes: The interlobar veins carry blood out between the pyramids toward the renal vein. They are veins, not capillaries; pick them if the question asked which vessels drain blood between the pyramids.

The peritubular capillaries wrap the tubules of the cortical nephrons, the short-looped nephrons that barely enter the medulla. Choose them if the question asked which capillaries serve cortical nephrons.
Correct. The vasa recta run alongside the long loops of juxtamedullary nephrons.

The arcuate arteries arch along the bases of the pyramids at the border of cortex and medulla. They are arteries, not capillaries, so pick them if the question asked which vessels curve along the pyramid bases.

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: During a dissection, you cut through the renal fascia around a kidney. Which layer will you meet next, and which layer still lies between that one and the kidney tissue?
options: The adipose capsule, with the renal fascia still beneath it
The adipose capsule, with the renal capsule still beneath it
The parietal peritoneum, with the renal capsule beneath it
The renal capsule, with the adipose capsule still beneath it
questions.why: From the kidney outward, the three layers are the renal capsule, the adipose capsule, and the renal fascia. Working inward from the fascia, you reverse that order, so the fat of the adipose capsule comes next. The thin renal capsule is the last layer, lying right on the kidney's surface.
notes: The adipose capsule is the right next layer, but the renal fascia is the layer you just cut. It is the outermost layer, not one that lies closer to the kidney.
Correct. Under the renal fascia is the fat of the adipose capsule, and the renal capsule sits on the kidney surface below that.
The parietal peritoneum lies in front of the kidneys, which is why they are called retroperitoneal. It is not one of the kidney's three layers, so you would not find it inside the renal fascia.
This reverses the two inner layers. The renal capsule is the innermost layer on the kidney itself, so it comes last, after the fat.
questions.answerText: The adipose capsule, with the renal capsule still beneath it

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: A surgeon removes a kidney together with its renal fascia, without opening the fascia. Which other organ comes out inside the same fascia, and which layer inside it cushions the kidney?
options: The liver, with the adipose capsule cushioning the kidney
The adrenal gland, with the renal capsule cushioning the kidney
The urinary bladder, with the renal capsule cushioning the kidney
The adrenal gland, with the adipose capsule cushioning the kidney
questions.why: The renal fascia is the outermost of the three layers around the kidney, and it wraps the suprarenal (adrenal) gland together with the kidney, so the gland comes out with it. Inside the fascia, the adipose capsule (perirenal fat) cushions the kidney and helps hold it in place. The renal capsule lies on the kidney surface itself, where it holds the kidney's shape and protects its surface.
notes: The liver sits above the right kidney and is why that kidney sits lower, but it is not wrapped in the renal fascia. The only other organ inside the fascia is the adrenal gland.
The adrenal gland is right, but the renal capsule is the thin, tough layer on the kidney surface that holds its shape and protects it. The cushioning layer is the fat of the adipose capsule.
The bladder is the urinary organ that stores urine, far below the kidney, and the ureter connects the two. It does not share the renal fascia, and the renal capsule is not the cushioning layer.
Correct. The renal fascia wraps the adrenal gland together with the kidney, and the adipose capsule inside it cushions the kidney.
questions.answerText: The adrenal gland, with the adipose capsule cushioning the kidney

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: A stab wound enters the back beside the vertebral column, just below the lowest ribs, at about the level of L1. Which organ is most likely injured, and must the peritoneal cavity have been opened to reach it?
options: The kidney, and no, because it lies behind the parietal peritoneum
The kidney, and yes, because it lies inside the peritoneal cavity
The urinary bladder, and no, because it lies behind the peritoneum
The adrenal gland only, and yes, because it lies in the peritoneal cavity
questions.why: The kidneys sit on the posterior abdominal wall beside the vertebral column, between about T12 and L3, with the lowest ribs covering their upper ends. They are retroperitoneal, which means they lie behind the parietal peritoneum and outside the peritoneal cavity. A wound coming in from the back can reach a kidney before it ever reaches the peritoneum.
notes: Correct. The kidney lies at about T12 to L3 against the back muscles, behind the peritoneum, so a wound from behind can reach it without entering the peritoneal cavity.
The kidney is the right organ, but it is retroperitoneal. It lies behind the parietal peritoneum, so reaching it from behind does not require opening the peritoneal cavity.
The bladder sits low in the pelvis, far below L1. A wound just under the lowest ribs beside the spine is at kidney level, not bladder level.
The adrenal gland caps the upper end of the kidney inside the same renal fascia, so it is also retroperitoneal. At L1 beside the spine, the kidney itself is the organ in the path.
questions.answerText: The kidney, and no, because it lies behind the parietal peritoneum

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: A small stone blocks one minor calyx and urine backs up behind it. Which part of the kidney is the backed-up urine coming from?
options: The renal pelvis and the ureter below it
The renal column beside that calyx
The pyramid whose papilla opens into it
Every renal pyramid in the kidney
questions.why: Urine drains out of tiny openings on the renal papilla, the tip of a renal pyramid, and each papilla empties into a cup called a minor calyx. A blockage makes urine back up into the parts above it. So the backup comes from the pyramid whose papilla opens into that calyx, while the rest of the kidney keeps draining through its own calyces.
notes: The renal pelvis and ureter are downstream of the minor calyx, so a stone in the calyx does not back urine up into them. They would back up only if the stone were lower, in the pelvis or ureter.
A renal column is cortex tissue reaching inward between two pyramids. Urine drains from the papillae of the pyramids, not from the columns.
Correct. Each papilla drains into a minor calyx, so the pyramid whose tip opens into the blocked calyx is the one that backs up.
The other pyramids drain into their own minor calyces, which are still open. Only the pyramid draining into the blocked calyx is affected.
questions.answerText: The pyramid whose papilla opens into it

questions.topic: Kidney gross anatomy and blood supply
questions.q: Which vessel carries blood out of the kidney at the hilum and empties into the inferior vena cava?
options: The interlobar vein
The renal artery
The renal vein
The ureter
questions.why: Blood leaving the kidney passes through veins that repeat the artery names in reverse: cortical radiate, arcuate, interlobar, and then the renal vein. The renal vein leaves the kidney at the hilum, alongside the renal artery and ureter. It empties into the inferior vena cava, which returns the blood to the heart.
notes: Interlobar veins run down through the renal columns toward the renal sinus. They join to form the renal vein, which is the vessel that actually leaves the kidney.
The renal artery also passes through the hilum, but it brings blood in. It branches off the abdominal aorta rather than draining into a vein.
Correct. The renal vein leaves at the hilum and empties into the inferior vena cava.
The ureter leaves at the hilum too, but it is a tube that carries urine to the bladder, not a blood vessel.

questions.q: Filtrate has just left the nephron loop. Which segment of the nephron does it enter next?
options: The distal convoluted tubule
The glomerular capsule
The collecting duct
The proximal convoluted tubule
questions.why: The segments are named in the order the filtrate meets them: capsular space, proximal convoluted tubule, nephron loop, distal convoluted tubule, and then the collecting duct. After the filtrate climbs the ascending limb of the nephron loop, it enters the distal convoluted tubule, the second coiled segment. Proximal means near the renal corpuscle and distal means farther from it, which makes the order easy to rebuild.
notes: Correct. The distal convoluted tubule follows the nephron loop.

The glomerular capsule is the cup around the glomerulus where filtrate first collects, at the very start of the nephron. It would be the answer for where filtrate enters the nephron, not where it goes after the loop.
The collecting duct comes one step later. It receives fluid from the distal convoluted tubules of many nephrons, so it is the answer for where filtrate goes after the distal convoluted tubule.

The proximal convoluted tubule is the first coiled segment, the one filtrate enters straight from the capsular space. It comes before the nephron loop, so pick it if the question asked where filtrate goes after leaving the glomerular capsule.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares cortical and juxtamedullary nephrons?
options: Cortical nephrons are about 85 percent and have short loops; juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops served by the vasa recta.
Cortical nephrons are about 15 percent and have long loops; juxtamedullary nephrons are about 85 percent and have short loops.
Juxtamedullary nephrons lie entirely within the medulla; cortical nephrons have no nephron loop at all.
Both types have the same loop length; they differ only in which kidney they are found in.
questions.why: Nephrons are sorted by how deep their loop reaches. Cortical nephrons make up about 85 percent of all nephrons, have short loops that barely enter the medulla, and are wrapped by peritubular capillaries. Juxtamedullary nephrons make up about 15 percent, have renal corpuscles near the border with the medulla (juxta means next to), and have long loops that reach deep into the medulla, served by the vasa recta. These long loops are what let the kidney concentrate urine.
notes: Correct. Cortical nephrons are the common short-looped type, and juxtamedullary nephrons are the long-looped type served by the vasa recta.
This statement swaps the numbers and the loop lengths. Most nephrons are cortical with short loops; only about 15 percent are juxtamedullary with long loops.
Every nephron has a nephron loop, and the renal corpuscles of juxtamedullary nephrons sit in the cortex next to the medulla, not inside it. Only their long loops dip deep into the medulla.

The two types differ mainly in loop length and the position of the corpuscle, and both types are found in each kidney. This choice comes from reading cortical and juxtamedullary as places rather than as nephron types.
questions.answerText: Cortical nephrons are about 85 percent and have short loops; juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops served by the vasa recta.

questions.q: What forms the parietal (outer) layer of the glomerular capsule?
options: Podocytes
Simple cuboidal epithelium
Simple squamous epithelium
Transitional epithelium
questions.why: The glomerular capsule has two layers with the capsular space between them. The outer, parietal layer is simple squamous epithelium, a single layer of flat cells that forms the wall of the cup. The inner, visceral layer is made of podocytes, which wrap the glomerular capillaries. Filtrate passes into the capsular space between the two layers.
notes: Podocytes form the inner, visceral layer that clings to the glomerular capillaries, and their foot-like processes form the filtration slits. Pick them if the question asked about the visceral layer.
Simple cuboidal epithelium lines the renal tubules, such as the proximal and distal convoluted tubules. It is the answer if the question asked about the tubule wall rather than the capsule.
Correct. The parietal layer is a thin wall of simple squamous epithelium.
Transitional epithelium is the stretchy lining of the ureters and urinary bladder. Choose it if the question asked which epithelium lines an organ that has to expand as it fills.

questions.q: Where are the juxtaglomerular (granular) cells located?
options: In the wall of the distal convoluted tubule
In the wall of the collecting duct
In the wall of the afferent arteriole
In the visceral layer of the glomerular capsule
questions.why: Juxtaglomerular cells are modified smooth muscle cells, mostly in the wall of the afferent arteriole, at the spot where the tubule passes beside its own renal corpuscle. Together with the macula densa cells in the tubule wall, they form the juxtaglomerular apparatus, which monitors the tubule fluid and the arteriole and helps adjust filtration. The JG cells release renin when blood pressure is low. Juxtaglomerular means next to the glomerulus.
notes: Macula densa cells sit in the tubule wall, where the ascending limb of the nephron loop ends and the distal convoluted tubule begins. Pick this location if the question asked where the macula densa is, not the JG cells.

The collecting duct gathers fluid from many nephrons and runs down into the medulla, away from the glomerulus. It is the answer if the question asked which duct receives fluid from many distal tubules.
Correct. The JG cells are modified smooth muscle in the afferent arteriole wall.
The visceral layer of the glomerular capsule is made of podocytes, which wrap the glomerular capillaries. It would be the answer if the question asked where the filtration slits are formed.
questions.answerText: In the wall of the afferent arteriole

questions.q: Near the tip of a renal pyramid, collecting ducts join into larger ducts that open on the renal papilla. What are these larger ducts called?
options: Papillary ducts
Minor calyces
Distal convoluted tubules
Ureters
questions.why: Collecting ducts run down through the renal pyramid and join into larger papillary ducts as they near the tip. The papillary ducts open on the renal papilla, where urine drips out into a minor calyx. The name tells you where they are: papillary ducts are the ducts of the papilla. They are on the lab structure list as the last part of the renal tubule system.
notes: Correct. The papillary ducts carry urine out onto the renal papilla.
The minor calyces are cups, not ducts, and they wrap around the papillae to catch urine. Pick them if the question asked what receives urine as it leaves the papilla.
The distal convoluted tubules are coiled segments of individual nephrons in the cortex. They empty into collecting ducts, so they come before the collecting ducts, not after.
The ureters are the paired tubes that carry urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder, well outside the pyramids. They would be the answer for the tube leaving the kidney at the hilum.

questions.q: What is the microscopic functional unit of the kidney?
options: The renal pyramid
The glomerulus
The nephron
The collecting duct
questions.why: The nephron is the microscopic structure that actually makes urine, so it is the functional unit of the kidney. Each nephron has a renal corpuscle that filters the blood and a renal tubule that processes the filtrate. Each kidney holds about one million of them.
notes: A renal pyramid is a large cone of medullary tissue that you can see without a microscope, and it holds parts of thousands of nephrons. Pick it if the question asked for the cone-shaped masses of the medulla.
The glomerulus is only one part of a nephron, the capillary tuft where blood is filtered. It would be the answer for where filtration happens, not for the whole working unit.
Correct. The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney.
The collecting duct gathers fluid from many nephrons, so it serves many units rather than being one. Choose it if the question asked which duct receives fluid from many nephrons.

questions.q: What is the tuft of capillaries where the blood is filtered?
options: The glomerulus
The peritubular capillaries
The renal tubule
The glomerular capsule
questions.why: The glomerulus is a tuft of leaky, fenestrated capillaries, meaning their walls are full of small pores. Blood enters it through the afferent arteriole, and water and small solutes are pushed out through the pores into the glomerular capsule as filtrate. Blood leaves through the efferent arteriole.
notes: Correct. The glomerulus is the filtering capillary tuft.
The peritubular capillaries are the second capillary bed, wrapping the renal tubules after blood leaves the glomerulus. Choose them if the question asked which capillaries surround the tubules.
The renal tubule is the long tube that processes the filtrate after it leaves the capsule. It would be the answer for the part of the nephron that changes the filtrate into urine.
The glomerular capsule is the cup that surrounds the glomerulus and collects the filtrate, but it is not made of capillaries. Pick it if the question asked what catches the filtrate.

questions.q: What is the cup-shaped structure that surrounds the glomerulus and collects the filtrate?
options: The collecting duct
The renal capsule
The renal pelvis
The glomerular capsule
questions.why: The glomerular capsule, also called Bowman's capsule, is a double-walled cup around the glomerulus. Filtrate pushed out of the glomerular capillaries collects in the capsular space inside it and then flows into the proximal convoluted tubule. The glomerulus and its capsule together make up the renal corpuscle.
notes: The collecting duct gathers fluid from many nephrons far downstream of the glomerulus. Choose it if the question asked what receives fluid from the distal convoluted tubules.

The renal capsule is the fibrous covering of the whole kidney, not a cup around one glomerulus. The similar names cause this mix-up; pick the renal capsule if the question asked about the kidney's outer covering.
The renal pelvis is the funnel-shaped cavity that collects urine from the calyces and passes it to the ureter. It would be the answer for the large collecting space at the center of the kidney.
Correct. The glomerular capsule surrounds the glomerulus and collects the filtrate.

questions.q: The renal corpuscle is made up of which two structures together?
options: A glomerulus enclosed in a glomerular capsule
A renal pyramid and a renal column
An afferent arteriole and an efferent arteriole
A renal tubule and a collecting duct
questions.why: The renal corpuscle is the filtering head of the nephron. It is a glomerulus, the tuft of capillaries where blood is filtered, sitting inside the glomerular (Bowman's) capsule, which catches the filtrate. The rest of the nephron, the renal tubule, carries and processes that filtrate.
notes: Correct. The renal corpuscle is the glomerulus inside its capsule.

Renal pyramids and renal columns are large regions of the kidney visible without a microscope. They would be the answer if the question asked what makes up the medulla and the cortex extensions between it.

The afferent and efferent arterioles carry blood into and out of the glomerulus, so they attach to the corpuscle but are not part of it. Choose them if the question asked which vessels serve the glomerulus.
The renal tubule and the collecting duct carry the filtrate after it leaves the corpuscle. Pick the renal tubule if the question asked for the second main part of the nephron.
questions.answerText: A glomerulus enclosed in a glomerular capsule

questions.q: Which part of the nephron is its filtering head?
options: The renal pelvis
The collecting duct
The renal corpuscle
The renal tubule
questions.why: A nephron has two main parts. The renal corpuscle, a glomerulus inside a glomerular capsule, is the filtering head where fluid is pushed out of the blood. The renal tubule then carries that filtrate and changes it into urine. All the renal corpuscles sit in the cortex.
notes: The renal pelvis is a large collecting cavity at the center of the kidney, not part of any nephron. It would be the answer for the funnel that passes urine to the ureter.
The collecting duct gathers fluid from many nephrons, so it is downstream of them rather than a part of one. Choose it if the question asked which duct receives fluid from many distal tubules.
Correct. The renal corpuscle is the filtering part of the nephron.

The renal tubule is the second main part of the nephron, the long tube that processes the filtrate after it is formed. Pick it if the question asked which part of the nephron carries the filtrate away from the corpuscle.

questions.q: Which segment of the nephron is the U-shaped part that dips down into the medulla?
options: The glomerular capsule
The nephron loop
The distal convoluted tubule
The proximal convoluted tubule
questions.why: The nephron loop, also called the loop of Henle, is the U-shaped segment between the two convoluted tubules. It has a descending limb that runs down into the medulla and an ascending limb that climbs back toward the cortex. In juxtamedullary nephrons the loop reaches deep into the medulla, and in cortical nephrons it barely enters it.
