notes: The glomerular capsule is the cup around the glomerulus at the start of the nephron, not a tubule segment. Choose it if the question asked what collects the filtrate first.
Correct. The nephron loop is the U-shaped segment that dips into the medulla.
The distal convoluted tubule is the second coiled segment, back in the cortex after the loop. It would be the answer for the segment that touches its own glomerulus at the juxtaglomerular apparatus.
The proximal convoluted tubule is the first coiled segment, lying in the cortex right after the capsule. Pick it if the question asked which segment has a brush border of microvilli.

questions.q: Which duct receives fluid from the distal convoluted tubules of many nephrons and carries it down through the pyramid?
options: The nephron loop
The distal convoluted tubule
The ureter
The collecting duct
questions.why: The collecting duct is shared by many nephrons. It receives fluid from their distal convoluted tubules and carries it down through a renal pyramid toward the renal papilla, where it joins into papillary ducts. Because it serves many nephrons, it is the last stage of the tubule system rather than a part of any single nephron.
notes: The nephron loop is the U-shaped segment of a single nephron between the two convoluted tubules. Choose it if the question asked which segment dips into the medulla and back.
The distal convoluted tubule belongs to a single nephron and empties into the collecting duct. Pick it if the question asked which segment comes right after the nephron loop.
The ureter carries urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder, outside the kidney tissue. It would be the answer for the tube that leaves the kidney at the hilum.
Correct. The collecting duct gathers fluid from many nephrons.

questions.q: The proximal convoluted tubule is called proximal because it is the segment closest to which structure?
options: The renal papilla
The collecting duct
The renal hilum
The renal corpuscle
questions.why: Proximal means nearer to the starting point and distal means farther away, the same words used for limbs. For the renal tubule, the starting point is the renal corpuscle. The proximal convoluted tubule begins right at the glomerular capsule, and the distal convoluted tubule comes later, after the nephron loop. Knowing this lets you rebuild the order of the segments.
notes: The renal papilla is the tip of a pyramid where urine drains into a minor calyx, near the end of the path. A segment closest to the papilla would be the papillary duct, not the proximal tubule.
The collecting duct is at the far end of the nephron, after the distal convoluted tubule. The segment closest to it is the distal convoluted tubule, which is the opposite of proximal.
The renal hilum is the notch on the kidney's medial border where vessels and the ureter pass. Tubule names are measured from the renal corpuscle, not from the hilum.
Correct. Proximal means closest to the renal corpuscle, where the tubule begins.

questions.q: Which part of the glomerular capsule wraps directly around the glomerular capillaries?
options: The renal capsule
The capsular space
The parietal layer
The visceral layer
questions.why: The glomerular capsule is a double-walled cup. Its inner, visceral layer is made of podocytes that wrap directly around the glomerular capillaries, and their foot-like processes form filtration slits. The outer, parietal layer forms the wall of the cup, and the capsular space between the two layers collects the filtrate. Visceral layers always cling to the organ, the same pattern as visceral pleura on the lung.
notes: The renal capsule is the fibrous covering of the whole kidney, not part of a nephron. The names are similar; choose it if the question asked what maintains the kidney's shape.
The capsular space is the gap between the two layers where filtrate collects, not a layer itself. It would be the answer for where filtrate gathers before entering the proximal convoluted tubule.
The parietal layer is the outer wall of the cup, made of simple squamous epithelium, and it does not touch the capillaries. Pick it if the question asked for the outer layer of the capsule.
Correct. The visceral layer of podocytes wraps the glomerular capillaries.

questions.q: Which segment is the second coiled part of the renal tubule, coming after the nephron loop?
options: The proximal convoluted tubule
The nephron loop
The distal convoluted tubule
The collecting duct
questions.why: The renal tubule has two coiled (convoluted) segments with the U-shaped nephron loop between them. The distal convoluted tubule is the second coil, lying back in the cortex after the loop climbs out of the medulla. Where the ascending limb ends and the distal convoluted tubule begins, the tubule passes beside its own renal corpuscle, and the macula densa cells there form part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus.
notes: The proximal convoluted tubule is the first coiled segment, right after the glomerular capsule and before the loop. Pick it if the question asked which segment filtrate enters first.
The nephron loop is the U-shaped, uncoiled segment between the two convoluted tubules. It would be the answer for the segment that dips into the medulla.
Correct. The distal convoluted tubule is the second coiled segment.
The collecting duct is not coiled and is shared by many nephrons, coming after the distal convoluted tubule. Choose it if the question asked where the distal tubules drain.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly traces filtrate through the nephron, from where it is captured to the collecting duct?
options: Glomerular capsule, distal convoluted tubule, nephron loop, proximal convoluted tubule, collecting duct
Glomerular capsule, proximal convoluted tubule, nephron loop, distal convoluted tubule, collecting duct
Glomerular capsule, nephron loop, proximal convoluted tubule, distal convoluted tubule, collecting duct
Glomerular capsule, distal convoluted tubule, proximal convoluted tubule, nephron loop, collecting duct
questions.why: Filtrate is captured in the glomerular capsule and flows next into the proximal convoluted tubule, the coil nearest the capsule. It then runs down and back up the nephron loop, through the distal convoluted tubule, and into the collecting duct. The segments are named in the order the filtrate meets them, so proximal comes before the loop and distal comes after it.
notes: This order runs the tubule backward, starting with the distal convoluted tubule. Distal means farther from the capsule, so the distal tubule is the last segment before the collecting duct.
Correct. Capsule, proximal convoluted tubule, nephron loop, distal convoluted tubule, collecting duct.
This order sends filtrate into the nephron loop before the proximal convoluted tubule. The proximal tubule is attached directly to the capsule, so it always comes first.
This order places both coiled segments before the loop. The nephron loop sits between the two convoluted tubules, so the proximal tubule leads into it and the distal tubule follows it.
questions.answerText: Glomerular capsule, proximal convoluted tubule, nephron loop, distal convoluted tubule, collecting duct

questions.q: About how many nephrons does each kidney hold?
options: About one thousand
About one million
About one hundred
About one billion
questions.why: Each kidney holds about one million nephrons, the microscopic functional units that make urine. Their renal corpuscles are packed into the cortex, and their loops and the collecting ducts they drain into fill the pyramids of the medulla. Because each nephron is so small, one kidney can hold that many.
notes: One thousand is far too low. Nephrons are microscopic, so each kidney holds far more of them than students who picture them as visible structures expect.
Correct. Each kidney holds about one million nephrons.
One hundred is far too few. Each kidney holds about ten thousand times that many, because each nephron is microscopic.
One billion overshoots by about a thousand times. Each nephron is built from many cells, so students who think of nephrons as single cells end up with a number that is far too large.

questions.q: Which two main parts make up a nephron?
options: The renal corpuscle and the renal tubule
The afferent and efferent arterioles
The glomerulus and the renal pelvis
The cortex and the medulla
questions.why: A nephron has two main parts. The renal corpuscle (a glomerulus inside a glomerular capsule) filters the blood, and the renal tubule (the proximal convoluted tubule, nephron loop, and distal convoluted tubule) carries the filtrate and turns it into urine. Learning these two parts first makes the smaller pieces easier to place.
notes: Correct. A nephron is a renal corpuscle plus a renal tubule.

The afferent and efferent arterioles carry blood into and out of the glomerulus. They serve the nephron but are blood vessels, so pick them if the question asked which vessels connect to the glomerulus.
The glomerulus is part of the renal corpuscle, but the renal pelvis is a large collecting cavity outside every nephron. Choose the renal pelvis if the question asked what funnels urine to the ureter.
The cortex and medulla are the two tissue regions of the whole kidney, each holding parts of many nephrons. Pick them if the question asked for the regions seen on a kidney section.
questions.answerText: The renal corpuscle and the renal tubule

questions.q: Where does filtrate collect inside the glomerular capsule before it enters the proximal convoluted tubule?
options: The renal pelvis
The minor calyx
The capsular space
The renal sinus
questions.why: The glomerular capsule has an inner visceral layer of podocytes and an outer parietal layer, with the capsular space between them. Fluid filtered out of the glomerulus passes into this space and then flows straight into the proximal convoluted tubule. The capsular space is the first stop in the path of the filtrate.
notes: The renal pelvis is the large funnel at the center of the kidney that passes urine to the ureter, far downstream of any nephron. Pick it if the question asked where the major calyces drain.
The minor calyx is the cup that catches urine from a renal papilla, at the end of the nephron's path rather than the start. Choose it if the question asked what receives urine from the papilla.
Correct. Filtrate collects in the capsular space first.
The renal sinus is the space inside the kidney, deep to the hilum, that holds the renal pelvis, calyces, vessels, and fat. It would be the answer for the cavity that the hilum opens into.

questions.q: What is another name for the glomerular capsule?
options: The renal capsule
The renal corpuscle
Bowman's capsule
The loop of Henle
questions.why: The glomerular capsule is also called Bowman's capsule, after the anatomist who described it. It is the double-walled cup around the glomerulus that collects the filtrate in its capsular space. You will see both names on models and in the lab structure list.
notes: The renal capsule is the fibrous covering of the entire kidney, not the cup around one glomerulus. It would be the answer for the layer that maintains the kidney's shape.
The renal corpuscle is the glomerulus and its capsule together, so it is larger than the capsule alone. Pick it if the question asked for the filtering head of the nephron as a whole.
Correct. Bowman's capsule is the other name for the glomerular capsule.
The loop of Henle is the other name for the nephron loop, the U-shaped segment of the tubule. Choose it if the question asked for another name for the nephron loop.

questions.q: Which segment of the renal tubule is lined with a brush border of microvilli?
options: The proximal convoluted tubule
The distal convoluted tubule
The nephron loop
The collecting duct
questions.why: The proximal convoluted tubule is the first coiled segment of the renal tubule, and its cells carry a dense brush border of microvilli on the side facing the filtrate. Microvilli are tiny finger-like folds of the cell membrane that add surface area. This is one of the features that lets you tell the proximal tubule from the distal tubule on a slide.
notes: Correct. The proximal convoluted tubule has the brush border of microvilli.

The distal convoluted tubule is the second coiled segment, and its cells have few microvilli, so it has no brush border. Pick it if the question asked which coiled segment comes after the nephron loop.
The nephron loop is the U-shaped segment that dips into the medulla, not the coiled segment with the brush border. It would be the answer for the segment with a descending and an ascending limb.
The collecting duct gathers fluid from many nephrons and is not lined by a brush border. Choose it if the question asked which duct receives fluid from many distal tubules.

questions.q: What is another name for the nephron loop?
options: The renal pelvis
The loop of Henle
Bowman's capsule
The collecting duct
questions.why: The nephron loop is also called the loop of Henle, after the anatomist who described it. It is the U-shaped segment between the proximal and distal convoluted tubules, with a descending limb that runs down into the medulla and an ascending limb that returns toward the cortex. Both limbs are on the lab structure list.
notes: The renal pelvis is the funnel-shaped collecting cavity at the center of the kidney. Pick it if the question asked what passes urine into the ureter.
Correct. The nephron loop is also called the loop of Henle.
Bowman's capsule is the other name for the glomerular capsule, the cup around the glomerulus. Choose it if the question asked for another name for the glomerular capsule.
The collecting duct is a shared duct that receives fluid from many nephrons, not a loop. It would be the answer for where the distal convoluted tubules drain.

questions.q: Which cells form the inner, visceral layer of the glomerular capsule?
options: Podocytes
Juxtaglomerular cells
Macula densa cells
Endothelial cells
questions.why: Podocytes are the cells of the visceral layer of the glomerular capsule. They wrap around the glomerular capillaries with foot-like processes, and the narrow gaps between those processes are the filtration slits. The name means foot cells, which describes their shape.
notes: Correct. Podocytes form the visceral layer of the capsule.

Juxtaglomerular cells are modified smooth muscle cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole that release renin. Pick them if the question asked which cells of the juxtaglomerular apparatus release renin.

Macula densa cells are tubule cells of the juxtaglomerular apparatus, where the ascending limb meets the distal convoluted tubule, and they sense the sodium chloride in the fluid. They would be the answer for the tubule cells of the juxtaglomerular apparatus.

Endothelial cells line the glomerular capillaries themselves, forming the fenestrated endothelium with its pores. Choose them if the question asked which layer of the filtration membrane blocks blood cells.

questions.q: Which type of nephron makes up about 85 percent of all nephrons?
options: Medullary nephrons
Papillary nephrons
Cortical nephrons
Juxtamedullary nephrons
questions.why: Cortical nephrons make up about 85 percent of nephrons. They have short loops that barely enter the medulla and are wrapped by peritubular capillaries. The other roughly 15 percent are juxtamedullary nephrons, whose long loops reach deep into the medulla.
notes: There is no nephron type called medullary. All renal corpuscles sit in the cortex, so this name comes from mixing up where the loops reach with where the nephrons are classified.
There is no nephron type called papillary; the papilla is the tip of a renal pyramid, where papillary ducts open. This choice borrows a real kidney word for a nephron type that does not exist.
Correct. Cortical nephrons are about 85 percent of nephrons.
Juxtamedullary nephrons are the minority, about 15 percent, with long loops served by the vasa recta. Pick them if the question asked which nephrons concentrate the urine.

questions.q: Which cells of the juxtaglomerular apparatus release renin when blood pressure is low?
options: The proximal tubule cells
The juxtaglomerular cells
The macula densa cells
The podocytes
questions.why: The juxtaglomerular (granular) cells are modified smooth muscle cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole. Their granules hold the enzyme renin, which they release when blood pressure is low. They sit where the tubule passes beside its own renal corpuscle, close to the macula densa cells in the tubule wall.
notes: Proximal tubule cells line the first coiled segment and carry a brush border of microvilli. They are not part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus; choose them if the question asked which segment has a brush border.
Correct. The juxtaglomerular cells release renin.

The macula densa cells are the tubule half of the juxtaglomerular apparatus, where the ascending limb meets the distal convoluted tubule. They sense the sodium chloride level of the fluid, so pick them for the sensing cells.
Podocytes form the visceral layer of the glomerular capsule and create the filtration slits. They would be the answer for the cells that wrap the glomerular capillaries.

questions.q: Which nephrons have long loops that reach deep into the medulla, and what share of nephrons are they?
options: Cortical nephrons, about 85 percent of nephrons
Juxtamedullary nephrons, about 85 percent of nephrons
Juxtamedullary nephrons, about 15 percent of nephrons
Cortical nephrons, about 15 percent of nephrons
questions.why: Juxtamedullary nephrons have their renal corpuscles in the cortex right next to the medulla, and their long loops reach deep into the medulla, where they are served by the vasa recta. They make up only about 15 percent of nephrons, but they are the ones that concentrate the urine. The other 85 percent are cortical nephrons with short loops.
notes: Cortical nephrons are the 85 percent, but they have short loops that barely enter the medulla. Pick this pairing if the question asked about the common short-looped nephrons.
Juxtamedullary is the right type, but they are the minority, not the majority. The 85 percent figure belongs to cortical nephrons.
Correct. Juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops and are about 15 percent of nephrons.
This pairing gives the cortical nephrons the juxtamedullary share. Cortical nephrons are the large majority with short loops, so both parts of this choice are mixed up.
questions.answerText: Juxtamedullary nephrons, about 15 percent of nephrons

questions.q: Which layer of the filtration membrane lets plasma pass but blocks blood cells?
options: The fenestrated endothelium
The slit membranes
The parietal layer of the glomerular capsule
The basement membrane
questions.why: Blood is filtered across a three-layer membrane. The first layer is the fenestrated endothelium, the wall of the glomerular capillary, which is full of pores (fenestrations means windows). The pores are large enough for plasma to pass but too small for blood cells, so the cells stay in the blood. The basement membrane and slit membranes then hold back proteins.
notes: Correct. The fenestrated endothelium blocks blood cells but lets plasma through.

The slit membranes bridge the filtration slits between podocyte feet and hold back most of the smaller proteins that get past the basement membrane. They would be the answer for the last layer of the filtration membrane.

The parietal layer is the outer wall of the capsule, made of simple squamous epithelium, and filtrate never has to cross it. Choose it if the question asked for the outer layer of the glomerular capsule.
The basement membrane is the middle layer, between the capillary and the podocytes, and it blocks large plasma proteins. Pick it if the question asked which layer holds back large proteins.

questions.q: Blood has just been filtered in the glomerulus. Which segment of the renal tubule does the filtrate enter first?
options: The proximal convoluted tubule
The collecting duct
The distal convoluted tubule
The nephron loop
questions.why: Filtrate collects first in the capsular space of the glomerular capsule, and the capsule opens directly into the proximal convoluted tubule. Proximal means closest, and this coil is the segment closest to the renal corpuscle. From there the filtrate moves on to the nephron loop, the distal convoluted tubule, and the collecting duct.
notes: Correct. Filtrate enters the proximal convoluted tubule first.
The collecting duct is the last stage, gathering fluid from many nephrons after their distal tubules. It would be the answer for where the distal convoluted tubule drains.
The distal convoluted tubule is the second coiled segment, after the nephron loop. Pick it if the question asked where filtrate goes after leaving the loop.
The nephron loop comes after the proximal tubule, not before it. Choose it if the question asked which U-shaped segment dips into the medulla.

questions.q: The proximal convoluted tubule is lined with a brush border of microvilli. How does this feature suit its job?
options: It forms filtration slits that hold back blood proteins
It adds surface area for reclaiming water and nutrients from the filtrate
It lets the tubule stretch as urine is stored inside it
It sweeps the filtrate along the length of the tubule the way cilia do
questions.why: The glomerulus filters far more fluid than the body can afford to lose, including water, glucose, and ions. The proximal convoluted tubule is the first place that fluid is reclaimed and returned to the blood. Microvilli are tiny finger-like folds of the cell membrane, and a dense brush border of them greatly increases the surface area for this reabsorption, the same design used by the lining of the small intestine.
notes: Filtration slits are formed by podocytes in the visceral layer of the glomerular capsule, not by tubule cells. Choose podocytes if the question asked which cells form the filtration slits.
Correct. The brush border increases surface area for reabsorption.

Stretching to store urine is the job of transitional epithelium in the bladder. The proximal tubule does not store urine, so pick transitional epithelium if the question asked about a lining that stretches.
Microvilli do not move; cilia are the longer, moving projections that sweep material along, as in the airways. Pick cilia if the question asked how mucus is moved up the trachea.
questions.answerText: It adds surface area for reclaiming water and nutrients from the filtrate

questions.q: Healthy urine contains almost no protein, even though plasma is full of large proteins. Which layer of the filtration membrane blocks large plasma proteins?
options: The renal capsule
The parietal layer of the glomerular capsule
The fenestrated endothelium
The basement membrane
questions.why: The filtration membrane has three layers, and each one holds back something different. The fenestrated endothelium blocks blood cells, the basement membrane between the capillary and the podocytes blocks large plasma proteins, and the filtration slits of the podocytes hold back most of the smaller proteins that get past it. Because large proteins stop at the basement membrane, they stay in the blood instead of entering the filtrate.
notes: The renal capsule is the fibrous covering of the whole kidney, far from the glomerulus. It would be the answer if the question asked what maintains the kidney's shape.

The parietal layer is the outer wall of the capsule, made of simple squamous epithelium, and it is not part of the filtration membrane. Choose it if the question asked for the outer layer of the glomerular capsule.

The fenestrated endothelium is the pored wall of the glomerular capillary, and its pores block blood cells rather than proteins. Pick it if the question asked which layer keeps blood cells out of the filtrate.
Correct. The basement membrane blocks large plasma proteins.

questions.q: Which layer of the filtration membrane holds back most of the smaller proteins that get past the basement membrane?
options: The capsular space
The basement membrane
The filtration slits of the podocytes
The fenestrated endothelium
questions.why: The filtration slits are the narrow gaps between the foot-like extensions of the podocytes, and thin slit membranes bridge them. They are the last of the three layers that filtrate crosses, and they hold back most of the smaller proteins that got past the basement membrane. Each layer catches something smaller than the one before it: blood cells at the endothelium, large proteins at the basement membrane, and smaller proteins at the slits.
notes: The capsular space is where filtrate collects after crossing all three layers, not a barrier itself. Choose it if the question asked where filtrate gathers before entering the proximal convoluted tubule.

The basement membrane is the middle layer, between the capillary and the podocytes, and it holds back large plasma proteins. The smaller proteins in this question have already passed it, so pick it if the question asked which layer stops the large proteins.
Correct. The filtration slits between podocyte feet, bridged by thin slit membranes, hold back most of the smaller proteins.
The fenestrated endothelium is the pored capillary wall, the first layer of the filtration membrane, and it blocks blood cells. Pick it if the question asked which layer keeps cells in the blood.
questions.answerText: The filtration slits of the podocytes

questions.q: Which cells of the juxtaglomerular apparatus sit in the tubule wall, where the ascending limb meets the distal convoluted tubule, and sense the sodium chloride in the fluid?
options: The macula densa cells
The podocytes
The juxtaglomerular cells
The endothelial cells
questions.why: The juxtaglomerular apparatus forms where the tubule passes beside the afferent and efferent arterioles of its own renal corpuscle. On the tubule side, where the ascending limb ends and the distal convoluted tubule begins, a patch of tall, tightly packed cells called the macula densa senses the sodium chloride level of the fluid passing by. Macula densa means dense spot, which describes how crowded these cells look. On the arteriole side, the juxtaglomerular cells release renin.
notes: Correct. The macula densa cells sit in the tubule wall at that junction and sense the sodium chloride level.
Podocytes form the visceral layer of the glomerular capsule and create the filtration slits. They would be the answer for the cells that wrap the glomerular capillaries.
The juxtaglomerular (granular) cells are the arteriole half of the apparatus, modified smooth muscle in the afferent arteriole wall. Pick them if the question asked which cells release renin.
Endothelial cells line the glomerular capillaries as the fenestrated endothelium. Choose them if the question asked which layer of the filtration membrane blocks blood cells.

questions.q: What is the microscopic functional unit of the kidney, the structure that actually makes urine?
options: The renal corpuscle
The nephron
The collecting duct
The renal pyramid
questions.why: The nephron is the microscopic functional unit of the kidney, and each kidney holds about one million of them. A nephron filters blood at its renal corpuscle and then adjusts that filtrate along its renal tubule, turning it into urine. All the larger kidney regions are simply organized groups of nephrons and the vessels and ducts that serve them.
notes: The renal corpuscle is only the filtering head of a nephron, the glomerulus inside its capsule. It filters blood but does not finish making urine, so choose it if the question asked where filtration happens.
Correct. The nephron filters the blood and processes the filtrate into urine.

A collecting duct gathers fluid from many nephrons and carries it toward the papilla. It is shared by several nephrons rather than being the unit itself; pick it if the question asked what drains several nephrons.

A renal pyramid is a visible cone of medulla holding parts of many nephrons and collecting ducts. It is far too large to be a microscopic unit; pick it if the question asked about the cone-shaped regions of the medulla.

questions.q: What are the two main parts of a nephron?
options: The afferent and efferent arterioles
The glomerulus and the collecting duct
The renal cortex and the renal medulla
The renal corpuscle and the renal tubule
questions.why: A nephron has two main parts. The renal corpuscle is the filtering head, made of the glomerulus (a capillary tuft) inside the glomerular capsule. The renal tubule is the long tube that follows, made of the proximal convoluted tubule, the nephron loop, and the distal convoluted tubule, where the filtrate is processed into urine.
notes: The afferent and efferent arterioles are the blood vessels that carry blood into and out of the glomerulus. They serve the nephron but are not part of it; choose them if the question asked which vessels supply the glomerulus.

The glomerulus is only part of the renal corpuscle, and the collecting duct is shared by many nephrons rather than belonging to one. This pairing mixes a piece of one part with a structure outside the nephron.
The cortex and medulla are the two regions of the whole kidney, and each nephron stretches across them. Pick them if the question asked for the outer and inner regions of kidney tissue.
Correct. Every nephron is a renal corpuscle followed by a renal tubule.
questions.answerText: The renal corpuscle and the renal tubule

questions.q: Which structure is the tuft of leaky, fenestrated capillaries where blood is filtered in the kidney?
options: The vasa recta
The peritubular capillaries
The glomerular capsule
The glomerulus
questions.why: The glomerulus is a ball of capillaries inside the glomerular capsule. Its walls are fenestrated, meaning they are full of small pores, which lets water and small solutes pass out of the blood easily. This makes the glomerulus the site of filtration, the first step in making urine.
notes: The vasa recta are long, straight capillaries that run beside the loops of juxtamedullary nephrons deep in the medulla. Pick them if the question asked which vessels follow the long nephron loops.

The peritubular capillaries come after the glomerulus and wrap around the renal tubules, where they take back useful substances. Pick them if the question asked which capillaries surround the tubules of cortical nephrons.

The glomerular capsule is the cup that surrounds the glomerulus and collects the filtrate. It is not made of capillaries; choose it if the question asked which structure catches the fluid that leaves the blood.
Correct. The glomerulus is the porous capillary tuft where blood is filtered.

questions.q: In the renal tubule, which segment does the filtrate enter right after it leaves the nephron loop?
options: The distal convoluted tubule
The glomerular capsule
The collecting duct
The proximal convoluted tubule
questions.why: The renal tubule segments are named in the order the filtrate meets them. After the glomerular capsule comes the proximal convoluted tubule, then the U-shaped nephron loop, then the distal convoluted tubule. Proximal means nearer the start of the tubule and distal means farther away, so the distal tubule comes after the loop.
notes: Correct. The distal convoluted tubule follows the ascending limb of the nephron loop.
The glomerular capsule is where filtrate first collects, before any tubule segment. It would be the answer if the question asked where the filtrate starts.
The collecting duct comes after the distal convoluted tubule and gathers fluid from many nephrons. It is one step too far; choose it if the question asked where the distal tubule drains.

The proximal convoluted tubule is the first coiled segment, right after the glomerular capsule and before the loop. Pick it if the question asked which segment receives filtrate straight from the capsule.

questions.q: Which list traces filtrate from the glomerulus through the nephron to the collecting duct?
options: Glomerular capsule, proximal convoluted tubule, distal convoluted tubule, nephron loop, collecting duct
Glomerular capsule, proximal convoluted tubule, nephron loop, distal convoluted tubule, collecting duct
Glomerular capsule, distal convoluted tubule, nephron loop, proximal convoluted tubule, collecting duct
Glomerular capsule, nephron loop, proximal convoluted tubule, distal convoluted tubule, collecting duct
questions.why: Filtrate leaves the glomerulus and collects in the capsular space of the glomerular capsule. It then flows through the proximal convoluted tubule, down and back up the nephron loop (the loop of Henle), and through the distal convoluted tubule. Finally the distal tubule drains into a collecting duct that serves many nephrons.
notes: This puts both coiled tubules before the loop. The nephron loop sits between them, linking the proximal tubule to the distal tubule.
Correct. The segments are named in the order the filtrate meets them.
This swaps the proximal and distal tubules. Proximal means near the start, so the proximal convoluted tubule must come right after the capsule; students pick this when they mix up the two terms.
This sends filtrate into the loop straight from the capsule. The proximal convoluted tubule always comes first, before the loop dips into the medulla.
questions.answerText: Glomerular capsule, proximal convoluted tubule, nephron loop, distal convoluted tubule, collecting duct

questions.q: What is the juxtaglomerular apparatus?
options: Where the collecting duct opens at the tip of a renal papilla
Where the distal tubule meets its own corpuscle's arterioles
Where the proximal tubule leaves its own glomerular capsule
Where a long nephron loop dips down beside the vasa recta
questions.why: Juxtaglomerular means next to the glomerulus. After the nephron loop rises back toward the cortex, the tubule passes right beside the afferent and efferent arterioles of its own renal corpuscle, where the ascending limb ends and the distal convoluted tubule begins. At that contact point, the macula densa cells in the tubule wall and the juxtaglomerular cells in the arteriole wall together form the juxtaglomerular apparatus, which monitors the tubule fluid and the arteriole and helps adjust filtration.
notes: Collecting ducts end as papillary ducts at the renal papilla, deep in the medulla and far from any glomerulus. Choose this if the question asked where urine leaves the pyramid.
Correct. The juxtaglomerular apparatus is the contact point between the distal tubule and its own arterioles.

The proximal convoluted tubule begins where it leaves the glomerular capsule, but that junction has no special name and is not where the tubule touches the arterioles. Pick the proximal tubule if the question asked which segment receives filtrate straight from the capsule.
Long nephron loops run beside the vasa recta in the medulla, but that is not next to the glomerulus. Pick this if the question asked which vessels follow the loops of juxtamedullary nephrons.
questions.answerText: Where the distal tubule meets its own corpuscle's arterioles

questions.q: Which list names the three layers of the filtration membrane, from the blood side to the capsule side?
options: Fenestrated endothelium, basement membrane, podocyte slit membranes
Renal capsule, adipose capsule, renal fascia
Basement membrane, fenestrated endothelium, podocyte slit membranes
Parietal capsule layer, capsular space, visceral capsule layer
questions.why: Blood in the glomerulus is filtered across three layers. First is the fenestrated endothelium, the pored wall of the capillary, which blocks blood cells. Next is the basement membrane, which blocks large plasma proteins. Last are the filtration slits between the feet of the podocytes, the cells of the capsule's inner layer, which hold back most of the smaller proteins.
notes: Correct. Fluid crosses the pored capillary wall, then the basement membrane, then the slits between podocytes.
These are the three tissue layers around the whole kidney, from inner to outer. Choose this list if the question asked what surrounds and anchors the kidney.

This puts the basement membrane first, but the capillary wall itself, the fenestrated endothelium, is the first layer the blood touches. The basement membrane lies between the capillary and the podocytes.

These are the parts of the glomerular capsule, which catches the filtrate. Only the visceral layer, made of podocytes, contributes to the filtration membrane; pick this list if the question asked for the parts of the capsule.
questions.answerText: Fenestrated endothelium, basement membrane, podocyte slit membranes

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the macula densa and the juxtaglomerular cells?
options: Both cell types sit in the glomerulus and filter the blood as podocytes do
Macula densa cells in the tubule wall sense the fluid; juxtaglomerular cells release renin
Macula densa cells line the afferent arteriole and release renin; juxtaglomerular cells sense the filtrate
Macula densa cells form the filtration slits; juxtaglomerular cells line the collecting duct
questions.why: The macula densa is a patch of tightly packed cells in the tubule wall, where the ascending limb meets the distal convoluted tubule, and it senses the sodium chloride level of the fluid passing by. The juxtaglomerular cells are modified smooth muscle cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole, and they release the enzyme renin when blood pressure is low. One is a tubule cell that senses, and the other is a vessel cell that releases an enzyme.
notes: Neither cell type is part of the filtration membrane. Filtering happens across the glomerular capillary wall, basement membrane, and podocyte slits, which would be the answer if the question asked about the filter itself.
Correct. The macula densa senses the fluid in the tubule, and the juxtaglomerular cells release renin.
This swaps the two cell types. The renin-releasing cells are the juxtaglomerular cells in the arteriole wall, and the macula densa is the tubule patch that senses the fluid.
The filtration slits are formed by podocytes in the glomerular capsule, and neither cell type lines the collecting duct. Pick podocytes if the question asked which cells form the filtration slits.
questions.answerText: Macula densa cells in the tubule wall sense the fluid; juxtaglomerular cells release renin

questions.q: Where does the renal corpuscle of a cortical nephron sit?
options: In the outer part of the cortex
In the deep cortex, next to the medulla
In the medulla, close to the renal papilla
In the medulla, beside the vasa recta
questions.why: Cortical nephrons have their renal corpuscles in the outer part of the cortex, and their short loops barely dip into the outer medulla. Juxtamedullary nephrons are the ones whose corpuscles sit in the deepest part of the cortex, right next to the medulla.
notes: Correct. The renal corpuscle of a cortical nephron sits in the outer part of the cortex.
The deepest part of the cortex, next to the medulla, is where juxtamedullary renal corpuscles sit. Juxta means next to.
Renal corpuscles sit in the cortex, not the medulla. Only the long loops of juxtamedullary nephrons reach deep, close to the renal papilla.
The vasa recta run deep in the medulla beside the long loops of juxtamedullary nephrons. Renal corpuscles sit in the cortex.
questions.answerText: In the outer part of the cortex

questions.q: The word juxtamedullary describes where these nephrons begin. What does the name tell you?
options: Their renal corpuscles sit next to the medulla
Their renal corpuscles sit inside the medulla
Their renal corpuscles sit in the outer cortex
They make up about 85 percent of all nephrons
questions.why: Juxta means next to, so a juxtamedullary nephron has its renal corpuscle in the deepest part of the cortex, right next to the medulla. From there, its long loop reaches deep into the medulla, close to the renal papilla.
notes: Correct. Juxta means next to, so the renal corpuscle sits in the deep cortex right next to the medulla.
Juxta means next to, not inside. The renal corpuscle stays in the cortex, at its deepest part beside the medulla.
Renal corpuscles in the outer cortex belong to cortical nephrons, the type with short loops.
About 85 percent is the share of cortical nephrons. Juxtamedullary nephrons are about 15 percent, and the name says nothing about numbers.
questions.answerText: Their renal corpuscles sit next to the medulla

questions.q: Why do juxtamedullary nephrons have the vasa recta running beside their loops, instead of only a capillary mesh in the cortex?
options: Their loops stay in the cortex, so they need straight capillaries to hold them
The vasa recta come straight from the renal papilla to supply the corpuscle
Their loops reach deep into the medulla, so the capillaries must reach deep too
Their corpuscles sit in the outer cortex, far from the peritubular capillaries
questions.why: Juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops that reach deep into the medulla, close to the renal papilla. A mesh that wraps the tubules in the cortex would not follow them, so long, straight capillaries, the vasa recta, run down and back up beside the loops. Cortical nephrons, with their short loops, are wrapped by the peritubular capillaries.
notes: Juxtamedullary loops do not stay in the cortex. They are long and reach deep into the medulla, which is why their capillaries must be long too.
The vasa recta are supplied by efferent arterioles leaving the glomeruli, not by the renal papilla.
Correct. The long loops reach deep into the medulla, so the straight vasa recta run deep beside them.
Juxtamedullary corpuscles sit in the deep cortex, next to the medulla. Corpuscles in the outer cortex belong to cortical nephrons.
questions.answerText: Their loops reach deep into the medulla, so the capillaries must reach deep too

questions.q: Which capillary bed wraps around the tubules of cortical nephrons in the cortex?
options: The peritubular capillaries
The straight vasa recta
The glomerular capillaries
The arcuate arteries and veins
questions.why: Cortical nephrons have short loops that stay mostly in the cortex. Their tubules are wrapped by the peritubular capillaries, a mesh of capillaries in the cortex. The long straight vasa recta belong instead to the deep loops of juxtamedullary nephrons.
notes: Correct. The peritubular capillaries form a mesh around the tubules in the cortex, the bed that runs with cortical nephrons.

The vasa recta are the long straight capillaries that run deep into the medulla beside the long loops of juxtamedullary nephrons. Cortical nephrons have short loops, so their bed is the peritubular mesh.
The glomerulus is the first capillary bed, where blood is filtered inside the renal corpuscle. The bed around the tubules is the second bed, which comes after the efferent arteriole.
The arcuate arteries and veins are not capillaries. They arch over the bases of the pyramids at the cortex and medulla border, well upstream of the beds that surround the tubules.

questions.q: Which vessels carry blood into both the peritubular capillaries and the vasa recta?
options: The interlobar veins
The efferent arterioles
The afferent arterioles
The segmental arteries
questions.why: Blood leaves each glomerulus through an efferent arteriole. Those efferent arterioles then supply the second capillary bed, the peritubular capillaries around cortical tubules and the vasa recta beside the long juxtamedullary loops. This is why the kidney has two capillary beds in a row, with an arteriole between them.
notes: Interlobar veins run down through the renal columns carrying blood out of the kidney. Veins drain capillary beds; they do not supply them.
Correct. Both capillary beds around the tubules are supplied by efferent arterioles leaving the glomeruli.
Afferent arterioles carry blood into the glomerulus, the first capillary bed. The beds around the tubules come after the glomerulus, so they are fed by the efferent arterioles.
Segmental arteries are branches of the renal artery in the renal sinus, near the start of the chain. Several more arteries and the glomerulus come before the beds around the tubules.

questions.q: A slide shows a renal corpuscle in the outer cortex, just under the renal capsule. How far will its nephron loop reach, and which capillaries will surround its tubule?
options: Deep into the medulla, with the vasa recta beside it
Deep into the medulla, with peritubular capillaries
Barely into the medulla, with the vasa recta beside it
Barely into the medulla, with peritubular capillaries
questions.why: Where the renal corpuscle sits tells you the nephron type. A corpuscle in the outer cortex marks a cortical nephron, which makes up about 85 percent of nephrons. Its loop is short and barely dips into the outer medulla, and its tubule is wrapped by the peritubular capillaries in the cortex.
notes: This describes a juxtamedullary nephron, whose corpuscle sits in the deepest cortex next to the medulla. A corpuscle just under the capsule belongs to a cortical nephron.
A long loop that reaches deep into the medulla belongs to a juxtamedullary nephron, not one starting in the outer cortex. Those long loops are paired with the vasa recta.
The short loop is right, but the vasa recta follow the long loops of juxtamedullary nephrons deep into the medulla. A short cortical loop is served by the peritubular capillaries.
Correct. A corpuscle in the outer cortex belongs to a cortical nephron, which has a short loop and is wrapped by peritubular capillaries.
questions.answerText: Barely into the medulla, with peritubular capillaries

questions.q: A disease mainly destroys the nephrons whose loops reach deep into the medulla. About what share of nephrons is affected, and which capillary bed loses the loops it runs beside?
options: About 85 percent, and the peritubular capillaries
About 85 percent, and the vasa recta
About 15 percent, and the vasa recta
About 15 percent, and the peritubular capillaries
questions.why: Nephrons with long loops reaching deep into the medulla are juxtamedullary nephrons. They make up about 15 percent of all nephrons, and their corpuscles sit in the deep cortex next to the medulla. The vasa recta, long straight capillaries, run down and back up beside these loops, so those are the vessels paired with the lost loops.
notes: This describes cortical nephrons, the majority, with short loops and peritubular capillaries. The question asks about the deep loops of juxtamedullary nephrons.
The vasa recta are right, but about 85 percent is the share of cortical nephrons, the ones with short loops. Juxtamedullary nephrons are the smaller group.
Correct. Long loops belong to juxtamedullary nephrons, about 15 percent of the total, and the vasa recta run beside them.
The share is right, but the peritubular capillaries wrap tubules in the cortex, the bed that goes with cortical nephrons. Deep loops are paired with the vasa recta.
questions.answerText: About 15 percent, and the vasa recta

questions.q: A cortex slide shows a patch of tall, crowded cells in a tubule wall pressed against the arterioles of its own renal corpuscle. Where in the nephron is this patch, and what do these cells sense?
options: In the glomerular capsule; they form filtration slits
In the afferent arteriole wall; they release renin
In the proximal convoluted tubule; they sense blood pressure
At the end of the ascending limb; they sense sodium chloride
questions.why: The tubule passes beside its own renal corpuscle between the afferent and efferent arterioles, forming the juxtaglomerular apparatus. The patch of tall, closely packed tubule cells there is the macula densa, which means dense spot. It sits where the ascending limb of the loop ends and the distal convoluted tubule begins, and its cells sense the sodium chloride in the passing fluid.
notes: Filtration slits are the gaps between podocyte feet on the glomerulus, part of the filtration membrane. The crowded cells in a tubule wall beside the arterioles are the macula densa.
The JG (granular) cells sit mostly in the afferent arteriole wall and release renin. The patch described here is in the tubule wall, which makes it the macula densa.

The macula densa is at the start of the distal convoluted tubule, after the loop has climbed back to the cortex. Sensing low blood pressure and releasing renin is the job of the JG cells in the arteriole.
Correct. Tall, crowded tubule cells beside the arterioles are the macula densa, at the end of the ascending limb, and they sense sodium chloride.
questions.answerText: At the end of the ascending limb; they sense sodium chloride

questions.q: A particle in glomerular blood slips through the pores of the capillary wall but is stopped at the very next layer. What kind of particle is it most likely, and which layer stopped it?
options: A large plasma protein, stopped by the basement membrane
A blood cell, stopped by the basement membrane
Glucose, stopped by the filtration slits
A smaller protein, stopped by the fenestrated endothelium
questions.why: The filtration membrane has three layers in a set order from the blood side: the fenestrated endothelium, the basement membrane, and the filtration slits of the podocytes. Each one holds back something smaller than the layer before it. A particle that passes the pores but stops at the next layer was stopped by the basement membrane, which holds back large plasma proteins.
notes: Correct. The basement membrane is the layer after the fenestrated endothelium, and it holds back large plasma proteins.
Blood cells and platelets are held back by the first layer, the fenestrated endothelium. A blood cell would not get through the capillary pores in the first place.
Glucose is a small dissolved substance that passes all three layers and becomes part of the filtrate. The filtration slits are also the third layer, not the one right after the pores.
The fenestrated endothelium is the pored layer the particle already passed. Smaller proteins that get past the basement membrane are held back by the filtration slits.
questions.answerText: A large plasma protein, stopped by the basement membrane

questions.q: In a kidney disease, the podocyte feet flatten and the filtration slits are lost, while the endothelium and basement membrane stay intact. What would start to appear in the filtrate?
options: Nothing new, since every protein is stopped earlier
Smaller proteins that pass the basement membrane
Red blood cells and platelets from the blood
Large plasma proteins from the blood plasma
questions.why: Each layer of the filtration membrane holds back a different size of particle: the fenestrated endothelium stops blood cells, the basement membrane stops large plasma proteins, and the filtration slits between podocyte feet stop most of the smaller proteins. If only the slits are lost, the first two layers still do their jobs. What gets through is the smaller protein the slits used to catch, which is one way protein ends up in the urine.
notes: The basement membrane stops large plasma proteins, but smaller proteins get past it. Those smaller proteins are what the missing slits used to catch.
Correct. The filtration slits hold back the smaller proteins that get past the basement membrane, so losing the slits lets those proteins through.
Blood cells and platelets are held back by the fenestrated endothelium, which is still intact here. Losing the slits would not let cells through.
Large plasma proteins are held back by the basement membrane, which is still intact. They never reach the slits, so losing the slits does not release them.
questions.answerText: Smaller proteins that pass the basement membrane

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Which pairing of a urinary organ with its job is correct?
options: Kidney: filters the blood and forms urine
Urethra: carries urine from the kidney to the bladder
Urinary bladder: carries urine out of the body
Ureter: stores urine until it is released
questions.why: The kidneys are the working organs of the urinary system. They filter wastes out of the blood and form urine. The other three organs only move and hold that urine: the ureters carry it down to the bladder, the bladder stores it, and the urethra carries it to the outside of the body.
notes: Correct. Filtering the blood and forming urine is the kidney's job; the rest of the system carries and stores the urine.
This pairing describes the ureter, not the urethra. The urethra is the single tube from the bladder to the outside, so match it with carrying urine out of the body.
This pairing gives the bladder the urethra's job. The urinary bladder is the muscular sac that stores urine, and it would be the right match for storage.
This pairing gives the ureter the bladder's job. The ureters are paired tubes that carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder, so match the ureter with transporting urine to the bladder.
questions.answerText: Kidney: filters the blood and forms urine

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Fluid leaves the distal convoluted tubule. Which sequence correctly traces it to the minor calyx?
options: Collecting duct, papillary duct, renal papilla, minor calyx
Collecting duct, renal papilla, papillary duct, minor calyx
Papillary duct, collecting duct, renal papilla, minor calyx
Collecting duct, papillary duct, major calyx, minor calyx
questions.why: The distal convoluted tubules of many nephrons drain into a collecting duct, which runs down through a renal pyramid. Near the tip of the pyramid, collecting ducts join into larger papillary ducts that open on the renal papilla. From there the urine drips into a minor calyx, the cup that fits around each papilla. The ducts get larger and fewer as you move toward the calyx.
notes: Correct. Collecting duct, then papillary duct, then out at the renal papilla into a minor calyx.
The papillary duct opens on the renal papilla, so it comes before the papilla, not after. The papilla is the tip of the pyramid where urine leaves the ducts.
This order puts the papillary duct first. Papillary ducts are formed when collecting ducts join near the papilla, so the collecting duct has to come before them.
This order sends urine to the major calyx before the minor calyx. Minor calyces receive urine from the papillae first and then join to form the major calyces.
questions.answerText: Collecting duct, papillary duct, renal papilla, minor calyx

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Which epithelium lines the inside of the ureter?
options: Transitional epithelium
Simple columnar epithelium
Simple cuboidal epithelium
Stratified squamous epithelium
questions.why: The ureter is lined by transitional epithelium, also called urothelium, the same stretchy lining found in the urinary bladder. Its cells can change from rounded to flattened as the wall stretches, which suits a tube that widens as each wave of urine passes. Beneath the lining are a lamina propria, a layer of smooth muscle that produces peristalsis, and an outer adventitia.
notes: Correct. Transitional epithelium lines the ureter and lets it stretch.
Simple columnar epithelium lines the stomach and intestines, where it absorbs and secretes. Pick it if the question were about the lining of the digestive tract.
Simple cuboidal epithelium lines the renal tubules inside the kidney. Choose it if the question asked about the wall of the proximal or distal convoluted tubule.
Stratified squamous epithelium protects surfaces that take abrasion, such as the mouth, esophagus, and skin. It would be the answer for the lining of the esophagus, not a stretching urine tube.

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the detrusor muscle?
options: Smooth muscle in the bladder wall that contracts to empty the bladder
Smooth muscle in the ureter wall that pushes urine to the bladder
Skeletal muscle around the urethra that gives voluntary control
A ring of smooth muscle that keeps the bladder outlet closed
questions.why: The detrusor muscle is the thick smooth muscle layer of the urinary bladder wall. When it contracts, it squeezes the bladder and pushes urine out into the urethra. Because it is smooth muscle, it works involuntarily, while conscious control of urination comes from the external urethral sphincter.
notes: Correct. The detrusor is the smooth muscle of the bladder wall that empties the bladder.
This describes the muscle layer of the ureter, which moves urine to the bladder by peristalsis. Choose it if the question asked how urine travels from the kidney to the bladder.
This describes the external urethral sphincter, the voluntary skeletal muscle ring that gives conscious control over urination. Pick it if the question asked how a person holds urine on purpose.
This describes the internal urethral sphincter, the involuntary smooth muscle ring at the bladder outlet. It would be the answer for the automatic ring that keeps urine from leaking.
questions.answerText: Smooth muscle in the bladder wall that contracts to empty the bladder

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Which sequence correctly names the regions of the male urethra, starting at the bladder?
options: Spongy, membranous, prostatic
Prostatic, spongy, membranous
Membranous, prostatic, spongy
Prostatic, membranous, spongy
questions.why: Each region of the male urethra is named for what it passes through. Leaving the bladder, it runs through the prostate gland as the prostatic urethra, then through the perineum as the short membranous urethra, and finally through the penis as the spongy (penile) urethra, which lies in the corpus spongiosum. The male urethra is longer than the female urethra and carries both urine and semen.
notes: This is the correct sequence read backward, from the outside of the body toward the bladder. It would only be right if the question asked you to start at the tip of the penis.
This order moves the membranous region to the end. The short membranous urethra crosses the perineum between the prostate and the penis, so it sits in the middle.
This order puts the membranous urethra first. The prostate sits directly below the bladder, so the urethra passes through it before reaching the perineum.
Correct. Prostatic, then membranous, then spongy.

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the internal and external urethral sphincters?
options: The internal sphincter is involuntary smooth muscle at the bladder outlet; the external sphincter is voluntary skeletal muscle around the urethra.
Both sphincters are involuntary smooth muscle, so neither one can be controlled consciously.
The internal sphincter is voluntary skeletal muscle at the bladder outlet; the external sphincter is involuntary smooth muscle around the urethra.
The internal sphincter lies in the wall of the ureter; the external sphincter lies at the bladder outlet.
questions.why: The bladder outlet is guarded by two rings of muscle. The internal urethral sphincter is involuntary smooth muscle where the bladder opens into the urethra, so it stays closed without any thought. The external urethral sphincter is voluntary skeletal muscle that surrounds the urethra farther along its path, and it gives conscious control over when urination happens.
notes: Correct. Internal is involuntary smooth muscle; external is voluntary skeletal muscle.
Only the internal sphincter is involuntary. The external sphincter is skeletal muscle, which is why people can hold urine on purpose, so this statement leaves out voluntary control entirely.
This statement swaps the two muscle types. The internal sphincter is the automatic smooth muscle ring, and the external sphincter is the skeletal muscle ring you can control.

Neither sphincter lies in the ureter; the ureters enter the bladder without a named sphincter. The internal sphincter is at the bladder outlet, and the external sphincter surrounds the urethra beyond it.
questions.answerText: The internal sphincter is involuntary smooth muscle at the bladder outlet; the external sphincter is voluntary skeletal muscle around the urethra.

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Which paired tubes carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder?
options: The ureters
The major calyces
The collecting ducts
The urethra
questions.why: The ureters are a pair of muscular tubes, one from each kidney, that carry urine from the renal pelvis down to the urinary bladder. Waves of smooth muscle contraction, called peristalsis, push the urine along. The names look alike, but there are two ureters, and the urethra is the single exit.
notes: Correct. The ureters carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder.
The major calyces are chambers inside the kidney that channel urine from the minor calyces into the renal pelvis. Choose them if the question asked what drains directly into the renal pelvis.
The collecting ducts are microscopic ducts inside the kidney that gather fluid from many nephrons. They would be the answer for a structure inside the renal pyramids, not a tube between organs.

The urethra is a single tube that carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body. Students often mix up the two names; pick the urethra if the question asked which tube empties the bladder.

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Which tube carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body?
options: The collecting duct
The renal pelvis
The urethra
The ureter
questions.why: The urethra is the last structure in the path of urine. It leaves the bladder at the internal urethral orifice and carries urine to the outside of the body, passing the internal and external urethral sphincters on the way. It is longer in males, where it also carries semen, and shorter in females.
notes: The collecting duct is a microscopic duct inside the kidney that gathers fluid from many nephrons. Choose it if the question asked about a duct in the renal pyramids.
The renal pelvis is the funnel-shaped cavity inside the kidney that collects urine and passes it into the ureter. It would be the answer for the space where the calyces drain.
Correct. The urethra carries urine from the bladder out of the body.
The ureter carries urine into the bladder from the kidney, not out of it. Pick the ureter if the question asked which tube connects each kidney to the bladder.

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: What is the smooth muscle layer of the bladder wall that contracts to empty the bladder?
options: The detrusor muscle
The internal urethral sphincter
The external urethral sphincter
The trigone
questions.why: The detrusor muscle is the thick smooth muscle layer that makes up most of the bladder wall. When it contracts, it squeezes the bladder and pushes urine into the urethra. The name comes from a Latin word meaning to push down or thrust away, which matches its job.
notes: Correct. The detrusor muscle empties the bladder.

The internal urethral sphincter is an involuntary smooth muscle ring at the bladder outlet that keeps urine in, not a layer of the whole wall. It would be the answer for the automatic ring at the bladder neck.
The external urethral sphincter is a ring of voluntary skeletal muscle around the urethra. Choose it if the question asked which muscle gives conscious control over urination.

The trigone is a smooth triangular area on the floor of the bladder, marked by the two ureter openings and the urethral opening. Pick it if the question asked about the landmark at the base of the bladder.

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Which muscular sac stores urine until it is released?
options: The ureter
The renal pelvis
The urinary bladder
The urethra
questions.why: The urinary bladder is a hollow, muscular sac in the pelvic cavity that stores urine. Its wall is lined with stretchy transitional epithelium and folds called rugae, so it can expand as it fills. When it is time to empty, the detrusor muscle in its wall contracts.
notes: The ureter is a transport tube that moves urine from the kidney to the bladder by peristalsis. It would be the answer for the structure that carries urine down to the bladder.
The renal pelvis is a funnel-shaped cavity inside the kidney that passes urine on to the ureter rather than storing it. Pick it if the question asked what collects urine from the calyces.
Correct. The urinary bladder stores urine.
The urethra is the exit tube from the bladder to the outside. Choose it if the question asked which structure carries urine out of the body.

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Where is the trigone found?
options: On the floor of the urinary bladder
Within the wall of the ureter
At the tip of a renal pyramid
Inside the renal pelvis
questions.why: The trigone is a smooth triangular area on the floor (base) of the urinary bladder. Its three corners are the two ureteral openings, where urine enters, and the internal urethral orifice, where urine leaves. Unlike the rest of the bladder lining, it stays smooth rather than folding into rugae.
notes: Correct. The trigone is on the floor of the urinary bladder.

The ureter wall has a transitional epithelium lining and a smooth muscle layer for peristalsis, but no triangular landmark. The ureters only meet the trigone where they open into the bladder at two of its corners.
The tip of a renal pyramid is the renal papilla, where urine drains into a minor calyx. Pick that location if the question asked about the renal papilla.
The renal pelvis is the funnel-shaped cavity inside the kidney that collects urine from the calyces. It has no trigone; choose it if the question asked where the major calyces empty.
questions.answerText: On the floor of the urinary bladder

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Which urethral sphincter is the voluntary ring of skeletal muscle?
options: The trigone
The detrusor muscle
The external urethral sphincter
The internal urethral sphincter
questions.why: The external urethral sphincter is a ring of skeletal muscle around the urethra, and skeletal muscle is under voluntary control. That is why a person can choose to hold urine or let it go. The internal urethral sphincter, closer to the bladder, is smooth muscle and works automatically.
notes: The trigone is a smooth triangular area on the bladder floor, a landmark rather than a muscle ring. Choose it if the question asked about the area marked by the ureter and urethral openings.
The detrusor muscle is the smooth muscle of the bladder wall that contracts to empty the bladder, not a sphincter. It would be the answer for the muscle that pushes urine out.
Correct. The external urethral sphincter is the voluntary skeletal muscle ring.
The internal urethral sphincter is an involuntary ring of smooth muscle at the bladder outlet. Pick it if the question asked which sphincter keeps the outlet closed without conscious effort.

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Which statement is true of the female urethra compared with the male urethra?
options: It has no external sphincter.
It is shorter and carries only urine.
It opens into the vaginal canal.
It is longer and also carries semen.
questions.why: The female urethra is short and carries only urine, opening to the outside between the clitoris and the vaginal opening. The male urethra is longer, passes through the prostate, perineum, and penis, and carries both urine and semen. The short female urethra is one reason urinary tract infections are more common in women.
notes: Both sexes have an external urethral sphincter of voluntary skeletal muscle. This choice confuses the shorter length of the female urethra with missing parts.
Correct. The female urethra is shorter and carries only urine.
The female urethra opens separately, between the clitoris and the vaginal opening, not into the vagina. This mix-up comes from the two openings sitting close together in the vulva.
This describes the male urethra, which runs through the prostate, perineum, and penis and carries both urine and semen. Pick it if the question asked about the male urethra.
questions.answerText: It is shorter and carries only urine.

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Glomerulonephritis is inflammation of which structures?
options: The ureters
The renal pelvis
The glomeruli
The renal pyramids
questions.why: Glomerulonephritis is inflammation of the glomeruli, the capillary tufts where blood is filtered. The name breaks down into glomerulo (the glomeruli), nephr (kidney), and itis (inflammation). Because the glomeruli are the filters, inflaming them impairs the kidney's ability to filter the blood.
notes: The ureters are the tubes from the kidneys to the bladder. They are where a kidney stone causes pain, so pick them if the question asked where a stone becomes painful.
The renal pelvis is the funnel that collects urine and passes it to the ureter, and it is where kidney stones often form. It would be the answer if the question asked where a stone first forms.
Correct. Glomerulonephritis is inflammation of the glomeruli.
The renal pyramids are the cone-shaped masses of the medulla that hold the nephron loops and collecting ducts. Choose them if the question asked what makes up the medulla.

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Urinary incontinence, the loss of voluntary control over urination, involves which structures?
options: The urethral sphincters
The renal pelvis
The glomeruli
The ureters
questions.why: Urinary incontinence is the loss of voluntary control over urination. The structures involved are the urethral sphincters, the detrusor muscle, and the pelvic floor. In stress incontinence a weak pelvic floor and external sphincter leak with coughing or lifting, and in urge incontinence the detrusor contracts too readily.
notes: Correct. The urethral sphincters guard the bladder outlet, so they are among the structures involved in incontinence.
The renal pelvis collects urine inside the kidney and passes it to the ureter. Choose it if the question asked where kidney stones often form.
The glomeruli are the filtering capillary tufts of the nephrons, far upstream of the bladder. Pick them if the question asked about glomerulonephritis.
The ureters carry urine to the bladder by peristalsis and play no part in holding urine in. They would be the answer for where a kidney stone causes pain.

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: How do the ureters move urine from the kidneys to the bladder?
options: By contraction of the external urethral sphincter
By waves of smooth muscle contraction (peristalsis)
By gravity alone, with no muscle action
By contraction of the detrusor muscle
questions.why: The ureter wall has a layer of smooth muscle that contracts in waves, called peristalsis, squeezing urine down toward the bladder. Because the muscle does the pushing, urine still reaches the bladder when a person is lying down. The same kind of wave moves food along the digestive tract.
notes: The external urethral sphincter is a skeletal muscle ring around the urethra that holds urine in on purpose. It would be the answer for voluntary control of urination, not transport down the ureter.
Correct. Peristalsis in the ureter wall moves urine to the bladder.
Gravity helps when a person is upright, but urine still reaches the bladder when someone lies flat. This choice comes from picturing the ureters as passive drainpipes rather than muscular tubes.
The detrusor muscle is in the bladder wall and contracts to empty the bladder into the urethra. Pick it if the question asked how urine leaves the bladder.
questions.answerText: By waves of smooth muscle contraction (peristalsis)

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Which inherited disorder fills the kidneys with many enlarging, fluid-filled cysts?
options: Polycystic kidney disease
Kidney stones
Glomerulonephritis
Renal failure
questions.why: Polycystic kidney disease is an inherited disorder in which many fluid-filled cysts grow in the kidneys and enlarge them. The name says it: poly means many, and cystic means cysts. As the cysts crowd out working kidney tissue, they can lead to renal failure.
notes: Correct. Polycystic kidney disease is the inherited cyst disorder.
Kidney stones are hardened mineral deposits that form in the kidney and can lodge in the ureter. Choose them if the question described solid deposits blocking the flow of urine.
Glomerulonephritis is inflammation of the glomeruli that impairs filtration, not an inherited cyst disease. Pick it if the question described inflamed filtering capillaries.

Renal failure is the loss of the kidney's ability to filter the blood, either acute or chronic. It can be the end result of polycystic kidney disease, but it is the outcome rather than the cyst disorder itself.

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Which disorder consists of hardened mineral deposits that form in the kidney and can lodge in the ureter?
options: Urinary incontinence
Kidney stones
Renal failure
Glomerulonephritis
questions.why: Kidney stones are hardened mineral deposits that form in the kidney, often in the renal pelvis. A stone can travel into the ureter, a tube only millimeters wide, where it scrapes the wall and blocks the flow of urine. That is why the pain usually starts when the stone enters the ureter.
notes: Urinary incontinence is the loss of voluntary control over urination, involving the detrusor, the urethral sphincters, or the pelvic floor. It would be the answer if the question described leaking urine.
Correct. Kidney stones are hardened mineral deposits in the urinary tract.
Renal failure is the loss of the kidney's ability to filter the blood. Choose it if the question described kidneys that can no longer clean the blood.
Glomerulonephritis is inflammation of the glomeruli, not a solid deposit. Pick it if the question described inflamed filtering capillaries that impair filtration.

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Which urinary disorder is an infection of the urethra, bladder, or kidneys, usually by bacteria?
options: Kidney stones
Urinary tract infection
Polycystic kidney disease
Renal failure
questions.why: A urinary tract infection is an infection anywhere along the urinary tract, usually by bacteria that enter through the urethra and climb toward the bladder and sometimes the kidneys. It is more common in women, in part because the female urethra is short and gives bacteria a shorter climb to the bladder.
notes: Kidney stones are hardened mineral deposits that can lodge in the ureter. Choose them if the question described a solid deposit causing sharp pain along the ureter.
Correct. A urinary tract infection is a bacterial infection of the urinary tract.
Polycystic kidney disease is an inherited disorder of many fluid-filled cysts in the kidneys. It would be the answer if the question described enlarged kidneys full of cysts.
Renal failure is the loss of the kidney's ability to filter the blood, not an infection. Pick it if the question described kidneys that can no longer clean the blood.

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Which structure is the involuntary smooth muscle ring at the bladder outlet?
options: The detrusor muscle
The external urethral sphincter
The trigone
The internal urethral sphincter
questions.why: The internal urethral sphincter is a ring of smooth muscle where the bladder opens into the urethra. Because it is smooth muscle, it works automatically and keeps the outlet closed without conscious effort. Farther along the urethra, the external urethral sphincter adds voluntary control.
notes: The detrusor muscle is the smooth muscle of the whole bladder wall, and it contracts to empty the bladder rather than close it. Pick it if the question asked which muscle pushes urine out.
The external urethral sphincter is a ring of voluntary skeletal muscle around the urethra, beyond the bladder outlet. It would be the answer for the sphincter you control on purpose.
The trigone is a smooth triangular area on the bladder floor, a landmark rather than a ring of muscle. Choose it if the question asked about the area marked by the ureter and urethral openings.
Correct. The internal urethral sphincter is the involuntary ring at the bladder outlet.

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: What is the smooth triangular area on the bladder floor, marked by the two ureter openings and the urethral opening?
options: The renal pelvis
The detrusor muscle
The trigone
The internal urethral orifice
questions.why: The trigone is the smooth triangle on the floor of the bladder. Its two back corners are the ureteral openings, where urine enters from the ureters, and its front corner is the internal urethral orifice, where urine leaves. Its name comes from the word for a triangle.
notes: The renal pelvis is the funnel inside the kidney that passes urine to the ureter, not part of the bladder. Choose it if the question asked where the calyces drain.
The detrusor muscle is the smooth muscle layer throughout the bladder wall, not a marked area on the floor. Pick it if the question asked which muscle contracts to empty the bladder.
Correct. The trigone is the triangle marked by the three openings.
The internal urethral orifice is only one corner of the trigone, the opening where urine leaves the bladder. It would be the answer if the question asked for the opening into the urethra.

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Which sequence correctly traces urine from the collecting duct to the ureter?
options: Collecting duct, renal papilla, minor calyx, major calyx, renal pelvis, ureter
Collecting duct, minor calyx, renal papilla, major calyx, renal pelvis, ureter
Collecting duct, renal papilla, major calyx, minor calyx, renal pelvis, ureter
Collecting duct, renal pelvis, major calyx, minor calyx, renal papilla, ureter
questions.why: Collecting ducts carry urine down through a pyramid to its tip, the renal papilla. Urine drips from the papilla into a minor calyx, several minor calyces join into a major calyx, and the major calyces empty into the renal pelvis. The renal pelvis narrows at the hilum into the ureter. The collecting spaces get larger at every step.
notes: Correct. Papilla, minor calyx, major calyx, renal pelvis, then ureter.
This order puts the minor calyx before the papilla. The papilla is the tip of the pyramid where urine leaves the tissue, so it must come first, and the minor calyx catches what drips from it.
This order swaps the minor and major calyces. Minor calyces catch urine from the papillae and then join to form the larger major calyces.
This order runs the collecting spaces backward after the collecting duct. The renal pelvis is the last and largest space, so it comes right before the ureter, not right after the collecting duct.
questions.answerText: Collecting duct, renal papilla, minor calyx, major calyx, renal pelvis, ureter

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
