questions.q: Which sequence correctly traces urine from the renal pelvis until it leaves the body?
options: Renal pelvis, ureter, urinary bladder, urethra
Renal pelvis, ureter, urethra, urinary bladder
Renal pelvis, urinary bladder, ureter, urethra
Renal pelvis, urethra, urinary bladder, ureter
questions.why: From the renal pelvis, urine flows into the ureter, which carries it down to the urinary bladder by peristalsis. The bladder stores the urine until it is released through the urethra to the outside. A quick check is that the bladder sits between the two look-alike tubes: ureter in, urethra out.
notes: Correct. Renal pelvis, ureter, urinary bladder, then urethra.
This order puts the urethra before the bladder. The urethra is the exit tube, so urine must be stored in the bladder before it reaches the urethra.
This order skips the ureter between the kidney and the bladder. The renal pelvis is inside the kidney and cannot drain directly into the bladder; the ureter connects the two.
This order swaps the ureter and urethra. The ureter leaves the kidney and enters the bladder, while the urethra leaves the bladder for the outside.
questions.answerText: Renal pelvis, ureter, urinary bladder, urethra

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Starting at the glomerular capsule, which sequence correctly traces fluid all the way out of the body?
options: Glomerular capsule, collecting duct, renal tubule, calyces, renal pelvis, ureter, bladder, urethra
Glomerular capsule, renal tubule, collecting duct, renal pelvis, calyces, ureter, bladder, urethra
Glomerular capsule, renal tubule, collecting duct, calyces, renal pelvis, ureter, bladder, urethra
Glomerular capsule, renal tubule, calyces, collecting duct, renal pelvis, bladder, ureter, urethra
questions.why: Filtrate captured in the glomerular capsule flows through the renal tubule of its own nephron and then into a collecting duct shared with other nephrons. From the renal papilla it drips into the calyces, gathers in the renal pelvis, and leaves the kidney through the ureter. The ureter carries it to the bladder for storage, and the urethra carries it out of the body.
notes: This order puts the collecting duct before the renal tubule. The renal tubule belongs to the nephron itself and empties into the collecting duct, so the tubule comes first.
This order swaps the calyces and the renal pelvis. The calyces catch urine from the papillae and then empty into the renal pelvis, which leads to the ureter.
Correct. Tubule, collecting duct, calyces, renal pelvis, ureter, bladder, urethra.
This order places the calyces before the collecting duct and the bladder before the ureter. Collecting ducts deliver urine to the calyces, and the ureter delivers urine to the bladder.
questions.answerText: Glomerular capsule, renal tubule, collecting duct, calyces, renal pelvis, ureter, bladder, urethra

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Which four organs make up the urinary system?
options: The kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder, and urethra
The kidneys, nephrons, glomeruli, and calyces
The renal artery, renal vein, ureter, and bladder
The cortex, medulla, renal pelvis, and ureter
questions.why: The urinary system is made of four organs: the two kidneys, which filter the blood and form urine; the two ureters, which carry urine down; the urinary bladder, which stores it; and the urethra, which carries it out of the body. Everything else in the urinary system, such as nephrons and calyces, is a part inside one of these organs.
notes: Correct. The kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder, and urethra are the four organs.
Nephrons, glomeruli, and calyces are all parts inside the kidney, not separate organs. Pick a list like this if the question asked for structures found within a kidney.
The renal artery and renal vein are blood vessels that serve the kidney. They belong to the circulatory system, so pick them if the question asked which vessels enter and leave at the hilum.
The cortex, medulla, and renal pelvis are regions inside a single kidney. This list would fit a question about what a frontal section of the kidney shows, not the organs of the system.
questions.answerText: The kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder, and urethra

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Which three openings mark the corners of the trigone?
options: One ureteral opening and two urethral openings
Two urethral sphincters and one ureteral opening
Two ureteral openings and the external urethral orifice
Two ureteral openings and the internal urethral orifice
questions.why: The trigone is the smooth triangular area on the floor of the bladder. Its two back corners are the ureteral openings, where each ureter delivers urine into the bladder, and its front corner is the internal urethral orifice, where urine leaves the bladder for the urethra. Two openings in and one opening out gives the triangle.
notes: There are two ureters but only one urethra, so the bladder has two ureteral openings and one urethral opening. This choice reverses the count.
The urethral sphincters are muscle rings around the outlet, not openings in the bladder floor. This choice mixes up the muscles that guard an opening with the openings themselves.
The external urethral orifice is at the far end of the urethra, on the outside of the body, not inside the bladder. Pick it if the question asked where urine finally exits the body.
Correct. Two ureteral openings and the internal urethral orifice mark the trigone.
questions.answerText: Two ureteral openings and the internal urethral orifice

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: After rapid weight loss, a patient's kidney loses its fat support and drops from its normal position, kinking the ureter. Which disorder is this?
options: Renal failure
Glomerulonephritis
Nephroptosis
Polycystic kidney disease
questions.why: Nephroptosis, also called a floating kidney, happens when the kidney drops from its normal position because the adipose capsule that holds it in place is lost. As the kidney sags, the ureter can kink and block the flow of urine. The name means a falling kidney: nephro (kidney) plus ptosis (drooping).
notes: Renal failure is the loss of the kidney's ability to filter the blood. A badly blocked ureter could eventually harm the kidney, but the dropped kidney itself is nephroptosis.
Glomerulonephritis is inflammation of the glomeruli that impairs filtration, not a change in the kidney's position. Pick it if the question described inflamed filtering capillaries.
Correct. A kidney that drops after losing its fat support is nephroptosis.
Polycystic kidney disease is an inherited disorder in which fluid-filled cysts enlarge the kidneys. It would be the answer if the question described kidneys full of cysts.

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: A kidney stone forms in the renal pelvis and causes no pain until it moves into the next tube along the path of urine, only millimeters wide. Which tube is that?
options: The urethra
The papillary duct
The ureter
The collecting duct
questions.why: Urine leaves the renal pelvis through the ureter, a narrow muscular tube only millimeters wide. A stone sitting in the roomy renal pelvis may cause no symptoms, but once it enters the ureter it scrapes the wall and blocks the flow of urine, causing sharp pain. Knowing the path of urine tells you where the pain will be.
notes: The urethra carries urine from the bladder to the outside, so a stone would have to pass the ureter and the bladder before reaching it. Pick it if the question asked about the last tube in the path.
The papillary duct opens on the renal papilla before urine reaches the calyces and pelvis, so it is upstream of the stone. It would be the answer for the duct that empties onto the papilla.
Correct. The ureter is the narrow tube that follows the renal pelvis.
The collecting duct is a microscopic duct inside a renal pyramid, upstream of the renal pelvis. A stone in the pelvis cannot move backward into it.

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: A patient's kidney filters are inflamed, and the kidneys cannot filter the blood properly. Testing shows the problem is in the capillary tufts of the nephrons. Which disorder fits?
options: Kidney stones
Glomerulonephritis
Urinary incontinence
Nephroptosis
questions.why: The capillary tufts of the nephrons are the glomeruli, so inflammation there is glomerulonephritis. Because the glomeruli are where the blood is filtered, inflaming them impairs filtration. Reading the name in pieces gives the answer: glomerulo (glomeruli), nephr (kidney), itis (inflammation).
notes: Kidney stones are hardened mineral deposits that can block the ureter, not inflammation of the filters. Pick them if the question described sharp pain as a stone moves down the ureter.
Correct. Inflammation of the glomeruli is glomerulonephritis.

Urinary incontinence is the loss of voluntary control over urination, involving the detrusor, the urethral sphincters, or the pelvic floor. It would be the answer if the question described leaking urine.
Nephroptosis is a kidney that drops out of position after losing its fat support. Choose it if the question described a sagging kidney that kinks the ureter.

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Urinary tract infections are more common in women. Which structural feature is one reason for this?
options: The female bladder is larger
The female ureters are wider
The female kidneys sit lower
The female urethra is shorter
questions.why: Most urinary tract infections start when bacteria enter through the urethra and climb up to the bladder. The female urethra is much shorter than the male urethra, so bacteria have a shorter distance to travel before they reach the bladder. The anatomy of the urethra helps predict who is at higher risk.
notes: Bladder size is not the reason infections are more common in women. This choice comes from assuming a bigger organ is more exposed, but the deciding feature is the length of the entry tube.

Bacteria usually climb in through the urethra, not the ureters, so the width of the ureters does not explain the higher risk. Pick the ureters only if the question asked how urine travels from kidney to bladder.

Kidney position does not differ by sex in a way that explains infection risk; the right kidney usually sits lower in both sexes because of the liver. That fact would answer which kidney sits lower, not why infections are more common.
Correct. The shorter female urethra gives bacteria a shorter climb to the bladder.

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: The bladder is lined with transitional epithelium and has folds called rugae. How do these features suit the bladder's job?
options: They keep the bladder at the same size whether it is full or empty
They let the bladder expand as it fills and shrink when empty without tearing
They move urine back into the blood through the thin wall of the bladder
They contract to push urine out of the bladder into the urethra
questions.why: The bladder changes volume greatly as it fills and empties. Transitional epithelium has cells that flatten as the wall stretches and round up again when it relaxes, and the rugae are folds that unfold as the bladder fills. Together they let the bladder hold a large volume and then return to a small size without damaging its lining.
notes: This is the opposite of what these features do. A lining that could not change size would tear as urine filled the bladder.
Correct. The stretchy lining and rugae let the bladder expand and shrink.
The bladder stores urine; it does not return urine to the blood. Reclaiming water and nutrients happens in the renal tubules, so pick the tubules if the question asked where filtrate is reabsorbed.
Contracting to push urine out is the job of the detrusor muscle in the bladder wall, not the epithelium or the rugae. Choose the detrusor if the question asked which layer empties the bladder.
questions.answerText: They let the bladder expand as it fills and shrink when empty without tearing

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Two sphincters guard the bladder outlet, one involuntary and one under conscious control. Why is it useful to have both?
options: The internal one keeps the outlet closed automatically, and the external one lets a person choose when to urinate
Both are voluntary, so a person must consciously hold each one closed at all times
The external one keeps the outlet closed automatically, and the internal one lets a person choose when to urinate
Both are involuntary, so urination happens on its own without any conscious control
questions.why: Continence needs both reliable closure and conscious timing. The internal urethral sphincter is smooth muscle, so it keeps the bladder outlet closed automatically and urine does not leak while a person is busy or asleep. The external urethral sphincter is skeletal muscle, so a person can hold urine or release it by choice. Each muscle type matches the kind of control it provides.
notes: Correct. The internal sphincter gives automatic closure and the external sphincter gives voluntary control.
Only the external sphincter is voluntary. If both needed conscious effort, a person would leak urine whenever their attention drifted or they fell asleep.
This choice swaps the two sphincters. The internal sphincter is smooth muscle and works automatically, while the external sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary control.
Only the internal sphincter is involuntary. The external sphincter of skeletal muscle is what lets people decide when to urinate, so this choice leaves out voluntary control.
questions.answerText: The internal one keeps the outlet closed automatically, and the external one lets a person choose when to urinate

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Which disorder is the loss of the kidney's ability to filter the blood, either acute or chronic?
options: Renal failure
Urinary tract infection
Nephroptosis
Urinary incontinence
questions.why: Renal failure is the loss of the kidney's ability to filter the blood. It can be acute, developing quickly, or chronic, developing over a long time. Other kidney disorders, such as glomerulonephritis or polycystic kidney disease, can lead to renal failure when they damage enough working tissue.
notes: Correct. Renal failure is the loss of the kidney's filtering ability.
A urinary tract infection is a bacterial infection of the urethra, bladder, or kidneys. Choose it if the question described bacteria climbing up the urinary tract.
Nephroptosis is a kidney that drops out of position after losing its fat support. It would be the answer if the question described a floating kidney that kinks the ureter.

Urinary incontinence is the loss of voluntary control over urination, involving the detrusor, the urethral sphincters, or the pelvic floor, while filtering may be normal. Pick it if the question described leaking urine.

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Where does the female urethra open to the outside of the body?
options: Between the clitoris and the vaginal opening
Between the vaginal opening and the anus
Inside the vaginal canal
On the glans of the clitoris
questions.why: The female urethra is short and carries only urine. Its external opening lies in the vulva, between the clitoris in front and the vaginal opening behind it. Knowing this order from front to back (clitoris, urethral opening, vaginal opening, then anus) is useful in the lab and in clinical skills such as placing a urinary catheter.
notes: Correct. The female urethra opens between the clitoris and the vaginal opening.

The skin between the vaginal opening and the anus is part of the perineum, and no urinary structure opens there. This choice comes from placing the urethra behind the vaginal opening instead of in front of it.
The urethra has its own separate opening and does not empty into the vagina. This choice comes from the two openings sitting close together in the vulva.
The clitoris contains no urethra in females, unlike the penis, which carries the spongy urethra. Choose the glans of the penis if the question asked where the male urethra opens.
questions.answerText: Between the clitoris and the vaginal opening

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Which list names the four organs of the urinary system?
options: Kidneys, ureters, prostate, urethra
Kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder, urethra
Kidneys, adrenal glands, ureters, urethra
Kidneys, renal pelvis, ureters, bladder
questions.why: The urinary system has four organs. The kidneys filter the blood and form urine, the ureters carry urine down to the bladder, the urinary bladder stores it, and the urethra carries it out of the body. Every other urinary structure you learn, such as the calyces or the renal pelvis, is a part of one of these four organs.
notes: The prostate surrounds the first part of the male urethra, but it is a male reproductive gland, and this list leaves out the bladder. Pick the prostate if the question were about which accessory gland the urethra passes through.
Correct. These are the four organs, in the order urine passes through them.

The adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys but they are endocrine glands, not urinary organs, so they never handle urine. Pick them if a question asked which glands cap the superior pole of each kidney.

The renal pelvis is a real urine-carrying space, but it is a part inside the kidney rather than a separate organ, so this list counts the kidney twice and leaves out the urethra. Choose the renal pelvis when a question asks what funnels urine from the calyces into the ureter.

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Which structure carries urine from the kidney to the bladder, and how is the urine moved?
options: The ureter, by gravity alone
The renal pelvis, by cilia
The ureter, by peristalsis
The urethra, by peristalsis
questions.why: Each ureter is a muscular tube that runs from the renal pelvis down to the urinary bladder. Waves of smooth muscle contraction called peristalsis push urine along the tube, the same kind of squeezing that moves food through the gut. Because of peristalsis, urine reaches the bladder even when a person is lying down.
notes: The ureter is right, but gravity alone does not move the urine. Urine still reaches the bladder when a person lies flat or is upside down, because muscle in the ureter wall pushes it along.

The renal pelvis collects urine and funnels it into the ureter, but it does not reach the bladder, and the urinary tract is not lined by cilia that sweep urine along. Choose the renal pelvis if the question asked what passes urine into the ureter.
Correct. The ureter moves urine to the bladder by peristaltic waves of smooth muscle.

The urethra carries urine from the bladder to the outside, not from the kidney to the bladder. Students mix up the two because the names are so close; pick the urethra if the question asked about the last tube of the system.

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Which feature of the bladder is the smooth triangular area at its base, marked by the two ureter openings and the urethral opening?
options: The detrusor
The internal urethral sphincter
The renal papilla
The trigone
questions.why: The trigone is a smooth triangle on the floor of the bladder. Its three corners are the two openings where the ureters enter and the single opening where the urethra leaves. Unlike the rest of the bladder lining, which folds into rugae when the bladder is empty, the trigone stays smooth.
notes: The detrusor is the smooth muscle layer of the whole bladder wall, not a marked area on its floor. Pick it if the question asked which muscle contracts to empty the bladder.

The internal urethral sphincter is a ring of involuntary smooth muscle at the bladder outlet, at only one corner of the trigone. Choose it if the question asked what keeps the bladder outlet closed without conscious effort.
The renal papilla is the tip of a renal pyramid inside the kidney, not part of the bladder. Pick it if the question asked which structure drains urine into a minor calyx.
Correct. The trigone is the triangle outlined by the two ureter openings and the urethral opening.

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Which muscle forms the bladder wall and contracts to empty the bladder?
options: The internal urethral sphincter
The external urethral sphincter
The detrusor muscle
The cremaster muscle
questions.why: The detrusor muscle is the thick layer of smooth muscle in the wall of the urinary bladder. When it contracts, it squeezes the bladder and pushes urine out through the urethra. The sphincters, in contrast, are rings that hold the outlet closed and must relax for urine to leave.
notes: The internal urethral sphincter is a ring of involuntary smooth muscle at the bladder outlet. It keeps the outlet closed and relaxes when the bladder empties, so choose it if the question asked about the involuntary ring at the bladder neck.

The external urethral sphincter is a ring of voluntary skeletal muscle around the urethra that holds urine in. It relaxes during urination rather than squeezing the bladder; pick it if the question asked which muscle gives conscious control over urination.
Correct. The detrusor is the smooth muscle of the bladder wall that contracts during urination.

The cremaster is a skeletal muscle in the spermatic cord that raises and lowers the testes. It has nothing to do with the bladder; pick it if the question asked which muscle adjusts the position of the testes.

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Which list traces urine from the collecting duct to outside the body?
options: Collecting duct, major calyx, minor calyx, renal pelvis, urethra, bladder, ureter
Collecting duct, minor calyx, major calyx, renal pelvis, urethra, bladder, ureter
Collecting duct, renal pelvis, minor calyx, major calyx, ureter, bladder, urethra
Collecting duct, minor calyx, major calyx, renal pelvis, ureter, bladder, urethra
questions.why: Collecting ducts carry urine to the renal papilla, which drains into a minor calyx. Minor calyces merge into major calyces, which empty into the renal pelvis, and the pelvis narrows into the ureter. The ureter carries urine to the bladder for storage, and the urethra carries it out of the body.
notes: This flips the calyces and also swaps the ureter and urethra. Students pick this when they mix up minor with major and ureter with urethra, two of the most common look-alike pairs in this system.

The kidney portion is right, but the tubes after the pelvis are reversed. The ureter leaves the kidney and the urethra leaves the bladder, so the ureter must come before the bladder and the urethra after it.
This puts the renal pelvis before the calyces. The pelvis is formed where the major calyces meet, so both calyces must come first.
Correct. The spaces inside the kidney grow larger as they merge, and then the ureter, bladder, and urethra carry urine out.
questions.answerText: Collecting duct, minor calyx, major calyx, renal pelvis, ureter, bladder, urethra

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: Which anatomical difference helps explain why urinary tract infections are more common in women?
options: The female bladder has no trigone, so bacteria settle more easily
The female urethra passes through the prostate, which traps bacteria
The female ureters are shorter, so bacteria reach the kidney sooner
The female urethra is shorter, so bacteria reach the bladder sooner
questions.why: Most urinary tract infections start when bacteria enter at the urethral opening and climb upward. The female urethra is much shorter than the male urethra, which runs the length of the penis, so bacteria have a shorter distance to travel before reaching the bladder. Its opening also lies close to the vaginal and anal openings.
notes: Both females and males have a trigone, the smooth triangle on the bladder floor. Pick the trigone if the question asked which area of the bladder is marked by the ureter and urethral openings.
Only the male urethra passes through the prostate, as the prostatic urethra. Pick this if the question asked why an enlarged prostate makes urination difficult.

Bacteria in a typical urinary tract infection climb up from the outside through the urethra, not down from the kidney, so ureter length is not the main factor. Students choose this when they mix up the ureter and the urethra.
Correct. The short female urethra gives bacteria a shorter path to the bladder.
questions.answerText: The female urethra is shorter, so bacteria reach the bladder sooner

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: When urine backs up behind a blockage, the renal pelvis and calyces swell. What is this swelling called?
options: Hydronephrosis
Nephroptosis
Glomerulonephritis
Pyelonephritis
questions.why: Urine travels one path from the calyces through the renal pelvis and ureter to the bladder. Any blockage along that path makes urine back up into the parts above it. When the backup reaches the renal pelvis and calyces, they swell, and that swelling is called hydronephrosis.
notes: Correct. Hydronephrosis is the swelling of the renal pelvis and calyces when urine backs up.
Nephroptosis is the kidney dropping out of its normal position when its fat cushion is lost. It can kink the ureter, but the term names the drop, not the swelling.
Glomerulonephritis is inflammation of the glomeruli, which damages the filtration membrane. It affects the filters, not the collecting spaces that swell with backed-up urine.
Pyelonephritis is an infection that has reached the renal pelvis and kidney tissue. It is named for infection, not for swelling from backed-up urine.

questions.topic: Ureters, bladder, urethra and the path of urine
questions.q: What is a urinary tract infection called once it reaches the renal pelvis and kidney tissue?
options: Glomerulonephritis
Hydronephrosis
Pyelonephritis
Cystitis
questions.why: In a urinary tract infection, bacteria, most often from the intestine, climb up the urine path and inflame its lining. Infection of the bladder is called cystitis. If it keeps climbing through the ureter to the renal pelvis and kidney tissue, it is called pyelonephritis.
notes: Glomerulonephritis is inflammation of the glomeruli that damages the filtration membrane. It is not named for a climbing infection of the renal pelvis.
Hydronephrosis is swelling of the renal pelvis and calyces when urine backs up behind a blockage. It is caused by blocked flow, not named for infection.
Correct. Pyelonephritis is infection that has climbed to the renal pelvis and kidney tissue.
Cystitis is infection of the urinary bladder, lower on the path. It becomes pyelonephritis only when it climbs to the kidney.

questions.q: Which hormone do the kidneys release to stimulate red blood cell production in bone marrow?
options: Erythropoietin
Aldosterone
Atrial natriuretic peptide
Thrombopoietin
questions.why: Peritubular cells sense low oxygen delivery and release erythropoietin, which drives erythroid precursors in marrow to mature. Thrombopoietin comes mostly from the liver and acts on platelets, not red cells. Aldosterone is adrenal, not renal, and acts on the collecting duct. Atrial natriuretic peptide comes from atrial muscle and promotes sodium loss.

questions.q: Which nitrogenous waste produced by protein breakdown is excreted in the largest amount by the kidney?
options: Uric acid
Creatinine
Urea
Bilirubin
questions.why: Amino groups stripped from amino acids become ammonia, the liver converts that ammonia to urea, and the kidney excretes urea in bulk. Bilirubin comes from heme breakdown and leaves mainly in bile, not urine. Uric acid comes from purines and is excreted in far smaller amounts. Creatinine comes from muscle creatine phosphate and is also excreted, but the daily mass is small compared with urea.

questions.q: Which waste in plasma is produced at a steady rate by skeletal muscle from creatine phosphate?
options: Uric acid
Creatinine
Ketone bodies
Urea
questions.why: Muscle converts creatine phosphate to creatinine at a rate that tracks muscle mass, which is why plasma creatinine is a useful steady baseline for judging excretory function. Urea production swings with dietary protein intake. Uric acid production swings with purine intake and cell turnover. Ketone bodies are liver products of fat breakdown and appear only in specific metabolic states.

questions.q: Which substance released by the granular cells of the kidney begins the renin angiotensin aldosterone cascade?
options: Angiotensinogen
Angiotensin converting enzyme
Aldosterone
Renin
questions.why: Granular cells in the afferent arteriole wall release renin, which cleaves circulating angiotensinogen to angiotensin I and starts the cascade. Angiotensinogen is the liver made substrate, not the trigger. Angiotensin converting enzyme acts later and comes largely from lung endothelium. Aldosterone is the adrenal end product of the cascade, not its first step.

questions.q: What is the kidney's role in vitamin D activation?
options: It stores vitamin D in large amounts until plasma calcium falls
It absorbs vitamin D from the diet along with dietary fat and calcium
It carries out the hydroxylation that converts 25 hydroxyvitamin D into calcitriol
It makes vitamin D from a cholesterol derivative using ultraviolet light
questions.why: The kidney holds the 1 alpha hydroxylase step, so it makes the active form calcitriol, which then raises intestinal calcium absorption. Dietary vitamin D is absorbed by the small intestine, not the kidney. Skin, not kidney, converts a cholesterol derivative to vitamin D under ultraviolet light. The liver does the earlier 25 hydroxylation and fat is the main storage site.
questions.answerText: It carries out the hydroxylation that converts 25 hydroxyvitamin D into calcitriol

questions.q: About what share of resting cardiac output do the kidneys receive?
options: About 20 to 25 percent
About 45 percent
About 5 percent
About 10 percent
questions.why: The kidneys take roughly a fifth of cardiac output, far more than their mass requires, because the flow serves filtration rather than their own metabolism. Five percent would be closer to resting skeletal muscle per unit mass. Ten percent understates renal flow and would not support a filtration rate of 125 mL/min. Forty five percent overstates it and would leave too little for the rest of the body.

questions.q: Which ion does the kidney regulate as the main determinant of extracellular fluid volume?
options: Mg2+
K+
Ca2+
Na+
questions.why: Sodium is the dominant extracellular solute, so retaining or excreting Na+ moves water with it and sets extracellular volume and blood pressure. K+ matters enormously for membrane potential but is mostly intracellular and contributes little to extracellular volume. Ca2+ is regulated for bone and signaling, not volume. Mg2+ is present in small amounts and does not drive fluid distribution.

questions.q: Which plasma buffer does the kidney reabsorb and generate as its main contribution to acid base balance?
options: Hemoglobin
HCO3-
Phosphate in bone
Plasma albumin
questions.why: The tubule reclaims filtered bicarbonate and makes new bicarbonate while excreting H+, which is how the kidney corrects an acid load over hours to days. Bone phosphate does buffer acid but is a skeletal reservoir, not a renal transport product. Plasma albumin buffers weakly and is not filtered or handled by the tubule. Hemoglobin buffers inside red cells and is not part of renal acid handling.

questions.q: A patient with long standing kidney failure is anemic despite normal iron stores. Which lost kidney function best explains this?
options: Reduced erythropoietin production
Reduced urea excretion
Reduced renin release
Reduced calcitriol production
questions.why: Damaged kidneys make less erythropoietin, so marrow gets a weaker signal and red cell production falls even when iron is available. Poor urea excretion raises blood urea nitrogen but does not by itself stop erythropoiesis. Low renin lowers blood pressure and sodium retention, a separate consequence. Low calcitriol produces low calcium and bone disease, not anemia.

questions.q: Kidney function falls to about fifteen percent of normal. Which acid base disturbance would you expect?
options: Respiratory acidosis
Respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis
questions.why: The kidney is the route for excreting the fixed acid produced daily by metabolism and for making new bicarbonate, so failing kidneys let acid accumulate and bicarbonate fall. Respiratory disturbances arise from changes in ventilation and PCO2, not from tubular transport. Metabolic alkalosis would require gaining bicarbonate or losing acid, the opposite of what a failing kidney does.

questions.q: Mean arterial pressure falls after blood loss. What is the kidney's immediate endocrine response?
options: Granular cells decrease renin secretion
Granular cells increase renin secretion
The tubule releases atrial natriuretic peptide
The kidney stops releasing erythropoietin
questions.why: Low perfusion pressure at the afferent arteriole is a direct stimulus for renin release, which raises angiotensin II and aldosterone and defends pressure and volume. Renin falls when pressure is high, which is the opposite situation. Atrial natriuretic peptide comes from stretched atria and would worsen the volume loss. Erythropoietin release actually tends to rise with low oxygen delivery, and in any case it acts over days.

questions.q: Why does chronic kidney disease tend to lower plasma calcium?
options: Erythropoietin normally drives calcium uptake into blood
Renin normally drives calcium reabsorption in the loop of Henle
More calcium is filtered because the filtration membrane is damaged
Less calcitriol is made, so the intestine absorbs less calcium
questions.why: The failing kidney cannot complete the 1 alpha hydroxylation step, so calcitriol falls and the intestine takes up less dietary calcium. Filtration of calcium is not the main problem, and filtration overall falls rather than rises in kidney disease. Erythropoietin acts on marrow and has no role in calcium transport. Renin acts on sodium and pressure through angiotensin, not on calcium handling.
questions.answerText: Less calcitriol is made, so the intestine absorbs less calcium

questions.q: A hiker goes twelve hours without water. What happens to the volume and osmolarity of the urine the kidney makes?
options: Volume rises and osmolarity falls
Volume falls and osmolarity falls
Volume falls and osmolarity rises
Volume rises and osmolarity rises
questions.why: Water conservation means reabsorbing water while still excreting the same solute load, so a small volume of concentrated urine leaves. Rising volume would waste the water the body is short of. Falling osmolarity with falling volume is impossible while solute output is maintained. Rising volume with rising osmolarity would mean excreting far more solute than was consumed.

questions.q: A person eats a meal very high in potassium. Which renal response protects the resting membrane potential of excitable cells?
options: Increased K+ secretion into the tubular fluid
Increased K+ reabsorption in the proximal tubule
Increased filtration of plasma proteins
Decreased Na+ excretion in the collecting duct
questions.why: Rising plasma K+ stimulates aldosterone and directly stimulates principal cells, and both increase K+ secretion so the excess leaves in urine before membrane potentials shift far. Extra proximal reabsorption would move K+ back into blood and make the problem worse. Protein filtration is not part of potassium handling. Holding onto sodium changes volume, not potassium balance.
questions.answerText: Increased K+ secretion into the tubular fluid

questions.q: Which plasma measurement is used as the routine index that the kidney's excretory function is declining?
options: Plasma calcium
Plasma albumin
Plasma glucose
Plasma creatinine
questions.why: Creatinine is produced at a near constant rate and cleared almost entirely by the kidney, so its plasma level rises predictably when filtration falls. Albumin reflects liver synthesis and protein loss, not filtration rate. Glucose reflects the pancreas and metabolism. Calcium can fall in kidney disease but is disturbed by many other conditions and moves late.

questions.q: A patient has narrowing of both renal arteries, so perfusion pressure reaching the kidneys is low even though systemic pressure is normal. Trace the expected sequence.
options: Renin falls, angiotensin II falls, and systemic blood pressure falls
Renin rises, angiotensin II rises, and systemic blood pressure is driven higher
Erythropoietin falls, red cell mass falls, and systemic blood pressure falls
Renin rises, aldosterone falls, and sodium is lost in the urine
questions.why: The kidney reads its own low perfusion pressure as whole body hypovolemia, so it releases renin, angiotensin II rises, vasoconstriction and aldosterone driven sodium retention follow, and systemic pressure climbs. Renin falling would require the kidney to sense high pressure, which the narrowing prevents. Erythropoietin changes act on red cell mass over weeks and do not explain the pressure change. Renin and aldosterone move in the same direction, so a rise in one with a fall in the other is inconsistent.
questions.answerText: Renin rises, angiotensin II rises, and systemic blood pressure is driven higher

questions.q: A patient with advanced kidney disease has anemia, a low plasma bicarbonate, and weak bones. Which grouping of lost kidney functions accounts for all three findings together?
options: Loss of erythropoietin production, loss of bicarbonate handling, and loss of calcitriol production
Loss of filtration only, with all three findings following from waste retention
Loss of aldosterone production, loss of vitamin D storage, and loss of protein synthesis
Loss of renin release, loss of urea excretion, and loss of potassium secretion
questions.why: Each finding maps to one lost function: no erythropoietin gives anemia, no bicarbonate reclamation and generation gives acidosis, and no calcitriol gives poor calcium absorption and weak bone. Renin, urea and potassium changes are real in kidney disease but do not produce anemia or bone disease. Waste retention alone does not explain a hormone deficiency. Aldosterone is adrenal, vitamin D is stored in fat, and plasma proteins are made by the liver.
questions.answerText: Loss of erythropoietin production, loss of bicarbonate handling, and loss of calcitriol production

questions.q: A drug selectively blocks renal 1 alpha hydroxylase. Predict plasma calcitriol, intestinal calcium absorption, and parathyroid hormone.
options: Calcitriol rises, intestinal calcium absorption rises, and parathyroid hormone falls
Calcitriol falls, intestinal calcium absorption rises, and parathyroid hormone falls
Calcitriol falls, intestinal calcium absorption falls, and parathyroid hormone rises
Calcitriol is unchanged, intestinal calcium absorption falls, and parathyroid hormone rises
questions.why: Blocking the enzyme stops the last activation step, so calcitriol falls, the intestine absorbs less calcium, plasma calcium drifts down, and the parathyroid glands respond by raising parathyroid hormone. A rise in calcitriol would require the enzyme to be working. Absorption cannot rise when its main hormonal driver is gone. Calcitriol cannot stay unchanged when the only enzyme that makes it is blocked.
questions.answerText: Calcitriol falls, intestinal calcium absorption falls, and parathyroid hormone rises

questions.q: Thirty minutes after a severe hemorrhage, what combination best describes renal blood flow, renin release, and sodium excretion?
options: Renal blood flow falls, renin release falls, and sodium excretion falls
Renal blood flow falls, renin release rises, and sodium excretion falls
Renal blood flow is unchanged, renin release rises, and sodium excretion rises
Renal blood flow rises, renin release falls, and sodium excretion rises
questions.why: Sympathetic vasoconstriction and lower perfusion pressure both cut renal blood flow, low pressure and sympathetic drive both raise renin, and the resulting angiotensin II and aldosterone cut sodium excretion so volume is defended. Renin cannot fall while pressure and sodium delivery are both low. Excreting sodium after hemorrhage would deepen the volume loss, so any answer with rising sodium excretion contradicts the regulation.
questions.answerText: Renal blood flow falls, renin release rises, and sodium excretion falls

questions.q: Which nephron segment reabsorbs about 65 percent of the filtered sodium and water?
options: The thick ascending limb
The distal convoluted tubule
The collecting duct
The proximal convoluted tubule
questions.why: The proximal tubule does the bulk work, reclaiming roughly two thirds of filtered sodium and water with a dense brush border and a large mitochondrial supply. The thick ascending limb handles about 25 percent and is the segment that builds the medullary gradient. The distal convoluted tubule fine tunes a small percentage. The collecting duct handles the final few percent under hormonal control.

questions.q: Which part of the loop of Henle is permeable to water but has low permeability to solute?
options: The distal convoluted tubule
The thick ascending limb
The descending thin limb
The thin ascending limb
questions.why: The descending thin limb lets water leave into the hyperosmotic medulla, which is why tubular fluid becomes progressively more concentrated toward the bend. The thick ascending limb is the reverse case, pumping salt while staying essentially water impermeable. The thin ascending limb also lacks water permeability and allows passive NaCl exit. The distal convoluted tubule sits in the cortex and does not participate in the countercurrent loop.

questions.q: Which transporter on the apical membrane of the thick ascending limb moves salt out of the tubular fluid?
options: The Na+ K+ 2Cl- symporter
The Na+ Cl- symporter
The Na+ H+ antiporter
The Na+ glucose symporter
questions.why: The thick ascending limb uses the Na+ K+ 2Cl- symporter, which is why loop diuretics act there and why this segment can move a large salt load into the medullary interstitium. The Na+ H+ antiporter is the proximal tubule exchanger tied to bicarbonate reclamation. The Na+ glucose symporter is also proximal and is spent by the end of that segment. The Na+ Cl- symporter belongs to the distal convoluted tubule.

questions.q: Which nephron segment carries the Na+ Cl- symporter that thiazide diuretics block?
options: The proximal convoluted tubule
The descending thin limb
The collecting duct
The distal convoluted tubule
questions.why: The distal convoluted tubule reabsorbs sodium and chloride together through the Na+ Cl- symporter and is the thiazide sensitive segment. The proximal tubule uses coupled transport driven by the sodium gradient but not this symporter. The descending thin limb moves water, not salt, by active transport. The collecting duct reabsorbs sodium through epithelial sodium channels in principal cells.

questions.q: Which collecting duct cell type secretes H+ and reclaims bicarbonate?
options: Principal cells
Intercalated cells
Macula densa cells
Granular cells
questions.why: Intercalated cells carry proton pumps and carbonic anhydrase and are the collecting duct's acid base workers. Principal cells sit alongside them but handle sodium, potassium and water. Macula densa cells are in the thick ascending limb and sense NaCl delivery. Granular cells are in the afferent arteriole wall and release renin.

questions.q: Which collecting duct cell inserts aquaporin 2 channels into its apical membrane when antidiuretic hormone is present?
options: The principal cell
The mesangial cell
The intercalated cell
The podocyte
questions.why: Antidiuretic hormone binds principal cells, raises cyclic AMP, and moves aquaporin 2 containing vesicles into the apical membrane so water can follow the medullary gradient. Intercalated cells handle H+ and bicarbonate and are not the water route. Podocytes are part of the filtration membrane in the renal corpuscle. Mesangial cells sit among glomerular capillaries and adjust filtration surface area.

questions.q: Which nephron type has long loops of Henle that descend deep into the medulla?
options: Both types equally
Neither type, since all loops stay in the cortex
Juxtamedullary nephrons
Cortical nephrons
questions.why: Juxtamedullary nephrons have glomeruli near the cortex medulla border and loops that reach far into the medulla, which is what allows a steep osmotic gradient to form. Cortical nephrons make up the large majority but have short loops that barely enter the outer medulla. The two types differ specifically in loop length, so treating them as equal misses the point. All loops entering the medulla is exactly what defines the juxtamedullary group.

questions.q: Which capillary network runs alongside the long loops of juxtamedullary nephrons?
options: The peritubular capillaries of the cortex
The vasa recta
The arcuate arteries
The glomerular capillaries
questions.why: The vasa recta are long straight capillaries that follow the loop into the medulla and remove reabsorbed water without washing out the salt gradient. Glomerular capillaries are the filtering bed inside the renal corpuscle. Cortical peritubular capillaries surround convoluted tubules in the cortex only. Arcuate arteries are supply vessels running along the cortex medulla junction, not exchange vessels.

questions.q: A nephron has a short loop that barely enters the medulla. Which capability is most limited?
options: Secreting H+ into the tubular fluid
Filtering plasma at the glomerulus
Reabsorbing filtered glucose
Producing a maximally concentrated urine
questions.why: Concentrating urine requires a steep medullary gradient, and that gradient is built by long loops, so a short looped cortical nephron contributes little to it. Glucose reabsorption happens in the proximal tubule and is unaffected by loop length. H+ secretion happens proximally and in the collecting duct. Filtration occurs at the renal corpuscle and does not depend on how far the loop descends.

questions.q: A patient cannot concentrate urine because the medullary osmotic gradient has collapsed. Which segment's transport function is most likely impaired?
options: The proximal convoluted tubule
The descending thin limb
The thick ascending limb
The distal convoluted tubule
questions.why: The thick ascending limb pumps salt into the medullary interstitium without letting water follow, and that single asymmetry is what builds the gradient. The proximal tubule reabsorbs isosmotically and adds nothing to medullary tonicity. The descending thin limb responds to the gradient rather than creating it. The distal convoluted tubule lies in the cortex, away from the medullary interstitium.

questions.q: A drug blocks the Na+ K+ 2Cl- symporter. What happens to the medullary osmotic gradient?
options: It becomes shallower
It becomes steeper
It is unchanged because the gradient depends on urea alone
It reverses so the medulla becomes dilute relative to cortex
questions.why: Blocking the symporter stops the thick ascending limb from loading salt into the interstitium, so medullary osmolarity falls toward plasma values and concentrating ability drops. The gradient cannot steepen when its main pump is off. Urea recycling contributes to the gradient but cannot maintain it without the salt component. Reversal would require actively pumping salt out of the medulla, which no segment does.

questions.q: Why is the fluid leaving the thick ascending limb hypo osmotic compared with plasma?
options: Urea is secreted into the tubular fluid
Both salt and water are removed in equal proportion
Water is added to the tubular fluid from the interstitium
Salt is removed while water cannot follow
questions.why: The segment is water impermeable, so pumping out Na+, K+ and Cl- lowers tubular osmolarity to roughly 100 mOsm/L, earning the name diluting segment. Water cannot move in because the segment blocks water flux in either direction. Urea secretion happens deeper in the medullary collecting duct and would not dilute the fluid. Removing salt and water together is isosmotic reabsorption, which is what the proximal tubule does instead.
questions.answerText: Salt is removed while water cannot follow

questions.q: What do macula densa cells sense in the tubular fluid?
options: The concentration of urea
The delivery rate of NaCl
The concentration of filtered albumin
The partial pressure of oxygen
questions.why: Macula densa cells sit where the thick ascending limb touches its own glomerulus and read NaCl delivery as a proxy for filtration rate, which drives tubuloglomerular feedback. Albumin should not be present in filtrate in appreciable amounts, so it carries no useful signal. Oxygen is sensed by peritubular cells for erythropoietin release. Urea concentration varies with water handling and is not the feedback signal.

questions.q: Antidiuretic hormone is released. Which segment changes its water permeability the most?
options: The collecting duct
The proximal convoluted tubule
The thick ascending limb
The descending thin limb
questions.why: The collecting duct is the segment whose water permeability is hormonally switchable, because aquaporin 2 insertion into principal cells is the regulated step. The proximal tubule is always highly water permeable through aquaporin 1 and is not regulated this way. The thick ascending limb stays water impermeable regardless of hormone. The descending thin limb is constitutively water permeable and also not regulated by the hormone.

questions.q: Aldosterone acts on principal cells of the collecting duct. Predict the movement of Na+ and K+.
options: Na+ reabsorption decreases and K+ secretion decreases
Na+ reabsorption increases and K+ secretion decreases
Na+ reabsorption increases and K+ secretion increases
Na+ secretion increases and K+ reabsorption increases
questions.why: Aldosterone raises the number of apical sodium channels and basolateral pumps, so sodium moves into the cell and blood while the resulting favorable electrical gradient drives potassium out into the tubule. Both falling together would describe removal of aldosterone. Sodium retention with potassium retention would leave the body unable to trade one for the other. The collecting duct does not secrete sodium or reabsorb potassium under aldosterone.
questions.answerText: Na+ reabsorption increases and K+ secretion increases

questions.q: Follow tubular fluid osmolarity through a juxtamedullary nephron. What is the sequence at the end of the proximal tubule, at the bend of the loop, and at the end of the thick ascending limb?
options: About 1200, then about 300, then about 100 mOsm/L
About 300, then about 1200, then about 100 mOsm/L
About 300, then about 100, then about 1200 mOsm/L
About 100, then about 300, then about 1200 mOsm/L
questions.why: Proximal reabsorption is isosmotic so fluid leaves at about 300, the water permeable descending limb concentrates it toward the medullary peak near 1200, and the salt pumping water impermeable ascending limb dilutes it to about 100. Diluting before concentrating reverses the anatomy of the limbs. Starting at 100 would require dilution in the proximal tubule, which reabsorbs isosmotically. Starting at 1200 would mean the filtrate was already maximally concentrated at the glomerulus.
questions.answerText: About 300, then about 1200, then about 100 mOsm/L

questions.q: A toxin selectively destroys juxtamedullary nephrons and spares cortical ones. Predict the maximum urine osmolarity the kidney can now reach and the effect on water conservation.
options: Maximum urine osmolarity is unchanged because antidiuretic hormone still acts on the collecting duct
Maximum urine osmolarity falls but water conservation improves because less solute is filtered
Maximum urine osmolarity rises and water conservation improves
Maximum urine osmolarity falls well below normal and water conservation is impaired
questions.why: Long loops build the medullary gradient, so losing them flattens the gradient and the collecting duct has nothing steep to draw water toward, capping urine osmolarity near plasma. Osmolarity cannot rise when the mechanism that raises it is gone. Antidiuretic hormone can still open water channels, but water only moves if a gradient exists, so hormone alone does not rescue concentration. Impaired concentration always worsens rather than improves water conservation.
questions.answerText: Maximum urine osmolarity falls well below normal and water conservation is impaired

questions.q: Blood flow through the vasa recta increases several fold. Predict the effect on the medullary interstitium and on urine concentrating ability.
options: Solute is washed out of the medulla but concentrating ability rises
Solute accumulates in the medulla and concentrating ability rises
Solute is washed out of the medulla and concentrating ability falls
The medulla is unaffected because the vasa recta carry only water
questions.why: The vasa recta work as countercurrent exchangers only when flow is slow enough for solute leaving the ascending limb of the vessel to reenter the descending limb, so high flow carries medullary solute away. Accumulation would require the vessels to deposit solute, which they do not. The vasa recta carry both water and solute, which is why washout is possible. Concentrating ability tracks the gradient, so it cannot rise while the gradient is being destroyed.
questions.answerText: Solute is washed out of the medulla and concentrating ability falls

questions.q: A patient has generalized proximal tubule dysfunction with normal function in all downstream segments. Which set of findings in the urine fits best?
options: Glucose, amino acids, and bicarbonate all appear in the urine
Only glucose appears in the urine, since other solutes are handled downstream
Only potassium wasting occurs, since the proximal tubule sets potassium balance
Urine is free of solute but the volume is very large
questions.why: The proximal tubule is where glucose, amino acids and most bicarbonate are reclaimed, and downstream segments have neither the transporters nor the capacity to make up for the loss, so all three spill. Isolated glucose loss would point to a single transporter defect rather than generalized segment failure. Potassium balance is set mainly in the collecting duct, which is intact here. A large solute free urine would describe a water handling problem such as diabetes insipidus.
questions.answerText: Glucose, amino acids, and bicarbonate all appear in the urine

questions.q: Which renal process moves fluid from glomerular capillary blood into the capsular space?
options: Reabsorption
Excretion
Secretion
Filtration
questions.why: Filtration is the bulk movement of protein free plasma across the filtration membrane, driven by pressure rather than by carriers. Secretion moves substances from peritubular blood into the tubule downstream of the glomerulus. Reabsorption runs the other way, from tubule back to blood. Excretion is what finally leaves the body in urine, not a step at the glomerulus.

questions.q: Which renal process moves a substance from the tubular fluid back into peritubular capillary blood?
options: Secretion
Reabsorption
Excretion
Filtration
questions.why: Reabsorption is the recovery step, and because most of what is filtered is useful, it accounts for the largest mass movement in the kidney. Filtration is the entry step at the glomerulus. Secretion moves in the opposite direction, from blood into tubule. Excretion is the final output and is what remains after reabsorption and secretion have acted.

questions.q: Which renal process adds a substance to tubular fluid from peritubular blood after the glomerulus?
options: Secretion
Reabsorption
Filtration
Excretion
questions.why: Secretion is a carrier mediated route that lets the kidney clear substances that were not fully filtered, including many drugs, H+ and K+. Reabsorption is the reverse direction. Filtration occurs only at the renal corpuscle and is pressure driven, not carrier driven. Excretion is the summed result appearing in urine.

questions.q: What term names the amount of a substance that actually leaves the body in the urine?
options: Filtration
Clearance
Excretion
Reabsorption
questions.why: Excretion is the net output, and it is measured as urine flow multiplied by urine concentration. Filtration is only the first of the three handling steps. Clearance is a derived volume per time, not an amount of substance. Reabsorption is a recovery step that reduces excretion rather than defining it.

questions.q: Which equation correctly relates the renal processes for any solute?
options: Excretion equals filtration plus reabsorption minus secretion
Excretion equals filtration minus reabsorption plus secretion
Filtration equals excretion minus reabsorption plus secretion
Excretion equals reabsorption plus secretion minus filtration
questions.why: What enters at the glomerulus, minus what is taken back, plus what is added later, is what leaves in urine. Adding reabsorption would mean recovery increases output, which reverses its meaning. Rearranging the equation with filtration on the left changes which quantity is being solved for and is not the standard statement. Making excretion depend on reabsorption plus secretion minus filtration inverts every sign.
questions.answerText: Excretion equals filtration minus reabsorption plus secretion

questions.q: How is the filtered load of a substance calculated?
options: Plasma concentration divided by urine concentration
Glomerular filtration rate divided by plasma concentration
Urine flow multiplied by urine concentration
Glomerular filtration rate multiplied by plasma concentration
questions.why: Filtered load is how much of a substance enters the tubule per minute, which is the filtered volume per minute times how concentrated the plasma is. Urine flow times urine concentration gives excretion rate, which is the output not the input. A ratio of concentrations has no units of amount per time. Dividing filtration rate by plasma concentration produces a nonsense quantity.
questions.answerText: Glomerular filtration rate multiplied by plasma concentration

questions.q: How is excretion rate calculated from a urine sample?
options: Urine flow rate divided by urine concentration
Urine concentration divided by plasma concentration
Urine flow rate multiplied by urine concentration
Urine flow rate multiplied by plasma concentration
questions.why: Multiplying volume per minute by amount per volume gives amount per minute, which is exactly the rate of loss in urine. Dividing flow by concentration inverts the units. A urine to plasma ratio is dimensionless and describes concentrating work, not output. Using plasma concentration with urine flow mixes two compartments and does not describe what left the body.
questions.answerText: Urine flow rate multiplied by urine concentration

questions.q: Which of the renal processes takes place across the filtration membrane rather than across tubular epithelial cells?
options: Filtration
Reabsorption
Secretion
Excretion
questions.why: Only filtration crosses the three layered filtration membrane in the renal corpuscle, and it is driven by Starling forces rather than transporters. Reabsorption and secretion both cross tubular epithelium using channels, carriers and pumps. Excretion is not a membrane crossing at all but the summed result that appears in urine.

questions.q: A solute is filtered at 100 mg/min and excreted at 20 mg/min, and it is not secreted. How much is reabsorbed?
options: 100 mg/min
120 mg/min
20 mg/min
80 mg/min
questions.why: With no secretion, excretion equals filtration minus reabsorption, so reabsorption is 100 minus 20, which is 80 mg/min. Getting 120 comes from adding rather than subtracting the excreted amount. Twenty is the excretion rate itself, not the amount recovered. One hundred would mean everything filtered was reabsorbed and nothing appeared in urine.

questions.q: A solute is filtered at 50 mg/min, secreted at 30 mg/min, and excreted at 60 mg/min. How much is reabsorbed?
options: 80 mg/min
20 mg/min
10 mg/min
40 mg/min
questions.why: Rearranging the equation, reabsorption equals filtration plus secretion minus excretion, so 50 plus 30 minus 60 is 20 mg/min. Ten would come from subtracting secretion instead of adding it. Forty ignores the secreted contribution entirely. Eighty is the total amount entering the tubule, before any recovery is subtracted.

questions.q: Glomerular filtration rate is 125 mL/min and plasma glucose is 100 mg/dL. What is the filtered load of glucose?
options: 125 mg/min
100 mg/min
12.5 mg/min
1250 mg/min
questions.why: A plasma glucose of 100 mg/dL is 1 mg/mL, so 125 mL/min times 1 mg/mL gives 125 mg/min. Getting 12.5 misplaces the decimal by treating plasma glucose as 0.1 mg/mL. Getting 1250 treats it as 10 mg/mL. One hundred simply repeats the plasma concentration without multiplying by the filtered volume.

questions.q: Urine flow is 1 mL/min and urine sodium concentration is 100 mEq/L. What is the sodium excretion rate?
options: 100 mEq/min
1 mEq/min
0.1 mEq/min
10 mEq/min
questions.why: One mL/min is 0.001 L/min, and 0.001 L/min times 100 mEq/L gives 0.1 mEq/min. One mEq/min would require ten times the urine flow or concentration. Ten and 100 mEq/min ignore the liter to milliliter conversion, and either value would represent a sodium loss the body could not sustain.

questions.q: A substance appears in urine at a higher rate than it is filtered. What must be true?
options: It undergoes net tubular reabsorption
It undergoes net tubular secretion
It is neither reabsorbed nor secreted
It is bound to plasma protein and cannot be filtered
questions.why: Output larger than input means the tubule added the substance downstream of the glomerulus, which is secretion. Net reabsorption would lower excretion below the filtered load. If neither process acted, excretion would exactly equal the filtered load. Heavy protein binding lowers the filtered load but by itself cannot make excretion exceed it.

questions.q: A freely filtered substance is neither reabsorbed nor secreted. What is the relationship between its filtration and excretion rates?
options: Excretion rate is half the filtration rate
Excretion rate exceeds the filtration rate
Excretion rate is zero
Excretion rate equals filtration rate
questions.why: With no tubular handling, whatever enters the tubule leaves in urine, which is exactly why inulin is used to measure filtration rate. Half would require reabsorption of half the filtered load. Exceeding filtration would require secretion. Zero excretion would mean complete reabsorption, which is the glucose case at normal plasma levels.

questions.q: Glomerular filtration rate is 125 mL/min and plasma sodium is 140 mEq/L. What is the filtered load of sodium?
options: 1.75 mEq/min
140 mEq/min
17.5 mEq/min
175 mEq/min
questions.why: Converting 125 mL/min to 0.125 L/min and multiplying by 140 mEq/L gives 17.5 mEq/min. Getting 1.75 misplaces the decimal by a factor of ten. Repeating 140 leaves out the filtered volume entirely. Getting 175 treats the filtration rate as 1.25 L/min, which is ten times too fast.

questions.q: Sodium is filtered at 17.5 mEq/min and excreted at 0.175 mEq/min. What fraction of the filtered sodium is reabsorbed?
options: About 99 percent
About 50 percent
About 65 percent
About 90 percent
questions.why: Excretion divided by filtered load is 0.175 divided by 17.5, which is 0.01 or one percent, so 99 percent is reabsorbed across the whole nephron. Sixty five percent is the proximal tubule's share alone, not the total. Ninety percent would leave ten times more sodium in urine than the numbers give. Fifty percent would represent a sodium loss incompatible with volume balance.

questions.q: For substance X, glomerular filtration rate is 100 mL/min, plasma concentration is 2 mg/mL, urine flow is 2 mL/min, and urine concentration is 150 mg/mL. What is the net tubular handling?
options: Net secretion of 300 mg/min
Neither reabsorption nor secretion
Net reabsorption of 100 mg/min
Net secretion of 100 mg/min
questions.why: The filtered load is 100 mL/min times 2 mg/mL, which is 200 mg/min, and excretion is 2 mL/min times 150 mg/mL, which is 300 mg/min, so the tubule added 100 mg/min. Reabsorption would require excretion below 200 mg/min. Three hundred is the total excretion rate, not the secreted increment. Equality of filtration and excretion would require an excretion rate of 200 mg/min.

questions.q: Para aminohippurate is filtered and then heavily secreted by the proximal tubule, so almost none remains in the renal vein. Which statement about its handling is correct?
options: Its excretion rate is below its filtered load because it is partly reabsorbed
Its excretion rate exceeds its filtered load because secretion adds to filtration
Its excretion rate cannot be measured because it is protein bound
Its excretion rate equals its filtered load because secretion balances reabsorption
questions.why: Filtration delivers only the plasma fraction that crosses the membrane, and secretion strips most of the rest from peritubular blood, so total output exceeds what filtration alone supplied. Equality would require no net secretion. Falling below the filtered load would require reabsorption, which the proximal tubule does not do for this substance. Excretion is measured from urine and is not blocked by protein binding.
questions.answerText: Its excretion rate exceeds its filtered load because secretion adds to filtration

questions.q: A drug is normally filtered and then secreted by the proximal tubule. A second drug blocks that secretory carrier. Predict the first drug's excretion rate and plasma concentration.
options: Excretion rate falls and plasma concentration rises
Excretion rate falls and plasma concentration also falls
Excretion rate is unchanged because filtration continues
Excretion rate rises and plasma concentration falls
questions.why: Removing the secretory component leaves only the filtered fraction to be excreted, so output drops and the drug accumulates in plasma until a new steady state is reached. A rise in excretion would require the blocker to help transport rather than hinder it. Plasma cannot fall while the route out of the body is narrowed. Filtration continuing does keep some excretion going, but at a lower total rate than before.
questions.answerText: Excretion rate falls and plasma concentration rises

questions.q: Which layer of the filtration membrane does plasma cross first?
options: The podocyte filtration slits
The parietal layer of the glomerular capsule
The fenestrated capillary endothelium
The glomerular basement membrane
questions.why: Plasma leaves the capillary lumen first, so the endothelium with its large pores is the first barrier and it excludes blood cells and platelets. The basement membrane is the middle layer. The podocyte slits are the last layer before the capsular space. The parietal layer lines the outside of the capsule and is not part of the filter.

questions.q: Which layer of the filtration membrane carries the fixed negative charge that repels anionic proteins?
options: The capillary endothelium
The basement membrane
The parietal capsule layer
The mesangium
questions.why: Heparan sulfate proteoglycans in the basement membrane give it a strong negative charge, so anionic plasma proteins are repelled before size alone would stop them. The endothelium contributes some surface charge but its fenestrations are large and its main job is excluding cells. The parietal layer is not part of the filter. The mesangium supports capillary loops and adjusts surface area rather than acting as a charge barrier.

questions.q: Which cells form the outermost layer of the filtration membrane?
options: Granular cells
Principal cells
Mesangial cells
Podocytes
questions.why: Podocytes wrap the capillary with foot processes whose interdigitating gaps form the final size selective barrier. Principal cells belong to the collecting duct and handle sodium and water. Mesangial cells lie between capillary loops and contract to change filtration surface area. Granular cells are in the afferent arteriole wall and release renin.

questions.q: What are the narrow gaps between adjacent podocyte foot processes called?
options: Gap junctions
Fenestrations
Filtration slits
Tight junctions
questions.why: The gaps are filtration slits, and each is bridged by a slit diaphragm that sets the effective size cutoff. Fenestrations are the pores through the capillary endothelium, one layer inward. Tight junctions seal neighboring epithelial cells and would prevent flow rather than permit it. Gap junctions connect cell interiors for electrical and chemical coupling.

questions.q: Which plasma protein is essentially excluded from normal filtrate, so that finding it in urine signals filtration membrane damage?
options: Albumin
Insulin
Angiotensin II
Myoglobin
questions.why: Albumin is both large and negatively charged, so a healthy membrane blocks it twice over and urine albumin points to a damaged barrier. Insulin is a small peptide that is filtered readily. Angiotensin II is a short peptide and crosses easily. Myoglobin is small enough to be filtered and appears in urine after muscle injury without any glomerular damage.

questions.q: Which blood component is completely excluded by the fenestrated endothelium of the glomerular capillary?
options: Water
Glucose
Sodium ions
Red blood cells
questions.why: Endothelial fenestrations are large by capillary standards but far smaller than a red blood cell, so formed elements never enter the filtrate and their presence in urine always signals a problem. Glucose is small and freely filtered. Sodium ions are tiny and pass without hindrance. Water crosses in bulk, since bulk water movement is the point of filtration.

questions.q: Which description best fits a substance that is freely filtered?
options: Its concentration in the filtrate is higher than in plasma water
Its concentration in the filtrate equals its concentration in plasma water
It appears in the filtrate only when plasma levels are high
It is actively pumped across the filtration membrane
questions.why: Free filtration means the membrane offers no resistance, so filtrate and plasma water hold the same concentration and the filtered load is simply filtration rate times plasma concentration. Filtration is pressure driven bulk flow, not active pumping. Concentrating a solute above plasma would require a transporter, which the membrane does not have. Appearing only at high plasma levels describes a partially restricted substance, not a freely filtered one.
questions.answerText: Its concentration in the filtrate equals its concentration in plasma water

questions.q: Roughly what molecular size passes the filtration membrane without restriction?
options: Molecules below about 5000 daltons
Molecules below about 70000 daltons
Molecules below about 200000 daltons
Molecules of any size, since only charge matters
questions.why: Small solutes under roughly 5000 daltons cross freely, which covers ions, glucose, amino acids and urea. Seventy thousand daltons is about the size of albumin, which is largely excluded rather than freely filtered. Two hundred thousand daltons is well above the cutoff and describes proteins that never appear in filtrate. Charge modifies filterability but size sets the primary limit.

questions.q: Which of the following is filtered most freely at the glomerulus?
options: A red blood cell
Albumin
Glucose
Hemoglobin bound to haptoglobin
questions.why: Glucose has a molecular weight of only 180 daltons and no charge barrier acting against it, so it enters filtrate at the same concentration as plasma. Red blood cells are stopped at the endothelium. Albumin is stopped by both size and negative charge. Hemoglobin bound to haptoglobin forms a complex too large to cross, which is why free hemoglobin is filtered but the bound form is not.

questions.q: Two molecules have the same radius, but one is negatively charged and one is neutral. Which is filtered more readily?
options: Neither is filtered, since charged molecules block the pores
The neutral molecule
The negatively charged molecule
They are filtered equally because size alone matters
questions.why: The fixed negative charge of the basement membrane repels anions, so at equal size the neutral molecule crosses more easily. The anion is the one held back, not favored. Charge does matter alongside size, which is why the two barriers are described separately. Charged molecules do not block pores, and small cations actually filter slightly better than neutral ones of the same size.

questions.q: A disease strips the negative charge from the glomerular basement membrane but leaves pore size normal. What appears in the urine?
options: Glucose
Nothing new, since pore size is unchanged
Red blood cells
Albumin
questions.why: Albumin sits close to the size limit and is held back mainly by charge repulsion, so removing charge alone lets it through. Red blood cells are excluded by size at the endothelium, which is intact. Glucose is already freely filtered and is fully reabsorbed proximally, so it does not appear. Charge loss by itself is enough to cause proteinuria, so nothing new is not correct.

questions.q: About forty percent of plasma calcium is bound to albumin. What happens to that bound fraction at the glomerulus?
options: It is filtered only when plasma calcium is low
It is filtered normally, since calcium ions are small
It is not filtered, because the albumin carrying it cannot cross
It is filtered and then completely secreted back
questions.why: Filterability depends on the size of the whole complex, so calcium riding on albumin stays in the capillary while free ionized calcium crosses easily. The small size of a calcium ion does not help once it is bound. Secretion is a tubular process and does not undo filtration at the glomerulus. Plasma calcium level changes how much is free but does not change the rule for the bound fraction.
questions.answerText: It is not filtered, because the albumin carrying it cannot cross

questions.q: A drug is 90 percent bound to plasma protein. What fraction of the plasma drug concentration is available for filtration?
options: 10 percent
90 percent
50 percent
100 percent
questions.why: Only the free drug crosses the filtration membrane, so the filterable fraction is the ten percent that is unbound and the filtered load is calculated from that portion. Ninety percent is the bound fraction, which is retained. Fifty percent does not match the stated binding. One hundred percent would apply only to a drug with no protein binding at all.

questions.q: A urine sample contains red blood cells and casts made of red blood cells. Where is the most likely site of injury?
options: The renal pelvis
The urethra
The urinary bladder wall
The glomerular filtration membrane
questions.why: Casts form inside tubules, so cells packed into a cast must have entered upstream, which means they crossed a damaged filtration membrane. Bleeding from the bladder puts cells into urine that has already left the tubule, so no casts form. Pelvic bleeding is likewise downstream of the tubules. Urethral bleeding is the furthest downstream of all.

questions.q: A small cation and a small anion have identical radii. Which crosses the filtration membrane more readily?
options: The anion
The cation
Both equally, because they are the same size
Neither, because ions require transporters
questions.why: The negatively charged basement membrane attracts cations and repels anions, so at equal size the cation is favored. The anion faces repulsion. Equal treatment would only be true if the membrane had no fixed charge. Ions do not need transporters to be filtered, since filtration is bulk flow through a porous barrier.

questions.q: A patient loses large amounts of albumin in the urine over several weeks. Trace the consequence for plasma colloid osmotic pressure and for tissue fluid.
options: Plasma colloid osmotic pressure falls and fluid accumulates in tissues
Plasma colloid osmotic pressure falls and tissues become dehydrated
Plasma colloid osmotic pressure is unchanged because the liver replaces albumin exactly
Plasma colloid osmotic pressure rises and fluid moves out of tissues
questions.why: Albumin is the main protein holding water in capillaries, so losing it lowers plasma colloid osmotic pressure and systemic capillaries reabsorb less at their venous ends, leaving fluid in the interstitium. Pressure cannot rise while the protein is being lost. Falling colloid osmotic pressure pushes fluid into tissues, not out of them. Liver synthesis increases but does not keep pace with heavy urinary loss.
questions.answerText: Plasma colloid osmotic pressure falls and fluid accumulates in tissues

questions.q: Three neutral molecules have radii of 1.5, 3.0, and 4.5 nanometers. Rank their filterability from highest to lowest.
options: 4.5 nanometers, then 3.0, then 1.5
3.0 nanometers, then 1.5, then 4.5
1.5 nanometers, then 3.0, then 4.5
All three are filtered equally because none carries a charge
questions.why: With charge held constant, filterability falls steadily as radius rises, because the slit diaphragm and basement membrane mesh impose a size limit. Ranking largest first reverses the physical barrier. Placing the middle size at the top has no mechanistic basis. Neutrality removes the charge penalty but does nothing to remove the size restriction.

questions.q: Podocyte foot processes flatten and fuse, widening the filtration slits. Predict what newly appears in the filtrate and what happens to urine protein.
options: Only water and small ions enter the filtrate and urine protein falls
Plasma proteins including albumin enter the filtrate and urine protein rises
Red blood cells enter the filtrate and urine protein is unchanged
Filtration stops completely and urine protein cannot be measured
questions.why: The slit diaphragm is the final size barrier, so losing its architecture lets proteins near the albumin size range cross and spill into urine. Water and small ions already crossed freely before the injury, so their passage is not new. Red cells are still held back by the endothelium unless that layer is also damaged. Filtration continues and may even rise as plasma protein falls.
questions.answerText: Plasma proteins including albumin enter the filtrate and urine protein rises

questions.q: A patient takes a drug that is 95 percent albumin bound. A second drug is added that competes for the same albumin binding sites, raising the free fraction of the first drug to 20 percent. What happens to the filtered load of the first drug?
options: It is unchanged because total plasma concentration has not changed
It falls to zero because the second drug occupies the transporter
