It falls by about half
It rises about fourfold
questions.why: Only free drug is filtered, so raising the free fraction from 5 percent to 20 percent multiplies the filterable concentration by four and the filtered load rises in proportion. A fall would require more binding, not less. Total plasma concentration is the wrong quantity, since the membrane sees only the unbound portion. Filtration uses no transporter, so competition at a carrier is not the mechanism here.

questions.q: Which pressure favors filtration at the glomerulus?
options: Peritubular hydrostatic pressure
Capsular hydrostatic pressure
Glomerular hydrostatic pressure
Glomerular colloid osmotic pressure
questions.why: Blood pressure inside the glomerular capillary is the only force pushing fluid out into the capsular space, and it is unusually high because both ends of the bed are arterioles. Capsular hydrostatic pressure pushes back from the filtrate side. Colloid osmotic pressure holds water in the capillary. Peritubular hydrostatic pressure acts downstream at the tubule, not at the filter.

questions.q: Which pressure opposes filtration because fluid already in the capsular space pushes back?
options: Capsular hydrostatic pressure
Capsular colloid osmotic pressure
Glomerular hydrostatic pressure
Glomerular colloid osmotic pressure
questions.why: Filtrate collecting in the capsule exerts a back pressure of roughly 15 mmHg that must be overcome by capillary pressure. Glomerular hydrostatic pressure is the driving force, not an opposing one. Glomerular colloid osmotic pressure also opposes filtration but does so by osmosis, not by fluid pressure. Capsular colloid osmotic pressure is essentially zero because the filtrate holds almost no protein.

questions.q: Which pressure opposes filtration because plasma proteins hold water inside the capillary?
options: Capsular hydrostatic pressure
Glomerular hydrostatic pressure
Renal interstitial pressure
Glomerular colloid osmotic pressure
questions.why: Proteins left behind in the capillary raise the osmotic pull of plasma, roughly 30 mmHg, and that pull resists water leaving. Capsular hydrostatic pressure also opposes filtration but through mechanical back pressure. Glomerular hydrostatic pressure is the force in favor. Renal interstitial pressure affects peritubular exchange rather than glomerular filtration.

questions.q: What is the typical glomerular hydrostatic pressure in a healthy adult?
options: About 30 mmHg
About 55 mmHg
About 90 mmHg
About 15 mmHg
questions.why: Glomerular capillary pressure sits near 55 mmHg, much higher than a typical systemic capillary, because an arteriole sits on each side of the bed. Fifteen mmHg is the usual capsular pressure. Thirty mmHg is the usual colloid osmotic pressure. Ninety mmHg would approach mean arterial pressure and would damage the filtration membrane.

questions.q: What is the typical capsular hydrostatic pressure?
options: About 15 mmHg
About 30 mmHg
About 45 mmHg
About 5 mmHg
questions.why: Filtrate in the capsular space generates roughly 15 mmHg of back pressure. Thirty mmHg matches the colloid osmotic pressure of plasma instead. Forty five mmHg would nearly abolish filtration on its own. Five mmHg would understate the resistance the capsule provides and would give a net filtration pressure well above the observed value.

questions.q: What is the typical glomerular colloid osmotic pressure?
options: About 55 mmHg
About 15 mmHg
About 30 mmHg
About 10 mmHg
questions.why: Plasma proteins produce about 30 mmHg of osmotic pull, and this value rises along the capillary as protein free fluid leaves. Ten mmHg is the net filtration pressure, not the protein contribution. Fifty five mmHg is the glomerular hydrostatic pressure. Fifteen mmHg is the capsular pressure.

questions.q: What is the typical net filtration pressure at the glomerulus?
options: About 25 mmHg
About 10 mmHg
About 40 mmHg
About 55 mmHg
questions.why: Taking 55 mmHg and subtracting 15 and 30 leaves about 10 mmHg, a modest net force that nonetheless produces 180 liters of filtrate per day because the surface area and permeability are so large. Twenty five mmHg would result from ignoring the capsular pressure. Forty mmHg would result from ignoring colloid osmotic pressure. Fifty five mmHg is the driving pressure before any opposition is subtracted.

questions.q: What is the normal glomerular filtration rate for a healthy adult?
options: About 1250 mL/min
About 12 mL/min
About 625 mL/min
About 125 mL/min
questions.why: A filtration rate near 125 mL/min works out to about 180 liters per day, of which more than 99 percent is reabsorbed. Twelve mL/min would represent severe kidney failure. Six hundred twenty five mL/min is closer to renal plasma flow, which is a different quantity. Twelve hundred fifty mL/min exceeds even total renal blood flow.

questions.q: Glomerular hydrostatic pressure is 60 mmHg, capsular pressure is 18 mmHg, and colloid osmotic pressure is 28 mmHg. What is the net filtration pressure?
options: 70 mmHg
32 mmHg
14 mmHg
42 mmHg
questions.why: Net filtration pressure is 60 minus 18 minus 28, which is 14 mmHg. Forty two comes from subtracting only the capsular pressure. Seventy comes from adding the opposing pressures instead of subtracting them. Thirty two comes from subtracting only the colloid osmotic pressure.

questions.q: Glomerular hydrostatic pressure is 50 mmHg, capsular pressure is 10 mmHg, and colloid osmotic pressure is 25 mmHg. What is the net filtration pressure?
options: 15 mmHg
40 mmHg
35 mmHg
25 mmHg
questions.why: Subtracting both opposing forces gives 50 minus 10 minus 25, which is 15 mmHg. Thirty five leaves out the colloid osmotic pressure. Twenty five leaves out the capsular pressure and mistakenly uses the colloid value. Forty adds the capsular pressure back instead of removing it.

questions.q: A stone partly obstructs the ureter, raising capsular hydrostatic pressure from 15 to 25 mmHg with glomerular hydrostatic pressure at 55 mmHg and colloid osmotic pressure at 30 mmHg. What is the new net filtration pressure?
options: 20 mmHg
5 mmHg
10 mmHg
0 mmHg
questions.why: The calculation is 55 minus 25 minus 30, which is exactly zero, so filtration stops in that kidney. Ten mmHg was the value before the obstruction. Twenty mmHg would require the capsular pressure to fall rather than rise. Five mmHg does not follow from any correct arrangement of these three numbers.

questions.q: Severe dehydration raises plasma protein concentration. What happens to net filtration pressure and glomerular filtration rate?
options: Both rise
Both fall
Net filtration pressure rises and filtration rate falls
Net filtration pressure falls and filtration rate rises
questions.why: More concentrated plasma protein raises colloid osmotic pressure, which is subtracted in the net filtration equation, so the net force and the filtration rate both drop. A rise would require protein to become more dilute. Net filtration pressure and filtration rate move together when the filtration coefficient is unchanged, so answers that split them apart are inconsistent.

questions.q: Advanced liver disease lowers plasma albumin substantially. What happens to net filtration pressure at the glomerulus?
options: It rises, because colloid osmotic pressure is lower
It rises, because capsular pressure is lower
It is unchanged, because filtration depends only on blood pressure
It falls, because colloid osmotic pressure is lower
questions.why: Colloid osmotic pressure is one of the two subtracted terms, so lowering it leaves a larger net force pushing fluid out. Falling net pressure would require the opposing forces to grow. Capsular pressure is set by filtrate outflow and is not changed by albumin levels. Filtration depends on all three pressures, not on blood pressure alone.
questions.answerText: It rises, because colloid osmotic pressure is lower

questions.q: Why is colloid osmotic pressure in the capsular space treated as essentially zero?
options: Podocytes actively pump protein back into the blood
The capsular space is too small to hold osmotic force
The filtrate contains almost no protein
Protein in the filtrate is neutralized by bicarbonate
questions.why: Colloid osmotic pressure comes from protein, and a healthy filtration membrane keeps protein in the capillary, so the capsular fluid exerts none. Volume of the space is irrelevant to osmotic pressure, which depends on concentration. Bicarbonate does not neutralize osmotic activity. Podocytes form a barrier but do not pump protein back.
questions.answerText: The filtrate contains almost no protein

questions.q: Disease destroys many glomeruli, reducing the total filtration surface area. Net filtration pressure is unchanged. What happens to glomerular filtration rate?
options: It is unchanged, because net filtration pressure sets the rate
It falls, because the filtration coefficient is smaller
It falls, because colloid osmotic pressure rises
It rises, because the remaining glomeruli work harder
questions.why: Filtration rate is the filtration coefficient multiplied by net filtration pressure, and the coefficient combines surface area with membrane permeability, so losing area lowers the rate even at unchanged pressure. Remaining glomeruli do compensate somewhat but cannot restore the lost surface. Net filtration pressure alone does not set the rate. Colloid osmotic pressure is unchanged in this scenario.
questions.answerText: It falls, because the filtration coefficient is smaller

questions.q: A kidney stone fully blocks one ureter. Capsular pressure rises from 15 to 30 mmHg while glomerular hydrostatic pressure stays at 55 mmHg and colloid osmotic pressure stays at 30 mmHg. What is the net filtration pressure and what happens to filtration?
options: Net filtration pressure is 25 mmHg, so filtration increases
Net filtration pressure is 40 mmHg, so filtration increases sharply
Net filtration pressure is 10 mmHg, so filtration continues normally
Net filtration pressure is negative 5 mmHg, so filtration in that kidney stops
questions.why: The arithmetic is 55 minus 30 minus 30, which is negative 5 mmHg, and a negative net force means no filtrate is formed. Ten mmHg is the value before the obstruction. Twenty five mmHg would require the capsular pressure to be zero. Forty mmHg would require ignoring the colloid osmotic term altogether.
questions.answerText: Net filtration pressure is negative 5 mmHg, so filtration in that kidney stops

questions.q: In nephrotic syndrome plasma protein loss lowers glomerular colloid osmotic pressure from 30 to 15 mmHg. Glomerular hydrostatic pressure is 55 mmHg and capsular pressure is 15 mmHg. How does net filtration pressure change?
options: It stays at 10 mmHg because hydrostatic pressure did not change
It falls from 10 to 5 mmHg
It rises from 10 to 25 mmHg
It rises from 10 to 40 mmHg
questions.why: Before the change the net force is 55 minus 15 minus 30, which is 10 mmHg, and afterward it is 55 minus 15 minus 15, which is 25 mmHg. A fall would require the opposing forces to grow. Forty mmHg would result from dropping the colloid term to zero rather than to 15. Because colloid osmotic pressure is part of the equation, the net pressure cannot stay fixed when it changes.

questions.q: Hemorrhage drops glomerular hydrostatic pressure from 55 to 40 mmHg while capsular pressure stays at 15 mmHg and colloid osmotic pressure stays at 30 mmHg. What is the net filtration pressure, and what does the result show?
options: Negative 5 mmHg, showing why autoregulation must defend glomerular pressure
5 mmHg, showing that filtration continues at a reduced rate
10 mmHg, showing that filtration is unaffected by blood loss
25 mmHg, showing that filtration increases to conserve solute
questions.why: The arithmetic is 40 minus 15 minus 30, which is negative 5 mmHg, so filtration would cease entirely, which is exactly why myogenic and feedback mechanisms work to hold glomerular pressure up when systemic pressure falls. Five mmHg would come from subtracting only one opposing force. Ten mmHg is the normal value and ignores the pressure drop. Twenty five mmHg would require glomerular pressure to rise, not fall.
questions.answerText: Negative 5 mmHg, showing why autoregulation must defend glomerular pressure

questions.q: The filtration coefficient is 12.5 mL/min per mmHg and net filtration pressure is 12 mmHg. What is the glomerular filtration rate?
options: 104 mL/min
1.04 mL/min
125 mL/min
150 mL/min
questions.why: Filtration rate is the coefficient times the net pressure, so 12.5 times 12 is 150 mL/min. One hundred twenty five would correspond to a net pressure of 10 mmHg, the normal value rather than the one given. One hundred four comes from dividing the coefficient into the pressure product incorrectly. Dividing 12.5 by 12 gives about 1.04, which inverts the relationship.

questions.q: Over roughly what range of mean arterial pressure does renal autoregulation hold glomerular filtration rate nearly constant?
options: About 60 to 90 mmHg
About 80 to 180 mmHg
About 20 to 60 mmHg
About 100 to 250 mmHg
questions.why: Within roughly 80 to 180 mmHg the myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback adjust arteriolar tone enough to keep filtration steady. Twenty to 60 mmHg is below the range where filtration can be sustained at all. One hundred to 250 mmHg sets the lower limit too high, since autoregulation still works at 90 mmHg. Sixty to 90 mmHg describes far too narrow a window for a mechanism that also protects against hypertension.

questions.q: What does the myogenic mechanism do when the afferent arteriole is stretched by rising blood pressure?
options: The smooth muscle contracts
The endothelium releases renin
The arteriole becomes more permeable to water
The smooth muscle relaxes
questions.why: Stretch opens mechanically gated channels, depolarizes the smooth muscle, and causes contraction, which narrows the vessel and blunts the rise in glomerular pressure. Relaxation would let the pressure surge reach the glomerulus. Renin comes from granular cells and is a slower endocrine response, not the myogenic reflex. Arteriolar water permeability is not part of this mechanism.

questions.q: Which cells provide the sensor for tubuloglomerular feedback?
options: Granular cells of the afferent arteriole
Podocytes of the glomerular capsule
Macula densa cells of the thick ascending limb
Principal cells of the collecting duct
questions.why: Macula densa cells lie where the thick ascending limb passes its own glomerulus and read NaCl delivery, which reports on filtration rate. Granular cells are the effector that releases renin, not the sensor. Podocytes form the filtration barrier. Principal cells respond to aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone far downstream.
questions.answerText: Macula densa cells of the thick ascending limb

questions.q: When macula densa cells detect high NaCl delivery, which signal do they release to constrict the afferent arteriole?
options: Antidiuretic hormone
Adenosine
Nitric oxide
Aldosterone
questions.why: High sodium chloride delivery makes macula densa cells release ATP that is converted to adenosine, and adenosine constricts the afferent arteriole to lower filtration. Nitric oxide is a vasodilator and would move filtration the wrong way. Aldosterone is an adrenal steroid acting on the collecting duct. Antidiuretic hormone acts on water permeability, not on this feedback loop.

questions.q: Sympathetic norepinephrine constricts renal arterioles by acting on which receptor?
options: Nicotinic receptors
Beta 2 adrenergic receptors
Muscarinic receptors
Alpha 1 adrenergic receptors
questions.why: Alpha 1 receptors on arteriolar smooth muscle mediate vasoconstriction, and in the kidney this reduces renal blood flow and filtration during strong sympathetic drive. Beta 2 receptors cause vasodilation in other beds. Muscarinic receptors respond to acetylcholine and are not the main renal vascular control. Nicotinic receptors sit at ganglia and the neuromuscular junction, not on vascular smooth muscle.

questions.q: Which cells release renin in response to low perfusion pressure and sympathetic stimulation?
options: Intercalated cells of the collecting duct
Macula densa cells of the thick ascending limb
Granular cells of the afferent arteriole wall
Mesangial cells between the glomerular capillaries
questions.why: Granular cells are modified smooth muscle in the afferent arteriole wall and are the only source of renin in this pathway. Macula densa cells sense NaCl and signal to the granular cells rather than releasing renin themselves. Mesangial cells adjust filtration surface area. Intercalated cells handle acid base transport in the collecting duct.
questions.answerText: Granular cells of the afferent arteriole wall

questions.q: Angiotensin II at moderate levels constricts which renal arteriole preferentially?
options: The efferent arteriole
Both equally
Neither, since angiotensin II acts only on the tubule
The afferent arteriole
questions.why: Efferent arterioles are more sensitive to angiotensin II, so constricting them raises the pressure upstream in the glomerulus and helps defend filtration when perfusion is low. Preferential afferent constriction would lower glomerular pressure and reduce filtration, the opposite of the hormone's protective role. Equal constriction would remove the pressure advantage. Angiotensin II acts on both vessels and tubule, not on tubule alone.

questions.q: What is the effect of atrial natriuretic peptide on the afferent arteriole and glomerular filtration rate?
options: It has no vascular effect and acts only on collecting duct sodium channels
It constricts the afferent arteriole and lowers filtration rate
It dilates the afferent arteriole and lowers filtration rate
It dilates the afferent arteriole and raises filtration rate
questions.why: Released when atria are stretched by volume overload, atrial natriuretic peptide dilates the afferent arteriole, raising glomerular pressure and filtration so that more sodium and water can be excreted. Constriction would retain the excess volume it is meant to remove. Afferent dilation cannot lower filtration, since it raises glomerular hydrostatic pressure. The peptide does inhibit collecting duct sodium reabsorption as well, but it also acts on the arterioles.
questions.answerText: It dilates the afferent arteriole and raises filtration rate

questions.q: The afferent arteriole constricts. What happens to glomerular hydrostatic pressure and glomerular filtration rate?
options: Both rise
Both fall
Glomerular hydrostatic pressure rises and filtration rate falls
Glomerular hydrostatic pressure falls and filtration rate rises
questions.why: Constricting the vessel that feeds the glomerulus reduces inflow, so pressure inside the capillary bed drops and filtration falls with it. Both rising would describe efferent constriction instead. Glomerular pressure and filtration move in the same direction when the other Starling forces are unchanged, so the two split answers are internally inconsistent.

questions.q: The efferent arteriole constricts to a moderate degree. What happens to glomerular hydrostatic pressure and glomerular filtration rate?
options: Both rise
Neither changes, because the constriction is downstream of the glomerulus
Both fall
Glomerular hydrostatic pressure falls and filtration rate rises
questions.why: The efferent arteriole is the outflow resistor, so narrowing it dams blood in the glomerular capillaries, raises hydrostatic pressure there, and raises filtration rate. A fall in both would describe afferent constriction. Glomerular pressure cannot fall when outflow is restricted. Being downstream is exactly why the constriction raises upstream pressure rather than leaving it unchanged.

questions.q: The afferent arteriole dilates. What happens to glomerular filtration rate?
options: It is unchanged
It falls at first and then rises above baseline
It rises
It falls
questions.why: Widening the inflow vessel lets more of the arterial pressure reach the glomerular capillaries, raising hydrostatic pressure and filtration. A fall would follow afferent constriction, not dilation. No change would require an opposing adjustment elsewhere that the question does not describe. There is no biphasic reversal here, since dilation acts in one direction only.

questions.q: The efferent arteriole dilates. What happens to glomerular hydrostatic pressure and glomerular filtration rate?
options: Both rise
Both fall
Glomerular hydrostatic pressure rises and filtration rate falls
Only renal blood flow changes, with no effect on filtration
questions.why: Opening the outflow resistor lets blood escape the glomerulus more easily, so capillary pressure drops and filtration falls even though total renal blood flow may increase. A rise in both would follow efferent constriction. Pressure cannot rise when outflow resistance is reduced. Renal blood flow and filtration can move in opposite directions here, which is exactly why filtration is affected.

questions.q: Mean arterial pressure rises from 100 to 160 mmHg. What does the myogenic mechanism do, and what happens to glomerular filtration rate?
options: The afferent arteriole constricts and filtration rate falls far below normal
The afferent arteriole dilates and filtration rate rises sharply
The efferent arteriole constricts and filtration rate rises sharply
The afferent arteriole constricts and filtration rate stays near normal
questions.why: Stretch triggers afferent contraction, which raises inflow resistance just enough to absorb the extra pressure and hold filtration close to its set value. Dilation would let the pressure surge reach the glomerulus and damage it. Efferent constriction would add to filtration rather than protect against the rise. The response is calibrated to hold filtration steady, not to drive it below normal.
questions.answerText: The afferent arteriole constricts and filtration rate stays near normal

questions.q: Macula densa cells detect an unusually high NaCl concentration in the tubular fluid. What is the feedback response?
options: The efferent arteriole constricts and filtration rate rises
Renin release increases and filtration rate rises
The afferent arteriole constricts and filtration rate falls
The afferent arteriole dilates and filtration rate rises
questions.why: High NaCl delivery means filtration is running too fast for the tubule to keep up, so adenosine constricts the afferent arteriole and brings filtration back down. Dilation would worsen the overload. Efferent constriction would also raise filtration and worsen the mismatch. Renin release rises with low NaCl delivery, which is the opposite signal.
questions.answerText: The afferent arteriole constricts and filtration rate falls

questions.q: During severe hemorrhage, strong sympathetic outflow reaches the kidney. What is the effect on the afferent arteriole and on filtration rate?
options: The afferent arteriole constricts and filtration rate falls
The afferent arteriole constricts and filtration rate rises
The afferent arteriole is unaffected because sympathetic nerves reach only the tubule
The afferent arteriole dilates and filtration rate rises
questions.why: Strong alpha 1 stimulation constricts the afferent arteriole, cutting filtration so that fluid stays in the vascular compartment and blood can be redirected to brain and heart. Dilation would waste volume the body is trying to keep. Afferent constriction lowers glomerular pressure, so filtration cannot rise. Sympathetic fibers innervate both the arterioles and the granular cells, not the tubule alone.
questions.answerText: The afferent arteriole constricts and filtration rate falls

questions.q: A patient whose kidneys are already poorly perfused is given a drug that blocks angiotensin II formation. Trace the effect on efferent tone, glomerular hydrostatic pressure, and filtration rate.
options: Efferent tone rises, glomerular hydrostatic pressure rises, and filtration rate rises
Efferent tone falls, glomerular hydrostatic pressure rises, and filtration rate rises
Efferent tone is unchanged and filtration rate rises because systemic pressure falls
Efferent tone falls, glomerular hydrostatic pressure falls, and filtration rate falls
questions.why: Angiotensin II was holding the efferent arteriole partly closed to defend glomerular pressure, so removing it opens the outflow, capillary pressure falls, and filtration falls with it. Losing angiotensin II cannot raise efferent tone. Falling efferent tone and rising glomerular pressure are contradictory, since the efferent vessel is the outflow resistor. A fall in systemic pressure lowers rather than raises filtration.
questions.answerText: Efferent tone falls, glomerular hydrostatic pressure falls, and filtration rate falls

questions.q: Filtration rate drops, so NaCl delivery to the macula densa falls. Trace the corrective response back to filtration rate.
options: Adenosine release rises and the afferent arteriole constricts, so filtration rate falls further
Renin release rises and the afferent arteriole dilates, so filtration rate rises back toward normal
Renin release falls and the efferent arteriole dilates, so filtration rate falls further
Renin release rises and the afferent arteriole constricts, so filtration rate falls further
questions.why: Low sodium chloride at the macula densa signals that filtration is too low, so the cells reduce adenosine, allow afferent dilation, and stimulate granular cells to release renin, and angiotensin II then adds efferent constriction, both of which raise glomerular pressure. Rising adenosine and afferent constriction are the response to high, not low, sodium delivery. Falling renin with efferent dilation would drive filtration further down. Renin rising alongside afferent constriction pairs two opposing responses.
questions.answerText: Renin release rises and the afferent arteriole dilates, so filtration rate rises back toward normal

questions.q: A dehydrated patient with high sympathetic drive takes a drug that blocks renal prostaglandin synthesis. Prostaglandins normally dilate the afferent arteriole. Predict the effect on filtration rate and explain the mechanism.
options: Filtration rate falls, because afferent constriction is now unopposed
Filtration rate is unchanged, because myogenic autoregulation compensates fully
Filtration rate rises, because prostaglandins normally constrict the afferent arteriole
Filtration rate rises, because the efferent arteriole constricts more
questions.why: Local prostaglandins are the counterweight that keeps the afferent arteriole partly open during sympathetic vasoconstriction, so blocking them leaves constriction unopposed and glomerular pressure and filtration drop. Efferent tone is not increased by this drug. Myogenic autoregulation works against pressure changes and cannot offset a loss of local vasodilator tone. Prostaglandins dilate rather than constrict the afferent arteriole.
questions.answerText: Filtration rate falls, because afferent constriction is now unopposed

questions.q: Efferent constriction is increased from moderate to very severe. What happens to renal plasma flow and to glomerular filtration rate?
options: Renal plasma flow rises and filtration rate falls
Both renal plasma flow and filtration rate rise further
Renal plasma flow falls sharply and filtration rate now falls as well
Renal plasma flow falls sharply while filtration rate continues to rise
questions.why: Moderate efferent constriction raises glomerular pressure and filtration, but severe constriction chokes flow so much that plasma lingers in the capillary, filters a large fraction of its water, and its colloid osmotic pressure climbs steeply, which cancels the pressure advantage and drives filtration back down. Continued rising filtration ignores that rising colloid osmotic pressure. Renal plasma flow cannot rise while the outflow vessel is being narrowed. Both rising further would require the flow limitation to disappear.
questions.answerText: Renal plasma flow falls sharply and filtration rate now falls as well

questions.q: Which equation defines the renal clearance of a substance?
options: Clearance equals plasma concentration times urine flow rate, divided by urine concentration
Clearance equals urine concentration times urine flow rate, divided by plasma concentration
Clearance equals urine concentration divided by plasma concentration
Clearance equals plasma concentration divided by urine flow rate
questions.why: Clearance asks how many milliliters of plasma would have to be stripped clean each minute to account for the amount appearing in urine, so the excretion rate goes on top and the plasma concentration on the bottom. Swapping plasma and urine concentrations inverts the ratio. A bare urine to plasma ratio has no units of volume per time. Dividing plasma concentration by flow yields neither a rate nor a volume.
questions.answerText: Clearance equals urine concentration times urine flow rate, divided by plasma concentration

questions.q: In what units is renal clearance expressed?
options: mg/dL
mOsm/L
mg/min
mL/min
questions.why: Clearance is a virtual volume of plasma cleared per unit time, so the units are volume over time. Milligrams per minute is an excretion rate or a transport maximum, an amount rather than a volume. Milligrams per deciliter is a concentration. Milliosmoles per liter is an osmolarity.

questions.q: Which substance is the reference standard for measuring glomerular filtration rate?
options: Glucose
Urea
Inulin
Para aminohippurate
questions.why: Inulin is freely filtered and is neither reabsorbed nor secreted nor metabolized, so its clearance equals filtration rate exactly. Para aminohippurate is heavily secreted and is used to estimate renal plasma flow instead. Glucose is almost completely reabsorbed, so its clearance is near zero. Urea is partly reabsorbed, so its clearance underestimates filtration.

questions.q: Which property makes a substance suitable for measuring glomerular filtration rate by clearance?
options: It is freely filtered and is neither reabsorbed nor secreted
It is not filtered but is heavily secreted
It is bound to plasma protein so it stays in the capillary
It is filtered and then completely reabsorbed
questions.why: If the tubule neither adds nor removes the substance, everything appearing in urine came from filtration, so clearance and filtration rate are the same number. Complete reabsorption gives a clearance near zero and tells you nothing about filtration. Heavy secretion gives a clearance larger than filtration rate. Protein binding keeps the substance out of the filtrate, so it cannot report on filtration.
questions.answerText: It is freely filtered and is neither reabsorbed nor secreted

questions.q: Which endogenous substance is used clinically to estimate glomerular filtration rate without an infusion?
options: Para aminohippurate
Albumin
Inulin
Creatinine
questions.why: Creatinine is produced continuously by muscle and is cleared almost entirely by filtration, so its clearance can be measured from ordinary blood and urine samples. Albumin is not normally filtered at all. Inulin works beautifully but is not made by the body and must be infused. Para aminohippurate also has to be infused and reports plasma flow rather than filtration.

questions.q: Why does creatinine clearance slightly overestimate glomerular filtration rate?
options: A small amount of creatinine is reabsorbed by the proximal tubule
A small amount of creatinine is secreted by the proximal tubule
Creatinine is partly broken down in the tubular fluid
Creatinine is not freely filtered at the glomerulus
questions.why: Organic cation transporters add a modest amount of creatinine to the tubular fluid, so urinary output slightly exceeds the filtered load and the calculated clearance runs a little high. Reabsorption would push the estimate low rather than high. Creatinine is not metabolized in the tubule. It is in fact freely filtered, which is what makes it useful in the first place.
questions.answerText: A small amount of creatinine is secreted by the proximal tubule

questions.q: What does the clearance of a substance actually describe?
options: The volume of plasma completely cleared of that substance each minute
The volume of urine produced each minute
The mass of the substance filtered each minute
The fraction of the substance bound to plasma protein
questions.why: Clearance is a calculated volume, the amount of plasma that would have to give up all of the substance to supply what shows up in urine. Mass filtered per minute is the filtered load, a different quantity. Protein binding affects filterability but is not what clearance measures. Urine volume per minute is the urine flow rate, one of the inputs to the clearance calculation.
questions.answerText: The volume of plasma completely cleared of that substance each minute

questions.q: What is the approximate inulin clearance in a healthy young adult?
options: About 1 mL/min
About 625 mL/min
About 125 mL/min
About 25 mL/min
questions.why: Because inulin clearance equals glomerular filtration rate, the normal value is the normal filtration rate of about 125 mL/min. Six hundred twenty five mL/min is roughly renal plasma flow, which is what para aminohippurate clearance reports. Twenty five mL/min would indicate advanced kidney failure. One mL/min is closer to a typical urine flow rate.

questions.q: Urine inulin is 100 mg/mL, urine flow is 1.5 mL/min, and plasma inulin is 1.2 mg/mL. What is the glomerular filtration rate?
options: 150 mL/min
125 mL/min
180 mL/min
80 mL/min
questions.why: Excretion rate is 100 times 1.5, which is 150 mg/min, and dividing by the plasma concentration of 1.2 mg/mL gives 125 mL/min. One hundred fifty is the excretion rate in mg/min, not the clearance. One hundred eighty comes from multiplying by the plasma concentration instead of dividing. Eighty does not follow from any arrangement of these numbers.

questions.q: Urine concentration of a substance is 30 mg/mL, urine flow is 2 mL/min, and plasma concentration is 0.5 mg/mL. What is its clearance?
options: 15 mL/min
30 mL/min
60 mL/min
120 mL/min
questions.why: Excretion rate is 30 times 2, which is 60 mg/min, and dividing by 0.5 mg/mL gives 120 mL/min. Thirty repeats the urine concentration. Sixty is the excretion rate in mg/min before dividing by plasma concentration. Fifteen comes from multiplying by 0.5 instead of dividing.

questions.q: Plasma creatinine is 1 mg/dL, urine creatinine is 100 mg/dL, and urine flow is 1.25 mL/min. What is the creatinine clearance?
options: 1250 mL/min
12.5 mL/min
125 mL/min
100 mL/min
questions.why: The urine to plasma ratio is 100 to 1, and multiplying that ratio by the urine flow of 1.25 mL/min gives 125 mL/min. Twelve and a half misplaces the decimal by using a ratio of ten. One hundred uses the ratio alone without the flow rate. Twelve hundred fifty overstates the ratio by a factor of ten.

questions.q: A 24 hour urine collection totals 1440 mL with a creatinine concentration of 1.2 mg/mL. Plasma creatinine is 1.2 mg/dL. What is the creatinine clearance?
options: 100 mL/min
120 mL/min
144 mL/min
10 mL/min
questions.why: Dividing 1440 mL by 1440 minutes gives a urine flow of 1 mL/min, plasma creatinine of 1.2 mg/dL equals 0.012 mg/mL, and 1.2 times 1 divided by 0.012 gives 100 mL/min. One hundred twenty results from forgetting to convert mg/dL to mg/mL correctly. One hundred forty four comes from misusing the collection volume as a flow rate. Ten mL/min is off by a factor of ten in the unit conversion.

questions.q: Creatinine production is unchanged but plasma creatinine has doubled and remains steady at the new value. What has happened to glomerular filtration rate?
options: It is unchanged
It has fallen to about one quarter of normal
It has doubled
It has fallen by about half
questions.why: At steady state the kidney must excrete creatinine as fast as muscle makes it, so if production is constant, the product of filtration rate and plasma concentration is fixed, and doubling the concentration means the filtration rate halved. Doubling filtration would lower plasma creatinine, not raise it. No change would leave plasma creatinine at its original value. A drop to one quarter would have quadrupled plasma creatinine.
questions.answerText: It has fallen by about half

questions.q: A patient's measured inulin clearance is 100 mL/min. What is the glomerular filtration rate?
options: 500 mL/min
100 mL/min
It cannot be determined without the urine flow rate
125 mL/min
questions.why: Inulin clearance equals filtration rate by definition, since inulin is filtered and then left alone by the tubule, so the answer is the clearance value itself. One hundred twenty five is the textbook normal, not this patient's measured value. Five hundred is in the range of renal plasma flow. Urine flow was already used inside the clearance calculation, so no further data are needed.

questions.q: A person drinks a large volume of water, and urine flow doubles while urine inulin concentration halves. What happens to the calculated inulin clearance?
options: It is unchanged
It falls to zero
It doubles
It halves
questions.why: Clearance depends on the product of urine flow and urine concentration, and doubling one while halving the other leaves that product the same, so filtration rate reads the same. Doubling would require the excretion rate to rise. Halving would require it to fall. A clearance of zero would mean no inulin appeared in urine at all.

questions.q: A patient's plasma creatinine rises from 1.0 to 2.0 mg/dL over six months while muscle mass and creatinine production stay constant. Baseline filtration rate was 120 mL/min. What is the approximate current filtration rate?
options: About 30 mL/min
About 240 mL/min
About 60 mL/min
About 120 mL/min
questions.why: With constant production, filtration rate and plasma creatinine are inversely related at steady state, so a doubling of plasma creatinine corresponds to a halving of filtration rate, from 120 to about 60 mL/min. Two hundred forty inverts the relationship. One hundred twenty ignores the change entirely. Thirty would require plasma creatinine to have risen four fold, to 4.0 mg/dL.

questions.q: In the same patient, inulin clearance is 120 mL/min and the clearance of a drug is 480 mL/min. What does this tell you about the drug's handling, and by what factor does the tubule add to its filtered load?
options: It is net reabsorbed, and reabsorption removes three quarters of the filtered load
It is net secreted, and secretion adds three times the filtered load
It is net secreted, and secretion adds four times the filtered load
It is neither secreted nor reabsorbed, since clearance is a multiple of filtration rate
questions.why: Clearance four times filtration rate means total excretion is four times what filtration supplied, so the extra three parts came from secretion. Reabsorption would put clearance below the inulin value. Saying secretion adds four times the filtered load double counts the filtered part. A clearance that differs from inulin clearance always signals tubular handling, whether or not the ratio is a whole number.
questions.answerText: It is net secreted, and secretion adds three times the filtered load

questions.q: Para aminohippurate clearance is 625 mL/min and inulin clearance is 125 mL/min. What is the filtration fraction?
questions.why: Filtration fraction is filtration rate divided by renal plasma flow, and since para aminohippurate clearance estimates plasma flow, the calculation is 125 divided by 625, which is 0.20. Five inverts the ratio and would mean more plasma is filtered than arrives. Point eight is the fraction that leaves in the efferent arteriole unfiltered, not the fraction filtered. Point five would require plasma flow of only 250 mL/min.

questions.q: A 24 hour urine collection totals 2160 mL with a creatinine concentration of 80 mg/dL. Plasma creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL. What is the creatinine clearance?
options: 120 mL/min
100 mL/min
150 mL/min
15 mL/min
questions.why: Urine flow is 2160 divided by 1440 minutes, which is 1.5 mL/min, and the urine to plasma ratio is 80 divided by 0.8, which is 100, so the clearance is 100 times 1.5, or 150 mL/min. One hundred twenty would follow from a urine flow of 1.2 mL/min. One hundred uses the ratio without the flow rate. Fifteen misplaces the decimal in the ratio.

questions.q: A substance has a clearance lower than the glomerular filtration rate. What does that indicate?
options: Net tubular reabsorption
Net tubular secretion
No tubular handling at all
Failure of the filtration membrane
questions.why: A clearance below filtration rate means less of the substance left in urine than filtration delivered, so the tubule took some back. Secretion would push clearance above the filtration rate. No tubular handling would make the two values equal. A damaged filtration membrane changes what enters the tubule but does not by itself lower clearance below filtration rate.

questions.q: A substance has a clearance higher than the glomerular filtration rate. What does that indicate?
options: The substance is protein bound
Net tubular reabsorption
No tubular handling at all
Net tubular secretion
questions.why: More appeared in urine than filtration supplied, so the tubule must have added the difference from peritubular blood. Reabsorption removes rather than adds and would lower clearance. Equal clearance and filtration rate means no net handling. Protein binding lowers the filtered load, which by itself would reduce not raise clearance.

questions.q: A substance has a clearance exactly equal to the glomerular filtration rate. What does that indicate?
options: It is heavily secreted
It is neither reabsorbed nor secreted
It is heavily reabsorbed
It is not filtered at all
questions.why: When output matches the filtered load exactly, the tubule neither added nor removed any, which is the defining property of a filtration marker like inulin. Heavy secretion would raise clearance well above filtration rate. Heavy reabsorption would push it far below. A substance that is not filtered and not secreted would have a clearance near zero.
questions.answerText: It is neither reabsorbed nor secreted

questions.q: What is the clearance of glucose in a healthy person with normal plasma glucose?
options: Essentially zero
About equal to the filtration rate
About 625 mL/min
About half the filtration rate
questions.why: Glucose is freely filtered but then completely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, so none appears in urine and the clearance calculation gives essentially zero. A clearance equal to filtration rate would mean glucose is left untouched by the tubule. Six hundred twenty five mL/min describes para aminohippurate, which is heavily secreted. Half the filtration rate would mean half the filtered glucose is lost each day.

questions.q: Para aminohippurate has a clearance of about 625 mL/min while filtration rate is 125 mL/min. What does that comparison show?
options: It is metabolized by tubular cells before excretion
It is filtered and then heavily reabsorbed
It is filtered and then heavily secreted
It is not filtered but is reabsorbed from the interstitium
questions.why: Clearing five times more plasma than filtration alone could account for means the proximal tubule stripped the substance from peritubular blood and added it to the tubular fluid. Heavy reabsorption would drive clearance below 125 mL/min. Substances are not reabsorbed from the interstitium into urine. Tubular metabolism would destroy the substance and lower rather than raise its urinary output.
questions.answerText: It is filtered and then heavily secreted

questions.q: Urea clearance is about 65 to 70 mL/min while filtration rate is about 125 mL/min. What does this reveal about urea handling?
options: Urea is secreted along the whole nephron
About half the filtered urea is reabsorbed
Urea is not filtered because of its charge
Urea is completely reabsorbed like glucose
questions.why: A clearance roughly half the filtration rate means roughly half the filtered urea is recovered, which happens passively as water is reabsorbed and concentrates urea in the tubule. Net secretion would put clearance above filtration rate. Urea is small and uncharged and is filtered freely. Complete reabsorption would give a clearance of zero, which is the glucose pattern, not the urea pattern.
questions.answerText: About half the filtered urea is reabsorbed

questions.q: What term describes the clearance of a substance divided by the glomerular filtration rate?
options: Renal threshold
Filtration fraction
Transport maximum
Fractional excretion
questions.why: Fractional excretion is the share of the filtered load that ends up in urine, so it is below one for a reabsorbed substance and above one for a secreted one. Filtration fraction is filtration rate divided by renal plasma flow, a different ratio entirely. Transport maximum is the saturation rate of a carrier system. Renal threshold is the plasma concentration at which a substance first appears in urine.

questions.q: A substance's fractional excretion is greater than 1. What does that mean?
options: The filtration rate was measured incorrectly
More is filtered than is excreted, so it is net reabsorbed
More is excreted than was filtered, so it is net secreted
The substance is not filtered at the glomerulus
questions.why: A fractional excretion above one means urinary output exceeded the filtered load, which requires the tubule to have added the difference. A value below one is what indicates net reabsorption. A substance that is not filtered would still show secretion, but the fractional excretion would be undefined rather than simply greater than one. Values above one are physiologically ordinary for secreted substances and do not signal a measurement error.
questions.answerText: More is excreted than was filtered, so it is net secreted

questions.q: Glomerular filtration rate is 120 mL/min and the clearance of substance A is 20 mL/min. How is A handled?
options: It is net reabsorbed
It is neither reabsorbed nor secreted
It is not filtered
It is net secreted
questions.why: A clearance of 20 mL/min against a filtration rate of 120 mL/min means only about one sixth of the filtered load reached the urine, so five sixths was reabsorbed. Secretion would raise the clearance above 120. Equality at 120 would indicate no tubular handling. Being unfiltered would give a clearance near zero unless secretion occurred.

questions.q: Glomerular filtration rate is 120 mL/min and the clearance of substance B is 300 mL/min. How is B handled?
options: It is filtered but then metabolized
It is net reabsorbed
It is neither reabsorbed nor secreted
It is net secreted
questions.why: Clearance far above the filtration rate means the kidney removed the substance from more plasma than it filtered, which only secretion can accomplish. Reabsorption would lower clearance below 120 mL/min. No handling at all would leave clearance at 120 mL/min. Tubular metabolism would reduce urinary output and lower the calculated clearance.

questions.q: Inulin clearance is 125 mL/min and the clearance of substance C is also 125 mL/min. What can you conclude about C?
options: It is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule and secreted in the distal tubule
It is freely filtered and not handled by the tubule
It is filtered and then equally secreted and metabolized
It is heavily protein bound
questions.why: Matching inulin exactly is the signature of a substance that enters by filtration and is then left alone all the way down the nephron. Secretion balanced by metabolism is possible in principle but is not the simple interpretation and would be unusual physiology. Heavy protein binding would lower the filtered load and give a clearance well below the inulin value. Equal reabsorption and secretion in different segments is speculative and not what the matching numbers indicate.
questions.answerText: It is freely filtered and not handled by the tubule

questions.q: The fractional excretion of sodium is 0.5 percent. What fraction of the filtered sodium is reabsorbed?
options: 99.5 percent
0.5 percent
95 percent
50 percent
questions.why: Fractional excretion is the share that leaves in urine, so the rest is reclaimed, and 100 minus 0.5 gives 99.5 percent reabsorbed. Fifty percent confuses the decimal point in the percentage. Half a percent is the excreted share, not the reabsorbed share. Ninety five percent would correspond to a fractional excretion of 5 percent.

questions.q: A substance is freely filtered but its clearance is zero. What is the tubule doing?
options: Reabsorbing half the filtered load
Secreting the substance heavily
Reabsorbing all of the filtered load
Blocking it at the filtration membrane
questions.why: Zero clearance means nothing appears in urine, and since the substance did enter the tubule by filtration, all of it must have been reabsorbed, which is the normal fate of glucose. Secretion would produce a large clearance. Blockage at the membrane is ruled out by the statement that it is freely filtered. Reabsorbing only half would leave a measurable clearance.
questions.answerText: Reabsorbing all of the filtered load

questions.q: A substance's clearance is essentially equal to the total renal plasma flow. What does that tell you?
options: It is filtered but not secreted
Nearly all of it is removed from the plasma in a single pass
It is reabsorbed as fast as it is filtered
It leaves the kidney unchanged in the renal vein
questions.why: If the clearance matches plasma flow, then every milliliter of plasma reaching the kidney gives up virtually all of the substance, which requires both filtration and near complete secretion. Filtration without secretion caps clearance at the filtration rate, roughly one fifth of plasma flow. Rapid reabsorption would drive clearance toward zero. Leaving in the renal vein unchanged would mean very low clearance.
questions.answerText: Nearly all of it is removed from the plasma in a single pass

questions.q: Glomerular filtration rate is 100 mL/min and plasma concentration of substance D is 2 mg/mL. Urine flow is 1 mL/min and urine concentration is 100 mg/mL. What is the net tubular handling of D?
options: Net reabsorption of 200 mg/min
No net handling, since clearance equals filtration rate
Net secretion of 100 mg/min
Net reabsorption of 100 mg/min
questions.why: Filtered load is 100 mL/min times 2 mg/mL, which is 200 mg/min, and excretion is 1 mL/min times 100 mg/mL, which is 100 mg/min, so 100 mg/min was recovered and the clearance of 50 mL/min falls below the filtration rate as expected. Secretion would require excretion above 200 mg/min. Two hundred would mean nothing at all reached the urine. Clearance is 50, not 100, so the no handling option is ruled out by the arithmetic.

questions.q: A drug's clearance is 400 mL/min while inulin clearance is 125 mL/min. A second drug is then given and the first drug's clearance falls to 120 mL/min. What changed?
options: The first drug became more tightly bound to plasma protein
The glomerular filtration membrane was damaged
The secretory carrier for the first drug was inhibited
Reabsorption of the first drug was inhibited
questions.why: A clearance of 400 mL/min required a large secretory component, and dropping back to about the inulin value means only filtration is left, so the shared carrier must have been blocked. Membrane damage would tend to increase what enters the filtrate rather than reduce excretion. Blocking reabsorption would raise clearance, not lower it. Tighter protein binding would lower clearance below the inulin value rather than to it.
questions.answerText: The secretory carrier for the first drug was inhibited

questions.q: A substance has a clearance of 130 mL/min while inulin clearance is 125 mL/min. Its organic anion transporter is then blocked. Predict the new clearance and the interpretation.
options: Clearance falls to about 125 mL/min, showing that the small excess came from secretion
Clearance falls to about 60 mL/min, showing that filtration also depends on the transporter
Clearance stays at 130 mL/min, showing that the substance is only filtered
Clearance rises to about 250 mL/min, showing that the transporter was reabsorbing it
questions.why: The five mL/min excess over inulin clearance is the secreted contribution, so removing the carrier leaves only the filtered portion and the clearance settles at the inulin value. A rise would mean the transporter had been removing the substance from urine, which describes reabsorption not secretion. Filtration is pressure driven and does not use the transporter, so clearance cannot fall below the filtration rate. Staying at 130 would mean nothing was secreted in the first place.
questions.answerText: Clearance falls to about 125 mL/min, showing that the small excess came from secretion

questions.q: In a patient with plasma glucose of 500 mg/dL, glucose clearance is 15 mL/min while inulin clearance is 120 mL/min. How should this be interpreted?
options: The filtration membrane is damaged, since glucose should not normally be filtered
Glucose transport has stopped completely, since the clearance is no longer zero
Glucose is now net secreted, since it appears in the urine at a high plasma level
Glucose is still net reabsorbed, but the transport maximum is exceeded so some now escapes
questions.why: A clearance of 15 mL/min is far below the filtration rate of 120, so most of the filtered glucose is still being recovered, but the carriers are saturated and the surplus spills into urine. Appearing in urine does not imply secretion, since it can equally reflect incomplete reabsorption. Glucose is normally filtered freely, so its presence in filtrate is not evidence of membrane damage. Transport has not stopped, because a complete stop would push clearance up toward 120 mL/min.
questions.answerText: Glucose is still net reabsorbed, but the transport maximum is exceeded so some now escapes

questions.q: Which pump on the basolateral membrane of the proximal tubule cell creates the low intracellular sodium concentration?
options: The Na+ glucose symporter
The Na+/K+ ATPase
The H+/K+ ATPase
The Ca2+ ATPase
questions.why: The Na+/K+ ATPase pumps sodium out of the cell into the interstitium, keeping intracellular sodium low so sodium keeps flowing in across the apical membrane. The H+/K+ ATPase handles acid secretion in the stomach and in some collecting duct cells. The Ca2+ ATPase moves calcium and does not set the sodium gradient. The Na+ glucose symporter uses the gradient rather than creating it.

questions.q: Which apical membrane transporter carries glucose into the proximal tubule cell?
options: The sodium glucose symporter, SGLT
The Na+/H+ antiporter
An aquaporin channel
A GLUT facilitated diffusion carrier
questions.why: SGLT binds sodium and glucose together and uses the inward sodium gradient to pull glucose into the cell against its own concentration gradient. GLUT carriers work on the basolateral side, moving glucose down its gradient into blood. The Na+/H+ antiporter is apical but exchanges protons for sodium, not glucose. Aquaporins carry water only.

questions.q: How does glucose leave the proximal tubule cell across the basolateral membrane?
options: By simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer
By primary active transport using ATP directly
By facilitated diffusion through a GLUT carrier
By cotransport with sodium
questions.why: Glucose accumulates inside the cell, so it can move down its concentration gradient into the interstitium through a GLUT carrier without any energy input. Direct ATP use is not needed once the gradient favors exit. Cotransport with sodium happens on the apical side, where glucose must be pulled uphill. Glucose is polar and does not cross the lipid bilayer at any useful rate.
questions.answerText: By facilitated diffusion through a GLUT carrier

questions.q: What type of transport is glucose uptake by SGLT in the proximal tubule?
options: Primary active transport
Secondary active transport
Simple diffusion
Osmosis
questions.why: SGLT moves glucose uphill but does not hydrolyze ATP itself, so it is secondary active transport powered by the sodium gradient the pump maintains. Primary active transport would require the carrier to split ATP directly, as the Na+/K+ ATPase does. Simple diffusion cannot move a solute against its gradient. Osmosis describes water movement, not glucose.

questions.q: Which apical exchanger of the proximal tubule secretes H+ into the tubular fluid while bringing Na+ into the cell?
options: The Na+ Cl- symporter
The Na+ K+ 2Cl- symporter
The Na+ amino acid symporter
The Na+/H+ antiporter
questions.why: The Na+/H+ antiporter uses the inward sodium gradient to push protons out into the lumen, which is the step that drives bicarbonate reclamation in this segment. The Na+ K+ 2Cl- symporter belongs to the thick ascending limb. The Na+ amino acid symporter also uses the sodium gradient but carries amino acids inward, not protons outward. The Na+ Cl- symporter is the distal convoluted tubule carrier.

questions.q: About what fraction of the filtered water is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule?
options: About 99 percent
About 20 percent
About 65 percent
About 90 percent
questions.why: Roughly two thirds of filtered water is recovered proximally, following the solutes that are reabsorbed there. Twenty percent understates the segment's bulk role. Ninety percent overstates it, since the loop and collecting duct still handle a substantial share. Ninety nine percent is the whole nephron total, not the proximal contribution.

questions.q: Which water channel makes the proximal tubule highly permeable to water at all times?
options: Aquaporin 1
Aquaporin 2
The Na+/K+ ATPase
The slit diaphragm
questions.why: Aquaporin 1 is constitutively present in proximal tubule membranes, which is why water follows solute there without any hormonal signal. Aquaporin 2 is the hormone regulated channel of collecting duct principal cells. The Na+/K+ ATPase moves ions, not water. The slit diaphragm is part of the filtration membrane in the renal corpuscle.

questions.q: What does it mean to say that proximal tubule reabsorption is isosmotic?
options: Water is reabsorbed without solute, so the fluid becomes concentrated
Osmolarity in the tubule rises to about 1200 mOsm/L by the end of the segment
Solute is reabsorbed without any water, so the fluid becomes concentrated
Water follows solute closely enough that tubular fluid osmolarity stays near that of plasma
questions.why: Because the segment is freely permeable to water, water tracks reabsorbed solute almost instantly and the fluid leaving stays close to 300 mOsm/L even though about 65 percent of the volume is gone. Reabsorbing solute alone would dilute the tubular fluid. Reabsorbing water alone would concentrate it. A value near 1200 mOsm/L belongs at the bend of a long loop of Henle, not at the end of the proximal tubule.
questions.answerText: Water follows solute closely enough that tubular fluid osmolarity stays near that of plasma

questions.q: A drug blocks the Na+/K+ ATPase in proximal tubule cells. What happens to glucose reabsorption?
options: It rises, because more sodium stays inside the cell to drive the carrier
It falls, because the sodium gradient that powers SGLT collapses
It is unchanged, because SGLT uses ATP directly
It falls, because glucose can no longer be filtered
questions.why: SGLT depends on sodium being much lower inside the cell than in the tubular fluid, and the pump is what maintains that difference, so blocking the pump removes the driving force. Sodium building up inside the cell weakens the inward gradient rather than strengthening it. SGLT does not hydrolyze ATP, so it is not independent of the pump. Filtration of glucose is pressure driven at the glomerulus and is unaffected by a tubular pump.
questions.answerText: It falls, because the sodium gradient that powers SGLT collapses

questions.q: Why is proximal glucose uptake called secondary active transport rather than primary?
options: The energy comes from the sodium gradient, which was built by a separate ATP using pump
No energy is required at all, since glucose simply moves down its own gradient
The transport happens second, after water has already been reabsorbed nearby
The carrier hydrolyzes ATP directly but does so more slowly than a primary pump
questions.why: Secondary means the carrier taps stored energy in an ion gradient rather than splitting ATP itself, and that gradient is maintained by the Na+/K+ ATPase on the other side of the cell. The SGLT carrier does not hydrolyze ATP at all. Energy is required, because glucose is moved against its own concentration gradient into the cell. The word secondary refers to the energy source, not to the order of events.
questions.answerText: The energy comes from the sodium gradient, which was built by a separate ATP using pump

questions.q: Amino acid reabsorption in the proximal tubule depends on which gradient?
options: The calcium gradient across the basolateral membrane
The chloride gradient established by the loop of Henle
The inward sodium gradient across the apical membrane
The outward potassium gradient across the apical membrane
questions.why: Amino acids are pulled into the cell by sodium coupled symporters, the same strategy used for glucose, so both share a dependence on the sodium gradient. Potassium moves outward and is not coupled to amino acid uptake. Calcium gradients drive signaling, not bulk amino acid recovery. The loop of Henle acts downstream and cannot supply a gradient to the proximal tubule.
questions.answerText: The inward sodium gradient across the apical membrane

questions.q: Why does water follow solute out of the proximal tubule?
options: An ATP dependent water pump in the basolateral membrane moves water into the interstitium
Solute reabsorption raises interstitial osmolarity, and water moves down that osmotic gradient
Hydrostatic pressure inside the tubule forces water across the epithelial tight junctions
Antidiuretic hormone opens aquaporin channels in this segment during dehydration
questions.why: Moving sodium, glucose and amino acids into the interstitium creates a small osmotic difference, and because aquaporin 1 makes the epithelium leaky to water, water follows almost as fast as solute leaves. There is no ATP driven water pump in any cell. Tubular hydrostatic pressure is low and is not the driving force here. Antidiuretic hormone acts on the collecting duct, while the proximal tubule is water permeable regardless.
questions.answerText: Solute reabsorption raises interstitial osmolarity, and water moves down that osmotic gradient

questions.q: What is the osmolarity of tubular fluid at the end of the proximal tubule compared with plasma?
options: Much higher, near 1200 mOsm/L
Slightly higher, near 600 mOsm/L
Much lower, near 100 mOsm/L
About the same, near 300 mOsm/L
questions.why: Isosmotic reabsorption removes solute and water in nearly equal proportion, so the volume shrinks while the concentration stays near plasma values. One hundred mOsm/L is what leaves the thick ascending limb, the diluting segment. Twelve hundred mOsm/L is reached at the bend of a long loop. Six hundred mOsm/L would require water to be reabsorbed faster than solute, which this segment does not do.

questions.q: If 125 mL/min is filtered, about how much fluid per minute leaves the proximal tubule and enters the loop of Henle?
options: About 1 mL/min
About 81 mL/min
About 44 mL/min
About 125 mL/min
questions.why: With about 65 percent reabsorbed, roughly 35 percent of 125 mL/min remains, which is about 44 mL/min. Eighty one mL/min is the amount reabsorbed, not the amount remaining. One hundred twenty five mL/min would mean no reabsorption occurred at all. One mL/min is the final urine flow after the entire nephron has acted.

questions.q: A drug blocks aquaporin 1 in the proximal tubule while leaving solute transport intact. What happens to the fluid leaving that segment?
options: Its volume is larger than normal and its osmolarity is below plasma
Its volume and osmolarity are both unchanged
Its volume is larger than normal and its osmolarity is above plasma
Its volume is smaller than normal and its osmolarity is above plasma
questions.why: Solute keeps leaving but water can no longer follow, so more fluid stays in the tubule and what remains is diluted below 300 mOsm/L. A smaller volume would require water reabsorption to continue. Nothing stays unchanged when the water route is closed. Rising osmolarity with rising volume would require solute to be added to the tubule, which is not happening here.
questions.answerText: Its volume is larger than normal and its osmolarity is below plasma

questions.q: Ouabain blocks the Na+/K+ ATPase in proximal tubule cells. Trace the effect on intracellular sodium, on SGLT driven glucose uptake, and on urine glucose.
options: Intracellular sodium is unchanged, SGLT uptake falls, and glucose appears in the urine
Intracellular sodium falls, SGLT uptake rises, and urine glucose stays at zero
Intracellular sodium rises, SGLT uptake rises, and urine glucose stays at zero
Intracellular sodium rises, SGLT uptake falls, and glucose appears in the urine
questions.why: With the pump off, sodium accumulates inside the cell, the inward sodium gradient flattens, SGLT loses its driving force, filtered glucose is not recovered, and it spills into urine. Intracellular sodium cannot fall when the only exit pump is blocked. Rising intracellular sodium reduces rather than increases the gradient available to SGLT. The pump is the sole determinant of intracellular sodium here, so it cannot stay unchanged.
questions.answerText: Intracellular sodium rises, SGLT uptake falls, and glucose appears in the urine

questions.q: A drug selectively inhibits SGLT2 in the early proximal tubule. Predict glucose reabsorption, urine glucose, and urine volume.
options: Glucose reabsorption falls, urine glucose is unchanged, and urine volume rises
Glucose reabsorption falls, urine glucose rises, and urine volume rises
Glucose reabsorption falls, urine glucose rises, and urine volume falls
Glucose reabsorption rises, urine glucose falls, and urine volume falls
questions.why: Blocking the main glucose carrier leaves glucose in the tubular fluid, and that unreabsorbed glucose holds water osmotically, so both glucose and water losses rise. Volume cannot fall when an osmotically active solute is retained in the tubule. Reabsorption cannot rise when its carrier is blocked. Urine glucose must rise, since the glucose left behind has nowhere else to go.
questions.answerText: Glucose reabsorption falls, urine glucose rises, and urine volume rises

questions.q: A person inherits a defect in the sodium coupled apical carrier for a specific group of amino acids. Predict the urine findings and whether glucose handling changes.
options: Those amino acids appear in the urine while glucose handling is normal
Both those amino acids and glucose appear in the urine
Neither amino acids nor glucose appear, since the sodium gradient is intact
Glucose appears in the urine but amino acid handling is normal
questions.why: Glucose and amino acids share a common energy source but use separate carriers, so a defect in one carrier spares the other and only the affected amino acids are lost. Losing glucose too would require a defect in SGLT or in the sodium gradient itself. An intact sodium gradient does not help if the carrier that uses it is missing. Nothing in the defect affects the glucose carrier.
questions.answerText: Those amino acids appear in the urine while glucose handling is normal

questions.q: Efferent arteriolar constriction raises the filtration fraction, so blood entering the peritubular capillaries has a higher protein concentration than usual. Predict the effect on proximal tubule reabsorption.
options: Reabsorption increases, because peritubular capillary hydrostatic pressure rises sharply
Reabsorption decreases, because higher peritubular colloid osmotic pressure opposes fluid uptake into the capillary
Reabsorption increases, because higher peritubular colloid osmotic pressure pulls more fluid into the capillary
Reabsorption is unchanged, because peritubular Starling forces have no effect on the tubule at all
questions.why: Once solute and water reach the interstitium, Starling forces at the peritubular capillary decide how much enters the blood, and a higher plasma protein concentration increases the osmotic pull, so more is taken up and less leaks back into the tubule. Colloid osmotic pressure in the capillary favors uptake rather than opposing it. Peritubular forces very much affect net reabsorption. Peritubular hydrostatic pressure actually falls behind a constricted efferent arteriole, which also favors uptake but is not the change described.
questions.answerText: Reabsorption increases, because higher peritubular colloid osmotic pressure pulls more fluid into the capillary

questions.q: What does the transport maximum for a substance describe?
options: The plasma concentration at which the substance first appears in urine
The fastest rate at which the tubular carriers can move that substance
The highest concentration the substance can reach in the filtrate
The amount of the substance filtered each minute
questions.why: Transport maximum is a saturation point of the carrier system, expressed as an amount per unit time, and once it is reached extra substance stays in the tubule. The plasma concentration at which the substance first appears in urine is the renal threshold, a related but different idea. Filtrate concentration matches plasma for a freely filtered solute and has no ceiling of this kind. The amount filtered each minute is the filtered load.
questions.answerText: The fastest rate at which the tubular carriers can move that substance

questions.q: What does the renal threshold for a substance describe?
options: The lowest plasma concentration the kidney is able to maintain at rest
The urine concentration at which the tubular carriers become saturated
The maximum rate at which the tubular carriers can transport the substance
The plasma concentration above which the substance begins to appear in the urine
questions.why: Renal threshold is a plasma concentration, the point at which the filtered load starts to outrun the reabsorptive capacity. The maximum transport rate is the transport maximum, expressed in amount per time rather than concentration. The kidney does not define a minimum maintainable plasma level this way. Carriers respond to what is delivered from plasma, so the threshold is described in plasma terms, not urine terms.
questions.answerText: The plasma concentration above which the substance begins to appear in the urine

questions.q: What is the approximate transport maximum for glucose in a healthy adult?
options: About 125 mg/min
About 180 mg/min
About 375 mg/min
About 600 mg/min
questions.why: The glucose carriers saturate at roughly 375 mg/min, which is about three times the filtered load at normal plasma glucose. One hundred twenty five mg/min is the filtered load at a normal plasma glucose of 100 mg/dL. One hundred eighty is the renal threshold in mg/dL, a concentration rather than a rate. Six hundred mg/min overstates the capacity of the transporters.

questions.q: What is the approximate renal threshold for glucose?
options: About 180 mg/dL of plasma glucose
About 375 mg/dL of plasma glucose
About 600 mg/dL of plasma glucose
About 100 mg/dL of plasma glucose
questions.why: Glucose starts appearing in urine when plasma glucose climbs above roughly 180 mg/dL. One hundred mg/dL is a normal fasting plasma glucose, well below the threshold, so no glucose appears. Three hundred seventy five is the transport maximum in mg/min, not a plasma concentration. Six hundred mg/dL is far above the threshold and would produce heavy glucose loss.

questions.q: Which pair of units correctly matches transport maximum and renal threshold?
options: Both in mg/dL
Transport maximum in mg/dL and renal threshold in mg/min
Both in mg/min
Transport maximum in mg/min and renal threshold in mg/dL
questions.why: Transport maximum is a rate of movement so it carries amount per time, while renal threshold is a plasma concentration so it carries amount per volume. Swapping them reverses both meanings. Two rates would leave no way to state the plasma level that triggers spillage. Two concentrations would leave no way to state carrier capacity.
questions.answerText: Transport maximum in mg/min and renal threshold in mg/dL

questions.q: What is splay in the glucose titration curve?
options: The sudden vertical rise in urine glucose once the transport maximum is passed entirely
The rounding of the curve caused by individual nephrons saturating at different points
The flat portion of the curve where no glucose at all is excreted in the urine
The gap between filtered load and excretion seen at very low plasma glucose
questions.why: Nephrons vary in their filtration rates and carrier numbers, so some spill glucose before others do and the transition from zero to full excretion is gradual instead of sharp. A vertical rise would be what a single uniform population of nephrons would produce. The flat portion below threshold shows complete reabsorption, not splay. At very low plasma glucose there is no gap between filtration and reabsorption to describe.
questions.answerText: The rounding of the curve caused by individual nephrons saturating at different points

questions.q: Which transporter saturating produces the glucose transport maximum?
options: SGLT in the proximal tubule apical membrane
The Na+ K+ 2Cl- symporter in the thick ascending limb
The Na+/K+ ATPase in the basolateral membrane
Aquaporin 1 in the apical membrane
questions.why: Glucose entry into the cell depends on a limited number of SGLT carriers, and once they are all occupied the reabsorption rate cannot rise further. The Na+/K+ ATPase supplies the gradient but is not the step that saturates first for glucose. Aquaporin 1 carries water. The Na+ K+ 2Cl- symporter handles salt in a different segment and has nothing to do with glucose.
questions.answerText: SGLT in the proximal tubule apical membrane

questions.q: How much glucose appears in the urine of a healthy person with a fasting plasma glucose of 90 mg/dL?
options: About half the filtered load
All of the filtered load
Essentially none
About one third of the filtered load
questions.why: At 90 mg/dL the filtered load is far below the transport maximum, so the carriers reabsorb every molecule and urine glucose is undetectable. One third or one half spilling would require a plasma glucose well above the renal threshold. Losing the entire filtered load would mean the carriers were absent altogether.

questions.q: Plasma glucose is 100 mg/dL and glomerular filtration rate is 125 mL/min, with a transport maximum of 375 mg/min. Will glucose appear in the urine?
options: Yes, because the filtered load of 375 mg/min equals the transport maximum
No, because the filtered load of 125 mg/min is well below the transport maximum
Yes, because plasma glucose is above the renal threshold
No, because glucose is not filtered at the glomerulus
questions.why: A plasma glucose of 100 mg/dL is 1 mg/mL, and multiplying by 125 mL/min gives a filtered load of 125 mg/min, only a third of the carriers capacity, so all of it is reclaimed. The filtered load here is 125, not 375. A plasma glucose of 100 mg/dL is below the threshold of about 180 mg/dL. Glucose is small and freely filtered, so it certainly enters the tubule.
questions.answerText: No, because the filtered load of 125 mg/min is well below the transport maximum

questions.q: Plasma glucose is 400 mg/dL, glomerular filtration rate is 125 mL/min, and the transport maximum is 375 mg/min. What is the glucose excretion rate?
options: 0 mg/min
500 mg/min
375 mg/min
125 mg/min
questions.why: A plasma glucose of 400 mg/dL is 4 mg/mL, so the filtered load is 4 times 125, which is 500 mg/min, and subtracting the 375 mg/min the carriers can recover leaves 125 mg/min in the urine. Five hundred is the filtered load before reabsorption. Three hundred seventy five is the amount reabsorbed. Zero would require the filtered load to stay under the transport maximum.

questions.q: At a plasma glucose of 200 mg/dL and a filtration rate of 125 mL/min, the filtered load is 250 mg/min, below the transport maximum of 375 mg/min, yet a small amount of glucose appears in the urine. What explains this?
options: Damage to the filtration membrane
An error in the transport maximum, which must actually be 250 mg/min
Splay, because some nephrons saturate before others do
Secretion of glucose by the distal tubule
questions.why: Nephrons are not identical, so a nephron with a high filtration rate or few carriers spills glucose while its neighbors are still well within capacity, which is why the threshold is lower than the transport maximum predicts. Glucose is not secreted anywhere in the nephron. A damaged filtration membrane would show protein and cells, not isolated glucose. The transport maximum is a whole kidney average and does not need to be revised to explain the finding.
questions.answerText: Splay, because some nephrons saturate before others do

questions.q: A patient's glomerular filtration rate falls from 125 to 62.5 mL/min while the glucose transport maximum stays at 375 mg/min. What happens to the plasma glucose level at which glucose starts to appear in urine?
options: It rises, because a lower filtration rate delivers less glucose per minute
It is unchanged, because the transport maximum did not change
It falls to zero, so glucose appears at any plasma level
It falls, because the kidney is damaged
questions.why: The filtered load is filtration rate times plasma concentration, so at half the filtration rate the plasma glucose must be twice as high to reach the same filtered load, and the threshold rises. Damage does not automatically lower the threshold when it also lowers delivery. The threshold depends on both filtration rate and transport maximum, so an unchanged transport maximum is not enough to keep it fixed. A threshold of zero would mean no glucose could ever be reabsorbed.
questions.answerText: It rises, because a lower filtration rate delivers less glucose per minute

questions.q: A drug lowers the effective glucose transport maximum. What happens to the renal threshold for glucose?
options: It is unchanged, because threshold depends only on filtration rate
It becomes undefined, because glucose can no longer be filtered
It rises, so a higher plasma glucose is needed before spilling
It falls, so glucose appears in urine at a lower plasma glucose
questions.why: With less carrier capacity, a smaller filtered load is enough to overwhelm reabsorption, so the plasma concentration at which spilling begins drops. A rise would require more capacity, not less. Threshold depends on both filtration rate and transport capacity, so it cannot be independent of the drug. Filtration is unaffected, since it is a pressure driven step at the glomerulus.
questions.answerText: It falls, so glucose appears in urine at a lower plasma glucose

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes transport maximum from renal threshold?
options: Both describe the same saturation point using different names
Transport maximum is a rate of reabsorption, while renal threshold is a plasma concentration
Transport maximum is a plasma concentration, while renal threshold is a rate of filtration
