Transport maximum applies to glucose only, while renal threshold applies to all solutes
questions.why: Transport maximum measures how fast the carriers can work, and renal threshold measures the plasma level at which the filtered load starts to exceed that capacity, so one is a rate and the other a concentration. They are related but not the same number, and splay separates them further. Reversing the two definitions inverts both. Transport maximum applies to many actively reabsorbed and secreted substances, not to glucose alone.
questions.answerText: Transport maximum is a rate of reabsorption, while renal threshold is a plasma concentration

questions.q: Glucose is spilling into the urine in large amounts. What happens to urine volume, and why?
options: Urine volume rises, because unreabsorbed glucose holds water in the tubule osmotically
Urine volume is unchanged, because glucose in the tubule is not osmotically active
Urine volume rises, because glucose directly blocks the sodium potassium pump
Urine volume falls, because glucose is reabsorbed together with water in the proximal tubule
questions.why: Glucose left in the tubular fluid raises its osmolarity, which opposes water reabsorption all the way down the nephron and produces an osmotic diuresis. If glucose were being reabsorbed with water, none would be spilling in the first place. Glucose is very much osmotically active, which is exactly why it drags water. Glucose does not inhibit the sodium potassium pump.
questions.answerText: Urine volume rises, because unreabsorbed glucose holds water in the tubule osmotically

questions.q: Glomerular filtration rate is 100 mL/min, plasma glucose is 600 mg/dL, and the transport maximum is 300 mg/min. What is the rate of glucose excretion?
options: 0 mg/min
600 mg/min
300 mg/min
100 mg/min
questions.why: A plasma glucose of 600 mg/dL is 6 mg/mL, so the filtered load is 6 times 100, which is 600 mg/min, and subtracting the 300 mg/min that the carriers can reclaim leaves 300 mg/min excreted. Six hundred is the filtered load before any reabsorption. One hundred is the filtration rate in mL/min, not a mass rate. Zero would require the filtered load to stay below the transport maximum.

questions.q: The glucose transport maximum is 375 mg/min and the filtration rate is 125 mL/min. At what plasma glucose would the filtered load exactly equal the transport maximum, and why is the observed threshold lower?
options: 500 mg/dL, and the observed threshold is lower because filtration is incomplete
300 mg/dL, and the observed threshold is lower because of splay
180 mg/dL, and the observed threshold matches this value exactly
375 mg/dL, and the observed threshold is lower because of protein binding
questions.why: Dividing 375 mg/min by 125 mL/min gives 3 mg/mL, which is 300 mg/dL, but because individual nephrons saturate at different plasma levels, spilling begins nearer 180 mg/dL. One hundred eighty is the observed threshold, not the calculated saturation point, so it cannot be both. Three hundred seventy five is the transport maximum in mg/min, not a concentration, and glucose is not protein bound. Five hundred does not follow from the numbers, and glucose is in fact filtered freely.
questions.answerText: 300 mg/dL, and the observed threshold is lower because of splay

questions.q: A person has glucose in the urine, a fasting plasma glucose of 85 mg/dL, and a normal filtration rate. What is the most consistent explanation?
options: A plasma glucose above the renal threshold
A damaged filtration membrane allowing extra glucose to be filtered
An increased filtered load from a high filtration rate
An inherited reduction in the glucose transport maximum
questions.why: With normal plasma glucose and normal filtration, the filtered load is ordinary, so glucose in urine must reflect reduced reabsorptive capacity, which lowers the threshold below the normal plasma range. A plasma glucose of 85 mg/dL is far below any normal threshold. Glucose is freely filtered even through an intact membrane, so membrane damage adds nothing. The filtration rate was stated to be normal, so a raised filtered load is ruled out.
questions.answerText: An inherited reduction in the glucose transport maximum

questions.q: Two people both have a plasma glucose of 250 mg/dL. One has a filtration rate of 125 mL/min and the other 60 mL/min, and both have a transport maximum of 375 mg/min. Who spills glucose into the urine?
options: Neither, because the transport maximum is the same in both
Only the person with the filtration rate of 60 mL/min
Only the person with the filtration rate of 125 mL/min
Both, because plasma glucose is above the usual renal threshold
questions.why: At 2.5 mg/mL the filtered load is 312 mg/min at 125 mL/min, close enough to the 375 mg/min ceiling that splay causes spilling, while at 60 mL/min the filtered load is only 150 mg/min, comfortably within capacity. The person with the lower filtration rate is protected, not the reverse. Threshold is not a fixed plasma number, since it shifts with filtration rate. An identical transport maximum does not make the two cases identical, because delivery differs.
questions.answerText: Only the person with the filtration rate of 125 mL/min

questions.q: In tubular secretion, which way does a substance move?
options: From tubular fluid into peritubular capillary blood
From glomerular capillary blood into the capsular space
From peritubular capillary blood into the tubular fluid
From tubular fluid into the interstitium and then into the loop of Henle
questions.why: Secretion adds material to the forming urine after filtration, so the substance leaves the blood of the peritubular capillaries and crosses the tubule cells into the lumen. Movement from tubular fluid back into blood is reabsorption, the opposite process. Movement from glomerular blood into the capsular space is filtration, which happens upstream at the renal corpuscle. The fourth option runs the wrong way and puts the fluid back into an earlier segment, which the nephron does not do.
questions.answerText: From peritubular capillary blood into the tubular fluid

questions.q: What is the main purpose of tubular secretion?
options: To recover filtered solutes such as glucose and amino acids before they are lost
To build the osmotic gradient in the renal medulla that allows urine to be concentrated
To generate the hydrostatic pressure inside the glomerular capillaries that drives filtration
To provide a second route for clearing substances from the blood beyond what filtration removes
questions.why: Only about a fifth of the plasma reaching the glomerulus is filtered, so secretion lets the tubule pull unwanted solutes out of the remaining four fifths and dump them into the urine. Recovering needed solutes is reabsorption, not secretion. Filtration pressure comes from glomerular capillary blood pressure set by the arterioles. The medullary gradient is built by the countercurrent multiplier in the loop of Henle, a separate mechanism.
questions.answerText: To provide a second route for clearing substances from the blood beyond what filtration removes

questions.q: Which ion is secreted by the tubule to help regulate blood pH?
options: H+
Ca2+
Cl-
Na+
questions.why: Secreting H+ into the tubular fluid removes acid from the body and is the kidney's main lever on blood pH. Ca2+ handling is dominated by reabsorption under parathyroid hormone control, not by secretion for pH. Cl- follows Na+ during reabsorption and is not the acid the kidney excretes. Na+ is heavily reabsorbed rather than secreted, since losing it would cost the body water and blood volume.

questions.q: Which tubule cells carry out most potassium secretion?
options: Intercalated cells of the collecting duct
Cells of the thick ascending limb
Cells of the descending limb of the loop of Henle
Principal cells of the collecting duct
questions.why: Principal cells have apical potassium channels and basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase, so they load K+ from blood and let it leak into the lumen, and this step is the one aldosterone controls. Intercalated cells are the acid and base handlers, secreting H+ or HCO3-. The thick ascending limb reabsorbs K+ through the NKCC2 cotransporter rather than secreting it. The descending limb moves water, not K+.
questions.answerText: Principal cells of the collecting duct

questions.q: Which nephron segment secretes most organic anions such as drug molecules?
options: The collecting duct
The proximal convoluted tubule
The thin descending limb
The distal convoluted tubule
questions.why: The proximal convoluted tubule carries the organic anion transporters that pull drug molecules and metabolic acids out of peritubular blood and push them into the lumen. The collecting duct is where H+, K+ and water handling are fine tuned, not where bulk drug secretion happens. The thin descending limb has no active transporters of this kind and simply loses water. The distal convoluted tubule adjusts Na+ and Ca2+, not organic anions.

questions.q: Penicillin is cleared from the blood largely by which renal process?
options: Tubular secretion
Glomerular filtration only
Tubular reabsorption
Countercurrent exchange
questions.why: Penicillin is an organic anion, and the proximal tubule's organic anion transporters secrete it, which is why its clearance exceeds the glomerular filtration rate. Reabsorption would return it to the blood and prolong its stay. Filtration alone would clear it no faster than inulin, but the measured clearance is higher than that. Countercurrent exchange preserves the medullary gradient and does not eliminate drugs.

questions.q: Secretion of which nitrogen containing ion helps the kidney excrete acid while making new bicarbonate?
options: Nitrate, NO3-
Creatinine
Urea
Ammonium, NH4+
questions.why: Proximal tubule cells break down glutamine to make NH4+, secrete it into the lumen, and release a new HCO3- into the blood, so acid leaves and buffer is gained. Nitrate is not a product of renal glutamine metabolism. Urea is a nitrogen waste that is filtered and partly recycled in the medulla but carries no acid load in this way. Creatinine is filtered and slightly secreted but does nothing for acid base balance.

questions.q: Which statement about creatinine handling by the tubule is correct?
options: It is secreted only, with no filtration
It is filtered freely and reabsorbed in large amounts
It is neither filtered nor secreted
It is filtered freely and secreted in small amounts
questions.why: Creatinine passes the filtration membrane freely and the proximal tubule adds a small extra amount by secretion, which is why creatinine clearance slightly overestimates the glomerular filtration rate. It is not reabsorbed, so once in the tubule it stays there. It is definitely filtered, which is what makes it useful clinically. Inulin, not creatinine, is the marker that is filtered and neither secreted nor reabsorbed.
questions.answerText: It is filtered freely and secreted in small amounts

questions.q: A drug is heavily bound to plasma albumin, so very little of it is filtered at the glomerulus. Yet it is cleared quickly. Which process best explains this?
options: Increased glomerular filtration rate driven by the drug
Reabsorption of the drug in the collecting duct
Tubular secretion by proximal tubule organic anion transporters
Countercurrent multiplication concentrating the drug
questions.why: Protein bound drug cannot cross the filtration membrane, but the transporters can strip it off albumin at the peritubular capillary and move it into the lumen, so secretion clears what filtration cannot. A drug does not raise the filtration rate on its own, and even if it did, the bound fraction would still not filter. Reabsorption would return the drug to blood and slow clearance rather than speed it. Countercurrent multiplication concentrates the medullary interstitium and has no drug transporters.
questions.answerText: Tubular secretion by proximal tubule organic anion transporters

questions.q: A patient's blood pH falls during a period of heavy exercise. How does the tubule respond?
options: It secretes less H+ and more HCO3-
It stops secreting K+ and secretes Na+ instead
It reabsorbs more H+ from the tubular fluid
It secretes more H+ into the tubular fluid
questions.why: Acidosis means excess H+ in the blood, and the tubule responds by pushing more H+ into the lumen so the acid leaves in the urine while HCO3- is returned to blood. Secreting bicarbonate is the response to alkalosis, when the body has too much base. Reabsorbing H+ would worsen the acidosis by adding acid back to the blood. Na+ is reabsorbed, not secreted, and swapping it for K+ secretion is not how the tubule handles an acid load.
questions.answerText: It secretes more H+ into the tubular fluid

questions.q: A substance has a renal clearance greater than the glomerular filtration rate. What does this tell you about its handling?
options: It is reabsorbed after filtration
It is neither filtered nor secreted
It is filtered only, with no secretion or reabsorption
It is secreted in addition to being filtered
questions.why: Clearance above the filtration rate means more of the substance leaves the blood than filtration alone could account for, so the tubule must be adding it to the urine by secretion. Reabsorption pulls the substance back and drops clearance below the filtration rate. A clearance exactly equal to the filtration rate is the signature of a purely filtered marker such as inulin. A substance that is neither filtered nor secreted would have a clearance near zero.
questions.answerText: It is secreted in addition to being filtered

questions.q: Probenecid competes with penicillin for the same proximal tubule organic anion transporter. What happens to plasma penicillin when probenecid is given with it?
options: It falls faster because penicillin reabsorption is blocked
It falls faster because secretion is increased
It is unchanged because penicillin is cleared only by filtration
It stays higher for longer because penicillin secretion is reduced
questions.why: Two organic anions competing for a limited number of carriers means less penicillin gets into the lumen, so its clearance drops and blood levels stay up. Competition at a shared carrier reduces transport of each substrate rather than increasing it. Penicillin is not cleared by filtration alone, which is exactly why blocking the carrier matters. Penicillin is secreted rather than reabsorbed, so there is no reabsorption step to block.
questions.answerText: It stays higher for longer because penicillin secretion is reduced

questions.q: A patient takes a drug that blocks the apical potassium channels of collecting duct principal cells. Predict the effect on plasma potassium.
options: Plasma potassium falls because more K+ is lost in the urine
Plasma potassium rises because less K+ is secreted into the urine
Plasma potassium is unchanged because K+ is handled entirely in the proximal tubule
Plasma potassium falls because K+ reabsorption in the collecting duct stops
questions.why: The apical channel is the exit route into the lumen, so blocking it strands K+ in the cell and in the blood and plasma levels climb. Losing more K+ requires that exit route to be open, not shut. The proximal tubule reabsorbs most filtered K+, but the amount that ends up in urine is set downstream at the principal cells. Blocking a secretory channel does not create a reabsorption problem, since reabsorption is not what the channel does.
questions.answerText: Plasma potassium rises because less K+ is secreted into the urine

questions.q: Aspirin is a weak acid. Making the urine more alkaline traps aspirin in its ionized form in the tubular fluid. What happens to aspirin excretion?
options: It increases, because the ionized drug cannot be reabsorbed back into blood
It decreases, because ionized drug is reabsorbed faster
It is unchanged, because urine pH does not affect drug handling
It decreases, because alkaline urine blocks organic anion secretion
questions.why: Charged molecules cannot slip back across the lipid membranes of the tubule, so trapping aspirin in the ionized form keeps it in the lumen and it leaves in the urine. Ionized forms are reabsorbed more slowly, not faster, which is the whole point of ion trapping. Urine pH strongly affects the excretion of any weak acid or weak base. Alkaline urine does not shut down the organic anion transporters, which work on the blood side of the cell.
questions.answerText: It increases, because the ionized drug cannot be reabsorbed back into blood

questions.q: A patient with poor kidney perfusion is given a drug cleared only by proximal tubular secretion. The drug accumulates to toxic levels even though the measured glomerular filtration rate is near normal. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The filtration membrane has become impermeable to the drug and no longer lets it enter
Reduced peritubular blood flow limits delivery of the drug to the secretory transporters
The collecting duct is reabsorbing the drug back into the blood before it is excreted
The countercurrent exchanger is trapping the drug in the medulla and returning it to blood
questions.why: Secretion depends on blood reaching the peritubular capillaries so transporters have substrate to grab, and a normal filtration rate does not guarantee good peritubular flow. The filtration membrane is not the route for this drug, since it is cleared by secretion, so its permeability is beside the point. Collecting duct reabsorption of an organic anion is not a normal pathway and would not appear suddenly. The vasa recta exchanger conserves the medullary gradient and has no role in drug handling.
questions.answerText: Reduced peritubular blood flow limits delivery of the drug to the secretory transporters

questions.q: A patient with severe metabolic acidosis is also hyperkalemic. Both H+ secretion and K+ secretion depend on the same collecting duct machinery. Which chain of reasoning best links the two findings?
options: When the cell secretes more H+ to handle the acid load, less electrochemical drive is left for K+ secretion, so K+ is retained
Acidosis raises aldosterone sharply, which increases both H+ and K+ secretion together, so potassium leaves in the urine faster
Acidosis increases the glomerular filtration rate, which washes K+ out of the blood faster than the tubule can reabsorb it
Acidosis blocks the Na+/K+ ATPase in the proximal tubule, which raises H+ in the blood and drives K+ out of the cells
questions.why: The collecting duct handles H+ and K+ with shared driving forces, so a heavy acid load pushes H+ into the lumen at the expense of K+ export and plasma K+ climbs. Aldosterone does raise both, but that would lower plasma K+ rather than produce the hyperkalemia described. A rising filtration rate is not a feature of acidosis, and even a higher rate would not explain retained K+. Proximal Na+/K+ ATPase inhibition is not what acidosis does, and it does not produce blood acidification by that route.
questions.answerText: When the cell secretes more H+ to handle the acid load, less electrochemical drive is left for K+ secretion, so K+ is retained

questions.q: An investigator infuses para aminohippurate, an organic anion, at a low plasma concentration and finds that nearly all of it is removed from the plasma in a single pass through the kidney. At a very high plasma concentration, a large fraction now remains in the renal vein. What accounts for the change?
options: Glomerular filtration has shut down at the higher concentration and no longer removes the substance
Renal blood flow falls sharply when plasma concentration rises, so less blood reaches the tubule cells
The substance begins to be reabsorbed once its concentration in the tubule is high enough to drive it back
The organic anion transporters have reached their transport maximum and cannot secrete the extra load
questions.why: Secretion runs on a fixed number of carriers, so once every carrier is occupied the extra molecules stay in the blood and the renal vein concentration rises. Filtration is not carrier limited and continues normally at higher plasma concentrations. Para aminohippurate is not reabsorbed, and no new reabsorptive pathway appears at high concentration. Renal blood flow is regulated by arteriolar tone and does not collapse just because a solute concentration was raised.
questions.answerText: The organic anion transporters have reached their transport maximum and cannot secrete the extra load

questions.q: A patient on a potassium sparing drug that blocks collecting duct sodium channels also develops a mild metabolic acidosis. Trace the reason.
options: Blocking Na+ entry makes the lumen more negative, which drives extra H+ out of the cells and into the blood
Blocking Na+ entry increases ammonium production in the proximal tubule, which acidifies the blood directly
Blocking Na+ entry raises aldosterone enough to strip bicarbonate from the blood as it is excreted
Blocking Na+ entry makes the lumen less negative, which reduces the driving force for both K+ and H+ secretion
questions.why: Sodium entering principal cells leaves the lumen negative, and that negativity pulls K+ and H+ out of the cells; remove the sodium current and both secretory steps weaken, so acid is retained along with potassium. Blocking sodium entry makes the lumen less negative, not more. Aldosterone may rise as volume falls, but the drug blocks the very channel aldosterone works through, so its effect is lost. Proximal ammonium production is driven by acid load and would rise as a compensation, not as the cause.
questions.answerText: Blocking Na+ entry makes the lumen less negative, which reduces the driving force for both K+ and H+ secretion

questions.q: What is the permeability of the thin descending limb of the loop of Henle?
options: Impermeable to water and permeable to NaCl
Permeable to water and largely impermeable to NaCl
Permeable to both water and NaCl
Impermeable to both water and NaCl
questions.why: Water leaves the descending limb into the salty medulla while the salt stays behind, which is why the fluid at the hairpin turn is the most concentrated in the nephron. Being impermeable to water and permeable to NaCl describes the ascending limb, the opposite half of the loop. If both moved freely, no osmotic difference could build between lumen and interstitium. If neither moved, the loop could not concentrate anything at all.
questions.answerText: Permeable to water and largely impermeable to NaCl

questions.q: What does the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle do?
options: It allows water out of the lumen and holds NaCl inside the tubule
It pumps NaCl out into the interstitium and is impermeable to water
It pumps NaCl into the lumen and lets water follow it osmotically
It is freely permeable to water, NaCl, and urea in both directions
questions.why: Active NaCl transport out of a water tight tube is the single effect that makes the interstitium salty and the tubular fluid dilute, and it is the engine of the whole multiplier. Letting water out while holding salt in describes the descending limb. Pumping NaCl into the lumen would dilute the medulla rather than concentrate it. Free permeability to everything would let all gradients collapse immediately.
questions.answerText: It pumps NaCl out into the interstitium and is impermeable to water

questions.q: Roughly what is the osmolarity of the interstitial fluid at the tip of the renal medulla in a well concentrated kidney?
options: About 1200 mOsm/L
About 600 mOsm/L
About 300 mOsm/L
About 100 mOsm/L
questions.why: The gradient runs from roughly 300 mOsm/L in the cortex to about 1200 mOsm/L at the deepest point of the medulla, which sets the maximum urine concentration the kidney can reach. About 300 mOsm/L is the cortical and plasma value, the starting point rather than the peak. About 600 mOsm/L is a midmedullary value along the way. About 100 mOsm/L is closer to the dilute fluid leaving the ascending limb.

questions.q: Which vessels form the countercurrent exchanger of the renal medulla?
options: The vasa recta
The peritubular capillaries of the cortex
The afferent arterioles
The arcuate veins
questions.why: The vasa recta are hairpin capillaries that dive into the medulla alongside the long loops and come back up, so solute and water they pick up on the way down are handed back on the way up. Cortical peritubular capillaries surround the proximal and distal tubules where there is no steep gradient to protect. Afferent arterioles deliver blood to the glomerulus and never enter the medulla. Arcuate veins drain blood at the corticomedullary border and do not form a hairpin.

questions.q: Which nephrons have the long loops of Henle that build the deepest part of the medullary gradient?
options: Cortical nephrons
Juxtamedullary nephrons
All nephrons equally
Nephrons whose glomeruli sit in the medulla
questions.why: Juxtamedullary nephrons have glomeruli near the corticomedullary junction and loops that reach far into the medulla, so they are the ones that generate the deep gradient. Cortical nephrons make up most of the total but have short loops that barely enter the medulla. The two types differ sharply in loop length, so treating them as equal misses the point. No nephron has its glomerulus in the medulla; all renal corpuscles sit in the cortex.

questions.q: How large is the osmotic difference the thick ascending limb can create between the tubular lumen and the surrounding interstitium at any one level?
options: About 900 mOsm/L
About 20 mOsm/L
About 1200 mOsm/L
About 200 mOsm/L
questions.why: The pump can only hold about a 200 mOsm/L difference at a single horizontal level, and the countercurrent arrangement multiplies that small single effect down the length of the loop into a much larger vertical gradient. About 900 or 1200 mOsm/L is the size of the finished gradient, not what one level of pumping produces. About 20 mOsm/L is far too small to build a gradient of the magnitude the kidney achieves.

questions.q: Besides NaCl, which solute contributes substantially to the osmolarity of the deep medullary interstitium?
options: Glucose
Bicarbonate
Albumin
Urea
questions.why: Urea recycles out of the inner medullary collecting duct into the interstitium and back into the loop, adding roughly half the osmolarity at the medullary tip. Glucose is fully reabsorbed in the proximal tubule and never reaches the deep medulla in quantity. Albumin is a plasma protein that is not filtered and stays in the capillary. Bicarbonate is reabsorbed proximally and is not a medullary osmole.

questions.q: What is the osmolarity of the tubular fluid leaving the thick ascending limb and entering the distal convoluted tubule?
options: About 1200 mOsm/L, highly concentrated
About 100 mOsm/L, dilute relative to plasma
About 300 mOsm/L, the same as plasma
About 600 mOsm/L, moderately concentrated
questions.why: The ascending limb strips out salt without letting water follow, so the fluid it delivers is more dilute than plasma, which is why this segment is called the diluting segment. Fluid near 1200 mOsm/L is what sits at the hairpin turn, before the ascending limb has done its work. Fluid at 300 mOsm/L is what entered the loop from the proximal tubule. A value of 600 mOsm/L would mean the pump had barely worked.
questions.answerText: About 100 mOsm/L, dilute relative to plasma

questions.q: A drug blocks the NKCC2 cotransporter in the thick ascending limb. What happens to the medullary osmotic gradient?
options: It strengthens, because more NaCl stays in the interstitium
It weakens, because the single effect that builds it is lost
It is unchanged, because urea alone maintains it
It strengthens, because water is retained in the descending limb
questions.why: NKCC2 is the transporter that moves NaCl out of the water tight ascending limb, so blocking it removes the pumping step and the medulla loses its saltiness. Blocking the transporter keeps NaCl in the lumen, not in the interstitium. Urea contributes to the gradient but depends on the concentrating process the loop drives, so it cannot hold the gradient alone. Water movement in the descending limb is a consequence of the gradient, not its source.
questions.answerText: It weakens, because the single effect that builds it is lost

questions.q: Why does the countercurrent arrangement multiply a small single effect into a large gradient?
options: Because the pump itself becomes progressively stronger deeper in the medulla, where the interstitium is saltiest of all levels
Because fluid flowing in opposite directions in the two limbs repeatedly exposes new fluid to the pumping step at each level
Because the vasa recta actively add salt to the interstitium as blood passes back up through the medulla
Because the descending limb pumps salt in at the same rate as the ascending limb pumps salt out of the lumen
questions.why: The hairpin means the fluid already concentrated by the descending limb is handed to the ascending limb, which pumps against it again, so each 200 mOsm/L step stacks on the one before. The transporters are not stronger at depth; the same modest single effect applies all the way down. The vasa recta exchange passively and add nothing of their own. The descending limb has no salt pump; it simply loses water.
questions.answerText: Because fluid flowing in opposite directions in the two limbs repeatedly exposes new fluid to the pumping step at each level

questions.q: Blood flow through the vasa recta increases sharply. Predict the effect on the medullary gradient.
options: The gradient becomes steeper
The gradient is unaffected because the vasa recta are impermeable
The gradient washes out and weakens
The gradient shifts to the cortex
questions.why: Slow flow is what lets the descending and ascending vasa recta trade solute and water with each other, and fast flow carries medullary solute away before it can be handed back, which is called medullary washout. Faster flow removes solute rather than concentrating it, so the gradient cannot steepen. The vasa recta are quite permeable to water and solute, which is exactly why flow rate matters. The gradient lives in the medulla by anatomy and does not relocate.
questions.answerText: The gradient washes out and weakens

questions.q: Fluid at the hairpin turn of a long loop of Henle is at about 1200 mOsm/L. What made it that concentrated?
options: Water left the descending limb into the salty interstitium while solute stayed in the lumen
NaCl was pumped into the descending limb from the interstitial fluid of the medulla
Urea was actively secreted into the descending limb from the medullary interstitium
Antidiuretic hormone opened extra aquaporins in the descending limb and let solute enter
questions.why: The descending limb concentrates its contents by losing water, not by gaining solute, because the interstitium around it is saltier than the lumen. There is no NaCl pump in the descending limb pulling salt inward. Urea does enter the thin limb in the deep medulla, but passively and as a smaller contribution, not by active secretion. Descending limb water permeability is constitutive, so it does not wait on antidiuretic hormone.
questions.answerText: Water left the descending limb into the salty interstitium while solute stayed in the lumen

questions.q: An animal is bred with unusually short loops of Henle. What would you predict about its maximum urine concentration?
options: It would be higher than normal
It would be unchanged because the vasa recta compensate
It would be unchanged because urea compensates
It would be lower than normal
questions.why: Longer loops multiply the single effect over more vertical distance, so shorter loops build a shallower gradient and the collecting duct has less osmotic pull to concentrate urine against. Shorter loops cannot produce a deeper gradient. Urea recycling depends on the concentrating machinery of the loop and collecting duct, so it cannot make up the shortfall. The vasa recta only preserve a gradient that already exists and cannot create one.
questions.answerText: It would be lower than normal

questions.q: Why does the descending vasa recta not simply carry the medullary solute away in the blood?
options: Because the descending vasa recta is impermeable to solute and picks none of it up on the way down
Because the vasa recta actively pump solute back into the interstitium as blood leaves the medulla for the cortex
Because the ascending vasa recta runs alongside it and hands solute back into the interstitium as blood returns
Because blood entering the vasa recta is already at 1200 mOsm/L and cannot take up any more solute
questions.why: The hairpin geometry means whatever solute diffuses into blood going down diffuses back out of blood coming up, so the medulla keeps its solute even though blood keeps flowing. The descending vasa recta is quite permeable to solute; the rescue comes from the return limb, not from a barrier. The exchange is entirely passive with no pumps involved. Blood entering the medulla is at plasma osmolarity of about 300 mOsm/L, not 1200.
questions.answerText: Because the ascending vasa recta runs alongside it and hands solute back into the interstitium as blood returns

questions.q: A patient is given a loop diuretic and their urine becomes large in volume and close to plasma osmolarity. Which step failed?
options: Aquaporin insertion in the collecting duct, so water could not be reabsorbed from the final urine
NaCl transport out of the thick ascending limb, so the fluid was neither diluted nor was the medulla made salty
Sodium reabsorption in the proximal tubule, so too much fluid was delivered on to the loop of Henle
Filtration at the glomerulus, so an abnormally large volume of filtrate entered the nephron each minute
questions.why: Loop diuretics block the ascending limb transporter, so the tubular fluid is not diluted on the way through and the medullary gradient that would let the collecting duct pull water back is gone, leaving a large volume of roughly isosmotic urine. Failed aquaporin insertion produces very dilute urine, not urine near plasma osmolarity, because the gradient is still intact. Proximal sodium reabsorption failure would also raise volume but would not specifically flatten the medullary gradient. Filtration is unchanged by a loop diuretic.
questions.answerText: NaCl transport out of the thick ascending limb, so the fluid was neither diluted nor was the medulla made salty

questions.q: A patient has been on prolonged high volume intravenous fluids and now cannot concentrate their urine even though antidiuretic hormone levels are high. Trace the most likely cause.
options: The collecting duct has lost the ability to make aquaporin-2, so water cannot cross its apical membrane even when stimulated
The thick ascending limb has become permeable to water, so the fluid leaving it is no longer dilute at all
High medullary blood flow has washed out the osmotic gradient, so there is no driving force for water to leave the collecting duct
The vasa recta have begun actively pumping urea into the blood and out of the medullary interstitium
questions.why: Even with aquaporins fully inserted, water only leaves the collecting duct if the interstitium is saltier than the lumen, and volume expansion speeds vasa recta flow enough to strip that saltiness away. A sudden loss of the aquaporin gene is not something intravenous fluid causes. The ascending limb does not change its water permeability under these conditions. Vasa recta exchange is passive, so an active urea pump is not part of the story.
questions.answerText: High medullary blood flow has washed out the osmotic gradient, so there is no driving force for water to leave the collecting duct

questions.q: An experimental animal has a loop of Henle in which the descending limb has been made impermeable to water while everything else is normal. Predict the consequence for the medullary gradient and the urine.
options: The gradient becomes steeper because no water enters the interstitium from the descending limb to dilute it
The gradient fails to multiply because fluid reaching the ascending limb is no longer preconcentrated, and the urine stays dilute
The gradient is unaffected because only the ascending limb pumping matters for building it, not anything the descending limb does
The urine becomes maximally concentrated because water stays in the tubule all the way through the loop
questions.why: Multiplication depends on the descending limb handing progressively saltier fluid to the ascending limb, so blocking that step leaves the pump working against a fixed 200 mOsm/L step with nothing to stack it on. Keeping water in the lumen does not add solute to the interstitium, so the gradient cannot steepen. The ascending limb provides the energy, but it cannot multiply without the descending limb's preconcentration. Water trapped in the tubule ends up as more urine, not more concentrated urine.
questions.answerText: The gradient fails to multiply because fluid reaching the ascending limb is no longer preconcentrated, and the urine stays dilute

questions.q: A patient on a protein restricted diet for months has a lower maximum urine concentrating ability than expected, though their loop of Henle and antidiuretic hormone system are intact. What is the best explanation?
options: Less urea is produced, so the urea contribution to medullary osmolarity is reduced
Less protein means less albumin filtered, which lowers the medullary gradient
Protein restriction directly inhibits NKCC2 in the ascending limb
Protein restriction closes aquaporin-2 channels in the collecting duct
questions.why: Urea comes from protein breakdown and supplies roughly half the deep medullary osmolarity, so a low protein intake leaves the medulla less salty and the ceiling on urine concentration drops. Albumin is not filtered in health and contributes nothing to the medullary gradient. Diet does not directly inhibit the ascending limb transporter. Aquaporin-2 insertion is controlled by antidiuretic hormone, which the question tells you is intact.
questions.answerText: Less urea is produced, so the urea contribution to medullary osmolarity is reduced

questions.q: Two nephrons are compared. Nephron A has a loop reaching the deep medulla; nephron B has a short loop confined near the corticomedullary junction. Both are exposed to the same high antidiuretic hormone level. Which statement about their collecting duct fluid is correct?
options: Only nephron A can concentrate its fluid, because the gradient belongs to that nephron alone and not to the neighboring nephrons in the medulla
Nephron B concentrates better, because its shorter loop loses less water on the way down into the medulla before the turn
Neither can concentrate, because antidiuretic hormone acts only on the loop of Henle rather than on the collecting duct itself
Both collecting ducts pass through the same medullary gradient and can concentrate their fluid, but the deep gradient depends on nephrons like A
questions.why: The gradient is a property of the medullary interstitium, shared by every collecting duct that runs through it, while the long looped nephrons are the ones that build it. The gradient is not private to the nephron that created it. Antidiuretic hormone acts on the collecting duct, inserting aquaporin-2, not on the loop. A short loop does not confer better concentrating ability; the long loop is the advantage.
questions.answerText: Both collecting ducts pass through the same medullary gradient and can concentrate their fluid, but the deep gradient depends on nephrons like A

questions.q: Where are the osmoreceptors that detect a rise in plasma osmolarity?
options: In the carotid sinus
In the posterior pituitary
In the juxtaglomerular apparatus
In the hypothalamus
questions.why: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors shrink when plasma osmolarity rises and increase their firing, which is the first step of the dehydration response. The carotid sinus holds baroreceptors for arterial pressure and chemoreceptors for blood gases, not osmoreceptors. The juxtaglomerular apparatus senses perfusion pressure and distal NaCl for renin release. The posterior pituitary stores and releases the hormone but does not do the sensing.

questions.q: Where is antidiuretic hormone released into the blood?
options: From the anterior pituitary
From the posterior pituitary
From the adrenal cortex
From the hypothalamus directly into the systemic circulation
questions.why: Hypothalamic neurons make the hormone and send their axons down the stalk to the posterior pituitary, where the axon terminals release it into the blood. The anterior pituitary makes its own tropic hormones under hypothalamic releasing factors and does not store antidiuretic hormone. The adrenal cortex makes aldosterone and cortisol. The hypothalamus makes the hormone but does not release it directly into the systemic circulation.

questions.q: Which water channel does antidiuretic hormone insert into the collecting duct?
options: Aquaporin-2
Aquaporin-1
The NKCC2 cotransporter
The epithelial sodium channel
questions.why: Aquaporin-2 sits in vesicles inside principal cells and is shuttled to the apical membrane when antidiuretic hormone binds, which is the regulated step in water reabsorption. Aquaporin-1 is constitutively present in the proximal tubule and descending limb and is not hormone regulated. NKCC2 is the salt transporter of the thick ascending limb. The epithelial sodium channel is the aldosterone target for Na+ reabsorption, not a water channel.

questions.q: Which membrane of the collecting duct principal cell gains aquaporin-2 when antidiuretic hormone acts?
options: The tight junctions between cells
The basolateral membrane facing the interstitium
The membrane of the mitochondria
The apical membrane facing the tubular lumen
questions.why: Water has to enter the cell from the lumen first, so the regulated channels go into the apical membrane; the basolateral side already carries aquaporin-3 and aquaporin-4 all the time. Adding channels only to the basolateral side would not let water in from the urine. Mitochondrial membranes have no role in transepithelial water movement. Tight junctions seal the space between cells rather than carrying channels.
questions.answerText: The apical membrane facing the tubular lumen

questions.q: Which receptor on the collecting duct principal cell does antidiuretic hormone bind?
options: The V1 receptor
The V2 receptor
The AT1 receptor
The beta-1 adrenergic receptor
questions.why: V2 receptors on the basolateral membrane of principal cells raise cyclic AMP and trigger aquaporin-2 trafficking. V1 receptors are on vascular smooth muscle and mediate the vasoconstrictor effect of the same hormone at high concentrations. AT1 receptors bind angiotensin II. Beta-1 receptors are the sympathetic receptors on the heart and on granular cells.

questions.q: What is the primary stimulus for antidiuretic hormone release?
options: A fall in plasma osmolarity
A fall in plasma glucose
A rise in plasma potassium
A rise in plasma osmolarity
questions.why: Osmolarity is the tightly defended variable here, and a rise of only one or two percent is enough to increase secretion. A fall in osmolarity does the opposite, shutting secretion off so dilute urine can be made. Plasma potassium is the direct stimulus for aldosterone, not for antidiuretic hormone. Plasma glucose drives insulin and glucagon rather than water balance hormones.

questions.q: What second messenger carries the antidiuretic hormone signal inside the principal cell?
options: Inositol trisphosphate
Calcium released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Cyclic AMP
Nitric oxide
questions.why: The V2 receptor is coupled to a G protein that activates adenylate cyclase, and the resulting cyclic AMP activates protein kinase A, which drives the aquaporin vesicles to the apical membrane. Calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum is a muscle contraction pathway. Inositol trisphosphate is the second messenger for the V1 vascular receptor, not the renal V2 receptor. Nitric oxide is a vasodilator signal in endothelium.

questions.q: What happens to urine volume and concentration when antidiuretic hormone levels are high?
options: Urine volume rises and urine concentration falls
Urine volume falls and urine concentration rises
Both urine volume and concentration rise
Both urine volume and concentration fall
questions.why: With aquaporins in place, water leaves the collecting duct into the salty medulla, so what remains is a small volume of concentrated urine. Large dilute urine is what happens when the hormone is absent and the collecting duct stays water tight. Volume and concentration move in opposite directions here because the solute load is roughly fixed while the water varies. Both falling together would require solute to disappear as well, which does not happen.
questions.answerText: Urine volume falls and urine concentration rises

questions.q: A hiker has been without water for eight hours. What is the expected sequence in their body?
options: Plasma osmolarity rises, osmoreceptors fire more, antidiuretic hormone rises, urine becomes concentrated
Plasma osmolarity falls, osmoreceptors fire more, antidiuretic hormone rises, urine becomes dilute
Plasma osmolarity rises, osmoreceptors fire less, antidiuretic hormone falls, urine becomes dilute
Plasma osmolarity falls, osmoreceptors fire less, antidiuretic hormone falls, urine becomes concentrated
questions.why: Losing water without losing solute concentrates the plasma, and every step downstream follows from that first rise. Dehydration raises osmolarity rather than lowering it, so any option starting with a fall is wrong from the first step. Osmoreceptors fire more when osmolarity rises, not less. Concentrated urine cannot follow a fall in antidiuretic hormone, since the collecting duct would be water tight.
questions.answerText: Plasma osmolarity rises, osmoreceptors fire more, antidiuretic hormone rises, urine becomes concentrated

questions.q: A person drinks a liter of water quickly. Predict the change in antidiuretic hormone and urine.
options: Antidiuretic hormone falls and a large volume of dilute urine is produced
Antidiuretic hormone rises and a small volume of concentrated urine is produced
Antidiuretic hormone rises and a large volume of dilute urine is produced
Antidiuretic hormone is unchanged because only solute intake affects it
questions.why: Water dilutes the plasma, osmoreceptors quiet down, secretion drops, aquaporins are pulled out of the apical membrane, and the collecting duct lets the water pass into the urine. A rise in the hormone would be the response to dehydration, the opposite situation. High hormone levels cannot coexist with a large dilute urine, since the aquaporins would be reabsorbing that water. Water intake changes osmolarity directly, so the hormone is very much affected.
questions.answerText: Antidiuretic hormone falls and a large volume of dilute urine is produced

questions.q: Alcohol suppresses antidiuretic hormone release. Predict its effect on urine output.
options: Urine output decreases because water is retained
Urine output is unchanged because the medullary gradient is intact
Urine output increases because the collecting duct stays water impermeable
Urine output increases because the glomerular filtration rate rises sharply
questions.why: Without the hormone, aquaporin-2 is not inserted, so water that reaches the collecting duct cannot be reclaimed and leaves as urine. Water retention requires the hormone to be present, not suppressed. An intact medullary gradient does nothing if the collecting duct has no channels for water to cross. Alcohol does not raise the filtration rate; the effect is entirely at the collecting duct.
questions.answerText: Urine output increases because the collecting duct stays water impermeable

questions.q: A patient produces large volumes of dilute urine, and giving synthetic antidiuretic hormone corrects it. Which problem does this identify?
options: The collecting duct cannot respond to the hormone
The medullary gradient has been washed out
The pituitary is not releasing enough hormone
The glomerular filtration rate is abnormally high
questions.why: Responding to the replacement hormone proves the kidney machinery works and the missing piece was the hormone itself, which is central diabetes insipidus. If the collecting duct could not respond, giving more hormone would change nothing, which is the nephrogenic form. A washed out gradient would also blunt the response to given hormone. A high filtration rate is not corrected by antidiuretic hormone.
questions.answerText: The pituitary is not releasing enough hormone

questions.q: A patient produces large volumes of dilute urine and does not respond to synthetic antidiuretic hormone. Where is the defect?
options: At the hypothalamic osmoreceptors, which are no longer sensing plasma concentration
At the thick ascending limb transporter, which is no longer pumping NaCl out of the lumen
At the posterior pituitary storage terminals, which cannot release the stored hormone
At the collecting duct, which cannot insert aquaporin-2 in response to the hormone
questions.why: Supplying the hormone bypasses everything upstream, so a failure to respond puts the defect in the target tissue, which is nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. A sensing problem in the osmoreceptors would be corrected by giving the hormone directly. A storage or release problem at the pituitary is the central form, which does respond to replacement. A thick ascending limb defect would produce a different picture, with salt wasting and a poor gradient rather than a pure failure to respond.
questions.answerText: At the collecting duct, which cannot insert aquaporin-2 in response to the hormone

questions.q: Antidiuretic hormone is secreted in very large amounts inappropriately. Predict the plasma sodium concentration.
options: It rises, because sodium is reabsorbed with the water
It is unchanged, because the hormone moves only water
It falls, because water is retained and dilutes the plasma
It rises, because the medullary gradient pulls sodium into the blood
questions.why: The hormone moves water without sodium, so retained water dilutes the sodium already in the plasma and the measured concentration drops. Sodium reabsorption is the job of aldosterone, not of this hormone. Moving only water is exactly why sodium concentration changes; the numerator stays put while the denominator grows. The medullary gradient pulls water out of the collecting duct, not sodium into the blood.
questions.answerText: It falls, because water is retained and dilutes the plasma

questions.q: Severe blood loss of twenty percent triggers antidiuretic hormone release even though plasma osmolarity has not risen. What sensed the change?
options: Baroreceptors reporting a fall in blood volume and pressure
Hypothalamic osmoreceptors detecting cell shrinkage
Macula densa cells detecting distal sodium delivery
Chemoreceptors detecting a fall in arterial PO2
questions.why: A large volume loss overrides the osmotic control through baroreceptor input, because defending pressure becomes more urgent than defending osmolarity. Osmoreceptors respond to concentration, and the question states osmolarity is unchanged. The macula densa signals to the granular cells for renin release, not to the pituitary. Arterial chemoreceptors adjust ventilation rather than water balance.
questions.answerText: Baroreceptors reporting a fall in blood volume and pressure

questions.q: A patient has been vomiting for two days and now has concentrated urine, high antidiuretic hormone, and a low plasma sodium concentration. Explain how the sodium can be low when the patient is clearly volume depleted.
options: The kidney is wasting sodium because antidiuretic hormone blocks sodium reabsorption in the collecting duct as well
Aldosterone has been suppressed by the volume loss, so sodium is no longer reabsorbed from the tubular fluid
Volume depletion drives antidiuretic hormone through baroreceptors, and the retained water dilutes the sodium that remains
The medullary gradient has collapsed, forcing sodium into the urine along with a large volume of water
questions.why: When volume is threatened, the body defends pressure first, holding onto water even at the cost of diluting the plasma, so a volume depleted patient can be hyponatremic. The hormone does not block sodium reabsorption; it acts on water channels only. Volume loss raises aldosterone rather than suppressing it, which conserves sodium. A collapsed medullary gradient would give dilute urine, not the concentrated urine described.
questions.answerText: Volume depletion drives antidiuretic hormone through baroreceptors, and the retained water dilutes the sodium that remains

questions.q: A patient with a head injury develops sudden polyuria with urine osmolarity of 80 mOsm/L and plasma osmolarity of 310 mOsm/L. Trace the failure and predict what happens if they cannot reach water.
options: Damage to the hypothalamic or pituitary pathway has stopped hormone release, so plasma osmolarity will keep climbing as water is lost
The collecting duct is oversensitive to the hormone, so water will be retained and plasma osmolarity will fall back toward normal
The loop of Henle has stopped pumping salt, so plasma sodium will fall as it is lost in a large urine volume
Aldosterone has risen sharply, so plasma osmolarity will fall as sodium is excreted over the next day or two
questions.why: Dilute urine in the face of concentrated plasma is the signature of absent hormone action, and after a head injury the release pathway is the likely break, so without drinking, the patient dehydrates further. Oversensitivity to the hormone would produce concentrated urine and a falling osmolarity, the reverse of these values. A loop failure would give urine near plasma osmolarity rather than 80 mOsm/L. Aldosterone conserves sodium and does not produce this pattern.
questions.answerText: Damage to the hypothalamic or pituitary pathway has stopped hormone release, so plasma osmolarity will keep climbing as water is lost

questions.q: An athlete drinks large volumes of plain water during a long race and becomes confused with a plasma sodium of 125 mEq/L. Which combination best explains the fall in sodium?
options: Sweat loss removed sodium while exercise related antidiuretic hormone release let the replacement water be retained
Exercise suppressed antidiuretic hormone, so all the water taken in was excreted along with sodium
The kidney secreted sodium directly into the urine under the influence of aldosterone released during the race
Water intake raised plasma osmolarity, which triggered further water intake and worsened the problem
questions.why: Sodium leaves in sweat, and the hormone stays elevated during hard exercise, so plain water taken in is held rather than excreted and the remaining sodium is diluted further. If the hormone were suppressed, the excess water would leave as dilute urine and sodium would not fall so far. Aldosterone conserves sodium rather than secreting it. Drinking water lowers plasma osmolarity, not raises it.
questions.answerText: Sweat loss removed sodium while exercise related antidiuretic hormone release let the replacement water be retained

questions.q: A patient with normal antidiuretic hormone levels and normal collecting duct receptors still cannot concentrate urine above 350 mOsm/L. Which single explanation fits all three findings?
options: The V2 receptors are present but not coupled to adenylate cyclase, so no cyclic AMP is made inside the cell
Aquaporin-1 is missing from the proximal tubule, so water cannot be reabsorbed there in bulk
The posterior pituitary has been surgically removed, so no hormone reaches the kidney at all
The medullary osmotic gradient has been lost, so there is no osmotic pull for water to leave the collecting duct
questions.why: Aquaporins can only move water down an osmotic gradient, so intact hormone and intact receptors still fail if the medulla is no longer salty, and 350 mOsm/L is about what you get with a flat gradient. A receptor coupling defect would mean the receptors are not normal, which the question rules out. Pituitary removal would drop hormone levels, which are stated to be normal. Proximal aquaporin-1 loss would change proximal water handling but is not the reason the final urine cannot be concentrated.
questions.answerText: The medullary osmotic gradient has been lost, so there is no osmotic pull for water to leave the collecting duct

questions.q: Which cells release renin?
options: Granular cells of the juxtaglomerular apparatus
Macula densa cells of the distal tubule
Principal cells of the collecting duct
Podocytes of the glomerulus
questions.why: Granular cells sit in the wall of the afferent arteriole and are modified smooth muscle cells that store and release renin. Macula densa cells sense sodium chloride in the distal tubule and signal to the granular cells, but they do not make renin themselves. Principal cells respond to aldosterone at the end of the pathway. Podocytes form the filtration slits and have no endocrine role of this kind.
questions.answerText: Granular cells of the juxtaglomerular apparatus

questions.q: Which of these is a direct stimulus for renin release?
options: A fall in perfusion pressure at the afferent arteriole
A rise in perfusion pressure at the afferent arteriole
A rise in sodium chloride delivery to the macula densa
Parasympathetic stimulation of the kidney
questions.why: Granular cells act as their own stretch sensors, and less stretch from lower pressure means more renin, which starts the pathway that restores pressure. A rise in perfusion pressure suppresses renin instead. High sodium chloride at the macula densa also suppresses renin, since it signals that filtration is adequate. Renin release is driven by sympathetic beta-1 stimulation, not parasympathetic input.
questions.answerText: A fall in perfusion pressure at the afferent arteriole

questions.q: What does renin act on in the plasma?
options: Angiotensinogen
Angiotensin I
Angiotensin II
Aldosterone
questions.why: Renin is an enzyme that cleaves angiotensinogen, a protein released continuously by the liver, into angiotensin I. Angiotensin I is renin's product, not its substrate. Angiotensin II is two steps downstream and is made by a different enzyme. Aldosterone is a steroid released from the adrenal cortex at the end of the pathway.

questions.q: Where is most angiotensin converting enzyme found?
options: In the liver, where angiotensinogen is made
In the adrenal cortex, near the glomerulosa
On the endothelium of the pulmonary capillaries
In the granular cells of the kidney cortex
questions.why: The lung has an enormous capillary surface area, and its endothelium carries most of the converting enzyme that turns angiotensin I into angiotensin II. The liver makes angiotensinogen, the substrate at the start of the chain. The adrenal cortex responds to angiotensin II by making aldosterone rather than making the enzyme. Granular cells make renin, the first enzyme in the sequence.
questions.answerText: On the endothelium of the pulmonary capillaries

questions.q: What effect does angiotensin II have on systemic arterioles?
options: It constricts them
It dilates them
It has no direct vascular effect
It constricts veins only
questions.why: Angiotensin II is one of the most potent vasoconstrictors in the body, and narrowing the arterioles raises total peripheral resistance and therefore arterial pressure. Dilation would lower pressure, which is the opposite of what the pathway is for. The vascular effect is direct and strong, acting through AT1 receptors on smooth muscle. The effect is not limited to veins; arterioles are the main target for resistance.

questions.q: Which zone of the adrenal cortex releases aldosterone?
options: The zona glomerulosa
The zona fasciculata
The zona reticularis
The adrenal medulla
questions.why: The outermost zone, the zona glomerulosa, is the only zone with the enzyme needed to make aldosterone, and it responds to angiotensin II and to plasma potassium. The zona fasciculata makes cortisol under ACTH control. The zona reticularis makes adrenal androgens. The adrenal medulla releases epinephrine and is not part of the cortex at all.

questions.q: Which two transport proteins does aldosterone increase in collecting duct principal cells?
options: The sodium glucose cotransporter and aquaporin-1 of the proximal tubule cell
Aquaporin-2 and the basolateral V2 receptor of the principal cell
NKCC2 and the apical potassium channel of the thick ascending limb
The apical epithelial sodium channel and the basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase
questions.why: Aldosterone increases the number of sodium channels letting Na+ in from the lumen and the number of pumps moving that Na+ into the blood, so sodium reabsorption rises and potassium secretion follows. Aquaporin-2 and the V2 receptor belong to the antidiuretic hormone pathway for water. NKCC2 is in the thick ascending limb, outside aldosterone's territory. Sodium glucose cotransporters and aquaporin-1 are proximal tubule proteins.
questions.answerText: The apical epithelial sodium channel and the basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase

questions.q: What is the net effect of aldosterone on sodium and potassium in the urine?
options: More sodium and more potassium in the urine
Less sodium and more potassium in the urine
Less sodium and less potassium in the urine
More sodium and less potassium in the urine
questions.why: Aldosterone reclaims sodium from the tubular fluid and drives potassium the other way into the lumen, so the two move in opposite directions. Losing both would not defend blood volume, which is the purpose of the hormone. Conserving both is not possible, because reabsorbing sodium leaves the lumen negative and pulls potassium out. Wasting sodium while keeping potassium describes what happens when aldosterone is absent.
questions.answerText: Less sodium and more potassium in the urine

questions.q: A patient's blood pressure falls after a hemorrhage. Predict what happens to renin release and why.
options: Renin release increases because the macula densa senses more sodium chloride
Renin release decreases because there is less blood to filter
Renin release is unchanged because renin responds only to plasma sodium
Renin release increases because the granular cells sense reduced stretch
questions.why: Granular cells respond to how much the afferent arteriole wall is stretched, and less pressure means less stretch and more renin, starting the pathway that raises pressure back up. Falling pressure calls for more renin, not less. Renin responds to perfusion pressure, macula densa signals, and sympathetic input, not to plasma sodium concentration directly. After hemorrhage the macula densa sees less sodium chloride, not more, and that also increases renin.
questions.answerText: Renin release increases because the granular cells sense reduced stretch

questions.q: A drug blocks angiotensin converting enzyme. Predict the effect on blood pressure and on aldosterone.
options: Blood pressure falls and aldosterone falls
Blood pressure rises and aldosterone rises
Blood pressure falls and aldosterone rises
Blood pressure rises and aldosterone falls
questions.why: Without the converting enzyme, angiotensin II is not made, so the vasoconstriction is lost and the adrenal stimulus for aldosterone disappears, and both pressure and aldosterone fall together. Blocking the pathway cannot raise pressure. Aldosterone cannot rise when its main driver is removed, unless plasma potassium climbs enough to stimulate it separately. Both effects follow from the same missing molecule, so they move in the same direction.
questions.answerText: Blood pressure falls and aldosterone falls

questions.q: A patient is put on a very low sodium diet. Predict the change in renin and aldosterone.
options: Both fall, because there is less sodium to handle
Renin rises but aldosterone falls
Both rise, to conserve the sodium that is available
Renin falls but aldosterone rises
questions.why: Low sodium intake lowers extracellular volume and reduces sodium chloride at the macula densa, both of which increase renin, and the extra angiotensin II then drives aldosterone up so the kidney holds onto sodium. Falling levels would waste the scarce sodium. Aldosterone follows angiotensin II in this setting, so renin and aldosterone move together. Renin falling with low sodium would be the reverse of the sensing mechanism.
questions.answerText: Both rise, to conserve the sodium that is available

questions.q: Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole more than the afferent arteriole. What does this preserve?
options: Renal blood flow, by increasing the volume of blood passing through the glomerulus
The glomerular filtration rate, by holding pressure up inside the glomerular capillaries
The medullary osmotic gradient, by slowing the flow of blood through the vasa recta
Sodium delivery to the macula densa, by speeding the flow of fluid through the tubule
questions.why: Squeezing the outflow while leaving the inflow more open raises glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure, which is what keeps filtration going when perfusion pressure is low. Renal blood flow actually falls with efferent constriction, since resistance is higher overall. The medullary gradient is a loop of Henle and vasa recta matter, not an efferent arteriole one. Sodium delivery to the macula densa falls in this setting rather than rising.
questions.answerText: The glomerular filtration rate, by holding pressure up inside the glomerular capillaries

questions.q: Besides its vascular and adrenal effects, angiotensin II acts on the brain. What does that produce?
options: Suppression of thirst and reduced antidiuretic hormone release
Increased respiratory rate and reduced thirst
Thirst and increased antidiuretic hormone release
Reduced sympathetic outflow to the heart
questions.why: Angiotensin II acts at the hypothalamus to make the person drink and to increase water retention, both of which add volume and support blood pressure. Suppressing thirst would work against the purpose of the pathway. Angiotensin II does not act as a respiratory stimulant. It raises sympathetic outflow rather than reducing it.
questions.answerText: Thirst and increased antidiuretic hormone release

questions.q: A patient is given a drug that blocks the aldosterone receptor. Predict the change in plasma potassium.
options: It falls, because potassium is lost in the urine
It rises, because potassium secretion in the collecting duct falls
It is unchanged, because aldosterone affects only sodium handling
It falls, because the sodium potassium pump starts working harder
questions.why: Aldosterone drives sodium in and potassium out at the principal cell, so blocking its receptor leaves potassium in the blood and plasma levels climb. Losing more potassium requires more aldosterone action, not less. Aldosterone handles sodium and potassium together, which is why blocking it affects both. Blocking the receptor reduces pump activity rather than increasing it.
questions.answerText: It rises, because potassium secretion in the collecting duct falls

questions.q: Sympathetic nerves to the kidney fire strongly during exercise. Which receptor on the granular cells mediates renin release?
options: The alpha-1 adrenergic receptor
The AT1 receptor
The muscarinic receptor
The beta-1 adrenergic receptor
questions.why: Beta-1 receptors on granular cells respond to norepinephrine by increasing renin release, which is why beta blockers lower renin. Alpha-1 receptors mediate vasoconstriction on the arterioles themselves rather than renin secretion. Muscarinic receptors respond to acetylcholine, and the kidney has little parasympathetic control of this kind. AT1 receptors bind angiotensin II and mediate the negative feedback that shuts renin off.

questions.q: A patient has a narrowed artery supplying one kidney. That kidney sees low perfusion pressure even though systemic pressure is high. Predict the renin level and the systemic blood pressure over time.
options: Renin falls because systemic pressure is already high, and blood pressure returns to normal
Renin falls and plasma potassium rises as aldosterone is withdrawn
Renin stays high but systemic pressure falls, because the other kidney compensates by excreting sodium
Renin stays high because the affected kidney senses low pressure, and systemic pressure climbs further
questions.why: The granular cells report only what they can sense, which is the pressure downstream of the narrowing, so the pathway keeps driving even though the rest of the body is hypertensive. Systemic pressure does not switch the sensor off, because the narrowing shields the sensor from it. The healthy kidney does excrete some sodium but cannot overcome continuous angiotensin II and aldosterone. Aldosterone rises rather than falls here, so potassium tends to drop.
questions.answerText: Renin stays high because the affected kidney senses low pressure, and systemic pressure climbs further

questions.q: A patient with heart failure has a low cardiac output. Their kidneys retain sodium and water aggressively, which worsens their swelling. Trace why the kidney behaves this way.
options: Low cardiac output raises renal perfusion pressure, which stimulates aldosterone directly and makes the kidney hold onto sodium and water
Low cardiac output damages the filtration membrane so protein is lost, and the missing protein pulls water into the tissues
Low cardiac output raises atrial natriuretic peptide, which retains sodium and water instead of promoting their loss in the urine
Low cardiac output lowers renal perfusion pressure, granular cells release renin, and angiotensin II and aldosterone retain sodium and water
questions.why: The kidney reads low perfusion the same way it reads blood loss and switches on volume conservation, which is unhelpful when the problem is a weak pump rather than a low volume. Low output lowers renal perfusion rather than raising it. Atrial natriuretic peptide does rise with atrial stretch in heart failure, but it promotes sodium loss, not retention. Filtration membrane damage causes proteinuria, which is a different problem from sodium retention.
questions.answerText: Low cardiac output lowers renal perfusion pressure, granular cells release renin, and angiotensin II and aldosterone retain sodium and water

questions.q: A patient takes an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor and their glomerular filtration rate drops sharply, more than expected from the fall in blood pressure alone. Which mechanism best explains the extra drop?
options: Loss of angiotensin II constricts the afferent arteriole and cuts inflow to the glomerular capillaries
Loss of aldosterone reduces the filtration surface area of the glomerulus and lowers the filtration rate
Loss of angiotensin II removes efferent arteriolar constriction, so glomerular capillary pressure falls further
Loss of renin lowers plasma oncotic pressure and reduces the net force favoring filtration at the glomerulus
questions.why: Angiotensin II holds the efferent arteriole partly closed, which props up glomerular pressure, and removing it lets pressure escape downstream so filtration falls beyond what the systemic pressure change would predict. Aldosterone works on tubular transport and has nothing to do with filtration surface area. Removing angiotensin II relaxes arterioles rather than constricting the afferent one. Plasma oncotic pressure comes from plasma proteins made by the liver and is not set by renin.
questions.answerText: Loss of angiotensin II removes efferent arteriolar constriction, so glomerular capillary pressure falls further

questions.q: An adrenal tumor secretes aldosterone continuously and independently of angiotensin II. Predict the pattern of renin, plasma potassium, and blood pressure.
options: Renin high, potassium high, blood pressure low
Renin high, potassium low, blood pressure high
Renin low, potassium low, blood pressure high
Renin low, potassium high, blood pressure low
questions.why: Unregulated aldosterone retains sodium and water, which raises pressure, and the higher pressure feeds back on the granular cells to shut renin off, while the same aldosterone drives potassium into the urine. High renin would mean the pathway is being driven from above, which is not the case with an autonomous tumor. Potassium cannot be high while aldosterone is high, since the hormone promotes its secretion. Blood pressure rises rather than falls with sodium retention.
questions.answerText: Renin low, potassium low, blood pressure high

questions.q: Which cells release atrial natriuretic peptide?
options: Granular cells of the juxtaglomerular apparatus
Endothelial cells of the renal arteries
Myocytes of the cardiac atria
Cells of the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex
questions.why: Atrial muscle cells store this peptide in granules and release it when the atrial wall is stretched, which makes the heart itself an endocrine sensor of blood volume. Renal endothelium releases nitric oxide and other local vasodilators, not this peptide. Granular cells release renin, the hormone this peptide opposes. The zona glomerulosa releases aldosterone, which this peptide inhibits.

questions.q: What is the stimulus for atrial natriuretic peptide release?
options: A fall in blood volume that reduces venous return
A rise in plasma potassium above the normal range
Stretch of the atrial wall from increased blood volume
A fall in arterial PO2 sensed by chemoreceptors
questions.why: More volume returning to the heart stretches the atria further, and that stretch is the signal to release the peptide so the kidney can shed the extra salt and water. A fall in blood volume does the opposite, reducing release. Plasma potassium is the direct stimulus for aldosterone from the adrenal cortex. Arterial PO2 is monitored by chemoreceptors that adjust ventilation.
questions.answerText: Stretch of the atrial wall from increased blood volume

questions.q: What does the word natriuretic mean?
options: Promoting sodium retention in the blood
Promoting sodium loss in the urine
Promoting potassium loss in the urine
Promoting water retention without sodium
questions.why: Natrium is sodium and uresis is urination, so a natriuretic agent makes the kidney put sodium into the urine, and water follows it out. Retaining sodium is what aldosterone does, which is the opposite. Potassium loss in the urine is kaliuresis, a different term. Retaining water without sodium describes the action of antidiuretic hormone.
questions.answerText: Promoting sodium loss in the urine

questions.q: What effect does atrial natriuretic peptide have on renin release?
options: It stimulates renin release
It inhibits renin release
It has no effect on renin release
It converts renin into angiotensin I
questions.why: Suppressing renin shuts down the whole angiotensin and aldosterone chain, which is the core of how this peptide opposes volume conservation. Stimulating renin would add to sodium retention, the reverse of its purpose. The effect on renin is real and is one of its main renal actions. Renin is itself an enzyme and is not converted into angiotensin I; it makes angiotensin I from angiotensinogen.

questions.q: What effect does atrial natriuretic peptide have on aldosterone secretion?
options: It increases aldosterone secretion
It increases aldosterone but blocks its receptor
It has no effect on aldosterone secretion
It decreases aldosterone secretion
questions.why: The peptide acts directly on the zona glomerulosa and indirectly by lowering angiotensin II, so less aldosterone is made and less sodium is reabsorbed. Increasing aldosterone would retain sodium and defeat the purpose. The adrenal effect is one of the well established actions of this peptide. It does not block the aldosterone receptor; that is what a receptor antagonist drug does.

questions.q: How does atrial natriuretic peptide affect the glomerular filtration rate?
options: It lowers it, by constricting the afferent arteriole and cutting glomerular pressure
It leaves it unchanged, acting only on the tubule and not on the arterioles at all
It lowers it, by reducing the filtration surface area available in each glomerulus
It raises it, by dilating the afferent arteriole and constricting the efferent arteriole
questions.why: Opening the inflow while narrowing the outflow raises glomerular capillary pressure, so more fluid is filtered and more sodium is presented to the tubule for excretion. Constricting the afferent arteriole would cut filtration, the opposite of what a natriuretic hormone needs. The peptide relaxes mesangial cells, which increases rather than decreases effective surface area. It acts on both the vessels and the tubule, not the tubule alone.
questions.answerText: It raises it, by dilating the afferent arteriole and constricting the efferent arteriole

questions.q: Which segment of the nephron does atrial natriuretic peptide inhibit sodium reabsorption in most directly?
options: The thin descending limb
The thick ascending limb
The medullary collecting duct
Bowman capsule
questions.why: The peptide closes sodium channels in the medullary collecting duct, which is the last chance the kidney has to reclaim sodium, so blocking it there sends sodium out in the urine. The thin descending limb handles water and has no sodium pump to inhibit. The thick ascending limb is the target of loop diuretics rather than of this peptide. Bowman capsule collects filtrate and does no reabsorption.

questions.q: What second messenger does atrial natriuretic peptide use in its target cells?
options: Cyclic GMP
Cyclic AMP
Inositol trisphosphate
Diacylglycerol
questions.why: Its receptor is itself a guanylate cyclase, so binding the hormone makes cyclic GMP directly without a separate G protein step. Cyclic AMP is the messenger for antidiuretic hormone at the V2 receptor and for many other hormones. Inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol come from the phospholipase C pathway used by angiotensin II at the AT1 receptor.

questions.q: A patient receives a large intravenous saline infusion. Predict the change in atrial natriuretic peptide and in urine sodium.
options: The peptide falls and urine sodium falls
The peptide rises and urine sodium rises
The peptide rises and urine sodium falls
The peptide falls and urine sodium rises
questions.why: Extra volume stretches the atria, release goes up, and the kidney answers by dumping sodium, which pulls water with it and returns volume toward normal. A fall in the peptide would follow volume loss, not volume loading. High peptide levels with low urine sodium contradicts the hormone's main action. Urine sodium rising while the peptide falls would need a different explanation entirely.
questions.answerText: The peptide rises and urine sodium rises

questions.q: Atrial natriuretic peptide and aldosterone are compared side by side. Which pair of effects is correct?
options: Both increase urinary sodium loss
The peptide increases urinary sodium loss while aldosterone decreases it
Both decrease urinary sodium loss
The peptide decreases urinary sodium loss while aldosterone increases it
questions.why: The two hormones are opposites on sodium handling, which is what lets the body correct volume in either direction.
