If both increased sodium loss, nothing would defend blood volume when it fell. If both decreased it, volume overload could not be corrected. The last option reverses each hormone's action.
questions.answerText: The peptide increases urinary sodium loss while aldosterone decreases it

questions.q: A patient in heart failure has chronically stretched atria. What would you expect their natriuretic peptide level to be, and why is the sodium loss still inadequate?
options: The level is low, because a failing heart cannot make the peptide
The level is high, but strong renin angiotensin aldosterone activity overrides it
The level is high, and sodium loss is therefore excessive
The level is normal, because atrial stretch does not change in heart failure
questions.why: Chronic stretch keeps the peptide elevated, but the kidney also sees low perfusion and drives the opposing pathway hard, and that pathway usually wins, so fluid accumulates anyway. A failing heart with stretched atria releases more of the peptide, not less. Sodium loss is inadequate in heart failure, not excessive, which is why swelling develops. Atrial stretch is markedly increased in heart failure.
questions.answerText: The level is high, but strong renin angiotensin aldosterone activity overrides it

questions.q: A drug prevents the breakdown of atrial natriuretic peptide. Predict its effect on blood pressure.
options: Blood pressure rises, because the peptide is a vasoconstrictor that raises peripheral resistance
Blood pressure is unchanged, because the peptide acts only on the kidney and not on blood vessels
Blood pressure falls, because more of the peptide is available to promote vasodilation and sodium loss
Blood pressure rises, because renin release increases when the peptide level stays higher for longer
questions.why: Slowing degradation raises the effective hormone level, and its combination of vessel relaxation and sodium excretion lowers both resistance and volume. The peptide dilates vessels rather than constricting them. Its actions include direct vascular effects, so the kidney is not the only site. Renin release is suppressed by the peptide, not increased.
questions.answerText: Blood pressure falls, because more of the peptide is available to promote vasodilation and sodium loss

questions.q: After a hemorrhage, what happens to atrial natriuretic peptide release and why does that make sense?
options: Release falls, because reduced venous return means less atrial stretch, and the body needs to keep sodium
Release rises, to help restore volume by making the kidney retain sodium and water after the loss
Release rises, because sympathetic drive stimulates the atria to secrete more of the peptide after blood loss
Release is unchanged, because the peptide responds only to plasma sodium concentration rather than to volume
questions.why: Less blood returning means less atrial stretch, so the natriuretic signal quiets down and the volume conserving pathways are left unopposed. The peptide promotes sodium loss, so more of it would worsen a hemorrhage rather than help. Sympathetic drive raises heart rate and contractility but is not the release stimulus for this peptide. The stimulus is mechanical stretch, not plasma sodium concentration.
questions.answerText: Release falls, because reduced venous return means less atrial stretch, and the body needs to keep sodium

questions.q: Brain natriuretic peptide is measured in a patient with shortness of breath and is markedly elevated. What does the elevation indicate physiologically?
options: The kidneys are failing to filter blood at an adequate rate each minute
The patient is dehydrated and the circulating volume has dropped
The ventricular wall is being stretched by increased volume or pressure
The adrenal cortex is producing too much aldosterone for the volume
questions.why: Despite its name, this peptide is released mainly by ventricular myocytes in response to wall stretch, so a high level reports on the loading of the heart. A failing filter would show up as a rising creatinine, not as a natriuretic peptide rise. Dehydration reduces stretch and lowers the level. Excess aldosterone would raise volume indirectly, but the peptide reports stretch itself rather than naming the hormone behind it.
questions.answerText: The ventricular wall is being stretched by increased volume or pressure

questions.q: A patient is given a large volume of intravenous fluid. Trace the sequence that returns blood volume toward normal through the natriuretic pathway.
options: Volume rises, atria stretch, renin rises, aldosterone rises, and sodium is retained until the arterial pressure normalizes again
Volume rises, atria stretch, the peptide is released, renin and aldosterone fall, filtration rises, and sodium and water leave in the urine
Volume rises, the peptide falls, antidiuretic hormone rises, and water is retained until plasma osmolarity normalizes
Volume rises, the peptide is released, the afferent arteriole constricts, and filtration falls so sodium is retained
questions.why: Each step follows from the one before, and the endpoint is losing the extra salt and water rather than holding it. Renin and aldosterone are suppressed by volume expansion, so a version where they rise contradicts the stimulus. Antidiuretic hormone also falls with volume expansion, so retaining water would be wrong. The peptide dilates the afferent arteriole, so filtration rises rather than falls.
questions.answerText: Volume rises, atria stretch, the peptide is released, renin and aldosterone fall, filtration rises, and sodium and water leave in the urine

questions.q: Two patients both have a blood pressure of 150 over 95. Patient A has a high renin and low natriuretic peptide; patient B has a low renin and high natriuretic peptide. Which statement best distinguishes their situations?
options: Patient A has an expanded volume and patient B has a contracted volume, since the two hormones track circulating volume directly in every case
Patient A has a pressure problem driven by vasoconstriction and sodium retention, while patient B has an expanded volume the heart is reporting
Both patients have identical physiology because their measured pressures match, so the hormone levels add nothing useful
Patient B is at higher risk of losing sodium in the urine, but only if renin also rises to match the peptide level
questions.why: The hormone pattern tells you what the body thinks is happening, so high renin points to a kidney sensing low perfusion while high natriuretic peptide points to atria sensing too much volume. The volumes are the other way around from the first option, since renin rises when volume is low. Equal pressures do not mean equal mechanisms, which is the whole point of measuring the hormones. A rise in renin would oppose sodium loss rather than enable it.
questions.answerText: Patient A has a pressure problem driven by vasoconstriction and sodium retention, while patient B has an expanded volume the heart is reporting

questions.q: An experimental animal has its natriuretic peptide receptors deleted. It is then given a salt load. Predict what happens compared with a normal animal.
options: Its blood pressure falls, because aldosterone acts unopposed and relaxes the systemic arterioles
It excretes the salt faster, because renin can no longer be suppressed and instead drives sodium out into the urine
It excretes the salt more slowly and its blood pressure rises more, because the opposing arm of volume control is missing
It shows no change, because the kidney handles salt loads without any hormonal help from the heart
questions.why: Without receptors, the peptide is released but nothing responds to it, so renin and aldosterone stay active, the collecting duct keeps reclaiming sodium, and volume and pressure climb. Losing the receptors removes suppression of renin, which slows salt excretion rather than speeding it. Unopposed aldosterone raises pressure rather than lowering it. Pressure natriuresis provides some hormone independent handling, but not enough to make the deletion invisible.
questions.answerText: It excretes the salt more slowly and its blood pressure rises more, because the opposing arm of volume control is missing

questions.q: A patient with a tumor secreting large amounts of atrial natriuretic peptide is studied. Predict the pattern of plasma volume, renin, and urine output.
options: Plasma volume rises, renin rises, and urine output falls as sodium is retained by the collecting duct
Plasma volume falls, renin is suppressed by the peptide despite the low volume, and urine output rises
Plasma volume falls, renin rises sharply, and urine output falls as sodium is conserved
Plasma volume rises, renin falls, and urine output falls despite the extra circulating volume
questions.why: Continuous peptide release drives sodium and water out and directly inhibits granular cells, so renin stays low even though the falling volume would normally raise it, and urine output remains high. Rising volume cannot follow from a natriuretic and diuretic hormone. Renin would rise if the peptide were not blocking it, so the third option ignores the direct inhibition. Falling urine output contradicts the diuretic effect of the hormone.
questions.answerText: Plasma volume falls, renin is suppressed by the peptide despite the low volume, and urine output rises

questions.q: What is the normal range of plasma potassium?
options: 135 to 145 mEq/L
8 to 10 mEq/L
3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L
0.5 to 1.5 mEq/L
questions.why: Plasma potassium is kept in a narrow band around 4 mEq/L, and even small deviations disturb the resting membrane potential of heart and nerve. The range of 135 to 145 mEq/L is plasma sodium. Values of 8 to 10 mEq/L would be dangerously high and are not a normal range. Values below 1.5 mEq/L are far too low to sustain excitable tissue.

questions.q: Where is most of the body's potassium located?
options: In the plasma
In bone mineral
Inside cells
In the interstitial fluid
questions.why: About 98 percent of body potassium sits in the intracellular compartment, which is why the small plasma fraction is so sensitive to shifts across the membrane. Plasma holds only a tiny fraction of the total. Bone mineral is the reservoir for calcium and phosphate, not potassium. Interstitial fluid, like plasma, is part of the small extracellular pool.

questions.q: Which cell type secretes potassium into the collecting duct lumen?
options: Principal cells
Intercalated cells
Macula densa cells
Podocytes
questions.why: Principal cells pump potassium into themselves from the blood side and let it leak into the lumen through apical channels, and this is the step aldosterone regulates. Intercalated cells handle acid and base and can reabsorb potassium when the body is depleted. Macula densa cells sense sodium chloride and signal renin release. Podocytes are part of the filtration barrier and do no secretion.

questions.q: A rise in plasma potassium has what direct effect on the adrenal cortex?
options: It inhibits aldosterone release
It stimulates aldosterone release
It stimulates cortisol release
It has no direct effect, since angiotensin II is required
questions.why: The zona glomerulosa responds directly to plasma potassium, so a rise drives aldosterone up and the extra aldosterone drives potassium into the urine, closing a tight feedback loop. Inhibiting aldosterone would let potassium climb further. Cortisol release is controlled by ACTH from the anterior pituitary. Angiotensin II is one stimulus for aldosterone, but potassium works on its own without it.

questions.q: Which transporter on the basolateral membrane of the principal cell loads potassium into the cell?
options: The epithelial sodium channel
NKCC2
The Na+/K+ ATPase
The sodium glucose cotransporter
questions.why: The pump moves three Na+ out into the blood and two K+ in from the blood, which keeps intracellular potassium high enough to leak into the lumen. NKCC2 is the apical transporter of the thick ascending limb, not the collecting duct. The epithelial sodium channel is on the apical membrane and moves sodium in from the lumen. The sodium glucose cotransporter is a proximal tubule protein.

questions.q: How does aldosterone change potassium excretion?
options: It increases potassium excretion only when plasma potassium is low
It decreases potassium excretion
It has no effect on potassium
It increases potassium excretion
questions.why: By adding sodium channels and pumps to principal cells, aldosterone raises intracellular potassium and makes the lumen more negative, and both changes push potassium into the urine. Decreasing excretion is what happens when aldosterone is absent or blocked. Potassium is one of aldosterone's two main targets, alongside sodium. The effect does not require low plasma potassium; in fact high plasma potassium is one of the stimuli that turns aldosterone on.

questions.q: Which class of diuretic is described as potassium wasting?
options: Sodium channel blockers of the collecting duct
Aldosterone receptor blockers
Loop and thiazide diuretics
Osmotic agents that block the aldosterone receptor
questions.why: Loop and thiazide agents block sodium reabsorption upstream, so more sodium and more fluid reach the collecting duct, and both changes increase potassium secretion. Aldosterone receptor blockers are potassium sparing, since they remove the hormone signal that drives secretion. Collecting duct sodium channel blockers are also potassium sparing, because they remove the negative luminal charge that pulls potassium out. Osmotic agents work by holding water in the tubule and do not block the aldosterone receptor.

questions.q: Besides aldosterone and plasma potassium, what else increases potassium secretion in the collecting duct?
options: A lower rate of sodium delivery to the collecting duct
A higher flow rate of fluid past the principal cells
A more positive electrical charge in the tubular lumen
A rise in the potassium concentration of tubular fluid
questions.why: Fast flow sweeps secreted potassium away, keeping luminal potassium low and the concentration gradient steep, so more potassium keeps leaving the cell. Less sodium delivery reduces secretion, because sodium entry is what makes the lumen negative. A positive lumen would repel potassium rather than attract it. Rising luminal potassium concentration flattens the gradient and slows secretion.
questions.answerText: A higher flow rate of fluid past the principal cells

questions.q: A patient starts a loop diuretic. Predict the effect on plasma potassium and explain the mechanism.
options: Plasma potassium rises, because the loop of Henle normally secretes potassium
Plasma potassium is unchanged, because the drug acts upstream of the collecting duct and never reaches it
Plasma potassium falls, because increased distal sodium delivery and flow drive potassium secretion
Plasma potassium falls, because the drug blocks the Na+/K+ ATPase in principal cells
questions.why: Blocking reabsorption in the thick ascending limb sends more sodium and more fluid downstream, and both of those raise potassium secretion at the principal cells, so potassium is lost. The loop reabsorbs potassium rather than secreting it. Acting upstream is exactly why the drug matters, since what arrives at the collecting duct is changed. The drug does not touch the sodium potassium pump.
questions.answerText: Plasma potassium falls, because increased distal sodium delivery and flow drive potassium secretion

questions.q: A patient eats a large potassium rich meal. Trace the immediate renal response.
options: Plasma potassium rises, aldosterone falls, and potassium is retained in the blood instead
Plasma potassium falls, aldosterone rises, and potassium is secreted into the urine anyway
Plasma potassium rises, aldosterone rises, and principal cells secrete more potassium into the urine
Plasma potassium rises, renin rises, and sodium is excreted in the urine rather than potassium
questions.why: The adrenal cortex reads the plasma potassium directly, so more hormone is released, and the collecting duct disposes of the excess within hours. Aldosterone rising is the whole point of the feedback loop, so a fall would be wrong. Eating potassium raises rather than lowers plasma potassium. Renin is suppressed rather than driven by high potassium, and the pathway here defends potassium, not sodium.
questions.answerText: Plasma potassium rises, aldosterone rises, and principal cells secrete more potassium into the urine

questions.q: A patient's aldosterone level is very low after adrenal damage. Predict their plasma sodium and potassium.
options: Sodium high and potassium low
Sodium low and potassium high
Both sodium and potassium high
Both sodium and potassium low
questions.why: Without aldosterone the collecting duct cannot reclaim sodium or push potassium out, so sodium is lost in the urine and potassium builds up in the blood. High sodium with low potassium is the pattern of excess aldosterone, not deficiency. The two ions move in opposite directions here because the same transport step handles both. Both falling together would not fit a loss of sodium reabsorption alone.

questions.q: A drug blocks the epithelial sodium channel on principal cells. Predict its effect on potassium secretion.
options: Secretion falls, because the lumen no longer becomes negative enough to pull potassium out
Secretion rises, because sodium and potassium compete for the same apical channel in the cell
Secretion is unchanged, because potassium uses a separate channel
Secretion falls, because the drug also blocks the potassium channel directly
questions.why: Sodium moving out of the lumen leaves negative charge behind, and that electrical gradient is what draws potassium into the lumen; block the sodium entry and the driving force disappears. Sodium and potassium use separate channels, so competition is not the mechanism. Potassium does use its own channel, but that channel depends on the luminal negativity created by sodium entry. The drug acts on the sodium channel only.
questions.answerText: Secretion falls, because the lumen no longer becomes negative enough to pull potassium out

questions.q: Plasma potassium falls from 4.0 to 2.8 mEq/L. Which way does the resting membrane potential of a skeletal muscle cell move?
options: It becomes more negative, moving further from threshold
It becomes less negative, moving closer to threshold
It does not change, because potassium is mostly intracellular
It becomes more positive, because potassium enters the cell
questions.why: A lower outside potassium concentration steepens the gradient for potassium to leave the cell, so more positive charge exits and the inside becomes more negative, which is why hypokalemia causes weakness. Becoming less negative is what happens when extracellular potassium rises. The small extracellular pool is exactly what sets the resting potential, so changes there matter a great deal. Potassium leaves rather than enters when the outside concentration falls.
questions.answerText: It becomes more negative, moving further from threshold

questions.q: Why does a patient on a loop diuretic often also need to watch their magnesium, given how potassium secretion works?
options: Low magnesium increases sodium reabsorption in the collecting duct and drives potassium out with it
Low magnesium blocks aldosterone release from the adrenal cortex, so potassium cannot be conserved either
Low magnesium removes a normal brake on the apical potassium channel, so potassium keeps leaking into the lumen
Low magnesium prevents the Na+/K+ ATPase from working in the proximal tubule, so potassium is lost
questions.why: Intracellular magnesium normally plugs the apical potassium channel from inside, so when magnesium is low the channel stays open and potassium loss continues even with replacement. Magnesium does not act as a switch for aldosterone release. Low magnesium does not increase collecting duct sodium reabsorption. Proximal pump function is not what makes potassium hard to replace in this setting.
questions.answerText: Low magnesium removes a normal brake on the apical potassium channel, so potassium keeps leaking into the lumen

questions.q: A patient on a thiazide diuretic develops muscle weakness and a plasma potassium of 2.6 mEq/L. Trace the chain from drug to symptom.
options: The drug increases potassium reabsorption in the loop of Henle, plasma potassium falls, and the muscle cells lose calcium from their internal stores
The drug blocks the aldosterone receptor, potassium is retained in the blood, and the depolarized muscle membrane slowly becomes inexcitable over several days
The drug blocks distal sodium reabsorption, more sodium and fluid reach the collecting duct, potassium secretion rises, and the hyperpolarized muscle is harder to excite
The drug increases the glomerular filtration rate, potassium is filtered faster than it can be reabsorbed, and the muscle membrane depolarizes
questions.why: Every step follows: more sodium arriving means more sodium entry at principal cells, a more negative lumen, more potassium out, and a hyperpolarized muscle membrane that will not reach threshold. Thiazides do not block aldosterone; they increase its effective consequences by delivering more sodium. Increasing loop reabsorption of potassium would not lower plasma potassium the way described. Filtration is not the regulated step for potassium, and the potential moves the other way.
questions.answerText: The drug blocks distal sodium reabsorption, more sodium and fluid reach the collecting duct, potassium secretion rises, and the hyperpolarized muscle is harder to excite

questions.q: A patient with kidney failure has a plasma potassium of 7.2 mEq/L and dangerous changes on their heart tracing. Explain the link between the number and the finding.
options: High extracellular potassium hyperpolarizes cardiac cells so they can no longer reach threshold during the pacemaker potential of the sinoatrial node cells
High extracellular potassium blocks calcium entry during the plateau phase, so contraction is shortened without any change in conduction at all
High extracellular potassium reduces the gradient for potassium to leave cardiac cells, so the resting potential is less negative and sodium channels stay inactivated
High extracellular potassium raises aldosterone sharply, and the hormone directly slows conduction through the heart within a few minutes
questions.why: With less driving force for potassium efflux, the cell sits at a less negative potential, and a chronically depolarized membrane leaves voltage gated sodium channels stuck in the inactivated state, which is what disturbs conduction. Hyperpolarization is the effect of low potassium, not high. Plateau calcium entry is affected secondarily but is not the primary reason for the tracing change. Aldosterone rises in response to high potassium but works on the kidney over hours, not on the heart in minutes.
questions.answerText: High extracellular potassium reduces the gradient for potassium to leave cardiac cells, so the resting potential is less negative and sodium channels stay inactivated

questions.q: A patient is given a drug that blocks the aldosterone receptor together with a loop diuretic. Predict the net effect on plasma potassium compared with the loop diuretic alone.
options: The fall in potassium is blunted, because the two drugs push potassium secretion in opposite directions
Potassium falls further, because both drugs increase distal flow past the principal cells at once
Potassium is unaffected by either drug, since both of them act on sodium handling and nothing else
Potassium rises sharply, because the loop diuretic is itself potassium sparing at higher doses
questions.why: The loop diuretic raises distal delivery and drives potassium out, while the receptor blocker removes the hormonal signal that opens that route, so the two partly cancel and potassium stays closer to normal. The receptor blocker does not increase distal flow; it acts at the principal cell. Both drugs change potassium handling as a consequence of changing sodium handling, so neither is potassium neutral. Loop diuretics are potassium wasting, not sparing.
questions.answerText: The fall in potassium is blunted, because the two drugs push potassium secretion in opposite directions

questions.q: A patient with severe diarrhea has lost a large amount of potassium from the gut. Their aldosterone level is high because of the volume loss. Predict what happens to their plasma potassium and explain the conflict.
options: Potassium falls sharply, because the volume driven aldosterone keeps promoting renal potassium loss even though the body is already depleted
Potassium rises, because aldosterone switches to conserving potassium whenever the body is already depleted of it by heavy gut losses
Potassium stays normal, because aldosterone switches off completely as soon as plasma potassium starts to fall
Potassium rises, because volume loss reduces the glomerular filtration rate to zero and nothing at all is excreted
questions.why: Aldosterone released to defend volume acts on the same principal cells regardless of the potassium situation, so the kidney adds renal losses to the gut losses and the deficit deepens. Aldosterone promotes potassium loss rather than conservation. Low plasma potassium does reduce the potassium driven component of aldosterone release, but the angiotensin II driven component keeps the hormone elevated. Volume loss lowers filtration but does not stop it entirely.
questions.answerText: Potassium falls sharply, because the volume driven aldosterone keeps promoting renal potassium loss even though the body is already depleted

questions.q: What is the receptor that starts the micturition reflex?
options: Chemoreceptors sensing urine osmolarity
Osmoreceptors in the urethra
Pressure receptors in the renal pelvis
Stretch receptors in the bladder wall
questions.why: As urine accumulates, the bladder wall is stretched, and those mechanoreceptors fire more and more as volume rises, which is the trigger for the reflex. Urine osmolarity is not monitored in the bladder, since the composition of urine is already fixed by the time it arrives. Renal pelvis pressure receptors do not initiate voiding. There are no osmoreceptors in the urethra.
questions.answerText: Stretch receptors in the bladder wall

questions.q: Which muscle contracts to empty the bladder?
options: The external urethral sphincter
The detrusor muscle
The levator ani
The psoas major
questions.why: The detrusor is the smooth muscle of the bladder wall, and its contraction raises bladder pressure and expels urine. The external urethral sphincter must relax rather than contract for voiding to occur. The levator ani supports the pelvic floor but is not the muscle that empties the bladder. The psoas major is a hip flexor with no urinary role.

questions.q: What type of muscle is the internal urethral sphincter, and is it under voluntary control?
options: Skeletal muscle, under voluntary control
Cardiac muscle, not under voluntary control
Smooth muscle, not under voluntary control
Smooth muscle, under voluntary control
questions.why: The internal sphincter is a thickening of bladder smooth muscle controlled by the autonomic nervous system, so it opens and closes without conscious command. Skeletal muscle under voluntary control describes the external sphincter, the one you can hold. Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart. Smooth muscle is by definition not under direct voluntary control here.
questions.answerText: Smooth muscle, not under voluntary control

questions.q: Which nerve carries the voluntary command to the external urethral sphincter?
options: The pelvic nerve
The hypogastric nerve
The pudendal nerve
The vagus nerve
questions.why: The pudendal nerve is a somatic motor nerve, so it commands the skeletal muscle of the external sphincter and lets you delay voiding. The pelvic nerve carries parasympathetic fibers that contract the detrusor. The hypogastric nerve carries sympathetic fibers that keep the bladder relaxed and the internal sphincter closed during filling. The vagus does not reach the bladder.

questions.q: At which level of the spinal cord is the micturition reflex integrated?
options: The sacral spinal cord
The cervical spinal cord
The upper thoracic spinal cord
The medulla oblongata
questions.why: Sacral segments hold the parasympathetic neurons that drive the detrusor and the motor neurons for the external sphincter, so the basic reflex circuit lives there. Cervical segments serve the diaphragm and upper limb. Upper thoracic segments hold the sympathetic outflow that keeps the bladder relaxed during filling. The medulla controls cardiovascular and respiratory reflexes, while the pons houses the higher micturition center.

questions.q: Which division of the autonomic nervous system contracts the detrusor during voiding?
options: The sympathetic division
The parasympathetic division
The somatic motor system
The enteric nervous system
questions.why: Parasympathetic fibers in the pelvic nerve release acetylcholine onto detrusor muscarinic receptors, contracting the bladder while the internal sphincter relaxes. Sympathetic activity does the opposite, relaxing the detrusor and closing the internal sphincter so the bladder can fill. The somatic system controls only the external sphincter. The enteric nervous system governs the gut wall.

questions.q: An adult decides to delay voiding despite a strong urge. Which action makes that possible?
options: Voluntary relaxation of the detrusor through the parasympathetic pelvic nerve
Voluntary reduction of the glomerular filtration rate to slow urine formation
Voluntary closure of the internal urethral sphincter, which is smooth muscle
Voluntary contraction of the external urethral sphincter through the pudendal nerve
questions.why: Only the external sphincter is skeletal muscle with somatic innervation, so it is the single point in the pathway a person can command directly. The detrusor is smooth muscle and cannot be relaxed at will, though descending signals can inhibit its reflex drive. The internal sphincter is autonomic and closes without conscious control. Filtration rate is not under voluntary control.
questions.answerText: Voluntary contraction of the external urethral sphincter through the pudendal nerve

questions.q: Bladder volume rises from 100 mL to 400 mL. Predict what happens to stretch receptor firing and to the urge to void.
options: Firing increases and the urge becomes stronger
Firing decreases and the urge fades
Firing is unchanged until the bladder is completely full
Firing increases but the urge decreases as the bladder adapts
questions.why: Stretch receptors are graded, so more wall stretch means a higher firing frequency and a stronger conscious signal, which is why the urge builds gradually. Firing does not fall as the bladder fills. There is no threshold at complete fullness; the first urge appears around 200 mL. Some accommodation occurs, but the urge grows rather than shrinks as volume climbs.
questions.answerText: Firing increases and the urge becomes stronger

questions.q: A patient has a spinal cord injury above the sacral level. What happens to their micturition?
options: The bladder can no longer contract at all, so urine simply accumulates in it
Reflex voiding continues but voluntary control over the external sphincter is lost
Voluntary control is preserved but reflex voiding stops below the injury
Urine production at the kidney stops completely until the injury heals
questions.why: The reflex arc lives in the sacral cord and stays intact below the injury, but the descending pathways that let the brain hold the external sphincter closed are cut. The detrusor still contracts, because its motor neurons are below the lesion. Voluntary control requires an intact route from the brain, which the injury has interrupted. The kidneys keep making urine regardless of spinal cord injury.
questions.answerText: Reflex voiding continues but voluntary control over the external sphincter is lost

questions.q: A drug blocks muscarinic receptors on the detrusor. Predict the effect on bladder function.
options: The detrusor contracts more strongly and voiding becomes urgent and frequent
The detrusor contracts more weakly, so the bladder holds more urine before voiding
The external sphincter relaxes and continuous leaking of urine occurs
The internal sphincter opens and voiding becomes continuous and involuntary
questions.why: Acetylcholine acting on muscarinic receptors is the signal that contracts the detrusor, so blocking those receptors weakens contraction and raises the volume the bladder tolerates. Blocking a receptor cannot strengthen the response it mediates. The external sphincter uses nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction, not muscarinic ones. The internal sphincter is held closed by sympathetic alpha receptors, which the drug does not touch.
questions.answerText: The detrusor contracts more weakly, so the bladder holds more urine before voiding

questions.q: During bladder filling, sympathetic activity to the bladder is high. What does that accomplish?
options: It contracts the detrusor and opens the internal sphincter
It relaxes both the detrusor and the internal sphincter
It relaxes the detrusor and keeps the internal sphincter closed
It contracts the external sphincter directly
questions.why: Sympathetic outflow through the hypogastric nerve lets the bladder expand at low pressure while holding the outlet shut, which is exactly what storage requires. Contracting the detrusor and opening the outlet is the voiding pattern driven by the parasympathetic system. Relaxing both would let urine escape as the bladder filled. The external sphincter is skeletal muscle and takes somatic, not sympathetic, commands.
questions.answerText: It relaxes the detrusor and keeps the internal sphincter closed

questions.q: An infant voids automatically whenever the bladder fills, while an adult can wait. Which developmental change accounts for the difference?
options: Descending pathways from the pons and cortex mature and can inhibit the sacral reflex and hold the sphincter closed
The sacral reflex arc disappears with age and is replaced by a direct pathway from the cortex to the bladder
The internal sphincter gradually becomes skeletal muscle during childhood and comes under voluntary control
Bladder stretch receptors stop firing in adults until the volume in the bladder becomes very high indeed
questions.why: The reflex is present from birth; what develops is the brain's ability to override it, which is why toilet training depends on nervous system maturation rather than on the bladder. The sacral arc persists throughout life, which is why it reappears after spinal cord injury. Muscle type does not change; the internal sphincter remains smooth muscle. Stretch receptors in adults still fire progressively from around 200 mL.
questions.answerText: Descending pathways from the pons and cortex mature and can inhibit the sacral reflex and hold the sphincter closed

questions.q: A patient has a lesion that destroys the sacral spinal cord segments. Predict the bladder findings and explain them.
options: The bladder fills without reflex contraction and overflows, because both the parasympathetic outflow and the sphincter motor neurons are gone
The bladder empties frequently and completely, because the sacral reflex has been released from the inhibition normally supplied by the brain
The bladder empties only under voluntary command, since the somatic pathway to the sphincter survives the lesion
The bladder cannot fill at all, because the internal sphincter is left permanently open after the injury
questions.why: Destroying the sacral segments removes the motor limb of the reflex, so the detrusor no longer contracts and urine accumulates until pressure forces some out. Frequent complete emptying is what happens when a higher lesion releases the intact sacral reflex from inhibition. The somatic motor neurons for the external sphincter also live in the sacral cord, so they are lost too. The internal sphincter is not held open by this lesion.
questions.answerText: The bladder fills without reflex contraction and overflows, because both the parasympathetic outflow and the sphincter motor neurons are gone

questions.q: An older patient has an enlarged prostate narrowing the urethra. Over months the detrusor thickens and the bladder does not empty completely. Trace the physiology.
options: The obstruction weakens the bladder stretch receptors, so the reflex never fires and the bladder fills silently over time instead
The detrusor must generate higher pressure against the obstruction, hypertrophies in response, and still leaves residual urine
The obstruction relaxes the internal sphincter, so urine leaks continuously and the bladder never fills properly
The obstruction lowers the glomerular filtration rate, so less urine is made and the bladder never fills at all
questions.why: Working against a higher outlet resistance is a load, and smooth muscle responds to chronic load by thickening, but the added force is often still not enough to empty fully, leaving residual volume. Stretch receptors are not damaged by outlet obstruction; the urge is usually stronger, not absent. Obstruction raises outlet resistance rather than relaxing the internal sphincter. Severe long standing obstruction can eventually back pressure up to the kidney, but that is a late consequence rather than the reason the bladder retains urine.
questions.answerText: The detrusor must generate higher pressure against the obstruction, hypertrophies in response, and still leaves residual urine

questions.q: What does urine specific gravity measure?
options: The acidity of urine compared with the acidity of plasma
The density of urine compared with the density of pure water
The volume of urine produced in one hour of collection
The total concentration of protein dissolved in urine
questions.why: Specific gravity is a ratio of densities, and because dissolved solute adds mass, it serves as a quick proxy for how concentrated the urine is. Urine pH is measured separately by the dipstick pad. Volume per hour is a flow rate, measured with a graduated cylinder and a clock. Protein has its own dipstick pad and is only one of many solutes contributing to density.
questions.answerText: The density of urine compared with the density of pure water

questions.q: What is the normal range of urine specific gravity?
questions.why: Urine is always at least slightly denser than water, and the wide range reflects the kidney's ability to make either very dilute or very concentrated urine. Values below 1.000 would mean urine less dense than water, which cannot happen with solute dissolved in it. Values above 1.100 are far beyond what the kidney can produce. Values of 2.00 or 3.00 are not in the physiological range at all.

questions.q: What is the typical pH of urine in a person on a mixed diet?
options: About 7.4
About 6.0
About 3.0
About 9.0
questions.why: Urine is normally slightly acidic because the kidney is excreting the daily acid load from metabolism, and about 6 is a common value. A pH of 7.4 is the tightly regulated value of arterial blood, not urine. A pH of 3.0 is below the lower limit of about 4.5 the kidney can reach. A pH of 9.0 is above the upper limit of about 8.0.

questions.q: How much glucose should appear in the urine of a healthy person?
options: None
About 100 mg/dL
About the same as plasma
Trace amounts only after water intake
questions.why: Glucose is filtered freely but is completely reabsorbed by the sodium glucose cotransporters of the proximal tubule, so a normal dipstick reads negative. A reading near 100 mg/dL would mean the transport maximum had been exceeded. Urine glucose equal to plasma glucose would mean no reabsorption at all. Drinking water changes urine volume and concentration but does not put glucose in it.

questions.q: Why is protein normally absent from urine?
options: Protein is secreted back into the blood by the collecting duct before excretion
The loop of Henle reabsorbs all filtered protein
Protein is destroyed by enzymes in the bladder
The filtration membrane holds back large negatively charged plasma proteins
questions.why: Both the size of the filtration slits and the negative charge on the basement membrane keep albumin and larger proteins in the capillary, so very little protein ever enters the filtrate. The collecting duct does not secrete protein back into blood. Enzymatic destruction in the bladder is not how protein is kept out of urine. Small amounts that do filter are taken up by the proximal tubule, not the loop of Henle.
questions.answerText: The filtration membrane holds back large negatively charged plasma proteins

questions.q: What are ketones in the urine a sign of?
options: Heavy reliance on fat breakdown for energy
Failure of the glomerular filtration barrier
Bacterial infection in the bladder
Excessive protein reabsorption in the proximal tubule
questions.why: When carbohydrate is scarce or unusable, the liver makes ketone bodies from fatty acids, and these small molecules are filtered and appear in the urine. A failed filtration barrier shows up as protein or blood in the urine, not ketones. Bacterial infection typically shows nitrites and leukocyte esterase. Ketones do not come from protein handling in the tubule.
questions.answerText: Heavy reliance on fat breakdown for energy

questions.q: What does a positive blood pad on a urine dipstick indicate?
options: Plasma proteins have crossed the filtration barrier
The urine pH is below 5.0
The urine is more concentrated than normal
Red blood cells or hemoglobin are present in the urine
questions.why: The blood pad reacts with the heme group, so it turns positive whether intact red cells or free hemoglobin is present, and either finding points to bleeding or to hemolysis. Plasma proteins register on the protein pad instead. Urine concentration is read from the specific gravity pad. Urine pH has its own pad and does not affect this one.
questions.answerText: Red blood cells or hemoglobin are present in the urine

questions.q: Which instrument gives a direct reading of urine specific gravity from a single drop of sample?
options: A hemocytometer
A spectrophotometer
A refractometer
A sphygmomanometer
questions.why: A refractometer measures how much the sample bends light, which tracks with dissolved solute, so one drop gives a specific gravity reading. A spectrophotometer measures light absorbed at a chosen wavelength and is used for colorimetric assays. A hemocytometer is a counting chamber for cells. A sphygmomanometer measures blood pressure.

questions.q: A urine sample has a specific gravity of 1.030. What does this tell you about antidiuretic hormone activity?
options: It is low, since the urine is dilute and little water was reabsorbed
It is high, but only if the urine also contains protein
It is unchanged, since specific gravity reflects only the glucose present
It is high, since the collecting duct has reabsorbed a great deal of water
questions.why: A high specific gravity means concentrated urine, which requires aquaporins in the collecting duct and therefore a high hormone level. A value of 1.030 is at the concentrated end, not the dilute end. Specific gravity reflects all dissolved solute, not glucose alone. Protein is not required for the interpretation, though heavy proteinuria can raise the reading.
questions.answerText: It is high, since the collecting duct has reabsorbed a great deal of water

questions.q: A student's urine tests positive for glucose. Their blood glucose is 260 mg/dL. Which renal process has been exceeded?
options: Filtration of glucose at the glomerulus has failed and let too much through into the tubule
Water reabsorption in the collecting duct has stopped and concentrated the glucose left behind
Secretion of glucose into the tubular fluid has increased well beyond the normal rate
Reabsorption by the proximal tubule sodium glucose cotransporters has hit its transport maximum
questions.why: Above a plasma glucose of roughly 180 mg/dL the carriers are saturated, and every extra glucose molecule filtered stays in the tubule and appears in the urine. Filtration of glucose is normal and freely occurring; that is not the failure. Glucose is not secreted by the tubule at all. Water handling in the collecting duct has nothing to do with glucose appearing in the urine.
questions.answerText: Reabsorption by the proximal tubule sodium glucose cotransporters has hit its transport maximum

questions.q: A urine sample shows a strongly positive protein result. Which renal process most likely failed?
options: The filtration barrier lost its ability to hold back plasma proteins
The collecting duct stopped secreting protein into the blood
The loop of Henle stopped concentrating the tubular fluid properly
The bladder failed to empty completely between voids
questions.why: Protein in the urine means proteins that should have stayed in the glomerular capillary got through, usually because the podocyte slits or the charge barrier are damaged. The collecting duct does not secrete protein, so there is no such process to fail. A concentrating failure shows up as a low specific gravity, not as protein. Incomplete bladder emptying changes volume, not protein content.
questions.answerText: The filtration barrier lost its ability to hold back plasma proteins

questions.q: A patient who has been fasting for two days has a urine dipstick positive for ketones and negative for glucose. What does this combination indicate?
options: Blood glucose has risen above the renal threshold of about 180 mg/dL
The glomerular filtration barrier has been damaged and is leaking solute
The proximal tubule has lost its glucose transporters and cannot reabsorb
Fat is being used for fuel while blood glucose remains below the renal threshold
questions.why: Fasting shifts metabolism to fat, so ketones appear, while blood glucose stays low enough that the tubule reabsorbs all of it and the glucose pad reads negative. Barrier damage would give protein or blood on the dipstick, not ketones. Losing glucose transporters would give glucose in the urine, which is exactly what is absent here. A blood glucose above 180 mg/dL would produce a positive glucose pad.
questions.answerText: Fat is being used for fuel while blood glucose remains below the renal threshold

questions.q: A sample has a specific gravity of 1.002 and a urine osmolarity of about 60 mOsm/L. What does this tell you about the collecting duct?
options: It is fully loaded with aquaporins and is reabsorbing water rapidly from the lumen
It is water impermeable, so the dilute fluid from the ascending limb passed straight through
It is actively secreting water into the lumen against the osmotic gradient of the medulla
It has lost its ability to reabsorb sodium from the tubular fluid passing through it
questions.why: Very dilute urine means the water that entered the collecting duct left in the urine, which happens when aquaporin-2 is not in the apical membrane. Aquaporins in place would produce concentrated urine with a high specific gravity. No segment of the nephron secretes water into the lumen. Sodium reabsorption failure would change urine sodium rather than producing this degree of dilution.
questions.answerText: It is water impermeable, so the dilute fluid from the ascending limb passed straight through

questions.q: A patient's urine pH is consistently 5.0. Which renal activity is this most consistent with?
options: Loss of the medullary osmotic gradient
Bicarbonate secretion by intercalated cells in response to alkalosis
Failure of the proximal tubule to reabsorb sodium
Active hydrogen ion secretion by the tubule in response to an acid load
questions.why: An acidic urine means the tubule is dumping H+ into the lumen, which is what the kidney does when the body has acid to get rid of. Bicarbonate secretion would raise urine pH toward 8, not lower it. Proximal sodium handling does not set urine pH directly. The medullary gradient governs concentration, which is read from specific gravity rather than pH.
questions.answerText: Active hydrogen ion secretion by the tubule in response to an acid load

questions.q: Two urine samples are collected from the same person, one first thing in the morning and one an hour after drinking a liter of water. Which sample has the higher specific gravity, and why?
options: The post water sample, because the extra water carried more solute into the urine
The morning sample, because overnight water conservation concentrated the urine
They are identical, because specific gravity is a fixed property of urine
The post water sample, because drinking raises plasma osmolarity
questions.why: During sleep no water is taken in, antidiuretic hormone stays elevated, and the urine that accumulates is concentrated, giving a higher specific gravity. Drinking water dilutes the urine rather than adding solute to it. Specific gravity varies widely with hydration and is not fixed. Drinking water lowers plasma osmolarity, which is why the hormone is switched off.
questions.answerText: The morning sample, because overnight water conservation concentrated the urine

questions.q: A urinalysis shows specific gravity 1.010, pH 6.0, glucose negative, ketones negative, protein strongly positive, and blood positive. Which single site of failure explains both abnormal findings?
options: The proximal tubule transport maximum for glucose has been exceeded by the filtered load
The collecting duct response to antidiuretic hormone has been completely lost
The glomerular filtration barrier, which normally excludes both plasma proteins and blood cells
The thick ascending limb NaCl transporter has stopped working and the gradient is flat
questions.why: Protein and red cells are both held back by the same three layer barrier, so a single defect there explains both positives while leaving concentration and glucose handling untouched. A glucose transport maximum problem would show glucose, which is negative here. A collecting duct problem would change specific gravity, which is squarely mid range. An ascending limb defect would flatten the gradient and show up as persistently dilute urine.
questions.answerText: The glomerular filtration barrier, which normally excludes both plasma proteins and blood cells

questions.q: A sample from an untreated diabetic shows specific gravity 1.040, glucose strongly positive, ketones positive, protein negative, and a large urine volume. Explain why the volume is high despite the concentrated reading.
options: Unreabsorbed glucose holds water in the tubule by osmosis, so a large volume of solute rich urine is produced
Antidiuretic hormone has been switched off completely, producing a large volume of dilute urine
The filtration barrier is leaking protein, which drags water with it into the tubular fluid
The collecting duct is secreting water into the lumen against the osmotic gradient of the medullary interstitium
questions.why: Glucose left in the lumen acts as an osmotic diuretic, so water follows it out even while the hormone system is trying to conserve, and the heavy solute load pushes the specific gravity up. Switched off hormone gives dilute urine with a low specific gravity, which does not match a reading of 1.040. Protein is negative here, so a leaking barrier is not part of this picture. No nephron segment secretes water.
questions.answerText: Unreabsorbed glucose holds water in the tubule by osmosis, so a large volume of solute rich urine is produced

questions.q: A student measures specific gravity with a refractometer as 1.032 but the dipstick pad reads 1.015 for the same sample. The sample is known to contain a large amount of glucose. Which explanation fits best?
options: The two methods measure different variables and cannot be compared with each other in any sample
The dipstick pad is a more accurate method than the refractometer, which needs to be recalibrated for every sample it reads
Glucose lowers the density of urine, so the refractometer overreads the true specific gravity of the sample
The refractometer responds to all dissolved solute including glucose, while the dipstick pad responds mainly to ionic solutes
questions.why: Glucose is a large uncharged molecule that adds substantially to density and refraction but contributes little to the ionic strength the dipstick pad detects, so the two methods disagree in a predictable direction. Neither method is simply more accurate; each measures a different aspect of solute content. Glucose raises density rather than lowering it. The two methods do measure related things and are routinely compared, which is why the discrepancy is informative.
questions.answerText: The refractometer responds to all dissolved solute including glucose, while the dipstick pad responds mainly to ionic solutes

questions.q: A patient produces 4 L of urine daily with a specific gravity of 1.002, negative glucose, negative protein, and normal pH. Giving synthetic antidiuretic hormone does not change the urine. Which renal process failed?
options: The collecting duct cannot insert aquaporin-2 in response to the hormone
The proximal tubule cannot reabsorb the glucose that is filtered
The glomerular filtration barrier is damaged and leaking protein
The tubule cannot secrete hydrogen ion into the tubular fluid
questions.why: Large dilute urine with an otherwise clean dipstick points to water handling, and failure to respond to the given hormone puts the defect at the target rather than at the gland. A glucose reabsorption defect would show glucose on the dipstick, which is negative. Barrier damage would show protein or blood, both negative here. An acid secretion problem would show up as an abnormal urine pH.
questions.answerText: The collecting duct cannot insert aquaporin-2 in response to the hormone

questions.q: What is the formula for renal clearance of a substance?
options: Clearance equals urine concentration times urine flow rate, divided by plasma concentration
Clearance equals plasma concentration times urine flow rate, divided by urine concentration
Clearance equals urine concentration divided by plasma concentration
Clearance equals plasma concentration times the glomerular filtration rate
questions.why: The numerator is the amount of substance leaving in the urine each minute and the denominator is how much of it each milliliter of plasma held, so the ratio is the volume of plasma cleared per minute. Swapping urine and plasma concentrations inverts the relationship and gives a meaningless number. Leaving out the flow rate drops the time dimension, so the result is a ratio rather than a rate. The last expression is the filtered load, a different quantity.
questions.answerText: Clearance equals urine concentration times urine flow rate, divided by plasma concentration

questions.q: In what units is renal clearance normally expressed?
options: mg/min
mL/min
mg/mL
mL
questions.why: Clearance is a virtual volume of plasma completely cleared of the substance each minute, so it carries volume over time units. Units of mg/min describe an excretion rate, the amount leaving per minute. Units of mg/mL describe a concentration. A plain volume in mL has no time component and cannot express a rate.

questions.q: Which substance is the ideal marker for measuring glomerular filtration rate?
options: Creatinine
Glucose
Para aminohippurate
Inulin
questions.why: Inulin is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so all of it that appears in the urine came from filtration and its clearance equals the filtration rate exactly. Creatinine is close but is slightly secreted, so it overestimates a little. Para aminohippurate is heavily secreted and is used to estimate renal plasma flow instead. Glucose is completely reabsorbed at normal plasma levels, so its clearance is near zero.

questions.q: What is the approximate normal glomerular filtration rate in a healthy adult?
options: 125 mL/min
25 mL/min
650 mL/min
1250 mL/min
questions.why: About 125 mL/min works out to roughly 180 L of filtrate a day, of which almost all is reabsorbed. A value of 25 mL/min would represent severely reduced kidney function. About 650 mL/min is closer to renal plasma flow, not filtration rate. A value of 1250 mL/min exceeds the total blood flow to both kidneys.

questions.q: A filtered load calculated from a renal data set comes out in which units?
options: Milligrams per deciliter, the same units as the plasma concentration
Milliliters per minute, the same units as the filtration rate
Milligrams per minute, an amount of substance per unit time
Milligrams per milliliter, a concentration in the filtrate
questions.why: Filtered load multiplies a filtration rate in mL/min by a plasma concentration in mg/mL, so the volume units cancel and what is left is mg/min, an amount arriving at the tubule each minute. Milligrams per deciliter is the plasma concentration you started from, not the product. Milliliters per minute is the filtration rate alone, before the concentration is applied. Milligrams per milliliter is a concentration, and filtered load is a rate, which is why it can be compared directly against an excretion rate to see how much was reabsorbed.
questions.answerText: Milligrams per minute, an amount of substance per unit time

questions.q: What does renal clearance of a substance actually describe?
options: The volume of plasma completely cleared of that substance per minute
The mass of the substance that is filtered at the glomerulus each minute
The fraction of the substance that the tubule reabsorbs each minute
The volume of urine the kidney produces in one minute
questions.why: Clearance is a virtual volume, the amount of plasma that would have to be stripped entirely of the substance each minute to account for the amount excreted. The mass filtered per minute is the filtered load. The fraction reabsorbed is a separate calculation comparing filtered load with excretion rate. Urine produced per minute is the urine flow rate, which appears inside the clearance formula but is not clearance itself.
questions.answerText: The volume of plasma completely cleared of that substance per minute

questions.q: What is the normal range of plasma creatinine in an adult?
options: About 3.5 to 5.0 mg/dL
About 8 to 20 mg/dL
About 70 to 110 mg/dL
About 0.6 to 1.2 mg/dL
questions.why: Creatinine comes from muscle at a steady rate, and a healthy kidney holds its plasma level near 1 mg/dL, so a doubling signals a large drop in filtration. A range of 8 to 20 mg/dL is blood urea nitrogen. A range near 70 to 110 mg/dL is fasting plasma glucose. A range of 3.5 to 5.0 belongs to plasma potassium in mEq/L.

questions.q: In the clearance formula, what does V represent?
options: The volume of plasma in the body
The urine flow rate, in mL/min
The volume of the bladder at the time of collection
The total volume of filtrate made per day
questions.why: V is the rate at which urine is produced, obtained by dividing the collected volume by the collection time, and it converts a urine concentration into an excretion rate. Plasma volume is a body compartment measurement and is not part of this formula. The bladder volume at one moment says nothing about the rate. Total daily filtrate is the filtration rate expressed over a day, not the urine flow rate.
questions.answerText: The urine flow rate, in mL/min

questions.q: Inulin is infused to steady state. Plasma inulin is 1 mg/mL, urine inulin is 100 mg/mL, and urine flow is 1.25 mL/min. What is the glomerular filtration rate?
options: 80 mL/min
100 mL/min
125 mL/min
1.25 mL/min
questions.why: Clearance is 100 mg/mL times 1.25 mL/min divided by 1 mg/mL, which is 125 mL/min, and because inulin is neither secreted nor reabsorbed this equals the filtration rate. A value of 80 mL/min would come from arithmetic that lost the flow rate multiplication. A value of 100 mL/min is the urine concentration copied over without completing the calculation. A value of 1.25 mL/min is the urine flow rate itself.

questions.q: A patient has a glomerular filtration rate of 125 mL/min and a plasma glucose of 1 mg/mL. What is the filtered load of glucose?
options: 1 mg/min
125 mL/min
125 mg/min
250 mg/min
questions.why: Filtered load is 125 mL/min multiplied by 1 mg/mL, giving 125 mg of glucose presented to the tubule each minute, comfortably below the transport maximum of about 375 mg/min. A result in mL/min would be a volume rate, not an amount. A value of 1 mg/min ignores the filtration rate entirely. A value of 250 mg/min would require either double the filtration rate or double the plasma concentration.

questions.q: Urine creatinine is 60 mg/dL, urine flow is 2 mL/min, and plasma creatinine is 1.2 mg/dL. What is the creatinine clearance?
options: 50 mL/min
120 mL/min
100 mL/min
72 mL/min
questions.why: Multiply 60 by 2 to get 120, then divide by 1.2 to get 100 mL/min; the dL units cancel so no conversion is needed. A value of 50 mL/min results from dividing before multiplying by the flow rate. A value of 120 mL/min is the numerator left undivided. A value of 72 mL/min does not follow from these numbers under any correct grouping.

questions.q: A substance appears in the urine at 12 mg/mL and the urine flow rate is 2 mL/min. What is its excretion rate?
options: 6 mg/min
24 mL/min
24 mg/min
12 mg/min
questions.why: Excretion rate is urine concentration times urine flow rate, so 12 mg/mL times 2 mL/min gives 24 mg of substance leaving the body each minute. A value of 6 mg/min comes from dividing instead of multiplying. A result in mL/min has the wrong units for an amount per time. A value of 12 mg/min ignores the flow rate.

questions.q: A substance has a clearance of 200 mL/min in a patient whose glomerular filtration rate is 125 mL/min. How is the tubule handling it?
options: It is being reabsorbed by the tubule after filtration
It is neither secreted nor reabsorbed
It is being secreted in addition to being filtered
It is not being filtered at all
questions.why: Clearing more plasma than the kidney filters is only possible if the tubule adds the substance to the urine from the peritubular blood. Reabsorption would pull the clearance below the filtration rate. A clearance equal to the filtration rate would indicate no net tubular handling. A substance that is not filtered would have a very low clearance unless it were entirely secreted, which is not what 200 relative to 125 describes.
questions.answerText: It is being secreted in addition to being filtered

questions.q: A person filters 180 L of plasma per day and their plasma sodium is 140 mEq/L. What is the daily filtered load of sodium?
options: 1,260 mEq/day
25,200 mEq/day
320 mEq/day
140 mEq/day
questions.why: Multiply 180 L/day by 140 mEq/L to get 25,200 mEq of sodium filtered daily, nearly all of which is reabsorbed since only about 150 mEq is excreted. A value of 1,260 mEq/day is off by a factor that does not follow from these numbers. A value of 320 mEq/day comes from adding rather than multiplying. A value of 140 mEq/day is the plasma concentration copied over without using the filtration volume.

questions.q: A patient produces 1440 mL of urine in 24 hours. What is the urine flow rate in mL/min?
options: 0.06 mL/min
24 mL/min
60 mL/min
1 mL/min
questions.why: There are 1440 minutes in a day, so 1440 mL divided by 1440 min is exactly 1 mL/min, a convenient number to remember as a typical output. A value of 24 mL/min comes from dividing by hours rather than minutes. A value of 60 mL/min would be an enormous urine output. A value of 0.06 mL/min is a hundredfold too small for a normal day's output.

questions.q: A patient has a glomerular filtration rate of 140 mL/min measured with inulin and a para aminohippurate clearance of 700 mL/min. What is the filtration fraction, and what does it mean?
options: 0.2, meaning twenty percent of the plasma reaching the glomerulus is filtered
5.0, meaning five times as much plasma is filtered as actually arrives at the glomerulus
0.2, meaning twenty percent of the filtrate is reabsorbed
0.5, meaning half the plasma reaching the glomerulus is filtered
questions.why: Filtration fraction is filtration rate divided by renal plasma flow, so 140 divided by 700 is 0.2, and about a fifth of arriving plasma becomes filtrate while the rest continues to the peritubular capillaries. A value of 5.0 comes from inverting the ratio, and more plasma cannot be filtered than arrives. Reabsorption of filtrate is a separate quantity and is closer to 99 percent. A fraction of 0.5 would require 350 mL/min of filtration at this plasma flow.
questions.answerText: 0.2, meaning twenty percent of the plasma reaching the glomerulus is filtered

questions.q: A patient's plasma creatinine rises from 1.0 to 2.0 mg/dL over a week while their muscle mass and creatinine production are unchanged. What has happened to the glomerular filtration rate?
options: It has doubled
It has fallen to about half its previous value
It is unchanged, because creatinine production is unchanged
It has fallen to about one quarter of its previous value
questions.why: At steady state, production equals excretion, and excretion is the filtration rate times the plasma concentration, so if production holds constant while plasma concentration doubles, the filtration rate must have halved. A doubling of filtration would lower plasma creatinine, not raise it. Unchanged production is the assumption that makes the inverse relationship valid, not a reason for the rate to be unchanged. A drop to one quarter would push plasma creatinine to about 4 mg/dL.
questions.answerText: It has fallen to about half its previous value

questions.q: A patient has a plasma glucose of 4 mg/mL and a glomerular filtration rate of 125 mL/min. The tubular transport maximum for glucose is 375 mg/min. How much glucose appears in the urine each minute?
options: 125 mg/min
500 mg/min
375 mg/min
0 mg/min
questions.why: The filtered load is 125 times 4, which is 500 mg/min, and the carriers can move only 375 mg/min, so the surplus of 125 mg/min stays in the tubule and is excreted. A value of 500 mg/min is the whole filtered load, which ignores the substantial reabsorption still happening. A value of 375 mg/min is the amount reabsorbed, not the amount excreted. Zero would be correct only if the filtered load stayed below the transport maximum.

questions.q: A substance has a plasma concentration of 4 mg/mL and a clearance of 25 mL/min in a patient whose glomerular filtration rate is 125 mL/min. At what rate is the tubule reabsorbing it?
options: 100 mg/min
25 mg/min
500 mg/min
400 mg/min
questions.why: The filtered load is 125 times 4, or 500 mg/min, the excretion rate is clearance times plasma concentration, or 25 times 4, which is 100 mg/min, and the difference of 400 mg/min must have been reabsorbed. A value of 100 mg/min is the excretion rate rather than the reabsorption rate. A value of 500 mg/min is the whole filtered load, which would mean nothing at all was excreted. A value of 25 mg/min mistakes the clearance number for an amount.

questions.q: Which chemical buffer system does most of the buffering in extracellular fluid?
options: The phosphate buffer system
The bicarbonate buffer system
The hemoglobin buffer system
The ammonia buffer system
questions.why: Bicarbonate is present in plasma at about 24 mEq/L, far more than any other buffer outside cells, and both of its members are under active control. Phosphate is only about 1 to 2 mEq/L in plasma, so it matters much more inside cells and in urine. Hemoglobin is a powerful buffer but it is locked inside the red blood cell. Ammonia is made by the kidney tubule and buffers urine, not plasma.

questions.q: Which member of the bicarbonate buffer system is controlled by the lungs?
options: Plasma albumin
Carbon dioxide
Bicarbonate ion
Phosphate ion
questions.why: Ventilation sets how fast carbon dioxide leaves the body, so the lungs control the acid member of the pair. Bicarbonate is the base member and is handled by the kidney. Phosphate and albumin belong to other buffer systems entirely and are not part of the bicarbonate pair. Having one member on a respiratory dial and the other on a renal dial is exactly what makes this system so useful.

questions.q: Which member of the bicarbonate buffer system is controlled by the kidneys?
options: Carbon dioxide
Carbonic anhydrase
Bicarbonate ion
Dissolved oxygen
questions.why: The kidney reclaims filtered bicarbonate and can generate new bicarbonate, so it sets the base member of the pair. Carbon dioxide is the acid member and is set by ventilation. Carbonic anhydrase is the enzyme that speeds the reaction, not a buffer component that gets adjusted. Dissolved oxygen has no acid or base role in this system.

questions.q: What is the normal concentration of bicarbonate in arterial plasma?
options: About 40 mEq/L
About 4 mEq/L
About 12 mEq/L
About 24 mEq/L
questions.why: Normal plasma bicarbonate runs 22 to 26 mEq/L, so 24 is the value to carry. About 4 mEq/L is closer to normal plasma potassium, a number students often swap in. A value near 12 mEq/L would be a marked metabolic acidosis. A value near 40 mEq/L would be a marked metabolic alkalosis.

questions.q: Which plasma protein does most of the protein buffering in blood plasma?
options: Albumin
Hemoglobin
Fibrinogen
Transferrin
questions.why: Albumin is by far the most abundant plasma protein, and its histidine side chains accept and release H+ near blood pH. Hemoglobin is an excellent buffer but it sits inside the red blood cell, not in plasma. Fibrinogen and transferrin are present in much smaller amounts and contribute little buffering.

questions.q: Which protein does most of the buffering inside the red blood cell?
options: Albumin
Phosphate
Hemoglobin
Carbonic anhydrase
questions.why: Hemoglobin is present at very high concentration inside the erythrocyte and its histidine residues accept H+ generated when carbon dioxide is hydrated. Albumin does the same job but in plasma, not inside the cell. Phosphate is an inorganic buffer and is important intracellularly, but hemoglobin dominates in the red cell. Carbonic anhydrase is the enzyme producing the acid, not the buffer absorbing it.

questions.q: Which buffer system forms titratable acid in the tubular fluid of the kidney?
options: The albumin system
The hemoglobin system
The bicarbonate system
The phosphate system
questions.why: Filtered phosphate accepts secreted H+ in the tubule and is excreted as dihydrogen phosphate, which is what titratable acid means. Bicarbonate in the tubule is reclaimed rather than excreted, so it carries no acid out of the body. Albumin is not filtered in appreciable amounts. Hemoglobin stays inside red blood cells and never reaches tubular fluid.

questions.q: How quickly do chemical buffers begin to limit a pH change after acid enters the blood?
options: Within 6 to 12 hours
Within 2 to 3 days
Within seconds
Within 10 to 30 minutes
questions.why: Chemical buffering is a reaction between molecules already present, so it works in seconds and is the first line of defense. Ten to thirty minutes is closer to the time the respiratory response needs to reach its full effect. Six to twelve hours is when the renal response becomes measurable. Two to three days is how long the kidney needs to finish compensating.

questions.q: The phosphate system has a pKa of 6.8, much closer to blood pH than the 6.1 of the bicarbonate system. Why is bicarbonate still the stronger plasma buffer?
options: Plasma holds far more bicarbonate, and both are regulated
The pKa of bicarbonate rises to 7.4 once albumin is present
Phosphate stays in plasma and cannot reach the tissues
Phosphate cannot bind a hydrogen ion at 37 C
questions.why: Buffer power depends on concentration as well as pKa, and plasma carries roughly 24 mEq/L of bicarbonate against 1 to 2 mEq/L of phosphate, while ventilation and the kidney can move each member on demand. Phosphate binds H+ perfectly well at body temperature, which is why it dominates inside cells where its concentration is high. The pKa of a buffer pair is a property of the chemistry and albumin does not change it. Phosphate is freely filtered and distributed, so confinement is not the issue.
questions.answerText: Plasma holds far more bicarbonate, and both are regulated

questions.q: A load of fixed acid enters the blood. What happens to plasma bicarbonate and to carbon dioxide before the lungs respond?
options: Bicarbonate falls and carbon dioxide rises
Bicarbonate rises and carbon dioxide falls
Both bicarbonate and carbon dioxide rise
Both bicarbonate and carbon dioxide fall
questions.why: The added H+ combines with bicarbonate to make carbonic acid, which breaks down to water and carbon dioxide, so the base is consumed and the gas accumulates until ventilation clears it. Bicarbonate cannot rise while it is being spent on the acid load. Carbon dioxide cannot fall, because it is the product of the buffering reaction. Both falling would require an entirely different disturbance, such as hyperventilation on top of the acid load.
questions.answerText: Bicarbonate falls and carbon dioxide rises

questions.q: Which sequence gives the correct time course of the three defenses against an acid load?
options: Ventilation in seconds, buffering in minutes, the kidney over days
Buffering in seconds, ventilation in minutes, the kidney over days
The kidney in seconds, buffering in minutes, ventilation over days
Buffering in seconds, the kidney in minutes, ventilation over days
questions.why: Buffers are already dissolved in the fluid, so they act instantly; ventilation must be driven by chemoreceptors and takes minutes to reach full effect; the kidney must change transporter and enzyme activity, which takes hours to days. Ventilation cannot beat a chemical reaction that needs no signaling. The kidney is always the slowest of the three, never the fastest. Reversing the last two puts the slow organ ahead of the fast one.
questions.answerText: Buffering in seconds, ventilation in minutes, the kidney over days

questions.q: Why does buffering a fixed acid with bicarbonate depend on normal lung function?
options: The lungs deliver the oxygen that binds the excess hydrogen ion
The lungs manufacture the bicarbonate used in the reaction
The lungs supply the carbonic anhydrase for the reaction
The carbon dioxide produced must be exhaled or buffering stalls
questions.why: Each H+ buffered turns into a molecule of carbon dioxide, and if that gas accumulates the equilibrium pushes back and the buffer loses its power. The kidney, not the lung, makes bicarbonate. Carbonic anhydrase is inside cells such as the erythrocyte and the tubule cell rather than being supplied by the lung. Oxygen does not bind H+ and plays no part in the buffering reaction.
questions.answerText: The carbon dioxide produced must be exhaled or buffering stalls

questions.q: Blood reaches a systemic capillary and hemoglobin releases its oxygen. What happens to its ability to buffer H+?
options: It falls, because the cell loses carbonic anhydrase activity
It falls, because oxygen is needed to hold H+
It increases, because deoxyhemoglobin accepts H+ more readily
It is unchanged, because buffering does not depend on oxygen binding
questions.why: Deoxygenated hemoglobin is a weaker acid than oxygenated hemoglobin, so it picks up H+ more readily exactly where carbon dioxide is being loaded, which is the Haldane effect. Oxygen is not required for proton binding; releasing it is what improves binding. Saying nothing changes misses the coupling between the two gases that makes the red cell so efficient. Carbonic anhydrase content does not change as hemoglobin unloads oxygen.
questions.answerText: It increases, because deoxyhemoglobin accepts H+ more readily

questions.q: A patient's plasma albumin falls to half its normal value. What happens to the buffering power of plasma?
options: Bicarbonate buffering rises to compensate exactly
Buffering is unchanged because albumin is not a buffer
Buffering rises because more free H+ can reach bicarbonate
The non bicarbonate buffering power of plasma falls
questions.why: Albumin supplies most of the protein buffering in plasma through its histidine side chains, so losing half of it removes a real share of the total buffer capacity. Bicarbonate concentration is set by the kidney and does not automatically rise to cover the loss. Albumin is very much a buffer, which is why low albumin also lowers the measured anion gap. More free H+ reaching bicarbonate means a larger pH swing, not better buffering.
questions.answerText: The non bicarbonate buffering power of plasma falls

questions.q: Why can the kidney excrete far more acid when phosphate is present in the tubular fluid?
options: Buffered H+ keeps urine pH from falling, so secretion continues
Phosphate is converted to bicarbonate inside the tubule cell
Phosphate raises the number of H+ ATPase pumps in the membrane
Phosphate carries H+ across the luminal membrane by symport
questions.why: The H+ pumps stall once urine pH reaches about 4.4, and a buffer soaks up secreted H+ so the free concentration stays low and the gradient stays workable. Phosphate does not carry H+ across the luminal membrane; the H+ ATPase and the Na+/H+ exchanger do that. Phosphate is not converted into bicarbonate, although trapping H+ on phosphate does let the cell add new bicarbonate to the blood. Pump number is regulated by acidosis and hormones, not by the amount of filtered phosphate.
questions.answerText: Buffered H+ keeps urine pH from falling, so secretion continues

questions.q: Equal amounts of acid are added to a sealed tube of bicarbonate solution and to the blood of an intact person. Which shows the smaller fall in pH, and why?
options: The sealed tube, because none of its bicarbonate is lost to urine
The intact person, because the carbon dioxide formed is exhaled
Both fall equally, because the chemistry of the buffer is the same
The sealed tube, because its temperature stays constant
questions.why: In the body the system is open at the lung end, so the carbon dioxide produced by buffering is blown off and the reaction keeps running forward, which is why an open bicarbonate system outperforms its pKa. In the sealed tube the carbon dioxide accumulates, the equilibrium backs up, and pH falls further. Urinary bicarbonate loss is far too slow to matter over the seconds this comparison covers. Temperature is not what separates the two systems here.
questions.answerText: The intact person, because the carbon dioxide formed is exhaled

questions.q: Why is the bicarbonate system a poor buffer for a rise in carbon dioxide itself?
options: It raises H+ and bicarbonate together, so the ratio still falls
Carbon dioxide is a base rather than an acid in this reaction
Carbon dioxide inactivates carbonic anhydrase at high partial pressure
Bicarbonate cannot accept a hydrogen ion once carbon dioxide is high
questions.why: Hydrating carbon dioxide produces one H+ and one HCO3- from the same molecule, so the base cannot mop up the acid it just created, and pH is set by the ratio of the two. That is why proteins, especially hemoglobin, do the real buffering of a respiratory acid load by taking up the H+ and leaving the bicarbonate free. Carbonic anhydrase is not inactivated by high carbon dioxide. Bicarbonate still binds H+ chemically; the problem is bookkeeping, not chemistry. Carbon dioxide behaves as the acid member of the pair.
