questions.answerText: It raises H+ and bicarbonate together, so the ratio still falls

questions.q: A sustained acid load continues for several hours. Where does a large share of the buffering shift, and what electrolyte change follows?
options: Into red blood cells only, with Cl- moving out of plasma
Into filtered phosphate only, with Na+ falling in plasma
Into cells and bone, with K+ moving out of cells into plasma
Into plasma proteins only, with Ca2+ falling in plasma
questions.why: Over hours H+ enters cells and is taken up by intracellular proteins and phosphate, and bone carbonate releases base as well, and to keep charge balanced K+ leaves the cell, which is why chronic acidosis tends to raise plasma potassium. Plasma proteins act within seconds and are saturated long before hours pass. Red cells help immediately but cannot absorb a sustained load on their own, and the chloride shift belongs to carbon dioxide transport, not to a fixed acid load. Filtered phosphate is a urinary buffer and does not pull sodium out of plasma.
questions.answerText: Into cells and bone, with K+ moving out of cells into plasma

questions.q: Arterial PCO2 rises acutely from 40 to 80 mmHg, and over the next few minutes plasma bicarbonate rises only from 24 to 26 mEq/L. What produced that small rise?
options: New bicarbonate generated by the proximal tubule within minutes
Hydration of carbon dioxide, with H+ taken up by proteins
Release of stored bicarbonate from red blood cell granules
Reduced loss of bicarbonate in sweat and gastric secretions
questions.why: Extra carbon dioxide is hydrated to H+ and HCO3-, and because hemoglobin and other proteins take up the H+, the bicarbonate is left behind and measured concentration edges up by roughly 1 mEq/L for each 10 mmHg rise. The kidney cannot generate meaningful new bicarbonate in minutes, which is exactly why this rise is so small. Red blood cells store no bicarbonate granules. Sweat and gastric losses of bicarbonate are trivial and far too slow to explain a change over minutes.
questions.answerText: Hydration of carbon dioxide, with H+ taken up by proteins

questions.q: Which enzyme speeds the combination of carbon dioxide and water to form carbonic acid?
options: Carboxypeptidase
Bicarbonate synthase
Carbonic anhydrase
Carbonic dehydrogenase
questions.why: Carbonic anhydrase catalyzes the hydration of carbon dioxide, and it is abundant in red blood cells and renal tubule cells where the reaction has to run fast. Carbonic dehydrogenase and bicarbonate synthase are not real enzymes of this pathway. Carboxypeptidase is a protein digesting enzyme from the pancreas and has nothing to do with acid base handling.

questions.q: What is the normal value for arterial PCO2?
options: About 40 mmHg
About 60 mmHg
About 100 mmHg
About 24 mmHg
questions.why: Arterial PCO2 normally sits between 35 and 45 mmHg, so 40 is the anchor value. A value near 24 is the number for plasma bicarbonate in mEq/L, which is easy to confuse with a gas pressure. About 60 mmHg would be marked carbon dioxide retention. About 100 mmHg is the normal figure for arterial PO2, not PCO2.

questions.q: What is the normal range for arterial pH?
questions.why: Arterial pH is held in the narrow band of 7.35 to 7.45, and the midpoint 7.40 is the reference for deciding which side of neutral a compensated blood gas sits on. Values from 7.20 to 7.35 are acidemic, not normal. Values from 7.00 to 7.20 are severe acidemia. Anything above 7.45 is alkalemia.

questions.q: What happens to arterial PCO2 during hyperventilation?
options: It rises and then falls below normal
It rises
It falls
It stays constant while PO2 falls
questions.why: Hyperventilation means alveolar ventilation exceeds the rate at which metabolism makes carbon dioxide, so the gas is cleared faster than it is produced and arterial PCO2 falls. A rise in PCO2 is the mark of hypoventilation. PCO2 cannot stay constant while ventilation changes, since it is set by the balance of production and removal. There is no transient rise before the fall.

questions.q: Arterial PCO2 rises. Which way does plasma pH move?
options: It rises
It falls
It rises then returns to 7.40
It does not change until bicarbonate changes
questions.why: Carbon dioxide is hydrated to carbonic acid, which dissociates and adds H+ to the blood, so more carbon dioxide always means a lower pH. A rise in pH would require carbon dioxide to fall or bicarbonate to rise. Nothing returns pH to 7.40 without compensation over hours. Bicarbonate does not have to change first, because the carbon dioxide itself supplies the H+.

questions.q: Where are the central chemoreceptors that respond to a rise in blood carbon dioxide?
options: In the carotid bodies
In the medulla oblongata
In the aortic arch
In the pulmonary capillaries
questions.why: Central chemoreceptors sit on the ventral surface of the medulla and sense the H+ of cerebrospinal fluid, which tracks arterial PCO2 because carbon dioxide crosses the blood brain barrier freely. The carotid bodies and the aortic bodies are the peripheral chemoreceptors and respond mainly to low PO2. Pulmonary capillaries carry blood past the alveoli but contain no chemoreceptors.

questions.q: Which stimulus do the central chemoreceptors actually detect?
options: The bicarbonate concentration of plasma
The H+ concentration of cerebrospinal fluid
The temperature of arterial blood
The partial pressure of oxygen in arterial blood
questions.why: Carbon dioxide crosses into cerebrospinal fluid and is hydrated there, and it is the resulting H+ that the medullary receptors sense, so they read carbon dioxide indirectly. Arterial oxygen is monitored by the peripheral chemoreceptors instead. Plasma bicarbonate and H+ cross the blood brain barrier poorly, which is why a metabolic disorder stimulates ventilation less directly than a respiratory one. Temperature affects ventilation but is not the chemoreceptor stimulus.
questions.answerText: The H+ concentration of cerebrospinal fluid

questions.q: How long does the respiratory response to an acid load take to reach its full effect?
options: Twelve hours
Three days
Milliseconds
Minutes
questions.why: Chemoreceptors fire within seconds and ventilation is fully adjusted in a matter of minutes, which makes the lung the second line of defense after chemical buffers. Milliseconds is the time scale of an action potential, not of a ventilatory adjustment. Twelve hours and three days describe the renal response, which is far slower but far more complete.

questions.q: A student breathes rapidly and deeply for two minutes during an anxiety episode. Predict the changes in PCO2 and pH.
options: PCO2 falls and pH rises
PCO2 falls and pH falls
PCO2 rises and pH falls
PCO2 rises and pH rises
questions.why: Blowing off carbon dioxide faster than it is made lowers arterial PCO2, removes acid from the blood, and drives pH up, which is respiratory alkalosis. PCO2 and pH move in opposite directions for a respiratory problem, so falling PCO2 with falling pH is not possible from hyperventilation alone. Rising PCO2 with falling pH describes hypoventilation, the opposite disturbance. Rising PCO2 with rising pH breaks the chemistry in both directions.

questions.q: A person takes a sedative that slows the respiratory rate. Predict what happens to arterial PCO2 and pH.
options: PCO2 rises and pH falls
PCO2 and pH both stay normal
PCO2 falls and pH rises
PCO2 rises and pH rises
questions.why: Less ventilation lets metabolically produced carbon dioxide accumulate, and the extra carbonic acid drives pH down, which is respiratory acidosis. Falling PCO2 would require more ventilation, not less. A rise in PCO2 can never raise pH, because carbon dioxide is the acid member of the buffer pair. Values cannot stay normal while carbon dioxide production continues and removal has slowed.

questions.q: Adding carbon dioxide to blood shifts the reaction CO2 + H2O to H2CO3 to H+ plus HCO3- in which direction, and what happens to bicarbonate?
options: To the right, and bicarbonate rises slightly
To the right, and bicarbonate falls slightly
To the left, and bicarbonate rises slightly
To the left, and bicarbonate falls slightly
questions.why: Extra reactant pushes the equilibrium toward products, so both H+ and HCO3- are produced and measured bicarbonate rises a little even though pH is falling. The reaction cannot run to the left when carbon dioxide is being added. Bicarbonate cannot fall while it is being generated by the same reaction. This is also why a rising bicarbonate on a blood gas does not automatically mean a metabolic alkalosis.
questions.answerText: To the right, and bicarbonate rises slightly

questions.q: Alveolar ventilation doubles while carbon dioxide production stays the same. What happens to arterial PCO2?
options: It stays the same because production is unchanged
It falls to roughly half its previous value
It falls by roughly 10 percent
It doubles
questions.why: Arterial PCO2 is set by carbon dioxide production divided by alveolar ventilation, so doubling the denominator with the numerator fixed roughly halves the value, taking 40 mmHg toward 20 mmHg. A ten percent fall would need only a small change in ventilation. PCO2 doubles when ventilation is halved, not doubled. Unchanged production is precisely why the ventilation change is free to move PCO2.
questions.answerText: It falls to roughly half its previous value

questions.q: Why does hyperventilation raise pH even though it also lowers plasma bicarbonate?
options: A lower bicarbonate raises pH all by itself
Bicarbonate does not affect pH, only carbon dioxide does
Carbon dioxide falls proportionally more, so the ratio rises
The lost bicarbonate is replaced by phosphate within seconds
questions.why: pH tracks the ratio of bicarbonate to dissolved carbon dioxide, and hyperventilation cuts the denominator sharply while the numerator drifts down only slightly, so the ratio and the pH both rise. Bicarbonate certainly affects pH; it is the base member of the pair. Phosphate is present at far too low a plasma concentration to replace bicarbonate. A fall in bicarbonate by itself lowers pH, which is why the reasoning has to be about the ratio.
questions.answerText: Carbon dioxide falls proportionally more, so the ratio rises

questions.q: A patient breathes into and out of a closed paper bag. Which change explains the fall in pH that follows?
options: Slower airflow reduces carbonic anhydrase activity
The bag lowers inspired oxygen and produces lactic acid
Rebreathed carbon dioxide raises arterial PCO2
The bag raises tidal volume and clears bicarbonate
questions.why: Rebreathing returns exhaled carbon dioxide to the alveoli, the alveolar to blood gradient shrinks, arterial PCO2 climbs, and pH falls, which is why the maneuver was used against hyperventilation. Oxygen does drop somewhat but not enough in a short trial to produce meaningful lactic acid. Bicarbonate is not cleared by the lungs at all. Carbonic anhydrase activity is not altered by how fast air moves.
questions.answerText: Rebreathed carbon dioxide raises arterial PCO2

questions.q: Which chemoreceptor group produces most of the ventilatory response to a modest rise in arterial PCO2?
options: The carotid bodies
The central chemoreceptors of the medulla
The aortic bodies
Stretch receptors in the airway wall
questions.why: Roughly two thirds to three quarters of the ventilatory response to carbon dioxide comes from the medullary receptors, because carbon dioxide crosses into cerebrospinal fluid readily and generates H+ there. The carotid and aortic bodies respond to carbon dioxide as well but contribute the smaller share, and their dominant stimulus is a low PO2. Airway stretch receptors regulate the depth and timing of a breath, not its chemical drive.
questions.answerText: The central chemoreceptors of the medulla

questions.q: A climber arrives at 4000 meters. Low PO2 drives hyperventilation. Trace the effect on PCO2, then on pH, then name the disorder.
options: PCO2 falls, pH rises, and the result is respiratory alkalosis
PCO2 falls, pH falls, and the result is metabolic acidosis
PCO2 rises, pH rises, and the result is metabolic alkalosis
PCO2 rises, pH falls, and the result is respiratory acidosis
questions.why: Hypoxia stimulates the peripheral chemoreceptors, ventilation increases, carbon dioxide is cleared faster than it is produced so PCO2 falls, and losing that acid drives pH above 7.45, which is a respiratory alkalosis. Rising PCO2 would need hypoventilation, the opposite of the hypoxic response. A metabolic label would require the primary change to be in bicarbonate, but here the primary change is in a gas. Nothing in this sequence raises bicarbonate.
questions.answerText: PCO2 falls, pH rises, and the result is respiratory alkalosis

questions.q: A student hyperventilates for one minute, then holds their breath as long as possible. What happens to pH across the two phases?
options: It stays constant, then falls sharply
It rises during both phases
It falls, then rises above normal
It rises, then falls back through normal
questions.why: Blowing off carbon dioxide first drives PCO2 down and pH up, then during the breath hold metabolism keeps making carbon dioxide with no route out, so PCO2 climbs and pH falls back toward and past normal. The order cannot be reversed, since hyperventilation always comes first here. pH cannot stay constant while PCO2 is changing. It cannot rise in both phases, because a breath hold retains acid rather than removing it.
questions.answerText: It rises, then falls back through normal

questions.q: A patient in metabolic acidosis hyperventilates. Why can this respiratory compensation never return pH fully to 7.40?
options: Bicarbonate rises as PCO2 falls and cancels the benefit
Carbonic anhydrase is saturated once ventilation doubles
The lungs cannot lower PCO2 below 35 mmHg under any circumstance
The falling PCO2 removes the stimulus driving the extra ventilation
questions.why: Ventilation increases because H+ and carbon dioxide stimulate chemoreceptors, so as pH climbs back toward normal the drive weakens and ventilation levels off short of full correction, which is why compensation is fast but incomplete. PCO2 can certainly go well below 35 mmHg; values in the twenties are common in severe metabolic acidosis. Bicarbonate falls slightly rather than rising when PCO2 drops. Carbonic anhydrase has enormous spare capacity and does not become the limiting step.
questions.answerText: The falling PCO2 removes the stimulus driving the extra ventilation

questions.q: Alveolar ventilation is halved in a sedated patient whose arterial values started at pH 7.40, PCO2 40 mmHg, HCO3- 24 mEq/L. Predict the new PCO2 and the direction of pH.
options: PCO2 near 80 mmHg with pH above 7.45
PCO2 near 40 mmHg with pH unchanged
PCO2 near 20 mmHg with pH above 7.45
PCO2 near 80 mmHg with pH below 7.35
questions.why: PCO2 varies inversely with alveolar ventilation at constant production, so halving ventilation roughly doubles PCO2 from 40 to about 80 mmHg, and with bicarbonate still near 24 mEq/L the ratio collapses and pH falls to roughly 7.10. A PCO2 near 20 mmHg would follow from doubling ventilation, not halving it. A high PCO2 with a high pH is chemically impossible without a large rise in bicarbonate, which cannot happen in minutes. PCO2 cannot stay at 40 when removal has been cut in half.
questions.answerText: PCO2 near 80 mmHg with pH below 7.35

questions.q: Which tubule segment reclaims most of the filtered bicarbonate?
options: The thin descending limb
The distal convoluted tubule
The collecting duct
The proximal convoluted tubule
questions.why: Roughly 80 to 85 percent of filtered bicarbonate is reclaimed in the proximal tubule, which is built for high capacity bulk reabsorption. The thin descending limb is permeable to water and handles no bicarbonate transport. The distal tubule and collecting duct recover only the small remainder and are where fine adjustment of acid excretion happens, not bulk reclamation.

questions.q: Which transporter moves H+ into the proximal tubule lumen in exchange for Na+?
options: The chloride bicarbonate exchanger
The sodium potassium ATPase
The sodium hydrogen exchanger
The sodium glucose cotransporter
questions.why: The Na+/H+ exchanger on the luminal membrane uses the inward sodium gradient to push H+ out into the lumen, which is secondary active transport. The Na+/K+ ATPase sits on the basolateral membrane and creates that gradient rather than secreting H+ itself. The sodium glucose cotransporter carries glucose, not H+. The chloride bicarbonate exchanger moves bicarbonate out of the cell on the basolateral side and does not secrete acid into the lumen.

questions.q: Which cell of the collecting duct secretes H+ into the tubular fluid during acidosis?
options: The type A intercalated cell
The type B intercalated cell
The macula densa cell
The principal cell
questions.why: Type A intercalated cells carry an H+ ATPase on the luminal membrane and send new bicarbonate back to the blood, so they are the acid exporters. Principal cells handle sodium, potassium, and water under aldosterone and ADH. Type B intercalated cells are the mirror image and secrete bicarbonate during alkalosis. The macula densa senses tubular sodium chloride for tubuloglomerular feedback and does not transport acid.

questions.q: Which cell secretes bicarbonate into the tubular fluid during alkalosis?
options: The principal cell
The type B intercalated cell
The mesangial cell
The type A intercalated cell
questions.why: The type B intercalated cell has its pumps and exchangers arranged in reverse, so it puts bicarbonate into the lumen and H+ back into the blood, which is how the kidney corrects an alkalosis. The type A cell does the opposite and is active in acidosis. Principal cells are not acid base cells. Mesangial cells sit in the glomerulus and regulate filtration surface area.

questions.q: Which amino acid do proximal tubule cells break down to make ammonium for acid excretion?
options: Arginine
Histidine
Glycine
Glutamine
questions.why: Glutamine is taken up by the proximal tubule and metabolized to two ammonium ions and the carbon skeleton that yields new bicarbonate for the blood. Glycine and arginine are not the substrates for renal ammoniagenesis. Histidine is the buffering side chain in proteins, which is a different acid base role entirely.

questions.q: What are the two main urinary buffers that let the kidney excrete large amounts of acid?
options: Albumin and hemoglobin
Phosphate and ammonia
Sulfate and lactate
Bicarbonate and chloride
questions.why: Filtered phosphate accepts H+ to form titratable acid, and ammonia made in the tubule cell traps H+ as ammonium, and together they carry the bulk of the daily acid load out in the urine. Bicarbonate in the tubule is reclaimed rather than excreted, so it removes no net acid. Albumin and hemoglobin never reach tubular fluid in meaningful amounts. Sulfate and lactate are anions in urine but are not significant H+ acceptors at urine pH.

questions.q: How long does full renal compensation for an acid base disorder take?
options: Two to three minutes
One to two hours
Two to three days
Two to three weeks
questions.why: Renal compensation begins within hours but takes two to three days to reach its full effect, because it depends on changes in transporter number and enzyme activity. Minutes is the time scale of the respiratory response. One to two hours is enough for the kidney to start but not to finish. Weeks overstates it; the kidney is slow but not that slow.

questions.q: In what chemical form does filtered bicarbonate actually cross the luminal membrane of the proximal tubule cell?
options: As carbonic acid on a channel
As ammonium bicarbonate
As bicarbonate ion on a symporter
As carbon dioxide
questions.why: Secreted H+ combines with filtered bicarbonate in the lumen to form carbonic acid, brush border carbonic anhydrase splits it to water and carbon dioxide, and the gas diffuses into the cell where the reaction is reversed. The luminal membrane has no bicarbonate symporter for this purpose. Carbonic acid is short lived and does not cross on a channel. Ammonium bicarbonate is not a transported species here.

questions.q: A patient has been acidotic for two days. Predict what has happened to renal H+ secretion and to ammonium production.
options: H+ secretion decreased and ammonium production increased
Both have increased
Both have decreased
H+ secretion increased and ammonium production decreased
questions.why: Acidosis upregulates the luminal Na+/H+ exchanger and H+ ATPase and also induces the enzymes of glutamine metabolism, so the kidney both pumps more acid and supplies more ammonia to carry it out. Both falling is the response to alkalosis, not acidosis. The two processes are regulated together because H+ secretion is useless without a buffer to trap it, so a split answer in either direction misses how the system is coupled.

questions.q: A patient has a metabolic alkalosis that has lasted three days. What is the kidney doing with bicarbonate?
options: Holding bicarbonate constant while excreting more chloride
Reclaiming all filtered bicarbonate and generating more
Excreting bicarbonate in the urine, making it alkaline
Converting bicarbonate to ammonium for excretion
questions.why: With plasma bicarbonate high, the filtered load exceeds what the proximal tubule can reclaim and type B intercalated cells actively secrete bicarbonate, so the urine turns alkaline and plasma bicarbonate is dragged back down. Reclaiming and generating more bicarbonate is the acidosis response and would worsen the alkalosis. Bicarbonate is not converted into ammonium; ammonium comes from glutamine. Chloride excretion alone would not correct the base excess.
questions.answerText: Excreting bicarbonate in the urine, making it alkaline

questions.q: A drug inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule. Predict the effect on urine and on plasma.
options: Bicarbonate is lost in urine and plasma bicarbonate falls
Urine turns strongly acidic and plasma pH rises sharply
Ammonium excretion rises and plasma pH rises sharply
Bicarbonate is retained and plasma bicarbonate rises
questions.why: Without carbonic anhydrase the lumen cannot break down carbonic acid, bicarbonate reclamation stalls, the alkaline urine carries base out of the body, and a metabolic acidosis develops. Retention of bicarbonate is what happens when the enzyme is working normally. The urine becomes more alkaline, not more acidic, since bicarbonate is left behind in it. Plasma pH falls rather than rises, which is exactly why this class of drug is used to blunt the alkalosis of altitude.
questions.answerText: Bicarbonate is lost in urine and plasma bicarbonate falls

questions.q: Secreted H+ combines with a filtered bicarbonate ion in the lumen. How much new bicarbonate has been added to the blood?
options: One new bicarbonate ion for each H+ that is secreted
Two new bicarbonate ions for each H+ secreted
None, because a bicarbonate was merely preserved
None, because the secreted H+ is reabsorbed unchanged
questions.why: Titrating filtered bicarbonate is reclamation, so the blood ends where it started, and net new bicarbonate is added only when secreted H+ is trapped by phosphate or ammonia and leaves the body. Counting one new bicarbonate per secreted H+ confuses reclamation with generation, which is the single most common error in this topic. Two is not the stoichiometry of any step here. The H+ is not reabsorbed unchanged; it is consumed making carbon dioxide and water.
questions.answerText: None, because a bicarbonate was merely preserved

questions.q: Why does the minimum urine pH of about 4.4 limit how much free H+ the kidney can excrete?
options: Free H+ is still a tiny fraction of the acid load
Tubule cells cannot survive a lower urine pH
Carbonic anhydrase stops working below that pH
The H+ ATPase reverses direction and reabsorbs acid
questions.why: A urine pH of 4.4 corresponds to only about 0.04 mEq of free H+ per liter, which is trivial next to a daily acid load near 70 mEq, so nearly all of the excreted acid must ride out bound to phosphate or ammonia. The H+ ATPase stalls against the gradient rather than reversing. Tubule cells are not destroyed at that urine pH; it is a normal daily occurrence. Carbonic anhydrase is not what sets this limit.
questions.answerText: Free H+ is still a tiny fraction of the acid load

questions.q: Aldosterone secretion rises. Predict the effect on H+ handling by the collecting duct.
options: H+ secretion is unchanged but bicarbonate secretion rises
H+ is reabsorbed instead of secreted
H+ secretion increases
H+ secretion decreases
questions.why: Aldosterone stimulates the H+ ATPase of type A intercalated cells and increases sodium reabsorption by principal cells, which leaves the lumen more negative and pulls H+ out, so excess aldosterone can produce a metabolic alkalosis. A fall in H+ secretion is the response to too little aldosterone. Bicarbonate secretion by type B cells is not the aldosterone response. There is no mechanism for reabsorbing free H+ across the collecting duct.

questions.q: Why is renal compensation more complete than respiratory compensation even though it is far slower?
options: The kidney works much faster once it gets started
The kidney removes acid from the body altogether
The kidney is not limited by carbonic anhydrase
The kidney changes pH without changing bicarbonate
questions.why: Excreting H+ on phosphate and ammonia and adding new bicarbonate physically removes the acid load, and the kidney keeps working until pH is near normal because its drive does not switch off as quickly as chemoreceptor drive does. Renal compensation is slower than respiratory compensation at every stage, not faster. Carbonic anhydrase limits neither system in practice. The kidney acts precisely by changing bicarbonate, so it cannot alter pH while leaving bicarbonate alone.
questions.answerText: The kidney removes acid from the body altogether

questions.q: A patient with chronic lung disease has had a PCO2 near 60 mmHg for several years. Predict plasma bicarbonate and urine pH.
options: Bicarbonate is high and the urine is alkaline
Bicarbonate is high and the urine is acidic
Bicarbonate is low and the urine is alkaline
Bicarbonate is normal and the urine is alkaline
questions.why: Years of carbon dioxide retention drive the kidney to secrete H+ and generate new bicarbonate, so plasma bicarbonate climbs into the thirties while the acid leaving in the urine keeps urine pH low. A low bicarbonate would make the acidemia worse rather than compensating for it. A normal bicarbonate would mean no compensation at all, which is not possible after years. Alkaline urine would mean the kidney was dumping the very bicarbonate it needs to retain.
questions.answerText: Bicarbonate is high and the urine is acidic

questions.q: A patient has vomited gastric contents for three days and is now volume depleted with a metabolic alkalosis. Why does the kidney keep reabsorbing bicarbonate rather than excreting it?
options: Vomiting removes the enzyme needed for bicarbonate secretion
A high plasma pH directly inhibits glomerular filtration
The kidney cannot excrete bicarbonate at any plasma concentration
Volume depletion drives sodium reabsorption, and H+ follows
questions.why: Low volume raises angiotensin II and aldosterone, both of which stimulate the Na+/H+ exchanger and the H+ ATPase, so the kidney keeps secreting acid and reclaiming bicarbonate and the urine stays acidic even in alkalosis, which is why restoring volume is what lets the alkalosis resolve. The kidney can normally excrete bicarbonate very effectively; that ability is being overridden here. Vomiting removes gastric acid and fluid, not renal enzymes. Filtration is not directly shut down by a high plasma pH.
questions.answerText: Volume depletion drives sodium reabsorption, and H+ follows

questions.q: A climber takes a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor before ascending. Trace the effect through the kidney to arterial pH and explain why it helps at altitude.
options: Bicarbonate is lost in urine, lowering pH and offsetting alkalosis
Ammonium excretion falls, raising plasma pH and blunting the hypoxia
H+ secretion rises, lowering plasma pH and slowing ventilation down
Bicarbonate is retained, raising plasma pH and deepening each breath
questions.why: Blocking the enzyme stops proximal bicarbonate reclamation, base is lost in an alkaline urine, plasma bicarbonate and pH fall, and that mild metabolic acidosis counteracts the respiratory alkalosis caused by hypoxic hyperventilation so ventilation can stay high. Retaining bicarbonate would raise pH and suppress the very drive the climber needs. Ammonium excretion changes are not the main mechanism and would not lower pH. H+ secretion falls rather than rises when carbonic anhydrase is inhibited, and the goal is more ventilation, not less.
questions.answerText: Bicarbonate is lost in urine, lowering pH and offsetting alkalosis

questions.q: A patient develops a metabolic acidosis this morning. Compare what has happened by ten minutes and by three days.
options: Ventilation rises in minutes, and the kidney corrects pH over days
Nothing changes for three days, when ventilation finally rises
Ventilation rises only after the kidney has finished at three days
Renal bicarbonate generation finishes in minutes, so pH is normal by ten minutes
questions.why: Chemoreceptors drive hyperventilation within minutes, which lowers PCO2 and limits the fall in pH but cannot fully correct it because the drive fades as pH improves; over two to three days the kidney excretes the acid load and regenerates bicarbonate, bringing pH close to normal. The kidney cannot generate meaningful bicarbonate in minutes. Something does change immediately, since buffering and then ventilation both act early. The order is fixed by the machinery involved, so ventilation cannot wait on the kidney.
questions.answerText: Ventilation rises in minutes, and the kidney corrects pH over days

questions.q: What term describes an arterial pH below 7.35?
options: Hypoxemia
Alkalemia
Acidemia
Hypercapnia
questions.why: Acidemia is the measured state of blood that is too acidic, and it is the first thing to read off a blood gas because it tells you which direction the primary problem is pushing. Alkalemia is the opposite, a pH above 7.45. Hypercapnia means a high PCO2, which is one possible cause of acidemia but is not the same statement. Hypoxemia refers to low arterial oxygen and is read from PO2, not pH.

questions.q: What term describes an arterial pH above 7.45?
options: Acidemia
Hypocapnia
Alkalemia
Alkaluria
questions.why: Alkalemia is blood that is too alkaline, and it points you toward either a low PCO2 or a high bicarbonate as the cause. Acidemia is the opposite condition. Hypocapnia means a low PCO2, which can produce alkalemia but describes the gas rather than the blood pH. Alkaluria refers to alkaline urine, which is a renal finding and not a statement about arterial blood.

questions.q: Which measured value on a blood gas tells you about the respiratory component of an acid base disorder?
options: PCO2
Bicarbonate
pH
PO2
questions.why: PCO2 is set by ventilation, so it is the respiratory number on the panel and any primary abnormality in it makes the disorder respiratory. Bicarbonate is the metabolic number, controlled by the kidney and by gains or losses of acid and base. pH tells you the net result but not which system caused it. PO2 reports oxygenation, which is a separate problem from acid base status.

questions.q: Which measured value on a blood gas tells you about the metabolic component of an acid base disorder?
options: Bicarbonate
PCO2
PO2
Oxygen saturation
questions.why: Bicarbonate reflects the body stores of base and changes with fixed acid gain, base loss, or renal handling, so it is the metabolic number. PCO2 is the respiratory number. PO2 and oxygen saturation both describe oxygen carriage and say nothing directly about acid base balance.

questions.q: In a primary respiratory disorder, how do pH and PCO2 move relative to each other?
options: In opposite directions
In the same direction
PCO2 changes while pH stays fixed
pH changes while PCO2 stays fixed
questions.why: Carbon dioxide is an acid, so a rise in PCO2 lowers pH and a fall in PCO2 raises it, and that opposite movement is the signature of a respiratory problem. Moving in the same direction is the signature of a metabolic problem, where bicarbonate tracks pH. A change in PCO2 always changes pH unless something else is compensating. If pH moved while PCO2 held still, the cause would be metabolic rather than respiratory.

questions.q: In a primary metabolic disorder, how do pH and bicarbonate move relative to each other?
options: In opposite directions
In the same direction
Bicarbonate changes while pH stays fixed
Bicarbonate always stays within its normal range
questions.why: Bicarbonate is the base member of the buffer pair, so losing it lowers pH and gaining it raises pH, and that same direction movement marks the disorder as metabolic. Opposite movement is what PCO2 does in a respiratory disorder, which is the distinction students most often collapse. A change in bicarbonate cannot leave pH untouched. Bicarbonate is by definition abnormal in a primary metabolic disorder.

questions.q: What is the name of the disorder in which pH is low and PCO2 is high?
options: Respiratory alkalosis
Respiratory acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis
questions.why: A high PCO2 means retained carbon dioxide, the acid member of the pair, so it is respiratory and it is an acidosis. Metabolic acidosis also lowers pH but does so through a low bicarbonate with PCO2 normal or low. Respiratory alkalosis has a low PCO2 and a high pH. Metabolic alkalosis has a high bicarbonate and a high pH.

questions.q: What is the name of the disorder in which pH is high and bicarbonate is high?
options: Respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis
Respiratory acidosis
questions.why: Bicarbonate is the metabolic number and it has moved in the same direction as pH, so the primary problem is a gain of base or a loss of fixed acid. Respiratory alkalosis raises pH but through a low PCO2, with bicarbonate normal or low. Metabolic acidosis has a low bicarbonate and a low pH. Respiratory acidosis has a high PCO2 and a low pH, and its bicarbonate rises only as compensation.

questions.q: Classify this blood gas: pH 7.25, PCO2 60 mmHg, HCO3- 26 mEq/L.
options: Respiratory acidosis
Respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis
questions.why: The pH of 7.25 is acidemic, and the PCO2 of 60 mmHg is high, which is the direction that makes blood more acidic, so the respiratory system is the cause. Bicarbonate at 26 mEq/L is at the top of normal and cannot explain an acidemia, so metabolic acidosis is ruled out. Both alkalosis labels are impossible with a pH this low.

questions.q: Classify this blood gas: pH 7.30, PCO2 40 mmHg, HCO3- 19 mEq/L.
options: Metabolic acidosis
Respiratory alkalosis
Respiratory acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis
questions.why: The pH of 7.30 is acidemic, PCO2 is exactly normal at 40 mmHg so the lungs are not responsible, and the bicarbonate of 19 mEq/L is low, which is the metabolic cause of the acidemia. Respiratory acidosis would require a PCO2 above 45 mmHg. Neither alkalosis fits a pH below 7.35.

questions.q: Classify this blood gas: pH 7.55, PCO2 40 mmHg, HCO3- 34 mEq/L.
options: Respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis
Respiratory acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis
questions.why: The pH of 7.55 is alkalemic, PCO2 is normal at 40 mmHg so ventilation is not the cause, and bicarbonate at 34 mEq/L is clearly high, which raises pH and marks the problem as metabolic. Respiratory alkalosis would require a PCO2 below 35 mmHg. Neither acidosis label can accompany a pH above 7.45.

questions.q: Classify this blood gas: pH 7.52, PCO2 28 mmHg, HCO3- 22 mEq/L.
options: Respiratory acidosis
Respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis
questions.why: The pH of 7.52 is alkalemic, and the PCO2 of 28 mmHg is low, which removes acid and raises pH, so the cause is respiratory. Bicarbonate at 22 mEq/L is at the low end of normal and could not have raised the pH, so this is not a metabolic alkalosis. Both acidosis labels are ruled out by the high pH.

questions.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.14, PCO2 80 mmHg, HCO3- 26 mEq/L. Which single value explains the acidemia?
options: Both values together
Neither value, so the sample is in error
The bicarbonate of 26 mEq/L
The PCO2 of 80 mmHg
questions.why: Only a value that has moved in the acidifying direction can explain a low pH, and a PCO2 of 80 mmHg is double normal while bicarbonate sits inside its normal range of 22 to 26 mEq/L. A bicarbonate of 26 is if anything faintly alkalinizing, so it cannot be the cause. Calling both responsible ignores that one of them is normal. The set is internally consistent, so there is no reason to suspect a sampling error.

questions.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.02, PCO2 40 mmHg, HCO3- 10 mEq/L. What does the normal PCO2 tell you?
options: The measurement of pH must be wrong
The disorder must be respiratory in origin
The lungs have not responded to the acidosis
The kidney has fully corrected the disorder
questions.why: A severe metabolic acidosis should drive hyperventilation and pull PCO2 well below 40 mmHg, so a normal value here means the expected respiratory response is missing, which is an important warning sign. A normal PCO2 rules the disorder out as respiratory rather than in. A fully corrected disorder would show a pH back near 7.40, not 7.02. The three values are consistent with each other, so the pH is not suspect.
questions.answerText: The lungs have not responded to the acidosis

questions.q: A patient loses a large volume of bicarbonate rich intestinal fluid through severe diarrhea. Which disorder develops?
options: Respiratory acidosis
Metabolic acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis
Respiratory alkalosis
questions.why: Intestinal secretions are rich in bicarbonate, so losing them strips base from the extracellular fluid, bicarbonate falls, and pH falls with it, which is a metabolic acidosis. Respiratory acidosis would require carbon dioxide retention, and nothing here impairs ventilation. Metabolic alkalosis follows loss of acid, as in vomiting gastric contents, which is the mirror image of this case. Respiratory alkalosis would require hyperventilation as the primary event.

questions.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.39, PCO2 55 mmHg, HCO3- 32 mEq/L. The pH is inside the normal range. Is there a disorder, and if so which one?
options: Yes, a metabolic alkalosis, since bicarbonate is high
Yes, a mixed disorder, since both values are abnormal here
No, since the pH is within the 7.35 to 7.45 range
Yes, a respiratory acidosis, since pH is on the acid side
questions.why: When compensation is complete the pH returns inside the normal range but stops short of 7.40, and the side it lands on identifies the primary problem, so a pH of 7.39 with a high PCO2 and a high bicarbonate is a fully compensated respiratory acidosis. A normal pH alone does not mean normal blood, since both other values are far from normal. Calling it metabolic alkalosis mistakes the compensation for the primary problem, since a primary alkalosis would leave pH above 7.40. In a mixed disorder the two values push pH the same way, and here they oppose each other.
questions.answerText: Yes, a respiratory acidosis, since pH is on the acid side

questions.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.11, PCO2 55 mmHg, HCO3- 17 mEq/L. Why can this not be a simple disorder with compensation?
options: The pH is too low for any compensation to have started
Bicarbonate and PCO2 can never be abnormal at the same time
Both values are pushing pH down, so neither is compensating
Compensation never changes bicarbonate, only PCO2
questions.why: A high PCO2 acidifies and a low bicarbonate also acidifies, so both a respiratory and a metabolic acidosis are present and there is no compensating move in either direction, which is why this reads as a mixed acidosis. Compensation absolutely does change bicarbonate; that is how the kidney compensates for a respiratory problem. A very low pH does not prevent compensation from starting, and in a simple disorder you would expect to see it. Both values are abnormal at once in every compensated disorder, so that alone is not the problem here.
questions.answerText: Both values are pushing pH down, so neither is compensating

questions.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.60, PCO2 32 mmHg, HCO3- 30 mEq/L. What does the combination indicate?
options: A respiratory alkalosis with full renal compensation
A metabolic alkalosis with full respiratory compensation
A mixed alkalosis, since both values raise pH
A normal result, since the two changes cancel out
questions.why: Compensation moves the second value in the same direction as the primary one to blunt the pH change, but here PCO2 has fallen while bicarbonate has risen, so both are driving pH up and the pH is extreme rather than corrected. Renal compensation for a respiratory alkalosis would lower bicarbonate, not raise it. Respiratory compensation for a metabolic alkalosis would raise PCO2, not lower it. The changes reinforce rather than cancel, which is exactly why the pH is 7.60.
questions.answerText: A mixed alkalosis, since both values raise pH

questions.q: A patient vomits gastric contents repeatedly for two days, losing hydrochloric acid. Predict bicarbonate and pH, then classify the disorder.
options: Bicarbonate rises, pH falls, respiratory acidosis
Bicarbonate falls, pH rises, respiratory alkalosis
Bicarbonate falls, pH falls, metabolic acidosis
Bicarbonate rises, pH rises, metabolic alkalosis
questions.why: Every H+ secreted into the stomach leaves a bicarbonate behind in the blood, so removing that acid by vomiting leaves the base unopposed, bicarbonate climbs, and pH rises, which is a metabolic alkalosis. Bicarbonate cannot fall when the acid that would have neutralized it is being discarded. A rising bicarbonate with a falling pH would require a large simultaneous rise in PCO2, which vomiting does not cause. Losing bicarbonate is what happens with diarrhea, from the other end of the gut.
questions.answerText: Bicarbonate rises, pH rises, metabolic alkalosis

questions.q: What does it mean to call an acid base disorder uncompensated?
options: The pH has returned to the normal range
The system that is not the cause is still normal
Both PCO2 and bicarbonate are abnormal
The kidney has excreted all of the excess acid
questions.why: Uncompensated means only the primary value has moved, so the other value still sits in its normal range and pH is left fully abnormal. A pH back in the normal range describes full compensation, the opposite situation. Both values abnormal describes partial or full compensation. Full renal excretion of the acid load is correction of the disorder, not compensation for it.
questions.answerText: The system that is not the cause is still normal

questions.q: What defines a fully compensated acid base disorder?
options: The pH is back inside 7.35 to 7.45
The pH has settled at exactly 7.40
The primary abnormality has fully resolved
PCO2 and bicarbonate are both back to normal
questions.why: Full compensation means the opposing system has pushed pH back inside the normal band, but it has done so by making its own value abnormal, so the panel shows a normal pH with two abnormal numbers. If both values returned to normal the disorder would be gone, not compensated. Compensation stops short of exactly 7.40, which is what lets you identify the primary problem. The primary abnormality persists throughout; that is why compensation is still needed.
questions.answerText: The pH is back inside 7.35 to 7.45

questions.q: Which system compensates for a primary metabolic acid base disorder?
options: The hepatic system
The gastrointestinal system
The respiratory system
The renal system
questions.why: A metabolic problem lives in the bicarbonate, so the lungs answer it by adjusting PCO2 within minutes, which is fast but incomplete. The kidney is the compensator for respiratory disorders, not for metabolic ones, and in a metabolic disorder it is often the organ that is failing or being overwhelmed. The liver and gut can cause acid base disturbances but neither is a compensating system.

questions.q: Which system compensates for a primary respiratory acid base disorder?
options: The respiratory system
The hepatic system
The renal system
The lymphatic system
questions.why: A respiratory problem lives in the PCO2, so the kidney answers it by retaining or dumping bicarbonate over hours to days, which is slow but nearly complete. The respiratory system cannot compensate for itself, since it is the source of the disturbance. The liver handles ammonia and lactate metabolism but is not a compensating organ here, and the lymphatic system plays no acid base role.

questions.q: In a fully compensated disorder, what tells you which system caused the problem?
options: Which side of 7.40 the pH sits on
Whether PO2 is normal
Whether the bicarbonate is above 24 mEq/L
Which value is further from its normal range
questions.why: Compensation brings pH back toward 7.40 but never crosses it, so a compensated pH of 7.37 points to an acidosis and a compensated pH of 7.43 points to an alkalosis, and the abnormal PCO2 or bicarbonate then names the system. Comparing how far each value strays is unreliable, because the compensating change can be large. PO2 reports oxygenation and is silent on acid base cause. A bicarbonate above 24 could be either a primary metabolic alkalosis or renal compensation for a respiratory acidosis.
questions.answerText: Which side of 7.40 the pH sits on

questions.q: Can compensation carry pH past 7.40 to the opposite side of neutral?
options: No, compensation never overshoots
Yes, but only renal compensation does
Yes, but only in the first hour
Yes, routinely, which is how overcorrection happens
questions.why: The stimulus for compensating is the abnormal pH itself, so as pH approaches 7.40 the drive fades and the response stops, which is why the compensated pH always stays on the side of the original problem. If a pH were found on the opposite side, the explanation would be a second primary disorder rather than overshoot. That is true for renal and respiratory compensation alike, and it does not change with time.

questions.q: In a partially compensated disorder, what is true of the pH and the two other values?
options: The pH is normal and one other value is abnormal
The pH is abnormal and both other values are abnormal
The pH is abnormal and both other values are normal
The pH is normal and both other values are normal
questions.why: Partial compensation means the opposing system has begun to move, so its value has left the normal range, but the response has not been enough to pull pH back inside 7.35 to 7.45. A normal pH with abnormal values is full compensation. An abnormal pH with two normal values is chemically impossible, since something has to explain the pH. All values normal is simply a normal blood gas.
questions.answerText: The pH is abnormal and both other values are abnormal

questions.q: During compensation, how does the compensating value move relative to the primary value?
options: In the same direction
It returns toward the middle of its normal range
It stays fixed until the primary value normalizes
In the opposite direction
questions.why: If a high PCO2 is the problem, the kidney raises bicarbonate; if a low bicarbonate is the problem, the lungs lower PCO2, so both numbers end up high or both end up low, which restores the ratio that sets pH. Moving in opposite directions would deepen the pH change rather than blunt it, and that pattern signals a mixed disorder. The compensating value leaves the normal range rather than centering itself in it. Waiting for the primary value to normalize would defeat the purpose of compensating.

questions.q: Determine the compensation status: pH 7.32, PCO2 60 mmHg, HCO3- 30 mEq/L.
options: Uncompensated
Partially compensated
Fully compensated
No compensation is possible for this disorder
questions.why: The pH of 7.32 is still acidemic, the high PCO2 identifies a respiratory acidosis, and the bicarbonate of 30 mEq/L is above normal, which is the kidney moving in the right direction but not far enough yet. Uncompensated would require a bicarbonate still inside 22 to 26 mEq/L. Full compensation would require the pH back inside 7.35 to 7.45. Renal compensation is very much possible here; it is simply incomplete.

questions.q: Determine the compensation status: pH 7.37, PCO2 60 mmHg, HCO3- 34 mEq/L.
options: Partially compensated
Uncompensated
Overcompensated
Fully compensated
questions.why: The pH is back inside the normal range while PCO2 and bicarbonate are both well outside theirs, which is the definition of full compensation, and the pH sitting just below 7.40 confirms the primary problem was an acidosis. Partial compensation would leave pH below 7.35. Uncompensated would leave bicarbonate normal. Overcompensation does not occur, because the drive to compensate disappears as pH nears 7.40.

questions.q: Determine the compensation status: pH 7.30, PCO2 40 mmHg, HCO3- 19 mEq/L.
options: Mixed disorder
Partially compensated
Fully compensated
Uncompensated
questions.why: Bicarbonate is low and pH is low, so this is a metabolic acidosis, and the PCO2 of exactly 40 mmHg shows the lungs have not yet responded at all. Partial compensation would require PCO2 below 35 mmHg. Full compensation would require pH back above 7.35. A mixed disorder would need both values pushing pH the same way, but here PCO2 is normal rather than high.

questions.q: Determine the compensation status: pH 7.50, PCO2 48 mmHg, HCO3- 36 mEq/L.
options: Fully compensated
Mixed alkalosis
Partially compensated
Uncompensated
questions.why: The high bicarbonate with an alkalemic pH marks a metabolic alkalosis, and the PCO2 of 48 mmHg is above normal, meaning ventilation has been reduced to retain acid, which is compensation that has not yet finished. Uncompensated would show a PCO2 in the normal 35 to 45 range. Full compensation would put pH back under 7.45. A mixed alkalosis would require PCO2 to be low, driving pH up further, rather than high.

questions.q: Determine the compensation status: pH 7.46, PCO2 28 mmHg, HCO3- 19 mEq/L.
options: Partially compensated
Uncompensated
Mixed alkalosis
Fully compensated
questions.why: The low PCO2 with an alkalemic pH marks a respiratory alkalosis, and the bicarbonate of 19 mEq/L is below normal, which is the kidney dumping base to bring pH down. The pH is still above 7.45, so compensation is incomplete rather than full. Uncompensated would show bicarbonate inside 22 to 26 mEq/L. A mixed alkalosis would require bicarbonate to be high, adding to the alkalemia instead of opposing it.

questions.q: Determine the compensation status: pH 7.37, PCO2 27 mmHg, HCO3- 15 mEq/L.
options: Mixed acidosis
Uncompensated
Partially compensated
Fully compensated
questions.why: The pH has returned inside the normal range while bicarbonate is markedly low and PCO2 is markedly low, which is full compensation, and the pH just under 7.40 identifies the primary problem as a metabolic acidosis. Uncompensated would leave PCO2 near 40 mmHg. Partial compensation would leave pH below 7.35. A mixed acidosis would require PCO2 to be high rather than low.

questions.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.33, PCO2 55 mmHg, HCO3- 28 mEq/L. Which organ is doing the compensating?
options: The lung
The kidney
The liver
No organ, since the disorder is uncompensated
questions.why: The high PCO2 with a low pH makes this a respiratory acidosis, so the lung is the source of the problem and the elevated bicarbonate of 28 mEq/L is the kidney retaining base in response. The lung cannot compensate for a disorder it is causing. The liver has no compensating role in acid base balance. Compensation is clearly underway, since bicarbonate has already left the normal range.

questions.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.43, PCO2 30 mmHg, HCO3- 19 mEq/L. Name the primary disorder and the compensating system.
options: A metabolic alkalosis compensated by the lung
A respiratory acidosis compensated by the kidney
A metabolic acidosis compensated by the lung
A respiratory alkalosis compensated by the kidney
questions.why: The pH is normal but sits above 7.40, so the primary problem was an alkalosis, and the low PCO2 is the value that raises pH, making it respiratory, with the low bicarbonate representing renal compensation. A metabolic acidosis would put pH below 7.40 and would be driven by the low bicarbonate instead. A metabolic alkalosis would require a high bicarbonate. A respiratory acidosis would require a high PCO2 and a pH below 7.40.
questions.answerText: A respiratory alkalosis compensated by the kidney

questions.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.44, PCO2 50 mmHg, HCO3- 33 mEq/L. Name the primary disorder and the compensating system.
options: A respiratory acidosis compensated by the kidney
A metabolic acidosis compensated by the lung
A metabolic alkalosis compensated by the lung
A mixed alkalosis with no compensation
questions.why: The pH is normal but above 7.40, so the primary problem was an alkalosis, and the high bicarbonate is the value that raises pH, making it metabolic, with the elevated PCO2 showing that ventilation has been reduced to hold acid in. A respiratory acidosis has the same two abnormal values but would leave pH below 7.40, which is why the side of neutral matters so much here. A metabolic acidosis would need a low bicarbonate. A mixed alkalosis would drive pH well above 7.45 rather than back to normal.
questions.answerText: A metabolic alkalosis compensated by the lung

questions.q: A patient develops a metabolic acidosis. Compare the blood gas twenty minutes later with the gas three days later.
options: At twenty minutes bicarbonate is already normal; by three days PCO2 has fallen
At twenty minutes PCO2 is low and pH still low; by three days pH is near normal
At twenty minutes nothing has changed at all; by three days PCO2 is low
At twenty minutes pH is already normal; by three days pH has fallen again
questions.why: Ventilation responds within minutes, so the early gas shows a low PCO2 that blunts but does not fix the acidemia, and only after two to three days has the kidney excreted the acid load and rebuilt bicarbonate enough to bring pH near normal. Bicarbonate cannot be back to normal in twenty minutes, since renal correction is the slow step. Something has certainly changed by twenty minutes, because chemoreceptors act long before that. The pH does not start normal and then deteriorate in a resolving disorder.
questions.answerText: At twenty minutes PCO2 is low and pH still low; by three days pH is near normal

questions.q: A patient has had a stable PCO2 of 60 mmHg for two weeks. Which bicarbonate value fits full renal compensation, and what pH would you expect?
options: About 18 mEq/L, with a pH near 7.10
About 24 mEq/L, with a pH near 7.22
About 34 mEq/L, with a pH just under 7.40
About 34 mEq/L, with a pH just over 7.45
questions.why: Two weeks is long enough for full renal compensation, which means bicarbonate rises far enough to restore the ratio and bring pH back inside the normal range but not past 7.40, and a bicarbonate near 34 mEq/L against a PCO2 of 60 mmHg does exactly that. A bicarbonate of 24 mEq/L would mean no compensation at all, leaving pH near 7.22. A pH above 7.45 would be an overshoot, which compensation does not produce. A bicarbonate of 18 mEq/L would push pH lower still and would indicate an added metabolic acidosis.
questions.answerText: About 34 mEq/L, with a pH just under 7.40

questions.q: What is the normal range for arterial PO2 in a healthy adult at sea level?
options: 100 to 120 mmHg
35 to 45 mmHg
80 to 100 mmHg
22 to 26 mmHg
questions.why: Arterial blood leaving normal lungs carries a PO2 of 80 to 100 mmHg, slightly below alveolar PO2 because of normal shunt and mismatch. The range 35 to 45 mmHg belongs to arterial PCO2. The range 22 to 26 is bicarbonate in mEq/L, not a gas pressure. A PO2 of 100 to 120 mmHg would require supplemental oxygen.

questions.q: What is the normal oxygen saturation of arterial hemoglobin?
options: 60 to 70 percent
75 to 80 percent
85 to 90 percent
95 to 100 percent
questions.why: At a PO2 of 80 to 100 mmHg the blood sits on the flat upper plateau of the oxygen hemoglobin curve, so saturation is 95 percent or better. About 75 percent is the normal saturation of mixed venous blood after tissue extraction. Values of 85 to 90 percent indicate real hypoxemia in arterial blood. Around 60 to 70 percent would be a severe deficit.

questions.q: Which value on a blood gas panel reports oxygenation rather than acid base status?
options: pH
PO2
PCO2
Bicarbonate
questions.why: PO2 describes how well oxygen is being loaded into arterial blood, and a patient can be severely hypoxemic with a perfectly normal pH. PCO2 is a gas but it is the respiratory acid base value, since carbon dioxide becomes carbonic acid. Bicarbonate is the metabolic acid base value. pH is the net acid base result and says nothing about oxygen.

questions.q: How is the bicarbonate value reported on a standard blood gas analyzer obtained?
options: It is measured after the sample is centrifuged
It is measured directly with a bicarbonate electrode
It is calculated from the measured pH and PCO2
It is estimated from the hemoglobin concentration
questions.why: The analyzer has electrodes for pH, PCO2, and PO2, and it derives bicarbonate from the Henderson Hasselbalch relationship, which is why the three acid base numbers on a gas are always internally consistent. There is no bicarbonate electrode in a standard analyzer. Hemoglobin concentration affects buffering but is not used to compute bicarbonate. Centrifugation separates plasma from cells and is not part of blood gas measurement.
questions.answerText: It is calculated from the measured pH and PCO2

questions.q: An air bubble is left in an arterial blood gas syringe. How does it change the measured values?
options: PO2 is falsely raised and PCO2 falsely lowered
Neither gas changes because the bubble is small
PO2 and PCO2 are both falsely raised
PO2 is falsely lowered and PCO2 falsely raised
questions.why: Room air has a PO2 near 160 mmHg and essentially no carbon dioxide, so gases equilibrate across the bubble, pushing the sample PO2 up and its PCO2 down, and the falsely low PCO2 also makes the reported pH too high. Both values cannot rise, since the bubble is high in one gas and empty of the other. The direction cannot be reversed for the same reason. Even a small bubble shifts values enough to change an interpretation.
questions.answerText: PO2 is falsely raised and PCO2 falsely lowered

questions.q: Why must an arterial blood gas sample be analyzed promptly or kept on ice?
options: Bicarbonate precipitates out of plasma at room temperature
Hemoglobin releases its bound carbon dioxide as the sample warms
Heparin loses its effect within minutes
Blood cells keep metabolizing, using oxygen and making carbon dioxide
questions.why: Leukocytes and red blood cells stay alive in the syringe, so a delayed sample shows a falsely low PO2, a falsely high PCO2, and a falsely low pH, and cooling slows that metabolism. Heparin keeps working well beyond the relevant time frame. Bicarbonate stays dissolved and does not precipitate. Hemoglobin does not spontaneously dump carbon dioxide as the sample sits.
questions.answerText: Blood cells keep metabolizing, using oxygen and making carbon dioxide

questions.q: How does venous blood differ from arterial blood in PCO2 and pH?
options: Venous PCO2 is higher and venous pH is lower
Venous PCO2 is lower and venous pH is higher
Both are identical to arterial values
Venous PCO2 is higher and venous pH is also higher
questions.why: Tissues add carbon dioxide to blood, so venous PCO2 runs about 6 mmHg above arterial and pH runs roughly 0.03 to 0.05 units lower, which is why an arterial sample is required to judge how well the lungs are working. Venous PCO2 cannot be lower, since carbon dioxide is added on the tissue side. Identical values would mean tissues had produced no carbon dioxide. More carbon dioxide always means a lower pH, not a higher one.
questions.answerText: Venous PCO2 is higher and venous pH is lower

questions.q: Which value should you read first when interpreting a set of arterial blood gas results?
options: The PCO2
The bicarbonate
The pH
The PO2
questions.why: The pH tells you whether the blood is acidemic or alkalemic, and that answer determines which of the other two values could possibly be the cause, so it anchors the whole interpretation. Starting with PCO2 or bicarbonate risks labeling a compensating change as the primary problem. PO2 belongs to the oxygenation question and is read separately.

questions.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.33, PCO2 55 mmHg, HCO3- 28 mEq/L. Which cause is most plausible?
options: Two days of vomiting gastric contents
Anxiety with rapid and deep breathing
Long standing airflow obstruction
Three days of profuse watery diarrhea
questions.why: The acidemic pH with a high PCO2 makes this a respiratory acidosis, and the raised bicarbonate shows the kidney has had time to begin compensating, which fits long standing airflow obstruction. Anxious hyperventilation lowers PCO2 and would give the opposite picture. Diarrhea loses bicarbonate and produces a metabolic acidosis with a low bicarbonate. Vomiting loses acid and produces a metabolic alkalosis with a high pH.

questions.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.27, PCO2 25 mmHg, HCO3- 11 mEq/L. Which cause is most plausible?
options: Uncontrolled diabetes with ketoacids
Several days of nasogastric suction
A panic attack with hyperventilation
A sedative overdose that slows respiration
questions.why: A low pH with a markedly low bicarbonate is a metabolic acidosis, and the low PCO2 is the deep rapid breathing that partially compensates, which is the classic picture when ketoacids accumulate. A sedative overdose raises PCO2 and causes a respiratory acidosis. Nasogastric suction removes gastric acid and causes a metabolic alkalosis with a high pH. A panic attack lowers PCO2 but raises pH, since there is no acid load to explain.

questions.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.52, PCO2 44 mmHg, HCO3- 35 mEq/L. Which cause is most plausible?
options: A pulmonary embolus causing rapid breathing
Severe diarrhea with bicarbonate loss
Two days of vomiting gastric contents
Opioid induced hypoventilation
questions.why: The alkalemic pH with a clearly high bicarbonate and a normal PCO2 is an uncompensated metabolic alkalosis, and losing hydrochloric acid from the stomach leaves bicarbonate unopposed in the blood. A pulmonary embolus drives hyperventilation and produces a respiratory alkalosis with a low PCO2. Diarrhea causes the mirror image, a metabolic acidosis. Opioid hypoventilation raises PCO2 and lowers pH.
questions.answerText: Two days of vomiting gastric contents

questions.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.49, PCO2 30 mmHg, HCO3- 22 mEq/L. Which cause is most plausible?
options: An acute panic attack with rapid breathing
A week of loop diuretic use
Chronic bronchitis with sputum retention
Renal failure with retained fixed acids
questions.why: The alkalemic pH with a low PCO2 and a normal bicarbonate is an acute uncompensated respiratory alkalosis, exactly what a burst of hyperventilation produces before the kidney has time to react. Diuretic use causes a metabolic alkalosis, which would show a high bicarbonate. Chronic bronchitis retains carbon dioxide and causes respiratory acidosis. Renal failure retains fixed acid and causes metabolic acidosis with a low bicarbonate.
questions.answerText: An acute panic attack with rapid breathing

questions.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.14, PCO2 80 mmHg, HCO3- 26 mEq/L. Which cause is most plausible?
options: Several days of severe vomiting
An opioid overdose that slows breathing
A drug overdose driving hyperventilation
Ascent to a high mountain altitude
questions.why: A very low pH with a PCO2 of 80 mmHg and a normal bicarbonate is an acute uncompensated respiratory acidosis, which means ventilation has abruptly fallen and the kidney has had no time to respond. Altitude drives hyperventilation and lowers PCO2. Vomiting produces a metabolic alkalosis with a high pH. Anything that drives hyperventilation lowers PCO2 rather than doubling it.
questions.answerText: An opioid overdose that slows breathing

questions.q: A patient has had watery diarrhea for three days. Which set of arterial values fits best?
options: pH 7.32, PCO2 60 mmHg, HCO3- 30 mEq/L
pH 7.46, PCO2 28 mmHg, HCO3- 19 mEq/L
pH 7.50, PCO2 48 mmHg, HCO3- 36 mEq/L
pH 7.28, PCO2 30 mmHg, HCO3- 14 mEq/L
questions.why: Losing bicarbonate rich intestinal fluid lowers plasma bicarbonate and pH, and the low PCO2 shows respiratory compensation already underway, so a low pH with low bicarbonate and low PCO2 is the expected pattern. A pH of 7.50 with a bicarbonate of 36 mEq/L is a metabolic alkalosis, which is what vomiting produces, not diarrhea. A PCO2 of 60 mmHg makes a set a respiratory acidosis, which needs a lung problem rather than a gut one. A pH of 7.46 with a PCO2 of 28 mmHg is a respiratory alkalosis, which diarrhea does not cause.

questions.q: A climber has been at 4200 meters for four days. Which set of arterial values fits best?
options: pH 7.40, PCO2 40 mmHg, HCO3- 24 mEq/L
pH 7.46, PCO2 26 mmHg, HCO3- 18 mEq/L
pH 7.46, PCO2 50 mmHg, HCO3- 34 mEq/L
pH 7.30, PCO2 26 mmHg, HCO3- 12 mEq/L
questions.why: Low inspired oxygen drives hyperventilation, so PCO2 falls and pH rises, and after several days the kidney has excreted bicarbonate to pull pH back toward normal, which gives a mildly alkalemic pH with both PCO2 and bicarbonate low. A PCO2 of 50 mmHg with a bicarbonate of 34 mEq/L is a metabolic alkalosis, and nothing about altitude raises PCO2. A pH of 7.30 is acidemic and would mean an acid load rather than hypoxic hyperventilation. A completely normal set would mean no ventilatory response to altitude at all.

questions.q: A patient in cardiac arrest has a blood gas of pH 7.10, PCO2 60 mmHg, HCO3- 18 mEq/L. Which two processes together explain these numbers?
options: Stopped ventilation plus lactic acid from hypoperfused tissue
Hyperventilation plus urinary loss of bicarbonate over hours
Retained carbon dioxide plus renal compensation already underway
Loss of gastric acid plus a reduced rate of ventilation
questions.why: The high PCO2 and the low bicarbonate both drive pH down, so there is no compensation here at all and two acidoses are present at once, from stopped ventilation and from anaerobic metabolism in tissue that is not being perfused. Hyperventilation would lower PCO2, not raise it to 60 mmHg. Renal compensation would raise bicarbonate above normal, and it could not act within minutes anyway. Loss of gastric acid raises bicarbonate and would push pH the other way.
questions.answerText: Stopped ventilation plus lactic acid from hypoperfused tissue

questions.q: A patient with a severe asthma attack initially had a PCO2 of 27 mmHg. An hour later it is 42 mmHg while the patient is still working hard to breathe. What has happened to alveolar ventilation and to pH?
options: Ventilation has risen further and pH has risen further
Ventilation has fallen and pH has come down toward normal and below
Ventilation is unchanged and pH is unchanged
Ventilation has fallen but pH has risen because bicarbonate rose
questions.why: A PCO2 of 27 mmHg means the patient was moving far more air than metabolism required, so a return to 42 mmHg with unchanged carbon dioxide production means alveolar ventilation has dropped, and the accumulating acid pulls pH back down from its alkalemic starting point. Rising ventilation would push PCO2 lower still. Unchanged ventilation cannot produce a fifteen mmHg swing in PCO2. Bicarbonate cannot rise fast enough in an hour to outweigh that carbon dioxide change.
questions.answerText: Ventilation has fallen and pH has come down toward normal and below

questions.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.48, PCO2 32 mmHg, HCO3- 23 mEq/L, PO2 55 mmHg. Interpret the acid base status and explain what links it to the oxygen value.
options: A metabolic alkalosis, with the low PO2 an unrelated finding
An uncompensated respiratory alkalosis driven by hypoxemic hyperventilation
A fully compensated respiratory acidosis, with hypoxemia from the same lung problem
A mixed alkalosis, with the low PO2 causing bicarbonate retention
questions.why: The alkalemic pH with a low PCO2 and a normal bicarbonate is an uncompensated respiratory alkalosis, and the PO2 of 55 mmHg explains it, because low arterial oxygen stimulates the peripheral chemoreceptors and drives ventilation, which blows off carbon dioxide. A metabolic alkalosis would require a high bicarbonate. A respiratory acidosis would require a high PCO2 and a pH at or below 7.40. A mixed alkalosis would need bicarbonate to be high, and hypoxemia does not cause the kidney to retain bicarbonate.
questions.answerText: An uncompensated respiratory alkalosis driven by hypoxemic hyperventilation

questions.q: Two patients both have a PCO2 of 60 mmHg. One has a pH of 7.24 and the other a pH of 7.38. What accounts for the difference?
options: The first has a higher PO2, which acidifies the blood
The first has a larger dead space in the lung
The second has a lower rate of carbon dioxide production
The second has had time for the kidney to raise bicarbonate
questions.why: pH is set by the ratio of bicarbonate to dissolved carbon dioxide, so with PCO2 identical the only way to hold pH near normal is a higher bicarbonate, which takes two to three days of renal compensation to build. Carbon dioxide production is not the issue, since PCO2 is already fixed at the same value in both. PO2 does not enter the Henderson Hasselbalch relationship and does not acidify blood. Dead space would change PCO2 itself rather than the pH at a given PCO2.
questions.answerText: The second has had time for the kidney to raise bicarbonate

questions.q: Total body water makes up about what fraction of body weight in a healthy adult?
options: About 40 percent
About 60 percent
About 80 percent
About 20 percent
questions.why: Water is roughly 60 percent of body weight, which is about 42 liters in a 70 kilogram adult and is the starting point for every compartment calculation. About 40 percent is the intracellular share of body weight, not the total. About 20 percent is the extracellular share. Eighty percent would leave almost no room for protein, mineral, and fat.

questions.q: What fraction of total body water is inside cells?
options: About two thirds
About one quarter
About one third
About one half
questions.why: Roughly two thirds of body water is intracellular and one third extracellular, so the intracellular compartment is the larger reservoir and absorbs much of any osmotic shift. One third is the extracellular share, which is the value most often swapped in by mistake. One quarter describes plasma as a fraction of extracellular fluid. One half would understate the intracellular volume considerably.

questions.q: Within the extracellular fluid, how is the volume divided between plasma and interstitial fluid?
options: About three quarters plasma and one quarter interstitial
Almost all plasma, with very little interstitial fluid
About one quarter plasma and three quarters interstitial
About half and half
questions.why: Of roughly 14 liters of extracellular fluid, about 3 liters is plasma and about 11 liters bathes the tissues, which is why a loss confined to plasma is a small share of extracellular volume. An even split would overstate the vascular compartment. Reversing the ratio would give a plasma volume that the heart could not accommodate. Interstitial fluid is by far the larger of the two.
questions.answerText: About one quarter plasma and three quarters interstitial

questions.q: What is the normal osmolarity of body fluids?
options: About 1200 mOsm/L
About 150 mOsm/L
About 290 mOsm/L
About 400 mOsm/L
questions.why: Plasma and intracellular fluid both sit near 290 mOsm/L, and because water crosses cell membranes freely the two compartments always end at the same osmolarity. About 150 mOsm/L would be severely dilute. Around 400 mOsm/L is markedly concentrated. About 1200 mOsm/L is the maximum concentration of urine, not of body fluid.

questions.q: Which solute is the main determinant of extracellular fluid osmolarity?
options: Glucose
Potassium with its accompanying anions
Sodium with its accompanying anions
Plasma albumin
questions.why: Sodium and the chloride and bicarbonate that follow it account for most extracellular particles, which is why plasma sodium concentration is the practical readout of extracellular osmolarity. Potassium is the dominant intracellular cation and is present in plasma at only about 4 mEq/L. Albumin has a large mass but very few particles, so it contributes almost nothing to osmolarity even though it sets colloid osmotic pressure. Glucose adds a small share that only becomes important when it rises far above normal.

questions.q: Which ion is the major cation of intracellular fluid?
options: Magnesium
Sodium
Calcium
Potassium
questions.why: Potassium is held at roughly 140 mEq/L inside cells by the Na+/K+ ATPase, and it is the counterpart to sodium outside. Sodium is the major extracellular cation and is kept low inside. Free intracellular calcium is measured in nanomolar amounts because it acts as a signal. Magnesium is present intracellularly but at far lower concentration than potassium.

questions.q: What is the difference between the osmolarity of a solution and its tonicity?
options: Osmolarity applies to plasma and tonicity to interstitial fluid
Tonicity counts only solutes that cannot cross the membrane
Tonicity counts only charged solutes
Osmolarity is measured at 37 C and tonicity at room temperature
questions.why: Tonicity describes what a solution does to cell volume, so only impermeant solutes count, which is why a urea solution can be isosmotic yet hypotonic as urea equilibrates and water follows into the cell. Charge is irrelevant, since glucose is uncharged and still contributes fully to tonicity. Temperature is not what separates the two terms. Both terms apply to any fluid, not to particular compartments.
questions.answerText: Tonicity counts only solutes that cannot cross the membrane

questions.q: What drives water movement between the intracellular and extracellular compartments?
options: The colloid osmotic pressure of albumin
Hydrostatic pressure across the cell membrane
The osmotic gradient across the cell membrane
Active pumping of water by the Na+/K+ ATPase
questions.why: Water moves toward the compartment with the higher osmolarity until the two are equal, and cell membranes cannot sustain a pressure difference, so osmosis alone sets the distribution. Hydrostatic pressure drives filtration across capillary walls, which is a different boundary. There is no water pump; the sodium pump moves solute and water follows. Albumin governs the split between plasma and interstitial fluid, not the split across the cell membrane.
questions.answerText: The osmotic gradient across the cell membrane

questions.q: One liter of isotonic saline is infused. Classify the disturbance and predict the fluid shift.
options: Isosmotic volume expansion, with no shift across the cell membrane
Hyperosmotic volume expansion, with water leaving cells
Isosmotic volume depletion, with no shift across the cell membrane
Hypoosmotic volume expansion, with water entering cells
questions.why: Isotonic saline has the same effective osmolarity as body fluid, so it stays where it is put, expanding the extracellular compartment while osmolarity and cell volume are unchanged. Water would enter cells only if extracellular osmolarity had fallen. Water would leave cells only if extracellular osmolarity had risen. Adding fluid is expansion, so depletion is ruled out at the start.
questions.answerText: Isosmotic volume expansion, with no shift across the cell membrane

questions.q: A person drinks two liters of plain water. Classify the disturbance and predict the fluid shift.
options: Hypoosmotic volume expansion, with water entering cells
Isosmotic volume expansion, with no shift
Hyperosmotic volume expansion, with water leaving cells
Hypoosmotic volume depletion, with water entering cells
questions.why: Pure water adds volume without solute, so extracellular osmolarity falls below intracellular, water crosses into cells, and both compartments end larger and more dilute. An isosmotic result would require the added fluid to carry solute at 290 mOsm/L. Water cannot leave cells when the outside has become more dilute. Drinking adds volume, so this cannot be depletion.
questions.answerText: Hypoosmotic volume expansion, with water entering cells

questions.q: One liter of hypertonic saline is infused. Classify the disturbance and predict the fluid shift.
options: Hyperosmotic volume depletion, with water leaving cells
Hypoosmotic volume expansion, with water entering cells
Isosmotic volume expansion, with no shift
Hyperosmotic volume expansion, with water leaving cells
questions.why: Concentrated salt raises extracellular osmolarity, so water is pulled out of cells, and the extracellular compartment grows by more than the volume infused while cells shrink. Water moves into cells only when the outside is more dilute. An isosmotic result would need the infusion to match body osmolarity. Total body volume rises here, so this is expansion rather than depletion.
questions.answerText: Hyperosmotic volume expansion, with water leaving cells

questions.q: An athlete sweats heavily for three hours and drinks nothing. Classify the disturbance and predict the fluid shift.
options: Hyperosmotic volume depletion, with water leaving cells
Hyperosmotic volume expansion, with water leaving cells
Isosmotic volume depletion, with no shift
Hypoosmotic volume depletion, with water entering cells
questions.why: Sweat is hypotonic, so more water than salt is lost, extracellular osmolarity climbs while extracellular volume falls, and water is drawn out of cells so both compartments shrink. An isosmotic loss would require sweat to match plasma osmolarity, which it does not. Water cannot enter cells when the outside has become more concentrated. Losing fluid is depletion, not expansion.
questions.answerText: Hyperosmotic volume depletion, with water leaving cells

questions.q: A patient loses two liters of blood through hemorrhage. Classify the disturbance and predict the immediate fluid shift across cell membranes.
options: Hyperosmotic volume depletion, with water leaving cells
Hypoosmotic volume depletion, with water entering cells
Isosmotic volume expansion, with no shift
Isosmotic volume depletion, with no immediate shift
questions.why: Whole blood is lost at the osmolarity of body fluid, so the extracellular compartment shrinks while osmolarity stays at 290 mOsm/L and cells are initially untouched. A hyperosmotic result would require losing relatively more water than solute, as in sweating. A hypoosmotic result would require losing relatively more solute than water. Losing volume is depletion, so expansion is ruled out.
questions.answerText: Isosmotic volume depletion, with no immediate shift
