questions.q: A patient with too little aldosterone loses sodium in the urine while water intake continues. Classify the disturbance and predict the fluid shift.
options: Hyperosmotic volume depletion, with water leaving cells
Hypoosmotic volume depletion, with water entering cells
Isosmotic volume depletion, with no shift
Hypoosmotic volume expansion, with water entering cells
questions.why: Losing sodium without an equal loss of water lowers extracellular osmolarity, so the extracellular compartment shrinks from the salt loss while water shifts into cells and makes that shrinkage worse. A hyperosmotic result would require water loss to exceed solute loss, the opposite of what happens here. An isosmotic loss would leave osmolarity at 290 mOsm/L. Extracellular volume falls, so this is depletion rather than expansion.
questions.answerText: Hypoosmotic volume depletion, with water entering cells

questions.q: A marathon runner sweats heavily and then drinks four liters of plain water. Trace extracellular osmolarity and cell volume across the two events.
options: Osmolarity rises then falls, so cells first shrink and then swell
Osmolarity rises in both phases, so cells shrink throughout
Osmolarity stays at 290 mOsm/L throughout, so cell volume never changes
Osmolarity falls then rises, so cells first swell and then shrink
questions.why: Hypotonic sweat concentrates the extracellular fluid and pulls water out of cells, and then replacing the losses with water alone dilutes the remaining solute below normal so water moves back into cells and past their starting volume, which is how exercise associated hyponatremia produces cerebral swelling. The order cannot be reversed, since sweating comes first. Osmolarity cannot keep rising once large volumes of pure water are added. It cannot stay fixed while solute free water is both lost and replaced.
questions.answerText: Osmolarity rises then falls, so cells first shrink and then swell

questions.q: A patient secretes too much antidiuretic hormone and retains water while sodium excretion continues normally. Classify the disturbance and predict what happens to cell volume.
options: Hypoosmotic volume depletion, with cells swelling
Isosmotic volume expansion, with no change in cell volume
Hyperosmotic volume expansion, with cells shrinking
Hypoosmotic volume expansion, with cells swelling
questions.why: Retaining solute free water adds volume while diluting the solute already present, so osmolarity falls, water follows into cells, and every compartment ends larger and more dilute, which is why plasma sodium is low in this condition. Cells cannot shrink when the fluid around them is dilute. Total volume rises, so this is expansion, not depletion. An isosmotic result would require sodium to be retained in proportion to the water.
questions.answerText: Hypoosmotic volume expansion, with cells swelling

questions.q: Two patients have each lost three liters of fluid, one through hemorrhage and one through pure water loss. Which lost more intracellular volume, and why?
options: The hemorrhage patient, because plasma volume fell fastest
The water loss patient, since osmolarity rose
Both lost the same, because total body water fell equally
Neither lost intracellular volume, because cells are protected
questions.why: Hemorrhage removes fluid at body osmolarity, so the loss stays extracellular and cells are spared, while pure water loss concentrates the extracellular fluid and drags water out of every cell, spreading the deficit across both compartments. Speed of plasma loss does not determine where the deficit ends up; osmolarity does. Equal total losses do not mean equal distribution, which is exactly the point of the comparison. Cells are not protected from osmotic gradients at all.
questions.answerText: The water loss patient, since osmolarity rose

questions.q: A hyperosmotic, volume depleted patient absorbs three liters of solute free water from the gut. Roughly how does that water distribute, and what does that mean for the extracellular deficit?
options: All three liters stay extracellular, filling the deficit completely
About two liters enter cells and one stays outside
All three liters enter cells, leaving the deficit unchanged
The water enters plasma alone, raising blood volume by three liters
questions.why: Solute free water follows the osmotic gradient until both compartments match, and since roughly two thirds of body water is intracellular, about two thirds of the added water ends up inside cells, so osmolarity is corrected far more effectively than volume. Water cannot stay entirely extracellular, because nothing holds it there once osmolarity falls. It cannot all enter cells either, since the shift stops when the two compartments are equal. Confining it to plasma would ignore the interstitial space, which is roughly three times larger than plasma.
questions.answerText: About two liters enter cells and one stays outside
